From his first lessons to his disciples until his final lessons before leaving this world, Srila Prabhupada quoted and taught this verse, which remains the banner of iskcon’s preaching to this day.

A further examination of the nature of consciousness will help us put the spotlight on the false ego and how it distances us from Krsna.

We have already touched on how the living entities who opt to enter the material world are dormant in the subtle, undifferentiated sum total of all material elements, pradhana. Thereafter, when pradhanais agitated by the time factor, it manifests the mahat tattva,which then passes through stages of creation in which living entities gradually awaken.

The initial, pure stage of the mahat-tattvais known as vasudeva whose presiding deity is Lord Sankarsana. This is the unfettered mode of goodness in which consciousness is still unadulterated, and in which awareness of the Supreme Lord is still natural. Such pristine consciousness is characteristic of the pure ego, the original identity of the living entity.

Let us briefly define the terms relating to consciousness.

**“What is the ego?”**

**“The sense of self!”**

In its original state the soul’s identity is pure, but in contact with the transformations of the mahat-tattvait becomes contaminated, and gives an erroneous sense of selfness.

That erroneous sense of identity is the false ego, ahankara.

Finally, awareness itself, or that state in which one is aware of one’s self and of other things, is consciousness, citta.

So, to the question posed earlier:

**“What is our** ***pramana*** **for studying the soul and its subtle coverings?”**

We answer:

**“Primarily, scripture; and secondarily, inference.”**

In a discussion on the false ego, an important point should also be clarified:

When we sometimes say, “the soul becomes contaminated,” we should understand that to mean “the soul’s sense of self, the ego, becomes contaminated.” The soul always remains pure. It is the aspects of the antah-karana—the soul’s coverings, like the mind—that become contaminated, giving the sense that the soul is equally covered. But the self, as Krsna goes to great pains to explain, can never he cut, dried, withered, diluted, and so on. It is the smallest indivisible spiritual substance and always retains its integrity

\* \* \* \*

Having established our pramana,let us return to our dissertation on the false ego.

When the pure stage of the mahat-tattva, vasudeva,is further agitated by time, the three modes of nature become active, and their first effect is the false ego, ahankara.Thus, the false ego is invested with three kinds of power—good, passionate, and ignorant, also expressed as serene, active, and dull. And it is from the three forms of false ego that all subsequent creation, subtle and gross, lakes place. The predominating deity of this false ego is Lord Sankarsana, and it is by His grace that one is again freed from the grasp of false misconceptions, ahankara.

To re-emphasise, and in summary, when in the mahat-tattva the modes of material nature become activated by the influence of time, then false ego manifests in the living entity. Because the active mahat-tattvameans creation, because creation means bodies, and because bodies mean instruments of misidentification, it is at this stage that the living entity again consciously turns away from Krsna and enters the material atmosphere. In Lord Kapila’s words:

*gunair vicitrah srjatim*  
*sa-rupah prakrtim prajah*  
*vilokya mumuhe sadyah*  
*sa iha jnana-guhaya*

*evam parabhidhyanena*  
*kartrtvam prakrteh puman*  
*karmasu kriyamanesu*  
*gunair atmani manyate*

**“Divided into varieties by her threefold modes, material nature creates the forms of the living entities, and the living entities, seeing this, are illusioned by the knowledge-covering feature of the illusory energy. Because of his forgetfulness, the transcendental living entity accepts the influence of material energy as his field of activities, and thus actuated, he wrongly applies the activities to himself.”**

Whatever exists is a transformation of false ego, thus in one sense false ego is all-pervading, which explains why it is so difficult to attain liberation from it. For example, false ego manifests as the doer in the form of the demigods, as the instrument in the form of the senses, and as the combination of doer and instrument in the form of material objects.

While false ego manifests everything created, it continues to remain as the cause, the subtlest aspect of the material energy, the juncture between matter and spirit. Like the air, false ego pervades all created beings and induces two kinds of thinking, ahantaand mamata:

**“I am this body!”**

and,

**“Everything related to this body is mine!”**

These are the two weapons in the aforementioned analogy of the chariot. In Chapter Four we have described the purification and spiritualisation of these two aspects of ego.

Further attributes evolving from these states of mind are:

**Lust for more; greed for what is not needed; anger at loss; fear of loss, especially from death; happiness and distress arising from these, and so on.**

In reality, all thinking behind conduct that is not in pursuance of pure devotional service—even if it is under other Vedic injunctions—is caused by false ego and results in desire and further bondage.

While we have previously explained how indifference to spiritual practice is inherent in the mind due to its misuse of independence, now, after elaborating on the manifestation and behaviour of the false ego, we can see how that indifference is further compounded by an equally ingrained attachment to self and to acquired belongings.

Since karma-yogaand jnana-yogafocus on the effects of both indifference and false ego, and not on their cause, those forms of yogaare unable to deliver the conditioned soul from bondage. Only pure bhakticleanses the consciousness of the jivaand revives its desire to serve. This is confirmed in Sanat-kumara’s advice to King Prthu:

*yat-pada-pankaja-palasa-vilasa-bhaktya*  
*karmasayam grathitam udgrathayanti santah*  
*tadvan na rikta-matayo yatayo 'pi ruddha-*  
*sroto-ganas tam aranam bhaja vasudevam*

**“The devotees, who are always engaged in the service of the toes of the lotus feet of the Lord, can very easily overcome hard-knotted desires for fruitive activities. Because this is very difficult, the non-devotees—the jnanisand yogis—although trying to stop the waves of sense gratification, cannot do so. Therefore you are advised to engage in the devotional service of Krsna, the son of Vasudeva.”**

In the previously mentioned Srimad-Bhagavatamanalogy involving the mind and the chariot, the consciousness was the impetus for movement. And we have mentioned that consciousness is the sense of awareness. The senses have their individual functions, which means they are empowered with a certain kind of awareness—seeing, hearing, and so on. By sensory awareness, the living entity connects with sense objects and thus charts a path through the jungle of sense gratificatory objects and experiences. In that way, consciousness becomes the impetus for the movement of the living entity.

However, that consciousness becomes contaminated by many base qualities sprouting from the sense of “I” and “mine.” And it is that contaminated consciousness and its role in the life of the conditioned soul that is worthy of brief attention.

However, before proceeding further, a fine point should be clarified in our definition of consciousness being identified as aware ness. And that point is: Srila Prabhupada at times equates con taminated consciousness with false ego, which in fact is more than awareness, it is the awareness of something.

So why in this book have we chosen the former definition?

The reason is that at other times, Srila Prabhupada and scriptures also define consciousness as awareness; they make a distinction between contaminated consciousness and false ego, and they also define the sequence in which the two appear. Let us look at an example of these quotes and their resolution.

In his commentary to the following verse, which clearly differentiates contaminated consciousness from false ego, Srila Prabhupada equates the two:

*mano buddhir ahankaras*  
*cittam ity antar-atmakam*  
*caturdha laksyate bhedo*  
*vrttya laksana-rupaya*

**“The internal, subtle senses are experienced as having four aspects, in the shape of mind, intelligence, ego, and contaminated consciousness. Distinctions between them can be made only by different functions, since they represent different characteristics.”**

The following is the entire purport to the verse:

**“The four internal senses, or subtle senses, described herein are defined by different characteristics. When pure consciousness is polluted by material contamination, and when identification with the body becomes prominent, one is said to be situated under false ego. Consciousness is the function of the soul, and therefore behind consciousness there is soul. Consciousness polluted by material contamination is called ahankara.”**

In the verse, Kapiladeva lists ego and contaminated consciousness as separate features of the antar-atmakam,the internal, subtle senses. And in the beginning of his purport, Srila Prabhupada acknowledges that listing, and then summarises how both come into being. However, in the last line of the purport, Srila Prabhupada clearly identifies contaminated consciousness as false ego:

**“Consciousness polluted by material contamination is called ahankara.”**

We have what seems to be a contradiction in the same purport: Srila Prabhupada states both things.

But in two other purports Srila Prabhupada clearly differentiates In tween false ego and contaminated consciousness:

**“The appearance of consciousness after the appearance of false ego.”**

and,

**“The subtle body is made of mind, intelligence, false ego, and contaminated consciousness.”**

What is the resolution of Srila Prabhupada’s seemingly contradictory statements?

The answer lies in Lord Kapila’s words, bhedo vrttya laksana-rupaya:

**“Distinctions between them can be made only by different functions, since they represent different characteristics.”**

Since both contaminated consciousness and false ego are part of the internal subtle senses, in one way they are the same; however in another way, when viewed from their functions and characteristics, they are different. Thus Srila Prabhupada’s different statements simply represent different contexts in which these two features of the subtle body are mentioned.

Therefore, returning to our definitions of consciousness and false ego, from the viewpoint of functions and characteristics, consciousness is awareness itself, false ego is awareness of the body as the self, and contaminated consciousness is false awareness covering the soul infected by false ego.

\* \* \* \*

Continuing our study of contaminated consciousness, it is interesting to note that in another Srimad-Bhagavatamverse, Srila Prabhupada’s translation of the word cittenais “along with reason.” This is quite understandable, as consciousness activates the reasoning faculty within the intelligence and, to a lesser extent, within the mind.

Consciousness is the symptom of the soul, and consciousness activates both the subtle and gross bodies with its power. Krsna says, ksetram ksetri tatha krtsnam prakasayati:

**“The living entity, one within the body, illuminates the entire body with consciousness.”**

Therefore, where the soul is present, consciousness is found. When the soul appears in the mahat-tattvawith a contaminated intent of being the enjoyer instead of the enjoyed, then its consciousness becomes equally contaminated. That contamination is caused by identification with the active modes of material nature, and thus manifests, and is manifested through, a variety of bodies.

The modes of nature are three in number, whilst their combinations are practically without limit. Thus the different conditions of these modes facilitate different bodies, and they in turn reflect variety in contaminated consciousness. Lord Kapila says:

*sva-yonisu yatha jyotir*  
*ekam nana pratiyate*  
*yoninam guna-vaisamyat*  
*tathatma prakrtau sthitah*

**“As fire is exhibited in different forms of wood, so, under different conditions of the modes of material nature, the pure spirit soul manifests itself in different bodies.”**

While in its pure state, the living entity’s consciousness spiritually enlivens the ego, mind, intelligence, and body. But when that mu pure consciousness becomes adulterated by the effect of the modes of nature, the bewildered soul embraces many kinds of false ego, with which are connected many kinds of bodies—subtle and gross-displaying a spectrum of contaminated consciousness.

For a conditioned soul, both bondage and liberation are difficult to conceive of, just as a person absorbed in a dream has little understanding of either the illusion of dreaming or the reality of being awake.

Srimad-Bhagavatamrepeatedly likens contaminated consciousness, its perception of the material world, and its absorption in sense gratification to the experience of a person engrossed in a dream. Such a contaminated state, while real, is temporary, and like a dream it is but a product of the material mind. Liberation means to awaken from the dream, and waking up is the call by which the Vedic literatures address humans. Bhaktivinoda Thakura sings:

*jiv jago, jiv jago, gauracanda bole*  
*kota nidra jao maya-pisacira kole*

**“Wake up sleeping soul! Wake up sleeping soul! Lord Caitanya is calling ‘How long will you sleep in the lap of** ***maya*****.’”**

The answer to Lord Caitanya’s question is that the living entity continues to dream as long as it voluntarily embraces the illusory potency of the Lord, maya,which convinces the jivathat dreaming is both reality and natural. Lord Brahma admits to Krsna:

*tasmad idam jagad asesam asat-svarupam*  
*svapnabham asta-dhisanam puru-duhkha-duhkham*  
*tvayy eva nitya-sukha-bodha-tanav anante*  
*mayata udyad api yat sad ivavabhati*

**“Therefore this entire universe, which like a dream is by nature unreal, nevertheless appears real, and thus it covers one’s consciousness and assails one with repeated miseries. This universe appears real because it is manifested by the potency of illusion emanating from You, whose unlimited transcendental forms are full of eternal happiness and knowledge.”**

A living entity begins the process of waking up when, by the acquisition of transcendental knowledge, it realises its folly and takes up sadhana-bhakti.And liberation, bhava-bhakti,is the waking state. Srila Prabhupada comments on the verse, muktir hitvanyatha rupam svarupena vyavasthitih:

**“Muktimeans liberation from the contaminated consciousness of this material world and becoming situated in pure consciousness.”**

King Rantideva is an example of a pure devotee who, being always fully Krsna conscious, was both free of material enchantment and entirely oblivious of maya,in the way that a dream has no exist ence for one who is awake.

To understand what is real and what is a dream, Narada Muni gives us a rule of thumb that he says is a secret of the Vedas:

*adṛṣṭam aśrutaṁ cātra*  
*kvacin manasi dṛśyate*  
*yathā tathānumantavyaṁ*  
*deśa-kāla-kriyāśrayam*

**“Everything happening within time, which consists of past, present, and future, is merely a dream. That is the secret understanding in all Vedic literature.”**

In the analogy of conditioned life being akin to a dream, we must conclude that only in the liberated state—in which one is free of the modes of material nature—is consciousness again pure. And to the degree that one is under the modes of material nature, to that degree one’s consciousness is contaminated, and one persists in the dream of illusion.

In that dream, sometimes one is a demigod and sometimes a spider. It all depends upon how deeply one is steeped in the illusions caused by the modes of nature. In any case, whether spider or Brahma, as Krsna says, mama maya duratyaya,it is difficult for anyone to overcome the material energy. The only way to do so is by surrendering to Krsna.

In his Jaiva-dharma,Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura classifies the spectrum development of consciousness through which conditioned souls pass as being five. These are consciousness that is covered, withdrawn, budding, blossoming, and blossomed. The first four are degrees of contaminated consciousness, the fifth is pure consciousness.

Souls in the bodies of plants have covered consciousness, animals have withdrawn consciousness, humans who are immoral and atheistic have budding consciousness, humans who are religious or who practise sadhana-bhaktihave blossoming consciousness, and pure Vaisnavas who have attained bhava-bhaktihave blossomed consciousness.

Keeping in mind that the consciousness in the chariot of the bodó directs the wayward soul, it is observed that the direction for plants is to grow; for animals to eat, sleep, mate, and defend; for the sinful humans to behave like animals; for believers and sadhakasto make spiritual advancement; and for bhava-bhaktasto attain full-blown prema.

The cultivation of the fourth stage of consciousness, which Bhaktivinoda Thakura calls mukulita-cetana,is the theme of this hook. A practising devotee has bhavaas his goal in life, and in his cultivation of Krsna consciousness he shuns anything that obstructs his attainment and embraces everything that qualifies him for it.

Rupa Gosvami explains that one takes to devotional service only because one has acquired qualification to strive towards Krsna in the previous life. For the rare devotee, such a sankalpamay begin as early as the seventh month in the womb. Lord Kapila narrates how a spiritually blossoming embryo expresses its determination lor perfection:

*tasmad aham vigata-viklava uddharisya*  
*atmanam asu tamasah suhrdatmanaiva*  
*bhuyo yatha vyasanam etad aneka-randhram*  
*ma me bhavisyad upasadita-visnu-padah*

**“Therefore, without being agitated any more, I shall deliver myself from the darkness of nescience with the help of my friend, clear consciousness. Simply by keeping the lotus feet of Lord Visnu in my mind, I shall be saved from entering into the wombs of many mothers for repeated birth and death.”**

When such a fortunate soul encounters a pure Vaisnava, hr. spiritual journey starts anew, and as the process of sadhana-bhakti purifies his consciousness, his direction in life becomes clear: “Back to Godhead.”

Gradually, by systematic sadhanaand progressive determination, such a devotee moves up the ladder of bhakti,his increasingly purified consciousness inspiring his mind and intelligence forward. In this way, by the causeless mercy of Vaisnavas and the Lord, such a devotee’s false ego gradually dissolves, just as fog evaporates with the rising of the sun. He becomes self-realised, free from all doubts, and increasingly sheltered by the hladini-sakti.

When finally the sadhakacrosses over the boundary of matter into the realm of spirit, all false egoistic conceptions disappear, and he realises his eternal ego as Krsna’s servant. Thus empowered, such a fortunate soul quickly achieves the ultimate goal of life, and with pure Krsna consciousness returns to the transcendental abode, never to return.

Thus the subtle body of mind, intelligence, false ego, contaminated consciousness—a result of the abuse of free will—and the vehicle that carries a bewildered soul through countless bodies, is, by the process of sadhana-bhakti,dissolved, as confirmed by Lord Kapila:

*jarayaty asu óa kosam*  
*nigirnam analo yatha*

**“Bhakti, devotional service, dissolves the subtle body of the living entity without separate effort, just as fire in the stomach digests all that we eat.”**

## Chapter Fourteen

**The Sanichya of Sanklalpa**

In this chapter we shall combine the workings of the mind, intelligence, false ego, and consciousness as they relate to a devotee’s sankalpathrough the stages of sadhana.Readers may question why, in the previous chapter, we elaborated on the process of creation, the formation of the subtle body, and how its parts work and interact. The answer, as stated at the beginning of Chapter Ten, is that knowledge of these activities is integral to understanding our goal.

Throughout Srila Prabhupada’s books, we are encouraged both by His Divine Grace as well as the books’ original authors, like Vyasa, not to shy away from an analytical study of the components of Krsna conscious philosophy. Even as a child, Prahlada Maharaja advised his equally-young friends to investigate the treasury of Vaisnava truths:

*anvaya-vyatirekena*  
*vivekenosatatmana*  
*svarga-sthana-samamnayair*  
*vimrsadbhir asatvaraih*

**“Sober and expert persons should search for the spirit soul with minds purified through analytical study in terms of the soul’s connection with, and distinction from, all things that undergo creation, maintenance, and destruction.”**

In this chapter we introduce an analogy that compares sankalpa to movements on a ladder. The evolution of the subtle and gross material elements mirrors the process of moving down a ladder from pure consciousness to contaminated consciousness. Much the same dynamics are also applicable to moving up the ladder, signifying the determined steps involved in spiritual progress.

In other words, knowledge of certain features of how living entities become conditioned is useful in knowing how they become liberated.

Narada also uses an analogy to illustrate the transmigration of the subtle body from one gross body to the next by showing how the body created in a dream is abandoned when one wakes to his actual living body. The acaryaalso explains that the mental condition of a person indicates something of his previous life, and also of what he will be in a future life. Indeed, this system of comparison is found throughout the Srimad-Bhagavatam,and it is one of the ten types of evidence accepted by the Vedic epistemology called upamana.A most beautiful analogy of the transmigration of the soul is also spoken by Narada:

*yatha trna-jalukeyam*  
*napayaty apayati ca*  
*na tyajen mriyamano 'pi*  
*prag-dehabhimatim janah*

*yavad anyam na vindeta*  
*vyavadbanena karmanam*  
*mana eva manusyendra*  
*bhutanam bhava-bhavanam*

**“The caterpillar transports itself from one leaf to another by capturing one leaf before giving up the other. Similarly, according to his previous work, the living entity must capture another body before giving up the one he has. This is because the mind is the reservoir of all kinds of desires.”**

Our first port of call is how the living entity makes his appearance in the elements of creation. The following paragraph describes how this takes place.

Prior to creation, the Supreme Lord rested upon the snake-bed Ananta, absorbed in divine trance, yoga-nidra. At that time, both the living entities and the external energy were dormant. Desiring to give the living entities a chance for perfection, Maha-Visnu inspired the time factor to interact with the mahat-tattva,in which the living entities then became active through the incitement of the inodes of material nature. Thus began the unfortunate jivas’ futile effort at material happiness, caused by forgetfulness of where real happiness lies—with Krsna. The mahat-tattvais the junction of matter and spirit, the shadow of pure consciousness wherein false ego is manifest in three ways—as cause, effect, and doer. Srimad-Bhagavatamsays that these developments all take place on a subtle mental plane.

In the paragraph above, as in scripture, terms like “then,” "when,” and “after” are employed to describe creation and the evolution of the subtle and gross bodies. These words give a sense of sequence and chronology that may not be exactly accurate, for our investigation is in a realm wherein time does not yet function as we experience it. Nonetheless, we must use such expressions to facilitate communication. Where time does follow the linear progression to which we are accustomed, such terms really do express an actual sequence of events.

From sastricnarrations of creation we generally suppose that the following is a chronological development:

False ego, mind, intelligence, and senses, followed by the material elements.

Srila Prabhupada’s translation of a verse of Srimad-Bhagavatam confirms this sequence:

**“Material activities are caused by the mahat-tattva’s being agitated. At first there is transformation of the modes of goodness and passion, and later—due to the mode of ignorance—matter, its knowledge, and different activities of material knowledge come into play.”**

Additionally, while we are speaking of such diverse products of creation and their intricate interaction, it is good to keep in mind the following:

**From the point of view of oneness, the subtle and gross bodies, sense perception, and their objects are all manifestations of the one Absolute Truth, while at the same time, from the perspective of duality, the supreme reality remains separate from them.**

Let us continue with the living entity’s desire for independence, which is the vehicle by which he enters the creation at Maha-Visnu’s bidding. Desire is the foundation of sankalpa Without it, no living entity, conditioned or liberated, would act.

Desire may be carried over from a previous creation, or it may be original, the cause of falldown from one’s role as a servant of the Lord. That desire is, as everything else, dormant until the will of the Supreme awakens false ego within the mahat-tattva,upon which both the jivaand his desires are activated. At this stage false ego is general, meaning that it does not reflect the details of the living entity’s individual desires. However, with the mixing of the time element, individual desires become activated, and then false ego is similarly characterised and individualised.

According to the jiva’sdesire, karma,and disposition, the living entity accedes to a corresponding mode of nature that then creates a suitably moulded mind, intelligence, senses, and eventually, body. The mind is created from the mode of goodness; intelligence and the senses from passion; and the material elements from ignorance. The sense of identification with these subtle and gross bodies, the false ego, is an adopted portion of the mahat-tattva,and the awareness that serves the sense of false identity is the contaminated consciousness. Sukadeva Gosvami gives a brilliant description of the false ego and its function as but a part of the Absolute Truth:

*yatha ghano ’rka-prabhavo ’rka-darsito*  
*by arkamsa-bhutasya ca caksusas tamah*  
*evam tv aham brahma-gunas tad-iksito*  
*brabmamsakasyatmana atma-bandhanah*

**“Although a cloud is a product of the sun and is also made visible by the sun, it nevertheless creates darkness for the viewing eye, which is another partial expansion of the sun. Similarly, material false ego, a particular product of the Absolute Truth made visible by the Absolute Truth, obstructs the individual soul, another partial expansion of the Absolute Truth, from realising the Absolute Truth.”**

If the jiva'sdesire is original and he has not previously been in the material world, he — according to Srila Prabhupada and Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura—first takes birth as Brahma. Srila Prabhupada writes:

**“Both the Lord and the living entity, being qualitatively spirit soul, have the tendency for peaceful enjoyment, but when the part of the Supreme Personality of Godhead unfortunately wants to enjoy independently, without Krsna, he is put into the material world, where he begins his life as Brahma and is gradually degraded to the status of an ant or a worm in stool.”**

If, however, the living entity is returning to the material world, he shoulders earlier desires and an earlier fate, and accepts a deserving position.

At this stage the components for the living entity’s first sankalpa are assembled and ready to be put to use.

In the case where the jivaaccepts his role as a human, the enchantress named Desire bewilders his intelligence, brings him under the influence of the mind, and makes him an instrument of the false ego. In this way the designation of the soul becomes the mind, and so its mental impressions, inspired by the external energy, become a source of further bondage.

Having taken the soul hostage, the mind, lacking discrimination, makes impulsive decisions, and when it accepts a certain direction of life it makes a corresponding commitment, which then becomes its first sankalpa,the first step down our figurative ladder.

A similar example of a first sankalpais when the aforementioned Brahma neglects the direction of the Vedas and, bewildered by his own creation, wants to enjoy in it. Thus he next takes a human body, forfeiting both his illustrious position and his chance for liberation.

In the introduction to this chapter, we emphasised a lack of clarity in chronology during the initial stages of creation. Because an event, a sankalpa,is time dependent, there is equal lack of clarity as to exactly where this first step of the jivainto mayais. We there fore take the maturing of the elements needed for a sankalpaas the “moment” of the first step down the ladder of entanglement.

Degradation is a process that feeds and amplifies itself. Just as the false ego inspires the mind to material attainment, thus soiling the consciousness and further obscuring the goal of life, sense gratification further nourishes the false ego, and empowers the mind to fresh mischief. In this way, one wrong step leads to another, and it does not take long before one has fallen from the status of a human or a Brahma to that of an insect. It is said that the mind is coloured by fruitive activity, karmatmaka,which means that all its activities are equally coloured by karma.

Sukadeva Gosvami tells Maharaja Pariksit that Lord Sankarsana is the presiding deity of false ego, and that it is He who dictates to the lusty soul, “I am the enjoyer. This world is for me.” Krsna reminds us of this same principle in the Bhagavad-gita:

*sarvasya caham hrdi sannivisto*  
*mattah smrtir jnanam apohanam ca*

**“I am seated in everyone’s heart, and from Me come remembrance, knowledge, and forgetfulness.”**

According to the type of body for which the jivais qualified, and according to the dictates of his fate, the infatuated mind seeks sense objects appropriate to the imagined fulfilment of its desire. In doing so, the mind enlists the intelligence in how to best eke out sense gratification from those objects with the never-to-be-fulfilled promise of happiness. Of course, the mind does not remain idle but does its part by continually accepting and rejecting according to newly surfacing circumstances, dragging the intelligence along with it as a willing—and sometimes an unwilling—accomplice.

The mind thus creates pious and impious activities as well as their concomitant karma,thereby conditioning the soul to a specific bodily appearance and behaviour. In this way the mind brings about birth in a variety of bodies and remains mired in the modes of material nature, just like “an independent, uncontrolled elephant.” The result is that it becomes submerged in a self-made pool of pious and impious activities, all because of a hopeless ideal that it will satisfy its senses.

One may argue that by performing pious activities under the higher modes of nature the false ego dissipates. However, this is not so! Neither can one attain liberation by piety. Narada Muni assures King Pracinabarhi:

*nabam mameti bhavo ’yam*  
*puruse vyavadbiyate*  
*yavad buddhi-mano-’ksartha-*  
*guna-vyuho hy anadiman*

**“As long as there exists the subtle material body composed of intelligence, mind, senses, sense objects, and the reactions of the material qualities, the consciousness of false identification and its relative objective, the gross body, exist as well.”**

As devotees well know, it is only devotional service that effectively dissolves the aforesaid subtle body and so brings an end to karma and the false ego. This is brilliantly exemplified by Lord Kapila to His mother:

*jarayaty asu óa kosam*  
*nigirnam analo yatha*

**“Bhakti,devotional service, dissolves the subtle body of the living entity without separate effort, just as fire in the stomach digests all that we eat.”**

In the downward journey of the soul, the mind is increasingly overcome by ignorance, and so it habitually engages the senses in fulfilling desires and taking successive sankalpas.In such a bewildered condition, the unfortunate living entity does not know that it will forfeit its valuable human form. It forgets that a consequence of impious deeds is that it becomes forced into species of life in which it has no say over its acts. As an animal, its only determination will be what is dictated by the instinct unique to its species.

Yet, while still in the human form, the jivagarners a host of con sequences from every sankalpahe makes. Decisions result in further desires, some happiness, mostly frustration, karmic reactions, increased lust, soaring greed, and—regardless of what mode of nature one is in—an increasingly bewildered consciousness.

Such bewilderment, burdened with the consequences of past deeds and compounded desires, impels the mind to look for new brands of sense gratification and happiness, moving down the ladder one rung after the other, and dragging with it the unfortunate soul and intelligence.

In the words of Sir Walter Scott, the living entity weaves an incredibly complex and “tangled web” of karmaand desires when it adopts a practice of deception in trying to commandeer Krsna’s supremacy for himself. The result is that the jivais impossibly ensnared in the material energy, and deeply illusioned. In their con versation with the Visnudutas, the Yamadutas wonderfully explain how the jivaentangles itself in maya’sweb:

*dehy ajno ’jita-sad-vargo*  
*necchan karmani karyate*  
*kosakara ivatmanam*  
*karmanacchadya muhyati*

**“The foolish embodied living entity, inept at controlling his senses and mind, is forced to act according to the influence of the modes of material nature against his desires. He is like a silkworm that uses its own saliva to create a cocoon and then becomes trapped in it, with no possibility of getting out. The living entity traps himself in a network of his own fruitive activities, and then can find no way to release himself. Thus he is always bewildered, and repeatedly he dies.”**

Sometimes, in an attempt to ease its conscience from sinful activities or to mitigate the suffering resulting from those deeds, the living entity adopts some form of karma, jnana,or yoga.But all to no avail! Should a rare soul even attain the liberated state, still, without some exceptional good fortune, he will once again fall into maya'sclutches, the result of his austerities foiled. In this regard Lord Brahma and the demigods say:

*ye ’nye ’ravindaksa vimukta-maninas*  
*tvayy asta-bhavad avisuddha-buddbayah*  
*arubya krcchrena param padam tatah*  
*patanty adho ’nadrta-yusmad-anghrayab*

**“O lotus-eyed Lord, although non-devotees who accept severe austerities and penances to achieve the highest position may think themselves liberated, their intelligence is impure. They fall down from their position of imagined superiority because they have no regard for Your lotus feet.”**

Exceptional good fortune is the mercy of pure devotees. Without this intercession of Vaisnava association, the living entity becomes hopelessly entangled, and after suffering in hell he is then tossed into the animal species. Such is the end result of his free will and the resolute steps he takes to be an independent enjoyer.

But good fortune sometimes does dawn in the life of a fallen jiva.

If somehow he is able to hear teachings from a pure Vaisnava, the effect of such transcendental knowledge brings about a revolution in the impious life of a misdirected soul. The effect of transcendental sound is to purify the consciousness and to rouse the intelligence, thus awakening a spark of desire for service to the Lord, and an inkling of one’s spiritual identity—a drastic contrast to the living entity’s earlier state of mind.

A new and dynamic course of events is in the making if the jiva hears and follows the teachings of true saints. In the same way that the mind was the cause of karma, it can now be the cause of destroying karma;as the mind was cause for entanglement, it can be the cause of liberation; as the mind swelled the false ego, it can find its real spiritual identity. How the instrument of bondage can also be the instrument of liberation is concisely explained by the sage Narada:

*amayo yas ca bhutanam*  
*jayate yena suvrata*  
*tad eva hy amayam dravyam*  
*na punati cikitsitam*

**“O good soul! Does not a thing, applied therapeutically, cure a disease which was caused by that very same thing?”**

In other words, the mind’s role may be reversed if it comes under the guidance of enlightened intelligence. And how the mind can be the instrument for a change of direction on the ladder is now the theme of the rest of this chapter.

\* \* \* \*

We begin by once again drawing attention to the importance that transcendental knowledge plays in the deliverance of the jiva.While other limbs of bhaktiare indispensable—most notably nama-sankirtana—the limb of sravanais given emphasis here because in our Krsna consciousness movement it is so neglected. Srila Prabhupada dedicated so much of his time to his mission of leaving transcendental literature for his followers’ education. Yet most “followers” tend to take the Bhaktivedanta Purports as casual reading at best, not as textbooks for their devotional schooling—textbooks from which to learn the sublime science of bhakti.

But Krsna praises the glories of transcendental knowledge as the boat by which to cross the ocean of miseries, and as the fire to burn up reaction to karmic activity. He also emphasises that one who is ajna,a fool with no knowledge of standard scriptures, and asraddadhana,without faith in the scriptures, does not attain God consciousness but falls down.

In his commentary to the same verse, Baladeva Vidyabhusana adds that one who has some faith but doubts that he can attain the goal is the most unfortunate fool.

In short, without the benefit of transcendental knowledge, the fledgling aspirant will not be able to take the substantial sankalpas necessary to reach bhava.For this reason, Krsna values the knowledge of transcendence as the greatest treasure. He says,

*na hi jnanena sadrsam*  
*pavitram iha vidyate*  
*tat svayam yoga-samsiddhah*  
*kalenatmani vindati*

**“In this world, there is nothing so sublime and pure as transcendental knowledge. Such knowledge is the mature fruit of all mysticism. And one who has become accomplished in the practice of devotional service enjoys this knowledge within himself in due course of time.”**

One may enquire:

**“What is required to be qualified to receive this transcendental gift?”**

The Lord continues:

*sraddhaval labhate jnanam*  
*tat-parah samyatendriyah*  
*jnanam labdhva param santim*  
*acirenadhigacchati*

**“A faithful man who is dedicated to transcendental knowledge and who subdues his senses is eligible to achieve such knowledge, and having achieved it he quickly attains the supreme spiritual peace.”**

In this translation, faith, dedication, and sense control are qualifications to receive knowledge. This implies that the preacher or Vaisnava gurumust be expert enough to instil in his follower a minimum of faith in Krsna, in the Bhagavad-gita,and in the process of hearing.

**“How much is a minimum of faith?”**

**“As much as will inspire the aspiring devotee to make the first commitment in Krsna consciousness, the step to bhajana-kriya.”**

Additionally, the aspirant must acquire attachment to what he has heard, which at this very initial stage often means attachment to the pure devotee preacher.

With faith in Krsna and attachment to his spiritual master, meaningful sankalpascan take place in a succession proportional to the degree of sense control that the novice is able to muster. These are the blessings upon a neophyte that arise from his fortuitous meeting with a pure devotee.

We should make clear that while transcendental knowledge is essential for spiritual advancement, faith—not knowledge—is the initial qualification for bhakti.Moreover, knowledge is a consequence of devotional service, and if one has both faith and devotion, one has the preliminary ingredients for perfection. Prahlada Maharaja gives a graphic example:

*bhavatam api bhuyan me*  
*yadi sraddadhate vacah*  
*vaisaradi dhih sraddhatah*  
*stri-balanam ca me yatha*

**“My dear friends! If you can place your faith in my words, simply by that faith you can also understand transcendental knowledge just like me, although you are small children. Similarly, a woman can also understand transcendental knowledge and know what is spirit and what is matter.”**

Nonetheless, Krsna points out in the Bhagavad-gitathat it is the exceptional devotee who can advance without knowledge of the process of bhakti.

To conclude, when a living entity becomes the beneficiary of serendipity, transcendental knowledge gradually strengthens his intelligence and gives him a semblance of control over his mind. This is the genesis of the determined effort necessary for the jivato elevate himself, and it is the inauguration of the first sankalpa.

\* \* \* \*

Let us first look at the general sequence of a few progressive pi ritual sankalpas,and then take a closer look at their commonly shared dynamics.

The first sankalpamay be no more than an interest in a Vaisnava function like Janmastami, a casual read of the Bhagavad-gita,or chanting Hare Krsna as part of a meditation fad. As previously indicated, this sankalpamust be anchored to a Vaisnava to take effect. Until it does, the candidate’s qualification may increase, but his actual upward progress will not.

If the intelligence is not sufficiently empowered, the mind may display fleeting interest in the divine, but due to its deeply entrenched search for sense gratification, it will avoid serious efforts at spiritual advancement. The intelligence must be adequately enlightened for it to entice the mind with devotional acts, even as non-devotional habits continue.

The whole idea is to somehow awaken the mind to a desire for bhakti.The mind is born of desire, and is also the cause of further desire. Just as a spark that touches tinder can transform into a conflagration, the mind’s smallest interest in Krsna can eventually awaken spiritual greed. It simply requires the fanning of Vaisnava association. Narada tells Yudhisthira Maharaja,

*katamo ’pi na venah syat*  
*pancanam purusam prati*  
*tasmat kenapy upayena*  
*manah krsne nivesayet*

**“Somehow or other, one must consider the form of Krsna very seriously. Then, by one of the five different processes mentioned above, one can return home, back to Godhead. Atheists like King Vena, however, being unable to think of Krsna’s form in any of these five ways, cannot attain salvation. Therefore, one must somehow think of Krsna, whether in a friendly way or inimically.”**

Thoughts and reflections give rise to desire, while desire results in acceptance and rejection, meaning sankalpa.In the way that Maya tempted the jivato enjoy through her covering and throw ing potencies, thereby creating further desire for enjoyment, so Vaisnavas must now tempt the illusioned jivato take up bhakti-yogaby their transcendental tactics, thereby creating further desire for it.

Granted! Greed for Krsna does not awaken as quickly as greed for maya.Descending a ladder is a swifter process than ascent, in the same way that it is easier to start a forest fire than to extinguish one. Yet to the degree that desire is purified, to that degree the senses can act for Krsna consciousness, thereby fueling an aspirant’s desire by offering him a higher taste through the experience of devotional acts.

There is, however, one great asset of the mind—believe it or not—and that asset is that it is born of the mode of goodness, and so it, like the soul, has a constitutional inclination for spiritual life and for Krsna’s service. The idea, therefore, of transferring desire to please Krsna is not one that is alien to the mind. For this reason, sadhana-bhaktiis partially about convincing the mind to give up the bad habits it has acquired in its sojourn down the ladder of material enjoyment.

As the false ego contacts an alternate identity as spirit soul, servant of Krsna, the mind and intelligence also acquire an alternate bearing, and so awaken to a determination for spiritual advancement. However, while material desires remain strong, the power of sankalpaswill be weak. So there is an inverse relationship between material desires and spiritual determination:

**The greater material desires, the weaker the determination; the weaker material desires, the stronger the determination.**

And so it is until ruciis attained. Up to nistha,the intelligence obliges the mind to adhere to the regulative principles of vaidhi-bhakti.At the stage of taste, sankalpabecomes natural, and at attachment it becomes greed, an overpowering urge that will be expressed in longings, known as lalasamayi.Such an overpowering desire for spiritual perfection is beautifully articulated by Kunti-devi:

*tvayi me ’nanya-visaya*  
*matir madhu-pate ’sakrt*  
*ratim udvahatad addha*  
*gangevaugham udanvati*

**“O Lord of Madhu! As the Ganges forever flows to the sea without hindrance, let my attraction be constantly drawn unto You without being diverted to anyone else.”**

Let us again return to our enquiring soul who has made first contact with bhakti.

The effect of reading Bhagavad-gitaor hearing the holy name will strengthen faith to the extent the jivaaccepts that his real identity is a servant of Krsna.

In his Introduction to Bhagavad-gita As It Is,Srila Prabhupada extends a helping hand to the fallen by proposing that the basis of an initial sankalpa—reading the Bhagavad-gita—may be as simple as a “theoretical” commitment to the content of the book. His Divine Grace writes,

**“So according to the statements of Bhagavad-gitaor the statements of Arjuna, the person who is trying to understand the Bhagavad-gita,we should at least theoretically accept Sri Krsna as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and with that submissive spirit we can understand the Bhagavad-gita."**

Starting with even such a theoretical commitment, the power of bhaktiis such that the sincere seeker comes to the second sankalpa in which devotional service appears like a reality of choice. Such an aspirant may not be up to the vows of initiation, but ongoing assn ciation will ensure that such a third commitment does take place in time. And with each of these sankalpas,the spiritual aspect of the subtle body increases and the material aspect decreases.

Of course, all sadhakaswill attest to the ongoing tug of war between the ideal ego and the false ego, spiritual desires and mate rial desires, thoughts of Krsna and the tenacity of the material mind, the call of the flute and the shackles of unwanted habits.

Added to this is the feeling that the effort to climb each successive rung of the ladder seems increasingly more exacting than climbing the previous one. And it is understandably so! Just as a student’s higher levels of education demand a corresponding calibre of knowledge and guidance, similarly a devotee’s progressive advancement demands correspondingly more elevated knowledge and mature association. Unfortunately, this is a point that devotees sometimes do not understand, and so they practise the same basic sadhanawith the anticipation of attaining progressively higher and higher levels of devotion. They think that a minimum practice is sufficient for the paramount attainment. It is not!

\* \* \* \*

As promised, let us now dissect an individual sankalpa.

We have established that all successive steps of a sankalpahave similar characteristics, albeit differently motivated and buttressed. But what is the common psychology and mechanics of making the determination to move up from one level of bhaktito the next?

Let us keep in mind that knowledge of the steps up the ladder of devotion are based on studying the steps a living entity takes down the ladder of conditioning. In other words, the premise is that the process of liberation is like the reverse of conditioning, just as the process of annihilation of the universe is similar to the reverse of creation. The Srimad-Bhagavatamconfirms this thesis:

*yatha jala-dhara vyomni*  
*bhavanti na bhavanti ca*  
*brahmanidam tatha visvam*  
*avayavy udayapyayat*

**“Just as clouds in the sky come into being and are then dispersed by the amalgamation and dissolution of their constituent elements, this material universe is created and destroyed within the Absolute Truth by the amalgamation and dissolution of its elemental, constituent parts.”**

We return to the example of a novice who has just contacted Krsna consciousness:

When the power of bhakti—if even in a shadowy form—touches the conditioned soul, the false ego, ahankara,weakens, and so a simple sense of spiritual identity is established.

The mind, affected by the inherent goodness of devotion, begins to casually probe this newly-proposed identity and its consequences. That is its nature—sankalpa, vikalpa.However, without guidance, the mind remains clueless as to how to properly process the newly-proposed ego.

Although lacking even the most basic understanding, a spark of spiritual desire has been awakened in the mind. And that desire will increase in proportion to both knowledge and purification. When desire reaches a critical stage, then it will initiate a sankalpa.That lid, if desire is not properly steered by transcendental knowledge, the jivawill not know how to move forward, or will err in doing so.

Thereafter, intelligence inspired by the goodness of bhaktiwill he inclined to guide the mind towards its new-found identity. But intelligence, too, without proper guidance, will neither know how nor be strong enough to do so.

But as the living entity acquires transcendental knowledge, the intelligence begins to process what it has learned by first understanding the information, then overcoming doubts, and finally by mapping out its course of application.

Originally, both the knowledge-acquiring senses and the working senses are meant to be under the direction of the intelligence. But without Krsna consciousness, the mind becomes increasingly empowered by passion and takes control of both kinds of senses, and makes them instruments of its contaminated desires. Now, however, with mind and intelligence seeing eye to eye on the path of purification, they conjointly direct the senses in appropriate ways.

Examples of such appropriate engagement are reading the Bhagavad-gitaand learning how to use japabeads.

By these activities, the intelligence is further empowered by good ness, thereby attaining a semblance of control over the mind. The use of the word “semblance” here indicates that there will be a constant competition between the developing desire of the intelligence for spiritual growth and the long-standing desires of the mind for enjoyment.

For the neophyte to progress, for him to be freed from the anchors of past deeds, he must remain in the fire of purification To do otherwise means to fall back into destructive habits. And that fire of purification burns only under the shelter of continuous sadhanaand wise Vaisnavas. Lord Krsna confirms:

*jata-sraddho mat-kathasu*  
*nirvinnah sarva-karmasu*  
*veda duhkhatmakan kaman*  
*parityage ’py anisvarah*

*tato bhajeta mam pritah*  
*sraddhalur drdha-niscayah*  
*jusamanas ca tan kaman*  
*duhkhodarkams ca garhayan*

**“Having awakened faith in the narrations of My glories, being disgusted with all material activities, knowing that all sense gratification leads to misery, but still being unable to renounce all sense enjoyment, My devotee should remain happy and worship Me with great faith and conviction. Even though he is sometimes engaged in sense enjoyment, My devotee knows that all sense gratification leads to a miserable result, and he sincerely repents such activities.”**

Finally, when the above-mentioned components are all in place— namely empowered intelligence, spiritual desire, purified consciousness, and a co-operative mind—at that time an empowered volition will move the mind, intelligence, the knowledge-acquiring senses, and the working senses to adopt a more gainful sadhana.

The initiative to embrace that new standard of sadhanais a sankalpa.

That intensified sadhana—which for our novice may now mean chanting eight rounds and becoming vegetarian—will initiate a heightened purification that becomes the cause of a similar transformation in the subtle body. When that transformation hits the next tipping point, then the next sankalpacan take place.

Again, the sequence of developments in the subtle body are:

Purification of consciousness, increased spiritual desire, strengthening spiritual identity, easing of false ego, enlightened intelligence, and decreasing material desire.

As a result of such enlightenment, the mind comes further under the control of purified intelligence, and hence becomes a better instrument both for sadhanaand for sankalpa.

This is as much detail as we shall describe of the mechanics of sankalpa.Readers deserve a basic understanding of the actual sub- \|ect of this book. Yet as they proceed from one rung to the next up the bhaktiladder, sadhakasneed not meditate on the intricacies of their transitions, rather they should keep in mind the greater picture of attaining their goal. This general picture and its attainment is summarised by Sukadeva Gosvami in this way:

*ghano yadarka-prabhavo vidiryate*  
*caksuh svampam ravim iksate tada*  
*yada hy ahankara upadhir atmano*  
*jijnasaya nasyati tarhy anusmaret*

**“When the cloud originally produced from the sun is torn apart, the eye can see the actual form of the sun. Similarly, when the spirit soul destroys his material covering of false ego by enquiring into the transcendental science, he regains his original spiritual awareness.”**

\* \* \* \*

Once the cloud of past bad habits has dissipated as a consequence of successful upward sankalpas,the mind begins to sober up and become a proactive participant in its own emancipation. Like the bad patient who finally begins to co-operate with the convalescence prescribed by his doctor, the mind begins to co-operate with the guidance directed by the intelligence.

While serious co-operation already begins at the stage of nistha. it transits from dutiful to natural at ruciand asakti.Spontaneous attraction is a phenomenon to be expected, since the mind is a product of goodness, and so service is its latent inclination. As purification brings the mind closer to its original state, it becomes increasingly inclined to spiritual practice until ultimately that inclination becomes exceedingly intense. That is spiritual greed.

Because the mind can be such a great asset to the controlled sadhaka,Krsna calls it a friend, bandhu. And while the mind can be a good friend, it is a friend one is advised to remain wary of. Spiritual authorities warn practicing devotees to never trust the mind, regardless of how much it co-operates with their sadhana-bhajana.For example, Sukadeva Gosvami warns,

*satyam uktam kintv iha va eke na manaso ’ddha visrambham*  
*anavasthanasya satha-kirata iva sangacchante*

**“My dear King! You have spoken correctly. However, after capturing animals, a cunning hunter does not put faith in them, for they might run away. Similarly, those who are advanced in spiritual life do not put faith in the mind. Indeed, they always remain vigilant and watch the mind’s action.”**

Since the contaminated mind is the repository of lust, anger, pride, greed, lamentation, illusion, and fear, which combined represent the shackles of material bondage, astute sadhakasdo not put faith in the mind at any time. Devotees worry that, if not restrained, the mind could once again welcome these enemies and compromise their austerities.

Examples of yogiswho fell from their perfection are Lord Siva, who became bewildered at the sight of Mohini, and Saubhari Muni, who was similarly stricken by seeing mating fish.

The lesson to learn is that while the mind may be an invaluable instrument, it should never be let loose. Considering the example of the chariot, the reins of the mind should be tightly held in the hands of a spiritually robust intelligence.

When a devotee ascends the ladder of successive sankalpas and arrives at the stage of mature attachment, his sadhanaqualities him for divine mercy, a shower of nectar which manifests in its own time. Until it does, a devotee can only cry and yearn for it. But when mercy descends upon a fortunate soul, he will have attained the goal of his devotions in the way it has been promised by learned authorities:

*suddha-sattva-visesatma*  
*prema-suryamsu-samya-bhak*  
*rucibhis citta-masrnya-*  
*krd asau bhava ucyate*

**“When devotional service is executed on the transcendental platform of pure goodness, it is like a sunray of love for Krsna. At such a time, devotional service causes the heart to be softened by various tastes, and one is then situated in bhava\[emotion\].”**

\* \* \* \*

The chapters of this part of Sankalpa-kaumudioffer a view into the workings of the various aspects of the subtle body, which, when properly aligned for bhakti,serve sadhakasin their determination to attain bhava.

In this chapter we have attempted to give a closer look at how the aspects of the subtle body work together to realise a devotee's vow to advance towards the goal of life. Knowledge of the inner dynamics of determination should be helpful to readers to make those sankalpashappen. Such knowledge is an instrument for sharpening the intelligence, and a spiritually astute intelligence is always welcome in keeping the mind under control and helping it make the right choices in Krsna consciousness.

By way of conclusion, we would like to offer a well-known verse as a means by which readers can easily understand and remember the process of sankalpa.This verse is a rule of thumb for what sankalpais and how it works:

*yam yam vapi smaran bhavam*  
*tyajaty ante kalevaram*  
*tam tam evaiti kaunteya*  
*sada tad-bhava-bhavitah*

**“Whatever state of being one remembers when he quits his body, Î son of Kunti, that state he will attain without fail.”**

Krsna’s explanation is clear. We paraphrase it slightly:

The nature that one attains at death by one’s accumulated actions throughout life determines, in detail, the kind of body and life one next attains.

In his purport, Srila Prabhupada writes:

**“One’s thoughts during the course of one’s life accumulate to influence one’s thoughts at the moment of death, so this life creates one’s next life.”**

Similarly, whatever sadhanaone has performed, the sankalpa into which that matures will determine one’s next sadhana.This is exemplified in Srimad-Bhagavatamwhere Brahma gave up his body in shame at thinking of forbidden sex. Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains that since Brahma's duration of life was already determined, his change of body was actually a change of mental disposition. Similarly, a sadhaka’srise from one rung of the devotional ladder to the next indicates a change in his mental disposition.

Thus the “state of being” at death in the above verse may also be understood as a change of disposition, or change of Krsna consciousness.

To summarise: the kind of Krsna consciousness one practises will result in a corresponding sankalpa,and that sankalpawill determine the next rung on the bhaktiladder, one’s next level of Krsna consciousness. This principle is shared by the maxim explained earlier, siddhasya laksanam yat syat sadhanam sadhakasya tat:

**“The practitioner and the means of practice should be in accord with their goal.”**

This completes our dissertation on the sankhyaof sankalpas.The next part of the book will give examples of determinations, both general and specific. We hope that as the reader progresses, he or she is able to better perceive the dynamics of moving up the ladder of sadhana-bhakti,and be increasingly inspired to do so.

## Part Four

**Types and Examples of Sankalpas**

## Chapter Fifteen

**Types of Sankalpas**

The chapters of Part Four chronicle both examples and types of sankalpas. This chapter elaborates on the latter, and the two chapters following give examples, both general and specific. The final chapter is dedicated to recommendations on how to formulate a determination.

Before continuing, we should again clarify our convention in lining the word “determination.”

When employing the word determination as a synonym for sankalpa,our primary use is as a noun, meaning a vow taken for the purpose of attaining an objective. The secondary use is as a verb, “determine,” thus indicating firmness of purpose. Obviously, the context of the word’s use will make clear whether the meaning in primary or secondary.

We begin by asserting that the principle of sankalpasis an aspect of every living entity’s nature. This claim is supported by the Vedic declaration, raso vai sah, rasam hy evayam labdhvanandi bhavati:

**“He is the embodiment of rasa,and the jivawho realises this rasabecomes fully ecstatic.”**

The import of this aphorism is that Krsna constantly strives to enjoy ever-increasing transcendental loving exchange, rasa.This desire of the Lord, and the endless ways He fulfils that desire, is also shared by His expansions—personal, energetic, and marginal, it is their shared inherent attribute! Thus the Lord appears in various incarnations with His associates and realises their mutual determinations for ever-new and variegated pastimes.

Sadly, when the marginal living entities come under the sway of the external potency, maya,they then direct their sankalpastowards efforts at material rasa.Such efforts are a will-of-the-wisp, since rasa is successful only when Krsna is its centrepiece. But when the living entity desires to re-establish a relationship with the Lord and con tinually makes efforts to do so, then he gradually revives the higher taste of pure devotional service and again tastes spiritual rasa.

Of particular interest to this book are sankalpasmade by a practising devotee, both for spiritual advancement and for perfection. The overarching principle defining a sadhaka’sefforts is Krsna's own quest for rasathrough the medium of loving exchange with confidential associates. Scholars in devotion explain that when a practising devotee mirrors the devotional activities of a perfect devotee, in time he, too, becomes perfect, having awakened loving devotion within himself.

The principle of a practitioner following an eternally perfect devotee as well as the all-prefect Lord is beautifully explained to Uddhava in this way:

*yatha sankalpayed buddhya*  
*yada va mat-parah puman*  
*mayi satye mano yunjams*  
*tatha tat samupasnute*

**“A yogiwho has faith in Me, absorbing his mind in Me and knowing that My purpose is always fulfilled, will always achieve his purpose by the very means he has determined to follow.”**

Krsna’s determination in loving exchange is always consummated to perfection. Therefore, a practising devotee who takes shelter of that loving exchange through bhakti-yogais also assured of the same success.

**“And what is the success of the sadhaka?”**

**“Attaining** ***bhava-bhakti*****, the blossoming bud of the flower of** ***prema*****!”**

Upon careful analysis of the meaning of sadhana-bhakti,we find very definite criteria for what constitutes an example of a sankalpa in the arena of pure devotion. Indeed, it was the import of this definition that contributed to our inspiration to undertake penning this work. We have already analysed this definition in order to establish its own integrity, to understand sadhana-bhakti,and to understand bhava.Now we take another approach and review it from the perspective of sankalpas.Rupa Gosvami's teachings are all encompassing. The definition is:

*krti-sadhya bhavet sadhya-*  
*bhava sa sadhanabhidha*  
*nitya-siddhasya bhavasya*  
*prakatyam hrdi sadhyata*

**“When transcendental devotional service, by which love for Krsna is attained, is executed by the senses, it is called sadhana-bhakti,or the regulative discharge of devotional service. Such devotion eternally exists within the heart of every living entity. The awakening of this eternal devotion is the potentiality of devotional service in practice.”**

In this verse the heart of a determination is expressed by the phrase krti-sadhya bhavet:

**“Activities of the senses that should be done.”**

Herein the vow is the resolve, and the means for realising it are the activities of the senses. Those activities then correspond to the goal, sadhya-bhava,which is the awakening of love of Godhead. Moreover, that awakening takes place in the heart, hrdi,where love has always been present in a potential state, sadhyata.

This definition establishes that a sankalpahas the following components:

**The goal, the means to attain the goal, and finally, where the goal leads—its result.**

Further reflection on the definition of sadhanamakes it obvious that for most practitioners bhava-bhaktiis not attained by just one sankalpa.For this reason, in the verses beginning adau sraddha tatah sadhu-sango 'tha bhajana-kriya, Rupa Cosvami lists seven steps that precede *bhava*. These seven steps could be said to be synonymous with seven sankalpas.That said, the reality for most practitioners is that each step takes multiple sankalpasto complete

For example, devotees usually make many efforts to go from unwanted habits, anartha-nivrtti,to steadiness, nistha.Therefore the phrase krti-sadhya bhavet,“activities of the senses that should be done,” implies multiple vows to reach the goal, in the way that it takes many steps to reach one’s destination.

Bhaktivinoda Thakura explains this stepwise elevation in the following way:

**“Conditioned souls are eligible to attain a very exalted position from a very low position. Between these two positions there are many other positions, each being a gradual step and a distinct level of advancement.**

**“Moreover, each and every gradual step has different prescriptions and prohibitions. Whenever a living entity steps to one level and stays there, he is obliged to follow the prescriptions and prohibitions of that step, following which he becomes eligible to attain the next step. If one is unable to attain the next step, he falls back to a lower step, which is called degradation. By contrast, attaining the higher step is called advancement.”**

In the chapters that follow, some examples of sankalpasthat we explore are from scripture, others from the lives of acaryas,and yet others of sadhana-bhakti.Since sadhanais the priority of this book, we shall study it in detail, citing examples of sankalpasin the seven stages of practice, in bhakti’sregulations, in varnasrama,and in preaching.

However, before proceeding with examples of sankalpas,we should first assess the different types of determinations that devotees make and that scriptures recommend. In doing so, we will see that examples of sankalpasfall into different categories. Some are absolutely essential for attaining bhava, and others less so. The sections that follow throughout this chapter explore major classifications of determination.

\* \* \* \*

While firmness of purpose to a desired goal is one, the variety of determinations are manifold. In studying sankalpa,this chapter aim at providing a better understanding of the different kinds of determination so that the sincere sadhakacan distinguish those that are favourable for premafrom those that are not.

Scriptural reference to the word determination is also manifold, at times simply due to linguistic diversity, at others due to difference in determinations. Without differentiating in usage, some primary words for determination found in the Srimad-Bhagavatam are: vyavasita, sahas, sankalpya, krta-niscaya, abhisandhi, asaya, nirbandha, drdha-vrata, nisthaya,and su-vrata.

Determinations in spiritual life can be categorised according to a host of factors including the following:

**The influence of the modes of nature; favourable or unfavourable circumstances; the stages of devotion aspired for; different secondary goals; earlier success or failure; impetus either by regulation or by natural taste; other kinds of inspiration by varnaand asrama;and primary or secondary considerations.**

While these factors may overlap or be interdependent, their individual influence should not be underestimated, and so each are described individually below. We begin with the influence of the modes of nature.

The Lord describes three kinds of determination—good, passionate, and ignorant—according to the modes of nature. The following is the definition of determination in goodness:

*dhrtya yaya dharayate*  
*manah-pranendriya-kriyah*  
*yogenavyabhicarinya*  
*dhrtih sa partha sattviki*

**“Î son of Prtha, that determination which is unbreakable, which is sustained with steadfastness by yoga practice, and which thus controls the activities of the mind, life, and senses is determination in the mode of goodness.”**

The specific characteristic of such determination is that it is never deviated from its purpose, avyabhicarinya.

Determination in passion is driven by desires for sense gratification, while that in ignorance is never successful and always meaningless. In summary, determination in goodness is for spiritual advancement, in passion for recognition, and in ignorance for no purpose.

In addition to the three modes of nature, a devotee’s determination may be favourable or unfavourable to his bhakti.

For example, Dhruva Maharaja was unmatched in his determinations, yet when the Lord appeared before him, the boy was ashamed of his motivations and begged forgiveness. He realised that his vows were unfavourable for pure devotion. From this example we learn that what may be favourable for mixed devotion may be unfavourable for pure devotion.

In a similar vein, Gopa-kumara took vows to serve different forms of the Lord, only to find that such determinations were unfavourable for service to Madana-gopala. His was also an example of determination for one form of pure devotion being unfavourable for that of another.

There are other things that exemplify how vows can adversely effect one’s devotions, a few of which are:

**Mistakenly taking a vow, being inspired by bad association, as a consequence of an offence, and ignorance of bhakti-tattva.**

These are exemplified below:

**The Mathura brahmanajoined the Vaisnavas in worshipping Bindu-Madhava in Prayaga until the Deity instructed him to abandon this mistaken sadhanaand go to Vraja.**

Due to bad association, Mukunda Datta thought that the studó of impersonal philosophy would enhance his devotion, but Caitanya Mahaprabhu thought otherwise.

By offending the Lord and His devotees, Ramacandra Puri thought stricter rules for renunciation were conducive to devotion, but this was not approved of by his godbrothers or by devotees in general.

And, due to ignorance of devotional science, Vyasa thought his composition of Mahabharatawould enhance his and others’ devotions, but Narada corrected him and explained that in this age only sankirtanaof Krsna’s names, forms, and pastimes would effect such a result. The sage said,

*yatha dharmadayas cartha*  
*muni-varyanukirtitah*  
*na tatha vasudevasya*  
*mahima hy anuvarnitah*

**“Although, great sage, you have very broadly described the four principles beginning with religious performances, you have not described the glories of the Supreme Personality, Vasudeva.”**

We also sometimes see that due to ignorance of devotional principles, a devotee becomes enamoured by excessive deity rituals, worship of Krsna’s incarnations, artificially taking sannyasa,accepting unnecessary austerities, and adopting excessive diets—to name a lew. Such commitments may well hamper a devotee’s spiritual life, despite being taken with the opposite intention.

Having touched upon the vows that are both favourable and unfavourable for bhakti,let us see those sankalpascharacteristic of the various stages of devotion.

The stages of devotion — from faith to ecstasy, as well as the divisions in each — require a corresponding and unique commitment. The distinctive impetus to rise from one level of devotion tî another is determined by corresponding degrees of faith and knowledge, and, at more advanced stages of bhakti,by attachment. Such determinations are both continuous and occasional. In any case, as in climbing a mountain, they require renewed and ever-new devotions to progress. These are, again, another kind of determination.

For example, the knowledge of devotional truths that is sufficient for one to progress from unsteady to steady devotion is insufficient to elevate one from steadiness to taste. To make this second step, a devotee will have to commit himself to regular hearing of Krsna's pastimes and qualities, which will not have been essential for him earlier.

Similarly, while for a novice initiation is not recommended, for a serious practitioner it is compulsory. Thus the determination atsraddhais much different than that at bhajana-kriya.

And finally, although by no means conclusively, to make the step from attachment to ecstasy, a devotee must be determined to do anything to attain Krsna’s mercy. Rupa Gosvami expresses this in the following way:

*krsna-bhakti-rasa-bhavita matih*  
*kriyatam yadi kuto 'pi labhyate*  
*tatra laulyam api mulyam ekalam*  
*janma-koti-sukrtair na labhyate*

**“Pure devotional service in Krsna consciousness cannot be had even by pious activity in hundreds and thousands of lives. It can be attained only by paying one price—that is, intense greed to obtain it. If it is available somewhere, one must purchase it without delay.”**

Now let us hear about determination for bhakti’ssecondary goals.

In the course of sadhana-bhakti,a devotee usually has a desire to cultivate activities not directly connected to devotion, such as studying non-devotional philosophy, practising various kinds of renunciation, learning devotional arts—such as playing music or painting—or becoming adept at astrology, gemology, or Ayurveda.

While such determination may inspire a devotee for devotion, bhaktiitself is independent of these practices. Nonetheless, a devotee who, for example, is inspired by playing melodious kirtana for Krsna will advance by the strength of the holy name, and thus such determination for a non-devotional aspect of bhakti—being attracted to and playing music—will be to Ins advantage.

Similarly, a devotee often adopts activities not connected to bhaktifor the purpose of preaching or making a livelihood. The aboove-mentioned astrology is an example of a Vedic science that non devotees are widely attracted to and which can become a means for giving others bhakti,and for paying bills. Such an astrologer may thus comfortably practise Krsna consciousness and also fulfil Lord Caitanya’s order to preach, and so, by his determination, benefit his own devotions.

\* \* \* \*

An interesting feature of determination is the success, failure, and even fall-down that may precede and inspire it. Obviously, success inspires success. Yet at the same time, Srila Prabhupada wrote:

**“Failures may not be detrimental; they may be the pillars of success.”**

Such an approach or mindset inspires in devotees a more calculated kind of determination.

Gopa-kumara was repeatedly successful in the chanting of his mantra,and so was elevated to increasingly spiritual realms. This success made him determined to advance further, even though great authorities like Narada advised him against such a difficult undertaking.

On the other hand, it can be seen that failure in bhaktileads to determination for the Lord’s lotus feet, either immediately or eventually. Saubhari Muni fell into household life as a result of his offence to Garuda. However, when, many years later, he meditated on the cause of his entanglement, he received renewed inspiration, and along with his wives, departed for Vrndavana forest.

In a similar vein, Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura was unable to understand how Kaviraja Gosvami identified the twenty-four and one half syllables of the Kama-gayatri mantra. Considering his inability to be an absolute failure, he contemplated suicide, in response to which Sri Radha appeared in a dream and resolved hi dilemma.

In these and many other ways, success and failure are an impetus for determined vows for perfection.

Another inspiration that gives birth to different kinds of determinations is the kind of bhaktibeing practised.

There are two kinds of sadhana,regulated and spontaneous.' The essence of regulated devotion is that determination is inspired by some external factor—scriptural injunction, order of the guru,or the need to advance. But spontaneous devotion is inspired by taste and attachment. A devotee does not have to be determined, he is already so because he has an insatiable desire to want to be so.

Let us first hear of sankalpasin regulated devotion.

The instructions and exemplary conduct of Vaisnavas are significant sources of inspiration, even when they appear to be indirect Take Prahlada Maharaja for example. He maintained an unimagi nable determination based on having heard from his guruNarada Muni, even while in his mother’s womb. And another young boy, Dhruva, left for the jungle to find God, an action based simply on the advice of his mother, a Vaisnavi.

No doubt readers have their own stories of becoming inspired to heights of devotion by reading the books of Srila Prabhupada, like Bhagavad-gitaor Srimad-Bhagavatam,or the commentaries of acaryaslike Jiva Gosvami and Visvanatha Cakravarti. There are many anecdotes of devotees who received one of Srila Prabhupada’s books, reading which they turned their backs on all material pur suits and gave their lives to serve Lord Gauranga’s mission.

Just a few weeks before writing these lines, the author was told of a recent story of a young man who saw no future for himself in the world and was wandering in a remote forest with the aim of ending his life—although he knew of no means by which to do that. Sitting down on a rock in the middle of nowhere, he looked down at the ground to see an invitation to a nearby Hare Krsna centre, “Yoga, meditation, and spiritual wisdom.” Just seeing a picture of Krsna awakened in him something very familiar, something very real, and so he returned to the world to become a devotee. That is determination arising from seeing a picture of Krsna and possibly from impressions of a previous life.

All the aforementioned examples are of regulative devotion. However, the fortunate sadhakawho has natural attraction for the service of the Divine Couple, either as a conditioned or a liberated soul, is inspired in a way that may be compared to an obsession.

In the following verse, Srimati Radharani gives vent to such obsession, admitting that despite His dishonest dealings, despite wanting to, She could not stop talking about Krsna:

*mrgayur iva kapindram vivyadhe lubdha-dharma*  
*striyam akrta virupam stri-jitab kama-yanam*  
*balim api balim attvavestayad dhvanksa-vad yas*
