*tad alam asita-sakhyair dustyajas tat-katharthah*

**“Like a hunter, He cruelly shot the king of the monkeys with arrows. Because He was conquered by a woman, He disfigured another woman who came to Him with lusty desires. And even after consuming the gifts of Bali Maharaja, He bound him up with ropes as if he were a crow. So let us give up all friendship with this dark-complexioned boy, even if we cannot give up talking about Him.”**

The contrast between spontaneous and regulative determination is clear. Whereas a regulative devotee takes vows to serve Krsna, a spontaneous devotee’s entire life is a vow, for he cannot but serve the Lord. His natural, realised condition is to be a servant.

Of course, the degree of Radha’s obsession with Krsna is unique. Still, Her spontaneous love exists to lesser degrees in those who follow Her style of devotion, and the devotion of the Vraja-vasis. This self-motivating, self-fuelling stimulus is also known as spiritual greed, as has been described in the earlier cited verse beginning with krsna-bhakti-rasa.

By way of conclusion, the determination of a spontaneous devotee is as unique as his brand of devotion. And yet that is the inspiration that a regulated devotee in the service of Lord Caitanya aspires for.

We have explained that determination may be spontaneous or forced, based on two kinds of practice, raga-bhaktiand vaidhi-bhakti, respectively. Additionally, because these two also mix, there is an additional range of vows that lead a devotee to Krsna's abodes, such as Goloka or Dvaraka, with pure spontaneous devotion, characterised by greed, leading to Vraja.

It may by now be obvious to the reader that the determinations driving bhaktiare manifold. In addition to the above vows we describe the following:

A devotee who is faithful to the varnasramasocial divisions will be enthused in his devotional practices by the callings of his varna or asrama.

For example, a grhastha-brahmanawill be encouraged to study Vaisnava scriptures to fulfil his duty to teach, while a grhastha vaisyawill be encouraged in his occupation so as to donate the results of his work to a devotional cause, such as the construction of a temple. In this way, both devotees are encouraged to serve through the calling of their work.

Similarly, as part of his new life, a novice brahmacariwill adopt devotional practices such as study of scripture, service to guru,and rising early, while a sannyasiwill renounce sense objects and use them in the service of Krsna.

Either directly or indirectly, when these vows and others are adopted by Vaisnava followers of the four varnasand asramas, those Vaisnavas progress further in devotion.

Determination to continue in devotional life, or to bring about a significant change in it, may come to a devotee in subtle or sublime ways.

There are many instances wherein dreams are the cause of determination.

For example, Krsnadasa Kaviraja dreamt that Lord Nityananda ordered him to leave his home and travel to Vrndavana, where all his desires would be fulfilled. Similarly, after repeatedly dreaming that his spiritual master was encouraging him towards renunciation, Srila Prabhupada left family life and began in earnest his mission of spreading Krsna consciousness all over the world.

A devotee of lesser calibre may have dreams of varying degrees of authenticity. And yet it is these very visions that often inspire a practitioner to higher stages of devotional service.

In the Bhagavad-gita,Lord Krsna speaks of another kind of inspiration of which He is the direct cause. Sitting within the heart of His devotee, Krsna often gives him guidance as the voice of his conscience, or in the form of a personal dictate. He says,

*tesam satata-yuktanam*  
*bhajatam priti-purvakam*  
*dadami buddbi-yogam tam*  
*yena mam upayanti te*

**“To those who are constantly devoted to serving Me with love, I give the understanding by which they can come to Me.”**

*teṣām evānukampārtham*  
*aham ajñāna-jaṁ tamaḥ*  
*nāśayāmy ātma-bhāva-stho*  
*jñāna-dīpena bhāsvatā*

**“To show them special mercy, I, dwelling in their hearts, destroy with the shining lamp of knowledge the darkness born of ignorance.”**

To summarise, there are multifarious causes of determination, and what may inspire one devotee may not inspire another. Ultimately, we may assess the value of an impetus by its result in furthering pure devotion. This conclusion follows Srila Prabhupada’s oft-quoted maxim of logic, phalena phala-karanam anumiyate:

**“By seeing a result, one can understand the cause of that result.”**

Thus, if a devotee finds a source of inspiration by which to rise closer tî bhava-bhakti,that source is a welcome component of his sadhana.

\* \* \* \*

The following section categorises sankalpasin relation to their relevance to bhava,the goal of sadhana-bhakti.It should be noted that this classification is a rule of thumb to assist devotees in evaluating how the varying types of sankalpasalready described relate to devotional practice. Is a determination essential, optional, or detrimental? The classifications below will help answer that question.

In both his Raga-vartma-candrikaand his summary study of Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu,Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura writes of five aspects of spontaneous devotion as they relate to a devotee's aspired-for perfection. These are:

*Bhavamaya:*

**A self-identification whose nature is in harmony with one’s aspired-for mood of eternal service.**

*Bhava-sambandhi:*

**Practices that are related to that mood.**

*Bhava-anukula:*

**Other practices that are favourable for it.**

*Bhava-aviruddha:*

**Further activities that are not opposed to it.**

*Bhava-viruddha*

**Those practices deemed detrimental to one’s aspired for mood of service.**

In this chapter we shall use these same divisions to illustrate the five kinds of determination relating to the attainment of ecstatic devotion, bhava.This means that the word bhava,unless otherwise specified, does not refer to the kind of service a raga-bhaktaaspires for, but rather to the stage of devotion following sadhanathat is aspired for by both regulated and spontaneous devotees.

Thus our convention in the five varieties of bhavais slightly different from that of CakravartI Thakura. Since our emphasis in this book is sadhana-bhakti,our convention relates to bhaktiin general and to the stage of ecstatic devotion, whereas that of the acarya relates to a raga-bhakta’syearning for a mood of perfection, such as that of a cowherd boy. The variance in the two usages is in reference to the kind of devotion and the kind of attainment that devotion targets.

It will be evident to the learned student that while sankalpasare an integral part of sadhana,they serve the purpose of sadhanain different ways. The different limbs of bhaktiserve different functions for the attainment of bhava,and so, too, do the sankalpasinherent in that development. Thus determinations, regulated and spontaneous, may be classified in five ways, and these will now be named and described in relation to how they serve the attainment of bhava.

*Bhavamaya-sankalpas:*

**These are the determinations of a devotee that are full of the desire for ecstatic devotion, bhava.**

As he advances in Krsna consciousness, a devotee will feel a compelling urgency to direct all aspects of his sadhanato its perfection, to bhava-bhakti.Those devotees who remain grounded in regulative devotion will be compelled to sadhanaby its very definition, whereas devotees who are awakened to spontaneous devotion will be increasingly compelled by the kind of perfectional mood they covet. In either case, when a devotee is consumed by attaining bhava-bhakti,his vows and resolve in sadhanaare bhavamaya.

Since most advanced, regulative devotees will also realise the purpose of Lord Caitanya’s teachings, eventually they, too, will covet the path of ragaand be drawn to its sweetness. If that transformation does not take place at the stage of sadhana,it will certainly do so at bhava.However, for an astute practitioner, spontaneous attraction will awaken at the stages of rucior asakti,thereby strengthening his resolve to progress to ecstatic devotion.

The spontaneity of sankalpasis proportional to the maturity of a devotee’s greed. Therefore, it is often found that aspirations driven mostly by regulations are weaker and more difficult to sustain. However, the blessings of advanced association will intensify a devotee’s eagerness, as well as the strength of his vows.

Nonetheless, whatever the strength, spontaneity, or accuracy of sankalpasmade by a devotee, when they are done to attain love for Krsna, sankalpasare said to be full, maya,of the desire for ecstatic devotion, bhava.

**“What does such a bhavamaya-sankalpalook like?”**

**“It depends on the kind of devotion by which one is inspired!”**

*Bhavamaya-sankalpa* is when a devotee says either:

**“I understand that the goal of sadhanais bhava-bhakti and that is the sole purpose of my life!”**

or:

**“My only desire is to attain ecstatic devotion, bhava-bhakti,so that I may follow that specific Vraja-vasi and serve like him or her!”**

The former is an example of a sankalpain regulative devotion, the latter an example in spontaneous devotion.

The second kind of determinations are the ingredient causes of love, *bhava-sambandhi-sankalpas:*

**These are vows that are related to bhava.**

A devotee’s determinations to attain premaby chanting the maha-mantra,reading scriptures, and remembering Krsna are of the nature of bhava-sambandhi.And as we know, these sankalpasmay be inspired either by dedication to regulations or by natural attraction.

In the way that a bhavamaya-sankalpais the very substance of ecstatic devotion, a bhava-sambandhi-sankalpais that impetus by which it is realised. The vows that a devotee takes shape the development of devotion leading to *bhava*. They begin with:

**“I will chant sixteen rounds of maha-mantradaily!”**

or:

**“I will read Srimad-Bhagavatamone hour a day!”**

Queen Kunti lists not only hearing, chanting, and remembering Krsna’s pastimes as activities leading to perfection, but also enabling others to do so. This is the mood of Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s sankirtanamovement, in which introducing others to the process of Krsna consciousness is an essential part of sadhana.A devotee who, throughout his life, makes progressive vows both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others certainly becomes a recipient of Krsna’s special grace. The Pandavas’ mother said,

*srnvanti gayanti grnanty abhiksnasah*  
*smaranti nandanti tavehitam janah*  
*ta eva pasyanty acirena tavakam*  
*bhava-pravahoparamam padambujam*

**“O Krsna, those who continuously hear, chant, and repeat Your transcendental activities, or take pleasure in others doing so, certainly see Your lotus feet, which alone can stop the repetition of birth and death.”**

Other vows that devotees must undertake to enable devotional success are:

**Following Ekadasi fasts, observing the festivities on Janmastami-day, and celebrating the month of Karttika.**

At this point a question may arise:

**“Why are acts like fasting or offering lamps to Lord Damodara the causes of attaining bhava?”**

The answer is seen in the two aspects to these observances. Not eating on Ekadasi for the pleasure of the Lord is not in itself a cause of bhava,but is instrumental or favourable for that attainment. The reason to restrict eating on Ekadasi is to engage in more nama-sankirtanaand other devotions. Hut doing ñṁḍṁ sankirtanawhen one is fasting on Ekadasi is an ingredient cause of bhava.

In the above-mentioned vows both instrumental and ingrediential factors are observed. For example, the Janmastami festival leads to both fasting and to remembrance of Krsna. Therefore, because of the presence of smarana,Janmastami is considered to he bhava-sambandhi.

And offering a lamp to Lord Damodara is instrumental to attain ing bhava,while singing Sri Damodarastakais the ingredient cause of bhava.

Subsequent to those vows that are essential for the attainment of ecstasy are bhava-anukula-sankalpas:

**Those sankalpasthat are favourable to bhava.**

These include the vow to mark the body with gopi-candana,to regularly circumambulate Tulasi-devi, and to wear neck beads.

A neophyte devotee sometimes neglects these basic practices, considering them external to the development of devotion However, like the instrumental austerities of Ekadasi, these commitments also have a material or ingrediential aspect.

For example, in marking the body with tilaka,a devotee simultaneously pronounces the different names of Lord Krsna and thus remembers Him. In this way a devotee does a kind of nama-sankirtana.This activity, then, is essential for the development of bhava.The same can be said of circumambulating Tulasi-devi, during which devotees sing the glories of Krsna’s dear associate. Thus, a Vaisnava attentive to the science of devotion does not fail to make these vows.

At this stage it is important to note that taking vows to serve Vaisnavas has the nature of the three aforementioned sankalpas.

When one vows to serve the spiritual master and predecessor acaryasby both following their instructions and by serving their mission, one’s determinations are full of bhava \[bhavamaya\], related to bhava\[bhava-sambandhi\], and favourable for bhava \[bhava-anukula\].The same can be said for any vow that serves pure Vaisnavas undertaken throughout the course of Krsna consciousness—they are beneficial for ecstatic devotion in all ways.

The fourth type of vows for devotion are those that have little direct relation to attaining love, bhava-aviruddha-sankalpa:

**Those vows that are neither favourable nor harmful, so may be said to be neutral.**

Making a vow to offer respect to brahmanasor cows is of the nature of bhava-aviruddha-sankalpa.Once again, when these acts are accompanied by remembrance or glorification of the Lord, they gain more substance.

The fifth classification of vows is called *bhava-viruddha-sankalpas:*

**Certain vows of devotion that are unfavourable for attaining bhava.**

The reader may wonder:

**“How can a determination in bhaktibe detrimental to one’s goal?”**

In the initial stages of devotion, a Vaisnava may make vows to meditate on Lord Narayana, Krsna’s various incarnations, or His Dvaraka associates. However, for the attainment of vraja-prema, the continuation of these vows becomes counterproductive in that they direct a practitioner to another goal. For this reason, saints explain that vows that are favourable at an initial stage of devotion may become unfavourable at a later stage. With the words tyaktva Laksmi-pati-ratim,Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami advises that under the guidance of the spiritual master, these kinds of vows for bhakti may be given up:

*asad-varta-vesya visrja mati-sarvasva-haranih*  
*katha mukti-vyaghrya na srnu kila sarvatma-gilanih*  
*api tyaktva Laksmi-pati-ratim ito vyoma-nayanim*  
*vraje radha-krsnau sva-rati-mani-dau tvam-bhaja manah*

**“Give up the prostitutes of friendship with non-devotees, prostitutes who will steal the treasure of your heart. Do not listen to the words of the tigress of impersonal liberation, which devours everyone. Give up attraction for Lord Narayana, which leads to the world of Vaikuntha. O mind, in Vraja worship Radha-Krsna, two philanthropists Who give away the jewel of pure love.”**

In summarising this chapter, it is worth repeating that a devotee's vows along the path of sadhana-bhaktifall into one of five can gories. As a devotee progresses in Krsna consciousness, he may evaluate the relevance of a new determination or of his sankalpas overall, with these five classifications. We repeat these five gradings of sankalpas.

*Bhavamaya:*

**The determinations that are full of the desire for ecstatic devotion, bhava.**

*Bhava-sambandhi:*

**Determinations that are the ingredient causes of bhava.**

*Bhava-anukula:*

**Determinations that are instrumental or favourable for bhava.**

*Bhava-aviruddha:*

**Further determinations that are not opposed to bhava, but are neutral to its accomplishment.**

*Bhava-viruddha:*

**Sankalpasthat are detrimental to attaining ecstatic devotion.**

We are hopeful that devotees become acquainted with these principles of devotion and review the relevance of their determinations in light of the five bhavas.

## Chapter Sixteen

**General Examples of Sankalpas**

We begin this chapter by citing examples of sankalpasfrom Srimad-Bhagavatamand Caitanya-caritamrta.The best examples of determinations are those shown by the Lord and His associates, for they fully reveal the components that constitute sankalpas.

At the twilight of Krsna’s descent to earth, all demons, along with their military might and divisions of soldiers, had been destroyed. Only Krsna’s own family, the Yadavas, were left as the greatest power in Yudhisthira Maharaja’s empire. However, the unchecked power of Krsna’s kin was a cause of concern for the Lord, for no force could defeat them—the sole military burden on the planet. Krsna thought,

**“If they turn against each other and, like a fire created from the friction of bamboo in a grove, annihilate each other, then My purpose would be achieved and I can return to My abode.”**

Sukadeva Gosvami then describes Krsna’s sankalpato initiate a quarrel between the Yadus:

*evam vyavasito rajan*  
*satya-sankalpa isvarah*  
*sapa-vyajena vipranam*  
*sanjahre sva-kulam vibhuh*

**“My dear King Pariksit! When the supreme almighty Lord, whose desire always comes to pass, had thus made up His mind, He withdrew His own family on the pretext of a curse spoken by an assembly of brahmanas.”**

This is an example of the satya-sankalpa isvarah,the Lord of Absolute Determination, making a sankalpa.Here we note that Krsna’s sankalpahas:

**A clear goal, the means to attain it, and knowledge of where that goal leads: to peace on earth and an accomplished mission.**

A similar sankalpawas made by Krsna some time later when He decided to descend as Caitanya Mahaprabhu in order to better comprehend Radha’s love. As the source of all rasa,Krsna could not understand how Sri Radha was able to give Him endless plea sure, what the qualities in Him were that gave Her pleasure, or what the actual bliss was that She savoured from Their exchange.

For these reasons Krsna decided to appear on earth again, but this time with a different form and mood:

*radha-bhava angikari’ dhari’ tara varna*  
*tina-sukha asvadite haba avatirna*

**“Therefore, assuming Srimati Radharani’s sentiments and bodily complexion, I shall descend to fulfil these three desires.”**

Again, we see that this sankalpahas all three determining attributes. Krsna is very consistent!

\* \* \* \*

In the Preface we mentioned that this book took inspiration from Sanatana Gosvami’s Brhad-bhagavatamrta.Therein we were particularly stirred by Gopa-kumara’s repeated determinations to attain a higher and higher perfection through the medium of his Gopala mantra. Yet the success of the young boy’s aspirations were not solely his own: his mantratoo would be the instrument of his success.

On their second meeting, his spiritual master thus encouraged Gopa-kumara to chant attentively, saying, yad yat sankalpya bho nijam mantram japisyasi:

**“Whatever you desire \[sankalpa\] while chanting your mantra,by its power you will fully achieve.”**

And so it was! Until this stage in his journey, Gopa-kumara’s chanting had transformed his life and made him king of a southern city without his being aware of it. But after meeting his guru in Puri, he understood the power of his mantra.By chanting with increased and focused determinations, he became king of Puri, then an Indra in heaven, a member of the Prajapatis in Maharloka, an associate of the Kumaras in Tapaloka, a Brahma in Satyaloka, a visitor to the brahmajyoti,a guest of the various Vaikuntha regions, and finally a brother to Sridama in Goloka Vrndavana.

Readers may lose their breath reading the sentence above. We loo were breathless contemplating the power of Gopa-kumara’s determined chanting, which pointed to an urgency in our personal chanting of the Hare Krsna mantraand other diksa-mantras.

Through his story’s hero, Sanatana Gosvami modelled the pilgrim’s journey for all pure Vaisnavas. And however that journey plays out for us, we cannot help but be moved by the great acarya’s pronouncement. Loud and clear, he proclaims that we can expect to go hack to Godhead only when we have a clearly defined goal to our sadhana,and when we take systematic steps towards that goal with sankalpasmade gainful by faithful nama-sankirtana.Thus Gopa-kumara is an ideal example for this book, Sankalpa-kaumudi. Readers who are not acquainted with Brhad-bhagavatamrtaand who are serious about their life’s goal are hereby advised to study Gopa-kumara’s journey and his sankalpas.

As a further comment, after reading and studying Brhad-bhagavatamrta many times, we would like to add that the Bhakti- vedanta Book Trust publication of His Grace Gopiparanadhana Prabhu’s rendition of this classic is a gold standard not even remotely approached by any other edition of the book.

Another example from the Srimad-Bhagavatamexemplifies a successful sankalpain devotional service, but for the wrong goal.

At the age of five, Dhruva Maharaja was offended by his father, and in a childish way demanded a kingdom to surpass that of his forefathers, including Lord Brahma. Fortunately for him, Dhruva was of aristocratic stock, and so had an unfailing determination enabling him to live alone in the jungle absorbed in austerity and mantra-japa.Thus, within the space of six months, Dhruva attracted the attention of the Lord and received the Pole Star as his eternal residence.

But when the Lord disappeared and Dhruva became the destined master of both the earth and the Pole Star, the boy was sorrowful Sukadeva Gosvami says,

*so ’pi sankalpajam visnoh*  
*pada-sevopasaditam prapya*  
*sankalpa-nirvanam*  
*natiprito 'bhyagat puram*

**“Despite having achieved the desired result of his determination by worshipping the lotus feet of the Lord, Dhruva Maharaja was not very pleased. Thus he returned to his home.”**

The reader may ask:

**“Why was Dhruva not pleased with such an incredible result?”**

The answer is:

**“Because in addition to his kingdom, Dhruva also received pure devotion from the Lord! Thus, with the perfect vision of an advanced Vaisnava, Dhruva lamented that he had stubbornly employed his touchstone mantrafor a trivial, material goal.”**

Here again we see all the parts of a sankalpaperfectly in place, except for one—Dhruva’s goal. Because the boy’s consciousness was impure, his motive was material, and thus he remains an example of a neophyte devotee who worships Krsna for material pain. Dhruva’s sadhakastatus is confirmed by Rupa Gosvami and Srila Prabhupada. That said, readers should note that after seeing the Lîrd, Dhruva was no longer a practitioner but a pure devotee of the highest calibre.

Dhruva’s example as a sadhakashould be a sobering one, especially in light of the words of Gopa-kumara’s guru:

**“Whatever you desire while chanting your mantra,by its power you will fully achieve.”**

If our desire is impure, we will attain a material goal, not bhava.

The Hare Krsna mantraand our diksa-mantrasare very powerful.

They will fulfil whatever we aspire for in devotional service, be that aspiration material or spiritual.

For example, if a devotee does nama-sankirtanawhile meditating on sensual enjoyment, desiring within his heart the opulence of the demigods, his mantramay well elevate him to heaven to enjoy along with its denizens. Such a result is far from the goal of a pure devotee.

Reader be warned!

Another example that a devotee should not emulate, but rather learn from, is that of Chota Haridasa.

For the offence of gazing lustfully at a woman, Lord Caitanya banned the renunciate from His association. Unable to placate the

Lord for a whole year, Chota Haridasa was determined that life without Caitanya Mahaprabhu was useless, and so he committed suicide by drowning. And while he attained an angelic body in which at night he sang for the Lord, Srila Prabhupada considered this scriptural atonement too extreme for the current time. Instead, His Divine Grace proposed that atonement be attained by the power of determination in devotional service. He would quote Lord Krsna’s words:

*ksipram bhavati dharmatma*  
*sasvac-chantim nigacchati*  
*kaunteya pratijanihi*  
*na me bhaktah pranasyati*

**“He \[the devotee who has sinned but who is humbly repentant\] quickly becomes righteous and attains lasting peace. Î son of Kunti, declare it boldly that My devotee never perishes.”**

Still, Chota Haridasa remains an example of how resolute a prat tising devotee should be in his sankalpa.Dhruva is an example of determination for a material goal; Chota Haridasa is an example of determination for bhava.

The last scriptural example is Maharaja Citraketu. We start with the time before he attained perfection in sadhana,when Narada was instructing him on the process of devotional service. The king and was beside himself with grief when rsisNarada and Angira appeared.

When the king was calm and ready for spiritual guidance Narada initiated him with a mantra.After chanting the mantra with the proper sankalpa,like Gopa-kumara, Maharaja Citraketu attained perfection, but unlike the boy, the king did so very quickly.

This example is therefore given to show that nama-sankirtana, when chanted with the right determination, can give fast results to the qualified sadhaka.The following verse depicts the king’s initiation and the swift timeline with which he was promised perfection:

*sri-narada uvaca*  
*etam mantropanisadam*  
*praticcha prayato mama*  
*yam dharayan sapta-ratrad*  
*drasta sankarsanam vibhum*

**“The great sage Narada continued: ‘My dear King! Attentively receive from me a mantra,which is most auspicious. After accepting it from me, in seven nights you will be able to see the Lord face to face.’”**

Sukadeva Gosvami continues to describe the detachment and other devotional practices taught to the king by Narada. He then reassures us that Narada’s words did come true, and that after a week and a few days Maharaja Citraketu attained the lotus feet of Anantadeva. This is an example of how one with faith in the words of one’s guruand in the sadhanahe prescribes quickly reaps the fruit of determination.

\* \* \* \*

We now move on to some examples of sankalpasexhibited by our acaryas,beginning with Lord Brahma.

After describing to Vidura the nine different natural creations and the tenth, the demigods, Maitreya goes on to explain how time overlaps these creations from the atom to the creator. But before explaining the workings of time, the wise friend of Vyasa comments,

*atah param pravaksyami*  
*vamsan manvantarani ca*  
*evam rajah-plutah srasta*  
*kalpadisv atmabhur harih*  
*srjaty amogha-sankalpa*  
*atmaivatmanam atmana*

**“Now I shall describe the descendants of the Manus. The creator, Brahma, as the incarnation of the passion mode of the Personality of Godhead, creates the universal affairs with unfailing desires in every millennium by the force of the Lord’s energy.”**

In this verse Brahma is described as having amogha-sankalpa, unfailing desires, or an unfailing determination to create. What is especially interesting about Brahma’s creative service is that he repeats the process of creation almost fourty-thousand times during his life. The conditioned mind may find such responsibility too repetitive to be interesting, but not Brahma. The word amogha also means spotless, invincible, and infallible. In addition to always remaining enthusiastic in recreating the universe, Brahma does it well, without rival and to completion.

Therefore, although a devotee may sometimes feel disheartened by the repeated attempts needed to succeed in a determination, or in the difficulties posed in moving on to the next, he should take heart from the example of our creator. In the way that Brahma receives empowerment from the Lord, so too does a sincere devo tee. Krsna’s own words confirm:

**“But those who always worship Me with exclusive devotion, meditating on My transcendental form—to them I carry what they lack, and I preserve what they have.”**

Let us move to a more current time and a more immediate predecessor, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura.

As a young man, the acaryatook a vow to chant one billion names at the rate of one hundred and ninety-two rounds a day. His purpose was to attain the purity and empowerment needed to fulfil Lord Caitanya’s prophecy of taking Krsna’s holy names all over the world.

While this was a one-off sankalpa,Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura had to dedicate almost ten years to its completion. This example provides inspiration for a devotee to remain fixed in the order of the Lord and in the inevitable efforts required to bring that order to fruition.

In this regard, Rupa Gosvami gives us six important qualities to cultivate that are as relevant to sankalpaas they are to sadhanain general. Of the six, we should especially keep in mind patience:

*utsāhān niścayād dhairyāt*  
*tat-tat-karma-pravartanāt*  
*saṅga-tyāgāt sato vṛtteḥ*  
*ṣaḍbhir bhaktiḥ prasidhyati*

**“There are six principles favourable to the execution of pure devotional service: being enthusiastic, endeavouring with confidence, being patient, acting according to regulative principles \[such as sravanam kirtanam visnoh smaranam— hearing, chanting, and remembering Krsna\], abandoning the association of non-devotees, and following in the footsteps of the previous deary as. These six principles undoubtedly assure the complete success of pure devotional service.”**

Contemplating Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura’s example, we can see how our parama-guruperfectly embodied these principles for the attainment of his goal.

Following in the footsteps of his spiritual master, Srila Prabhupada displayed those same qualities in fulfilling the order given to him, namely to take Krsna consciousness throughout the English speaking world. Although spiritually fulfilled living in Vrndavana, Srila Prabhupada ventured to a strange land, and in the space of twelve years empowered those who knew nothing of bhakti-yoga to help him in a global effort that continues to this day.

Srila Prabhupada’s father called him Abhay Charan, and in his sankalpato realise the disciplic succession’s will, Srila Prabhupada showed—among other qualities—absolute fearlessness, abhaya.

Devotees often find that the path to loving devotion is fraught with daunting circumstances. We may therefore take inspiration from Srila Prabhupada, who came to the West alone, and from Brahma, who was tasked with his service while being the only living entity in the universe. They were both on a lonely mission!

There were many individual steps to the fulfilment of Srila Prabhupada’s goal of a worldwide Krsna consciousness movement. One was his taking sannyasain 1959. It was a decision prompted by multiple dreams in which Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura was calling him towards renunciation. Srila Prabhupada’s preaching would be incomplete without sannyasa.He said,

**“My godbrother insisted to me, ‘Bhaktivedanta Prabhu, you must do it. Without accepting the renounced order of life, nobody can become a preacher.’”**

There were other, more worldly challenges to Srila Prabhupada’s venture; getting passage aboard the Jaladuta, acquiring a passport, and receiving government clearance to travel were just some. Each required a determined effort, and each brought Srila Prabhupada closer to the West.

And then there was the adventure across the Atlantic, in wich Srila Prabhupada had to face heart attacks without any medical assistance. But in what appeared to be Srila Prabhupada’s darkest hour, Krsna came to reassure him of success on his journey, and in its purpose.

A final example was Srila Prabhupada’s daily regimen of rising at one in the morning to translate and comment on Srimad-Bhagavatam,a cornerstone of his mission in giving the world the means for self-realisation.

These are but some of the sankalpasthat Srila Prabhupada took to realise the overarching and very difficult determination to do justice to Lord Caitanya’s prediction that Krsna’s name would resound throughout the world:

*prthivite ache yata nagaradi grama*  
*sarvatra pracara haibe mora nama*

**“In every town and village, the chanting of My name will be heard.”**

And that prediction has now come to pass through the medium of Srila Prabhupada and the grace of the Lord. As Prabhupada narrated in 1968:

**“On the first day of my sannyasaI never thought... But I remembered that I’ll have to speak in English. I remember on that sannyasaday when there was a reception. So I first of all spoke in English. So it is all arrangement of Krsna, higher authority.”**

While not in the category of the acaryasmentioned above, Jayananda Prabhu is certainly regarded by members of ISKCON as a saint. Srila Prabhupada requested his disappearance to be marked on the Vaisnava calendar, and that his picture be on Ratha-yatra carts when they roll through the cities of the world. These accolades speak for themselves.

And while Jayananda Prablu is remembered primarily for his dedication to realising Ratha-yatra, there is another example that we would like to share in order to highlight his sankalpa.

Jayananda was diagnosed with leukaemia and passed away in 1977, while Srila Prabhupada was still present on the planet. He had vowed that he did not want to take medication that would in mv way dull his consciousness and obstruct his ability to remember Krsna. And he was in great pain, pain that increased as his condition deteriorated. Still he refused medication until the last. That was an example of resolute determination which today may he considered extreme, but which in another way may be no less dun the willpower required of us to attain *vraja-bhava.*

\* \* \* \*

Let us move to some examples of sankalpas with which a devotee enhances his qualification for bhakti, and with which he progresses in sadhana. This section and the next are an application of Narada’s instructions to Yudhisthira Maharaja that specifically discuss the results of different determinations.

After the great sage recounted the history of Prahlada Maharaja and Nrsimhadeva, he described in detail the principles of varnasrama-dharma.At the conclusion of his teachings, Narada gave a list of determinations and the enhanced character and conduct to which they raise members of a divine society. An example of his instructions on sankalpais the following:

*asankalpaj jayet kamam*  
*krodham kama-vivarjanat*  
*arthanartheksaya lobham*  
*bhayam tattvavamarsanat*

**“By making plans with determination, one should give up lusty desires for sense gratification. Similarly, by giving up envy one should conquer anger, by discussing the disadvantages of accumulating wealth one should give up greed, and by discussing the truth one should give up fear.”**

We have adapted the teachings of the above verse and those that follow it to mirror a devotee’s journey along the progressive path of sadhana-bhakti.In this way we highlight the sankalpasof a sadhakaand the results he can expect from them, based on the lessons given by the professor of devotional service, Narada Muni The first sankalpais when one comes in contact with scrip tures and makes even the most casual effort to read them. That reading or discussion of the teachings of Bhagavad-gitaand Srimad-Bhagavatamawakens in a person feelings of satisfaction and happiness. For the first time in countless lives a jivais finally in touch with the truth, the Absolute Truth. In Krsna’s words, devotees,

**“Derive great satisfaction and bliss from always enlightening one another and conversing about Me.”**

The second sankalpais when a neophyte contemplates, and perhaps discusses with others, what is reality and what is illusion, how he is not this body, and how he has been entangled. As a result of this little effort, a beginner feels himself fearless even in the face of maya.This topic was wonderfully explained in the far distant past by Sri Kavi to Maharaja Nimi in this famous verse:

*bhayam dvitiyabhinivesatah syad*  
*isad apetasya viparyayo ’smrtih*  
*tan-mayayato budha abhajet tam*  
*bhaktyaikayesam guru-devatatma*

**“Fear arises when a living entity misidentifies himself as the material body because of absorption in the external, illusory energy of the Lord. When the living entity thus turns away from the Supreme Lord, he also forgets his own constitutional position as a servant of the Lord. This bewildering, fearful condition is effected by the potency for illusion, called maya.Therefore, an intelligent person should engage unflinchingly in the unalloyed devotional service of the Lord under the guidance of a bona fide spiritual master, wlmm he should accept as his worshipable deity and as his very life and soul.”**

Of course, to be fully fearless a devotee must be fully liberated from all bodily connection. But transcendental knowledge is so empowering that even theoretical understanding makes one bold enough to turn away from further sense gratification and begin sadhana-bhakti.

Commitment to such spiritual discussion is further exemplified by regular attendance in Srimad-Bhagavatamclass, in which a devotee recognises that it is not he, but Krsna Who is the enjoyer and proprietor—the only one. By embracing this truth, a devotee sets out on the path to conquering all lamentation and illusion.

At this stage, a novice becomes conscious of the constraints on Ins devotions caused by past bad habits, and seeks to free himself from the reactions to pious and impious deeds. This is the third sankalpa. One such bad habit is greed; the sadhanafor this impiety is to systematically hear the disadvantages of accumulating wealth, and the sadhyais that covetousness gradually dissipates.

But bhaktiis about more than passive hearing. It is about active service. In the association of Vaisnavas, one realises that pride in wealth, learning, social status, and physical beauty reinforce those same bad qualities that obstruct spiritual advancement. In her prayers to Lord Krsna, Queen Kunti elaborates on this spiritual development:

*janmaisvarya-sruta-sribhir*  
*edhamana-madah puman*  
*naivarhaty abhidhatum vai*  
*tvam akincana-gocaram*

**“My Lord, Your Lordship can easily be approached, but only by those who are materially exhausted. One who is on the path of \[material\] progress, trying to improve himself with respectable parentage, great opulence, high education and bodily beauty, cannot approach You with sincere feeling.”**

A devotee thus vows to overcome conceit by offering respect to and serving all living entities according to their position. Among those living entities, a devotee should specifically worship and serve a great devotee who exhibits all the traits of humility. To surrender to a spiritual master is the fourth sankalpa,and a result of surrendering to a saint is that the servant assumes the quality of the master.

Until now we have described four sankalpas.For the rest of this chapter we shall avoid the numbering and leave it to the reader to discern each successive determination.

A devotee new to Krsna consciousness knows that the fossilised desires for sense gratification are very difficult to wear away. And without sankalpasfor doing so, material desires remain an obstruction to all aspects of sadhana.To this problem Narada gives a very pragmatic solution, one which today’s lifestyle and leadership guruswould no doubt praise. The great sage says, asankalpaj jayet kamam:

**“By making plans with determination, one should give up lusty desires for sense gratification.”**

In his commentary, Srila Prabhupada quotes Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s insightful gloss on Narada’s counsel. He writes,

**“One cannot give up thinking of women, for thinking in this way is natural; even while walking on the street, one will see so many women. However, if one is determined not to live with a woman, even while seeing a woman he will not become lusty. If one is determined not to have sex, he can automatically conquer lusty desires. The example given in this regard is that even if one is hungry, if on a particular day he is determined to observe fasting, he can naturally conquer the disturbances of hunger and thirst.”**

If we follow the reasoning of Cakravarti Thakura, we see that a devotee can quickly reach the goal of giving up active engagement in sense gratification by making the appropriate plans to do so, even while the vestiges of desires linger in the heart. This is quite a significant sankalpa,one which we shall explore further on in the chapter.

Being determined to be in full control of one’s senses is the underlying purpose of iskcon’s regulative principles. This attainment itself becomes the sankalpafor another goal, which is to control the tendency to envy others. Unfortunately, all conditioned souls have this propensity, for it is a primary cause of their fall to the material world. And if envy dominates a devotee’s conduct, it leads to offending Vaisnavas, which is the most serious obstruction to progressive sadhana.

A practitioner who has determined to observe only good qualities in others and who ignores their apparent faults will also gradualló conquer anger, which is the third gate leading to darkness.

Following freedom from envy, the next sankalpais a Vaisnava’s commitment to good behaviour.

Conduct befitting a Vaisnava means not just following the regulative principles, but simultaneously cultivating both the twenty-one qualities of a human being and the twenty-six qualities of a Vaisnava. This dedication to goodness in thought, word, and deed invokes a life of goodness and bestows freedom from the sufferings imposed by other living entities. Such a determination is the fulfilment of the maxim,

**“Do unto others as you would have them do unto you.”**

This golden rule is based on Jesus’ teachings on the Mount in which he said, “All things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them.” While the source is not a Vaisnava scripture, the teaching is certainly universal in its scope.

The next section elaborates further on this topic.

\* \* \* \*

Sufferings that obstruct living entities and thus their devotional practice are of three types, *adhibhautika*, *adhidaivika*, and *adhyatmika*:

**Those arising in the course of everyday social intercourse; those brought about by the environment; and those caused by our bodies and minds, respectively.**

To one degree or another, these troubles are inevitable in the mate rial world. Still, a sadhakamust make lifestyle choices that mini mise disturbances and thereby avoid the unnecessary challenges these obstructions pose. Liberated souls also conduct themselves in that way. The prose of the Bhagavatamsays,

*kvacic ca sita-vatady-anekadhidaivika-bhautikatmiyanam*  
*dasanam pratinivarane ’kalpo duranta-cintaya visanna aste*

**“Being unable to protect himself from the threefold miseries of material existence, the conditioned soul becomes very morose and lives a life of lamentation. These threefold miseries are miseries suffered by mental calamity at the hands of the demigods \[such as freezing wind and scorching heath miseries offered by other living entities, and miseries arising from the mind and body themselves.”**

Determination for good behaviour and freedom from envy of others helps counteract the sufferings that others impose upon us, adhibhautika.An underlying principle of devotional service is that Krsna is present within all within all beings, and so a wise person offers respect to all manner of living entities according to their station. The result is that Krsna, Who resides in the hearts of every living entity, reciprocates with the well-mannered. While speaking of varnasrama,Krsna says,

*samuddharanti ye vipram*  
*sidantam mat-parayanam*  
*tan uddharisye na cirad*  
*apadbhyo naur ivarnavat*

**“Just as a ship rescues those who have fallen into the ocean, similarly, I very quickly rescue from all calamities those persons who uplift brahmanasand devotees who are in a suffering condition.”**

Similarly, the hardships imposed upon a person by the demigods through the environment, adhidaivika,can be both mitigated and tolerated by the strength of a devotee’s nama-sankirtana.By being resolutely absorbed in the sacrifice prescribed for this age, the demigods are appeased, and they look favourably upon a sadhaka. Krsna confirms this in the verse beginning with istan bhogan hi vo deva:

**“In charge of the various necessities of life, the demigods, being satisfied by the performance of yajna \[sacrifice\], will supply all necessities to you.”**

The third and last trouble to beset a devotee arises from his own body and mind. Readers can no doubt attest to the obstacles that their gross and subtle bodies place in the way of devotional progress. The Srimad-Bhagavatamemphasises that in the age of Kali, people are especially disturbed. This relentless anxiety, coupled with bad dietary habits and intense harassment from the other two troubles, klesas,are the source of untold physical, emotional, and mental problems. The World Health Organisation reports that despite unprecedented medical advances, the overall physical health of the global population is decreasing, while mental illness is almost uncontrollably and alarmingly increasing.

While devotional service, bhakti-yoga,is itself not effected by any material impediments, unfortunately the conditioned souls who practise bhakti-yogaare. Both Narada Muni and Srila Prabhupada recommend, by way of prevention as well as remedy, the practice of “mystic hatha-yoga.”

Breathing exercises and meditation are certainly effective. However, we should keep in mind both the lifestyle and dietary habits of hatha-yogis,for these two factors make their yogapractices effective.

So while, in today’s world, and especially for the working population, it may not be practical to retire to the forest and subsist on fruits and roots, it is practical to withdraw from an excessively passionate lifestyle and observe a mostly violence-free diet.

When a devotee makes a determination for such a life, then he can be assured that the inconveniences of his physical body are but the vestiges of his karma,arranged by Krsna as hurdles to be crossed over on the path to a trouble-free life, a vaikunthalife. Krsna’s assurance that such a sankalpatruly ends in the targeted attainment is spoken of by Lord Brahma, and is a verse well known to serious sadhakas:

*tat te ’nukampam su-samiksamano*  
*bhunjana evatma-krtam vipakam*  
*hrd-vag-vapurbhir vidadhan namas te*  
*jiveta yo mukti-pade sa daya-bhak*

**“My dear Lord, one who earnestly waits for You to bestow Your causeless mercy upon him, all the while patiently suffering the reactions of his past misdeeds and offering You respectful obeisances with his heart, words, and body, is surely eligible for liberation, for it has become his rightful claim.”**

Finally, one overarching determination—highly recommended by saints and yet perhaps least accepted by sadhakasin a close-knit social milieu—is the principle of mauna,silence. It is said that by keeping silent, one can avoid all three klesason the path of bhakti-yoga—adbyatmika, adhibhautika,and adhidaivika.

For a Vaisnava, silence means avoiding prajalpa,or speech that denigrates others, especially other devotees. Rupa Gosvami says that such language is born of envy, jealousy, and pride, and is a major impediment on the path of spiritual growth. The resulting impediment will be Vaisnava aparadha,of which no more need be said. Lord Krsna therefore advises the wise practitioner to make and keep to a sankalpaof silence, or an austerity of speech:

*anudvega-karam vakyam*  
*satyam priya-hitam ca yat*  
*svadhyayabhyasanam caiva*  
*van-mayam tapa ucyate*

**“Austerity of speech consists in speaking words that are truthful, pleasing, beneficial, and not agitating to others, and also in regularly reciting Vedic literature.”**

A practitioner would do well to heed the Lord’s advice and adopt vaisnava mauna.To avoid offensive speech, Krsna has given four pro-active practices to embed in our sadhana—speak truthfully, speak in a pleasing way, speak words that are beneficial, and regularly read scripture. Such positive conduct will elicit a spiritual taste much superior to the bitter taste of criticism and gossip.

As a final comment to this section, we should emphasise that avoiding the inconveniences of material existence should never be the motivation for nama-sankirtana,or bhaktiin general. The fundamental definition of pure devotional service is one that shuns the quest for liberation, or even the desire to be freed of the inconveniences of material life. Thus the motivation for devotional service should be for self-purification and for the pleasure of the Lord, not to be freed from suffering. Thus, as the verse beginning with tat te ’nukampamexplains, a devotee accepts all disturbances as Krsna’s mercy, while living in a way that is in harmony with the demigods, other living entities, and his very self. Why? Because he knows that this is the most trouble-free path of sadhana.

Thus concludes our study of Narada Muni’s teachings on sankalpasas they apply to the advancement of a sadhaka.We continue our review of sankalpasin the following chapter.

## Chapter Seventeen

**Specific Examples of Sankalpas**

The previous chapter was dedicated to scriptural examples of sankalpas: sankalpasof acaryas, sankalpasthat enhance qualification for bhakti,and sankalpasto minimise disturbances. This chapter is dedicated to examples of sankalpain pure devotional service.

To preface, an important aspect of devotional service is the foundation upon which it is built; in other words the modes of nature in which bhaktiis practised. A learned devotee knows all too well that devotion in the lower modes is not as conducive to perfection as that in goodness. Indeed, spiritual authorities recommend that a practitioner rise to the mode of goodness by cultivating those things that are in goodness, for in that mode spiritual practices become second nature. Krsna explains:

*sattvikany eva seveta*  
*puman sattva-vivrddhaye*  
*tato dharmas tato jnanam*  
*yavat smrtir apohanam*

**“Until one revives one’s direct knowledge of the spirit soul and drives away the illusory identification with the material body and mind caused by the three modes of nature, one must cultivate those things in the mode of goodness. By increasing the mode of goodness, one automatically can understand and practise religious principles, and by such practice transcendental knowledge is awakened.”**

The whole idea is that by fostering the things that are in goodness, a devotee can overcome his passionate and ignorant habits, and then by cultivating practices of transcendental goodness, he eventually overcomes material goodness. It is interesting to note that the sadhanaof simulating the things in goodness to invoke goodness is similar to the sadhanaof simulating the things in transcendence to invoke bhava.

Obviously, a devotee must study well the characteristics of goodness and make a firm resolve to practise them. While many of these determinations are included in the activities of sadhana,many are not. If a sadhakamakes a sankalpato rise to goodness, then he must ensure that he cultivates all the things in goodness that are both inside and outside the immediate sphere of sadhana.An example of the latter is a vow for cleanliness at all times and in all places—not just on the altar during arati.

When in time the practice of goodness becomes spontaneous, then one becomes situated in goodness, bad habits are eradicated, sadhanabecomes all the easier, one is fixed in devotion, and—with the right association—bbavaquickly arises.

The sankalpasto cultivate goodness are important in order that a devotee acquires a clear idea of the science of sadhana-bhakti, for that enlightenment will also guide him to the transcendental platform.

We should reiterate here Krsna’s warning to be alert when goodness becomes dominant in a devotee’s life, as one may, at that time, become attracted to the material happiness which that mode affords. The Lord explains this clearly:

*tatra sattvam nirmalatvat*  
*prakasakam anamayam*  
*sukha-sangena badhnati*  
*jnana-sangena canagha*

**“O sinless one, the mode of goodness, being purer than the others, is illuminating, and it frees one from all sinful reactions. Those situated in that mode become conditioned by a sense of happiness and knowledge.”**

In other words, there is a danger when a devotee makes his initial sankalpas,as a result of which his sufferings are diminished and he acquires a semblance of devotional steadiness. The danger is that at that point, due to distractions—such as the obligations of household life—a devotee becomes complacent and does not make the further sankalpasneeded to progress towards bhava.Even the sadhyasof sankalpashave their hazards!

But Narada gives us a fast-track summary of how devotees can ascend through and overcome the influence of the modes. He says, etat sarvam gurau bhaktya puruso hy anjasa jayet:

**“Faithfully serve the spiritual master.”**

This does not mean that a devotee need not make the effort to practise sadhana,study sastra,and make systematic determinations. Those things, as we learned from the example of service to Srila Prabhupada, are all part and parcel of service to the spiritual master.

Let us now move on to the examples of sankalpasin bhakti.

Lord Krsna explains that four kinds of people make the initial step to become devotees—albeit not pure devotees. These are the distressed, those searching after wealth, the inquisitive, and those striving for transcendental knowledge. To come to the path of sadhana,in their own way and for their own reasons, these four all make their first sankalpas.

After that initial commitment, and following Rupa Gosvami’s instruction comes guru-padasraya,that the practitioner may accept a guru. In the context of a global institution, that means accepting guidance of senior devotees, which is then followed by accepting a diksa-guru—hopefully one who not just initiates, but one who also systematically instructs his followers.

The sankalpaof accepting an initiator is one of the best-known determinations. iskcon today has provided an excellent education through its Guru-Disciple Course, which truly educates and guides an aspirant in the sankalpaof accepting a guru.A devotee may take note that the quality education behind making this one sankalpais indicative of how well he should educate himself in successfully making other sankalpas.Vows are not acts of whimsy!

Examples of whimsical vows can he seen in Arjuna, when once, upon hearing of his son’s death, and on another occasion on hearing the complaint of a brahmana,he vowed to achieve his goal, or otherwise immolate himself. Although ultimately Krsna helped His friend achieve his purpose, when the dust had settled the Lord chastised Arjuna for making such hasty and extreme vows. This is one rare example in which we should not follow Arjuna.

The sankalpaof accepting an initiator is followed by the actual act of initiation, in which a devotee publicly pronounces both his vow to follow the four regulative principles and to daily chant a minimum of sixteen rounds of the maha-mantra.

The sankalpaof the initiation ceremony is instructive in many ways, which we shall review later in this chapter. And while other steps in devotion are more private and not as generic to all devotees, individualised sankalpasdeserve a similar declaration and a similar clarity of purpose.

Readers may reflect on the different steps that a sadhakatakes in moving from sraddhato asakti.Each successive step requires a concerted effort, which necessitates clear definition and the fulfilment of consistent necessaries. Additionally, there are similar steps within each stage, such as those required to go from anisia-bhajana-kriyato nistha-bhajana-kriya,or from taste dependent on the excellence of devotion to taste that is independent of the same. To elaborate on all these would take a book in itself, so while being attentive to not over-extend the size of this chapter, we shall, in the next section, give a few examples of these sadhana-sankalpas.

\* \* \* \*

Let us begin this section with devotional activities that we may take for granted, and which are very clear examples of sankalpasin devotional service. From there we shall look at examples in more advanced devotion, examples that are built on the foundation of solid, regulated practice.

Srila Prabhupada repeatedly and emphatically instructed his followers that they should chant a “minimum” of sixteen rounds a day. This means an initiate is duty-bound to chant sixteen rounds, and he could chant more. So when a devotee either occasionally or regularly vows to chant extra rounds, he has taken a serious sankalpa,one that Srila Prabhupada would no doubt approve of. Over many years we have experienced that Srila Prabhupada’s initiates and subsequent followers rarely exceed chanting sixteen rounds, and some—or perhaps more than some—even neglect to follow the vow of sixteen. But that is another story.

Readers may consider that in addition to accepting vows that are obligatory, they also accept vows that are:

Voluntary, public or private, essential or optional, general or personalised.

An example of voluntary sankalpasare those that a devotee makes for reading. These are not part of obligatory vows for initiation, but are certainly part of commitments that Srila Prabhupada expected his followers to make in order to perfect the process of bhakti-yoga.

There are many good examples in iskcon today of devotees reading Srila Prabhupada’s books, and the books of our acaryas.We know of one godbrother who successfully adheres to the vow of reading Srila Prabhupada’s four main books every year. Another godbrother follows a vow to spend the month of Karttika in Vrndavana in a daily six-hour group-reading. And still another reads aloud to guests the entire Srimad-Bhagavatamover the course of a year, every year.

There are other devotees who are extremely studious and who, for the purpose of facilitating proper education in Srila Prabhupada’s teachings, have organised educational institutions in iskcon. This was very much in line with the desires of Srila Prabhupada, who as early as 1966 wrote to the managers of the Radha-Damodara temple in Vrndavana about establishing a school on the temple property:

“Now if your father is agreeable to the proposal, the construction of the buildings can now be taken up and my American disciples are ready to spend for the proposed building of Sri Rupanuga Para Vidya Pitha \[The place where transcendental knowledge is taught in line with the teachings of Rupa Gosvami and his followers\].”

With the availability of such educational facilities, a practitioner may make determinations to better enter the realm of sravanain general, or to fulfil Srila Prabhupada’s other desire, which was that followers qualify for educational degrees like bhakti-sastrior bhakti-vedanta.

Chanting extra rounds and systematically reading Srila Prabhupada’s books are examples of sankalpasthat are dear to His Divine Grace. These determinations certainly fix a devotee in sadhana and quickly propel him to its goal. And as a sadhakabecomes absorbed in these devotional acts, attracted by Krsna’s wonderful earthly pastimes, he naturally wants to hear more about Krsna in Vrndavana.

While this kind of reading may in the beginning just be a preference, it may later become a sankalpa.Wanting to hear about Vrndavana-Krsna will not exclude willingness to hear or speak about other devotional topics, but it certainly includes a commitment to begin spiritual development in the line of vraja-bhakti. Such determination will be most natural with good sadhana.

With the development of taste and attachment, a devotee’s attraction becomes specific, and his determination to hear Krsna’s pastimes equally so. A devotee who is inspired by the principle îf tad-anuragi jananugami—serving Krsna under the guidance of one of His eternal associates—will want to hear about Krsna’s deal devotees; Subala for example. And while such a sadhakamay not make a formal vow, his natural determination may be more effective than any proclamation.

Another example is the focused hearing of a devotee who is enchanted by the service of the maidservants of Srimati Radharani, the manjaris.Such a devotee may avail himself of books like Govinda-lilamrtaor Krsna-bhavanamrta-mahakavya,in which the conjugal rasaof Lord Krsna is dominant. By reading such books, an advanced devotee remains absorbed in thoughts of Krsna, thoughts that are in line with his transcendental aspiration. Because Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s special contribution was to make known conjugal love for Krsna, and because He instructed His followers to write on the subject, we find that there are innumerable books on madhurya-rasain Gaudiya Vaisnava literature. And Srila Prabhupada taught us that the determination to read such literature nurtures a sadhaka’sdevotions. After encouraging serious practitioners to read books like Krsna-bhavanamrta-mahakavya, His Divine Grace writes,

**“Any book of krsna-lila,even this book, Krsna,or our Teachings of Lord Caitanya,is actually solace for devotees feeling separation from Krsna.”**

On the topic of separation, it should be noted that the intensity of such devotional emotion will correspond to the level to which attachment has developed. The more one is in love with Krsna, the more intense will be the feeling of separation from Him. And, as separation intensifies, so too does a devotee’s determination in sadhana.In other words, the pain of separation from Krsna will increasingly inspire a practitioner to hear about and remember how an associate of the Lord serves Him and His favourite consort. This is the basic dynamic that gives rise to natural or spontaneous vows. Part Seven of this book elaborates on this topic in depth.

Rupa Gosvami gives a very interesting vow towards which a sadhakain spontaneous devotion may be inspired. That vow is residence in Vrndavana. In the following verse he invites such a devotee to live in Vraja, which may also be interpreted to mean to live in any place representative of Vraja, like a temple of Krsna, or even in Vraja-consciousness:

*tan-nama-rupa-caritadi-sukirtananu-*  
*smrtyoh kramena rasana-manasi niyojya*  
*tisthan vraje tad-anuragi jananugami*  
*kalam nayed akhilam ity upadesa-saram*

**“The essence of all advice is that one should utilise one’s full time—twenty-four hours a day—in nicely chanting and remembering the Lord’s divine name, transcendental form, qualities, and eternal pastimes, thereby gradually engaging one’s tongue and mind. In this way one should reside in Vraja and serve Krsna under the guidance of devotees. One should follow in the footsteps of the Lord’s beloved devotees, who are deeply attached to His devotional service.”**

In a subsequent verse of the same book, the acaryaadvises a devotee who has actually developed spontaneous love to make a vow of specifically living in Radha-kunda, the most exalted of all holy places. He writes, tadiya-sarasi tam nasrayet:

**“Who will not take shelter of Sri Radha’s divine lake?”**

Once again, this injunction applies to residing by Radha-kunda in Bhauma-Vrndavana, or any facsimile thereof.

In his teachings on raganuga-bhaktiin Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu, Rupa Gosvami reiterates the importance of living in Vraja, and in so doing further names some confidential commitments favourable for the development of raga. These vows are both internal and external, and it is understood that a sadhakais meant to practie both, simultaneously.

Internal vows are meditation on Krsna, selecting and following a vraja-bhakta,and conversing with the like-minded about that eternal associate. External vows are reinforcing the conduct that is characteristic of a regulative devotee. As mentioned above, such an advanced devotee who is inclined to, or who has entered, the realm of spontaneous devotion, should simultaneously follow both internal and external vows.

\* \* \* \*

Let us briefly consider how the two verses paraphrased above would apply to a devotee drawn to natural attraction. The actual slokasare:

**seva sadhaka-rupena**  
**siddha-rupena catra hi**  
**tad-bhava-lipsuna karya**  
**vraja-lokanusaratah**

**“The advanced devotee who is inclined to spontaneous loving service should follow the activities of a particular associate of Krsna’s in Vrndavana. He should execute service externally as a regulative devotee, as well as internally from his self-realised position. Thus he should perform devotional service both externally and internally.”**

*krsnam smaran janam casya*  
*prestham nija-samihitam*  
*tat-tat-katha-ratas casau*  
*kuryad vasam vraje sada*

**“The devotee should always think of Krsna within himself and should choose a very dear devotee who is a servitor of Krsna in Vrndavana. One should constantly engage in topics about that servitor and his loving relationship with Krsna, and one should live in Vrndavana. If one is physically unable to go to Vrndavana, he should mentally live there.”**

The basis for entering spontaneous devotion is to be advanced in regulated devotion and to have an inclination for vraja-bhakti.

An advanced devotee is one who, for a considerable time, has been steadfast in keeping the vows of initiation and in practising the regulative principles of sadhana.This steadfastness could be said to be a marginal characteristic of eligibility, the primary characteristic being the inclination to serve in the way of the Vraja-vasis.

The inclination to obtain ragatmika-bhaktiis an advanced sadhaka’simpetus for raga-bhakti.Srila Prabhupada’s use of the word “inclination” speaks to an interest in or liking for something, and implies that the practitioner does not yet have it. However, by diligently studying Srila Prabhupada’s books, such as Caitanya-caritamrta,an advanced sadhaka’sblossoming attachment will be increasingly inspired by Krsna’s personality and decreasingly by His divinity. In this way, by hearing more and more, natural attraction becomes stronger and more assertive, and in time it becomes fully spontaneous.

This predisposition towards spontaneous devotional service is an aspect of self-realisation wherein a practitioner intellectually understands that being Krsna’s eternal servant means, for him, being a vraja-vasi.This is the foundation of his siddha-rupa.Rupa Gosvami explains that this attraction is primarily intellectual:

*tat-tad-bhavadi-madhurye*  
*srute dhir yad apeksate*  
*natra sastram na yuktim ca*  
*tal lobhotpatti-laksanam*

**“When an advanced, realised devotee hears about the affairs of the devotees of Vrndavana—-in the mellows of santa, dasya, sakhya, vatsalya,and madhurya—he becomes inclined in one of these ways, and his intelligence becomes attracted. Indeed, he begins to covet that particular type of devotion. When such covetousness is awakened, one’s intelligence no longer depends on the instructions of sastraor on logic and argument.”**

The words srute dhirindicate that unless a devotee already has spontaneous attraction from a previous birth, interest in raga-bhaktican be awakened by hearing from an advanced devotee or by studying scripture. In other words, an intelligent devotee will come to the conclusion that spontaneous devotional service is more pleasing to Krsna than regulative service, and that he has to make efforts to cultivate it. After all, this is what is explicitly stated in Srila Prabhupada’s books. For example, in Caitanya-caritamrta we find Krsna thinking in the following way:

*aisvarya-jnanete saba jagat misrita*  
*aisvarya-sithila-preme nahi mora prita*

**“All the universe is filled with the conception of My majesty, but love weakened by that sense of majesty does not satisfy Me.”**

And a little further on in the same passage, Krsna discloses that the purpose of revealing His pastimes to the world was to attract devotees to the practice of raganuga-bhakti:

*vrajera nirmala raga suni bhakta-gana*  
*raga-marge bhaje yena chadi’ dharma-karma*

**“Then, by hearing about the pure love of the residents of Vraja, devotees will worship Me on the path of spontaneous love, abandoning all rituals of religiosity and fruitive activity.”**

This interest in spontaneous devotional service as a function of the intelligence will impel a practitioner to take vows to cultivate spontaneous devotion through hearing and remembering Krsna’s vraja- lilaand vrajaassociates.

At this point we should raise the red flag that Srila Prabhupada so often waved:

**A neophyte to raganuga-bhaktishould not speculate about his relationship with Krsna, nor should he imagine himself as serving Him. This kind of guesswork will only deviate him from his aspiration.**

A sadhakashould be patiently confident that in the way hearing and nama-sankirtanaled to the inclination for spontaneous service, in that way they will also cause maturation of the same.

That said, readers may note that in the previously mentioned verse beginning with seva sadhaka-rupena,Rupa Gosvami advises one who is seriously inclined to raganuga-bhaktito become an avowed follower of an associate of Krsna.

One may ask:

**“How can such a sankalpaauthentically manifest?”**

**“By continued hearing under the guidance of the spiritual master, a devotee will become attracted to one of the live kinds of services to Krsna, and in time those same devotional activities will awaken attraction to one of the associates of whom a** ***sadhaka*** **hears.”**

Readers may note that the way of ragais not to immediately identify as an associate of the Lord, but rather to identify as the follower of an associate, as an aspirant for a certain type of service. In this way, attachment to that kind of identity and service develops, and along with such attachment so, too, absorption develops.

In the verse beginning with krsnam smaran janam casya,Rupa Gosvami further guides a practitioner to another sankalpa,and that sankalpais hearing and speaking about the associate of Krsna whom he follows.

Much more could be written about the vows that Rupa Gosvami advises for the devotee practising raganuga-bhakti.To serve that purpose, the topic of determinations in raga-bhaktithrough the stages of nama-bhajanais described in Part Six of this book. And for further information on the subject of spontaneous devotion in general, readers may refer to the author’s previously published work entited The Awakening of Spontaneous Devotional Service.

\* \* \* \*

Scriptures provide many disciplines through which devotees may purify their consciousness and advance towards transcendence. The acaryaof an institution is duty-bound to select those vows that are most relevant to his followers, as is a spiritual master for his disciples.

For example, based on the principle of guror hitam,or living in the gurukulaonly for the benefit of the guru,Srila Prabhupada directed his followers to Narada Muni’s vow of brahmacarya—for men and women. And Srila Prabhupada’s entreaty to his followers was that they daily participate in either nama-sankirtanaor book distribution.

Currently the membership of the Krsna consciousness movement is spreading mainly within its congregation, the majority of whom rarely adopt the student life or evangelism that Srila Prabhupada prescribed. And while such believers may follow the basic tenets of their faith, without adopting the cultural vows prescribed by the Founder it is questionable whether they have the spiritual foundation or the bountiful grace needed to make trouble-free advancement towards bhava.

A related and important sankalpathat Srila Prabhupada set out for his followers was to adopt the varnasramasocial order upon which iskcon could transit from being solely a church to a broad-based spiritual society. And although most of the duties of asramashave been followed since iskcon’s early days, Srila Prabhupada envisaged that the principles of varnasramawould be adopted to guide all aspects of life, including education, leadership, laws, and members’ social duties—the varnas.

Like the brahmacari asramaand missionary zeal mentioned, this social foundation for sadhakasis suffering from neglect. Even its relevance to iskcon often comes under question, despite Srila Prabhupada’s clear instructions regarding its importance for neophyte devotees. The following excerpt from a well-known conversation is one of many that reflect His Divine Grace’s desire:

Prabhupada: Therefore varnasrama-dharmais required. Simply show-bottle will not do. So the varnasrama- dharmashould be introduced all over the world.

**Satsvarupa: Introduced, starting with ISKCON community?**

**Prabhupada: Yes. Yes. Brahmana, ksatriyas.There must be regular education.**

In his books, His Divine Grace further encouraged his followers to adopt varnasramaas a means to come to, and progress forward in, pure devotional service. He wrote,

**“Therefore, since this sanatana-dharmasystem \[varnasrama\] is eternal, one can elevate himself to the highest standard of spiritual life by following the Vedic principles.”**

In addition to the overarching system of varnasramaare other vows of both varnaand asramathat are optional, although generally regulated by one’s nature.

For example, a brahmacarimay or may not decide to get married, although his superiors and astrological reading may provide a clear vision as to which option would be best for him. However, whether brahmacarior grhastha,a man must follow the dos and don’ts of his asrama,because the proper execution of dharmahelps situate him in goodness, and hence in pure devotion.

Krsna gives the following principle duties for members of the asramas:

**The brahmacarishould serve the spiritual master; the grhasthashould give shelter to others; the vanaprastha should practise austerity; and the sannyasishould teach the other orders.**

And while it is not compulsory for a brahmacarito become a grhasthaor for a grhasthato become a sannyasi,it is compulsory for a grhasthato become a vanaprastha.A serious devotee makes such social commitments as both a way to instruct others and to further his own spiritual journey. And it is important that every sadhakabears in mind that all the vows that he takes must be constructive to the goal of developing and attaining love for Krsna.

Another vow related to the dharmaof a grhasthais one of charity, a vow that is not an ingredient of devotional service but which helps a grhasthaadopt the right mentality for bhakti.As a quality created by Krsna, Srila Prabhupada says that giving in charity is the “main function” of a grhastha.And while one may be charitable in many ways, including opening one’s home to others, the most generic way to be charitable is to give in charity a percentage of one’s income. Srila Prabhupada is quite specific in this regard:

**“To give charity is one of the householder’s main functions, and he should be prepared to give in charity at least fifty percent of his hard-earned money.”**

Once again, the vow of giving in charity is compulsory, but the amount seems to be optional. In the quote above, Srila Prabhupada speaks of giving at least fifty percent of one's earnings, and at other times he encouraged householders to give according to their means. While all giving helps in freeing one from the concept of “I and mine,” donating one’s wealth is perhaps the most practical, as it fulfils all kinds of needs. And while all kinds of charity are beneficial for both the donor and the recipient, charity most conducive for the donor is that which is in the mode of goodness. Krsna describes this kind of giving in the following way:

*datavyam iti yad danam*  
*diyate ’nupakarine*  
*dese kale ca patre ca*  
*tad danam sattvikam smrtam*

**“Charity given out of duty, without expectation of return, at the proper time and place, and to a worthy person is considered to be in the mode of goodness.”**

The Lord’s instructions show that there are different ways to make vows, and according to the mode of nature in which a vow is taken, a different benefit is accrued by the donor. Of all persons or causes to benefit from charity, the best are those that directly serve Krsna, and the best service to the Lord is that which facilitates others’ devotional service to Him.

An example of a charitable cause is building a temple or being one of many donors who builds a temple for the deity of the Lord. Krsna says that depending on the motive, such a donor attains either spiritual perfection or unlimited wealth.

One can just imagine the absorption in Krsna of a person who works to construct a home for the Supreme Lord. Such absorption certainly results in a spiritual pleasure that inspires the donor to render further service and to advance spiritually. Like the example of building a temple, a grhasthadevotee may make sankalpas relating to some project that furthers the mission of the Krsna consciousness movement. Such was Srila Prabhupada’s expectation from his followers.

\* \* \* \*

Having touched upon vows relevant to the varnasramasystem, let us conclude this section by examining a few vows repeatedly recommended in Srimad-Bhagavatam.

One vow is to show respect to all living things. This sankalpa is an aspect of sadhanain which a devotee sees the Supreme Lord in every living entity. While the respect offered to different living beings is shown in different ways, the Lord directs His devotee to show esteem for His presence with all his faculties. He says,

*yavat sarvesu bhutesu*  
*mad-bhavo nopajayate*  
*tavad evam upasita*  
*van-manah-kaya-vrttibhih*

**“Until one has fully developed the ability to see Me within all living beings, one must continue to worship Me by this process \[offering obeisances\] with the activities of his speech, mind, and body.”**

After Krsna liberated them from confinement as trees and transformed them into pure devotees, Nalakuvara and Manigriva also vowed to worship Krsna in all things. Praying to the Lord for the empowerment to do so, the two demigods said,

**“May our heads offer our obeisances to everything within this world, because all things are also Your different forms...”**

Sri Prahlada Maharaja is another example of a devotee who followed this vow.

Another vow in the same vein, though more generic, is to learn to see Krsna not only in animate but also in inanimate things. In the Bhagavad-gita,Krsna gives many examples of how in one sense He is everything—like the taste of water, the light of the sun, the scent of the earth, and so on. Srila Prabhupada would often instruct his disciples on how to adopt this vision in order to easily see Krsna, not Maya, in the world around them.

While this is the sadhanaof jnanis,it is one that a regulated devotee may adopt in order to purify his consciousness. The theme of not seeing things separate from the supreme transcendence is one that permeates Srimad-Bhagavatam,a theme that is recommended as an intellectual determination for a devotee to adopt until that time when he naturally sees Krsna everywhere. That stage of perfection is described by Caitanya Mahaprabhu in this way:

*sthavara-jangama dekhe, na dekhe tara murti*
