It would be hard to imagine that a practising devotee could sustain a resolute determination to progress from one stage of devotion to the next without the encouragement and guidance of Vaisnavas in general, and his spiritual master in particular. The exemplary conduct of other devotees, their subsequent success in spiritual life, and most importantly, Vaisnavas’ guidance to their dependants and peers, are causes for a sadhaka’s sankalpa.Rupa Gosvami summarises this by citing a beautiful verse by Sri Autkala:

*tebhyo namo ‘stu bhava-varidhi-jirna-panka-*  
*sammagna-moksana-vicaksana-padukebhyah*  
*krsneti varna-yugala-sravanena yesam*  
*anandathur bhavati nartita-roma-vrndah*

**“I offer my respectful obeisances to the devotees of the Lord. Simply by hearing the two syllables ‘Krs,’ ‘na,’ their bodily hairs stand up in ecstasy and they are moved to dance in ecstatic bliss. As they dance they mercifully inspire to devotion the fallen souls sunk in the mire at the bottom of the ocean of birth and death.”**

Like sadhu-sanga,the process of sadbana-bbakti—especially chanting Krsna’s holy names and hearing Srimad-Bhagavatam—so cleanses the heart that a devotee spontaneously feels inspired to make the next step in his spiritual journey.

The very nature of bhakti,as attested to by the maxim bhaktya sanjataya bhaktya,is to enrich itself. Therefore, sadhanais itself an impetus to meet newer and newer spiritual challenges.

If, however, a devotee is careless in devotional practices, he will certainly become stagnant in his progress and lose enthusiasm to attain his goal. Thus we sometimes hear a devotee say,

**“I am not one of those who can go back to Godhead in one lifetime.”**

Tî such a Vaisnava we can only reply,

**“Such complacency comes from inattentive chanting, neglecting the study of Srimad-Bhagavatam,and over-familiarity with the material energy. If you correct those faults, you will think otherwise.”**

The wisdom of transcendental knowledge obtained through the association of Vaisnavas and from sadhanaitself is an essential feature of renewed determination for service.

Whenever Gopa-kumara gained knowledge of higher realms, he became determined to attain them. By the agency of his Gopala mantra, he travelled to places like heaven, Janaloka, Tapaloka, and Brahmaloka. Gopa-kumara’s underlying determination was to become Krsna’s friend, and according to his evolving knowledge of that goal, his sankalpastook on increased maturity.

Common sense dictates that knowledge of a goal is essential in order to generate the determined effort required to get there. And so it is with Krsna consciousness. For that reason, Lord Krsna proclaims that transcendental knowledge is the greatest treasure of this world:

*na hi jnanena sadrsam*  
*pavitram iha vidyate*  
*tat svayam yoga-samsiddhah*  
*kalenatmani vindati*

**“In this world, there is nothing so sublime and pure as transcendental knowledge. Such knowledge is the mature fruit of all mysticism. And one who has become accomplished in the practice of devotional service enjoys this knowledge within himself in due course of time.”**

Knowledge effects an increased desire for devotional service within the heart, and that desire is the foundation for progressive sankalpas.

For example, by hearing Krsna’s pastimes a devotee is initially inspired to become His servant, then to enter His divine sports, and eventually to adopt a certain relationship with Him.

Knowledge of the goal is generally accompanied by knowledge of the process of achieving it. For this reason the science of abhidheya jnanahas been extensively addressed in the previous chapter.

\* \* \* \*

The primary responsibility of a spiritual master is to guide his disciple in the techniques of sadhana,which begin with instructions on the meaning of the maha-mantra.Even by mechanically contemplating those meanings, a devotee is empowered to progress in his sadhana,and as he becomes attached to the mantrahis progress becomes more spontaneous. Thus, fidelity to the instructions of the spiritual master is a cause for making a sankalpa.In this regard Srila Narottama Dasa Thakura writes,

*sri-guru-carana-padma, kevala-bhakati-sadma,*  
*bando mui savadhana mate*  
*jahara prasade bhai, e bhava toriya jai,*  
*krsna-prapti hoy jaha ha’te*

**“The lotus feet of my spiritual master are the only way by which one can attain pure devotional service. I bow to his lotus feet with great awe and reverence. By his grace one can cross the ocean of material suffering and obtain the mercy of Krsna.”**

Indeed, so potent is the principle of faith in the instructions of the spiritual master that even though a disciple may not initially have a clear picture of either the goal or the complete sadhanato attain it, by acting out of obligation to guruhis spiritual path is revealed, and his determination to march forward enriched.

Gopa-kumara is a classic example of such a disciple. When first initiated, the boy had no understanding of the purpose of his mantraor how to chant it. But out of respect for the great soul who initiated him, he remained faithful to his sketchy sadhana.As a result, the goal of chanting, the means to attain it, and the determination to do so were all systematically revealed.

This marvel of spiritual life—faith in the spiritual master—reaps its reward in the form of a similar spiritual marvel: the mercy of the spiritual master and the mercy of Vaisnavas.

Srila Prabhupada exquisitely expressed the meaning of guru-krpa with the phrase “your ever well-wisher.” The well-wishes and blessings of the spiritual master ensure that Krsna is quickly responsive to a devotee’s spiritual aspirations. A sadhakameditates daily on this principle during mangala-aratias he sings,

*yasya prasadad bhagavat-prasado*  
*yasyaprasadan na gatih kuto ’pi*

**“By the mercy of the spiritual master one receives the benediction of Krsna. Without the grace of the spiritual master, one cannot make any advancement.”**

The mercy of the spiritual master awakens in the disciple the desire to see Krsna, and the combined appeal of the guru’smercy and the sadhaka’sdetermination induces Krsna to eventually reveal Himself. This is the wonder of close adherence to the disciplic succession. In the words of Sanatana Gosvami,

**“If by the mercy of guruand the Vaisnavas one is eager to see the Supreme Person, nothing can stand in the way of success.”**

While the mercy of guruand the Vaisnavas may come unexpectedly—without cause or qualification—generally a devotee’s state of mind is a governing factor in taking progressive steps in sadhana.

As explained in earlier chapters, the origin of the mind is false ego in goodness, and when the mind is ruled by the mode of goodness, the resulting sankalpais conducive to spiritual life. However, if the mind is overcome by passion or ignorance, vows for spiritual advancement are either impeded by sensuality or brought to a standstill by lethargy.

To ensure that his consciousness is sheltered by goodness and his spiritual desires unfettered, a devotee must be attentive to his sadhanaand must associate with things in the mode of goodness. Then, as Krsna Himself explains, the sadhaka’sdetermination for Krsna consciousness will be spontaneous:

*sattvad dharmo bhaved vrddhat*  
*pumso mad-bhakti-laksanah*  
*sattvikopasaya sattvam*  
*tato dharmah pravartate*

**“When the living entity becomes strongly situated in the mode of goodness, then religious principles, characterised by devotional service to Me, become prominent.**  
**One can strengthen the mode of goodness by cultivation of those things that are already situated in goodness, and thus religious principles arise.”**

Another significant cause for a devotee to make a sankalpais the conviction of success that comes from previous successful sankalpas.In other words, from the power of precedent.

Having experienced that determined chanting of his mantra transported him to heaven, Gopa-kumara was convinced that he would meet with the same success if he chanted to attain Mahar-loka. He did! The successful result of earlier vows inspired Gopa-kumara to further determinations, which ultimately found their rest at Krsna’s lotus feet. That attainment was the promise of his guru:

*yad yat sankalpya bho vatsa*  
*nijam mantram japisyasi*  
*tat-prabhavena tat sarvam*  
*vanchatitam ca setsyati*

**“My dear boy, whatever you desire while chanting your mantra, by its power you will fully achieve. Indeed, you will attain more than you desire.”**

In contrast to a successful precedent as a cause for making vows stands the imposing challenge of the goal itself. The rarity and difficulty of perfecting love of God is also a cause of vows. The very idea of a challenge is the impetus to meet it, and Srila Prabhupada, like Napoleon, did not consider “impossible” as part of his life.

Napoleon Bonaparte said,

**“The word impossible is not in my dictionary.”**

Similarly, Srila Prabhupada said,

**“‘Impossible’ is a word in a fool’s dictionary.”**

While Narada Muni was monitoring Gopa-kumara’s progressive journey to Vaikuntha, he was amazed that a simple cowherd boy could remain so steadfast in his determination for the most difficult ,md most rare of spiritual attainments. The sage had even warned his disciple:

**“My dear boy! How is it that you are so eager to take shelter of the lotus feet of this Gopaladeva and see all those sweet pastimes? Dear brother! You must understand that to attain Him is exceedingly difficult, especially because of the devotional discipline required. Of this I am fully convinced.”**

And yet Gopa-kumara was not deterred by the gravity of his undertaking. Instead, he took the final step from Dvaraka to Vraja as a challenge, a challenge that he successfully met due to his strong desire to serve Krsna as a gopa.

While a devotee may sometimes doubt his ability to achieve his goals, the success of other sadhakaslike Gopa-kumara, Narada, and Dhruva will reassure him that sincere efforts are never thwarted. The maha-mantraand sadhana-bhaktiare all-powerful, and they grant a sincere devotee his desired goal.

Humility is a factor that both causes and nourishes sankalpa. Since the latter is described below and the former is referred to in multiple places throughout this book, we will not elaborate here on how humility is a cause of sankalpa.

Of the many factors that bring about determination in the heart of a devotee, we have described but a few prominent ones. The underlying axiom of “utility is the principle” applies to a devotee’s inspiration to meet the challenges of progressive Krsna conscious ness. This axiom parallels Rupa Gosvami’s own statement, tasmat kenapy upayena manah krsne nivesayet:

**“Somehow or other, one should engage in Krsna consciousness.”**

In other words, a devotee may accept any pure motivation for progress as a valid cause for a sankalpa.

\* \* \* \*

We shall now describe those factors that nurture sankalpa,such as:

Knowledge, faith, attachment, humility, and tastes arising from bhakti.

Devotional service in practice is like building a house one brick at a time. A mason has determination not only to see the house completed, but he also has a recurrent determination with every brick he puts in place. And there are conditions that make the mason’s tiring efforts easier and more fruitful. Similarly, the determination of a sadhakais enhanced by favourable considerations, just as they are hindered by those unfavourable.

Earlier chapters cited Rupa Gosvami’s assertion that a devotee’s advancement in bhaktiis measured by his knowledge of, faith in, and attachment to Krsna. These very factors also nourish the devotee’s determination to progress towards the goal. Krsna gives a wonderful analogy in this regard:

*yatha yathatma parimrjyate ‘sau*  
*mat-punya-gatha-sravanabhidhanaih*  
*tatha tatha pasyati vastu suksmam*  
*caksur yathaivanjana-samprayuktam*

**“When a diseased eye is treated with medicinal ointment, it gradually recovers its power to see. Similarly, as a conscious living entity cleanses himself of material contamination by hearing and chanting the pious narrations of My glories, he regains his ability to see Me, the Absolute Truth, in My subtle spiritual form.”**

As a devotee experiences the enchanting tastes and increasing wonders of devotional service, he becomes progressively knowledgeable, faithful, and attached. These spiritual assets give him strength to advance further.

To make the transition from one stage of devotion to another, a devotee must know how to enhance his practices and why he should do so.

Becoming familiar with the truths of devotion, a practitioner recognises the importance of progressive sadhana.In the words of Suta Gosvami:

*tac chraddadhana munayo*  
*jnana-vairagya-yuktaya*  
*pasyanty atmani catmanam*  
*bhaktya sruta-grhitaya*

**“The seriously inquisitive student or sage, well equipped with knowledge and detachment, realises that Absolute Truth by rendering devotional service in terms of what he has heard from the Vedanta-sruti.”**

Moreover, by hearing of the excellence and sweetness of vraja-bhakti,a spontaneous desire for it will eventually arise within a devotee, and that determination will spur him on to his coveted destination.

Without knowledge of the great importance of sankalpa,and without knowledge of the next stage of advancement, a devotee will hardly be inclined to make the required changes to his sadhana— rejecting and accepting practices as appropriate. Additionally, a devotee must have insight into the mysteries of nama-sankirtana,his primary means of progress. Such insight comes through the guidance of the spiritual masters and, if appropriate, from Krsna within.

The following is an example of how knowledge nurtures deter mination:

In his early days of Krsna consciousness, an aspirant is encouraged to chant Hare Krsna according to his ability, and not much attention is given to the number or quality of rounds. “Just chant Hare Krsna!” is the maxim.

But in time, an aspirant comes to know that Srila Prabhupada required a minimum of sixteen rounds, and that that number is mandatory for initiation. Hearing this, the serious aspirant vows to chant the desired number of rounds.

Perhaps preceding this vow, but certainly subsequent to it, a devotee realises that his chanting must also be free of the ten offences in order to return to Godhead. Knowing this, he makes the next determination to chant offencelessly, a determination he declares publicly at the time of initiation.

In the same way, to reach the stage of prema-sankirtanaand the shelter of Krsna’s lotus feet, the mature devotee must be equipped with knowledge of the process leading there. That will empower him to make the requisite commitments.

Hearing this a reader may enquire:

**“What should a devotee know?”**

The answer to this is:

**“If, in the words of Srimad-Bhagavatam,a practitioner ‘attentively and submissively’ studies Srila Prabhupada’s books, he will know everything that needs to be known.”**

Additionally, if a sadhakareads the books of our acaryas,his knowledge will be further enhanced. That knowledge includes an understanding of the characteristics of the stages of devotion, the truths of devotional service, and the truths relating to Krsna.

Aside from jnana,a devotee must have vijnana,realisation. A devotee must know how to apply transcendental knowledge to his devotional life. That means he must know what stage of bhaktihe is at, how far along that stage he has progressed, what the subsequent stage is, and how he must enhance his devotions to qualify lor the next stage of sadhana.

The reader may note that while a practitioner’s realisation matures in tandem with purification of heart, the sadhakais not excluded from having knowledge of things beyond his level of realisation. How can one journey along his path if he cannot see what is ahead of him?

Although his disciples were mostly neophytes, Srila Prabhupada translated Krsna Bookand Sri Caitanya-caritamrta,both replete with confidential pastimes far beyond contemporary devotees’ advancement or understanding. Still, His Divine Grace thought his followers should know that such pastimes exist. After all, these pastimes are what going back to Godhead means. An endearing example of how Srila Prabhupada sometimes divulged confidential truths is recorded in his biography:

**“Kim’s sister, who was only sixteen, also wanted to get initiated. ‘Are there offences in the spiritual world?’ she asked Prabhupada at one evening lecture. Prabhupada turned to the audience. ‘See?’ he said. ‘This little girl, she wants to go back to Godhead.’ And in the course of the answer, he said, ‘Krsna may kiss you.’ When he said that, Kim’s sister blushed, and everyone laughed.”**

At this point we shall make a further comment in regard to a devotee knowing about subjects beyond his realisation.

Because of Srila Prabhupada’s ample warnings about practising bhaktibeyond one’s attainment, it is routine for devotees to mistakenly call knowing of approved topics beyond one’s attainment sahajiyaism. Such an unfortunate misunderstanding, and its dissemination, are serious obstacles to advancement in Krsna consciousness.

That said, sahajiyaism exists, and the learned sadhakashould be able to recognise it for what it is. Of the many examples that Srila Prabhupada gives of this wayward devotion, the following is very much to the point:

**“One must be so eager that without Krsna consciousness, one should become mad. One should become mad. That is Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s teaching: separation, not direct contact. Direct contact is not possible. Neither that is the way of worshipping by the method of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu. That is sahajiya- vada.T am talking with Krsna. Krsna is snatching my cloth.’ There is a book, one lady has written her experience, that Krsna comes, He talks with her and snatches her cloth. She has written openly. But this is not Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s way.”**

Returning to our theme, inspiration for spiritual progress necessitates that a devotee is aware of what lies ahead in devotional service. And it is the responsibility of the spiritual master to ensure that a devotee’s eyes are wide open, lest he succumb to the pitfalls of the age.

While a young devotee may be excused for having a very general understanding of devotional principles, a decades-old practitioner is not.

For a novice, the goal of practice may be a general “go back to Godhead,” but for a veteran, the goal should be to go back to Goloka Vrndavana and serve Krsna in a specific mellow. Full realisation of Vraja’s mellows may yet be forthcoming, but knowledge of it should be comprehensive.

Both personal wisdom and the guidance of spiritual masters will prevent a devotee from running ahead of himself and entering into forbidden territory. But the risk of misusing transcendental knowledge is not a reason to remain in ignorance. In this oft-cited verse, the Lord describes the rule of thumb in transiting from one stage of bhaktito the next:

*sve sve ’dhikare ya nistha*  
*sa gunah parikirtitah*  
*karmanam jaty-asuddhanam*  
*anena niyamah krtah*  
*guna-dosa-vidhanena*  
*sanganam tyajanecchaya*

**“It is firmly declared that the steady adherence of transcendentalists to their respective spiritual positions constitutes real piety, and that sin occurs when a transcendentalist neglects his prescribed duty. One who adopts this standard of piety and sin, sincerely desiring to give up all past association with sense gratification, is able to subdue materialistic activities, which are by nature impure.”**

By way of example, let us summarise the important role that transcendental knowledge plays in a devotee’s march to perfection.

Although Gopa-kumara was a pure-hearted practitioner, so much so that he was able to directly serve forms of the Lord even as a sadhaka,his progress to vraja-bhaktiwas firmly determined by his level of knowledge. As his knowledge matured, so too did his practices. Thus, the general principle is that the determination to advance in Krsna consciousness corresponds to one’s level of wisdom.

Having said that, it is a fact that faith in one’s mantra,in one’s spiritual master, and in favourable devotional experiences also keep a devotee determined on the path of bhakti.But that determination does not elevate a sadhaka.Rather, it qualifies him to acquire the knowledge by which he can be elevated, while affording him the strength to remain fixed in his practices.

Like knowledge, both faith and attachment nurture progressive devotion, but they too need to be bolstered with a mastery of bhakti.

Gopa-kumara had deep faith in and a natural attraction to Madana-gopala, although he did not quite know who Madana-gopala was. That faith and attraction protected him from distractions, and in tandem with his budding knowledge, helped raise him to the realm of liberation. However, his limited devotion could not give him admittance to Vaikuntha. Therefore, he had to augment the sadhanaof chanting his mantrawith learning the full truths about Krsna from Srimad-Bhagavatam.

\* \* \* \*

We shall now look at how humility stimulates determined sadhana. While sadhana-bhaktirequires meaningful effort, no undertaking, including scriptural study, can be successful without Krsna’s grace. Brahma wonderfully describes this truth in this way:

*atkapi te deva padambuja-dvaya-*  
*prasada-lesanugrhita eva hi*  
*janati tattvam bhagavan-mahimno*  
*na canya eko ’pi ciram vicinvan*

**“My Lord! If one is favoured by even a slight trace of the mercy of Your lotus feet, he can understand the greatness of Your personality. But those who speculate to understand the Supreme Personality of Godhead are unable to know You, even though they continue to study the Vedas for many years.”**

Thus, the inspiration and ability to climb the mountain of bhakti must be nurtured by Krsna’s grace, and a key element by which that grace is attracted is the modest conduct of a devotee, his humility.

Sanatana Gosvami says that humility, more than any other trait, helps a devotee achieve success in loving devotion. Humility, dainya,is the root and most essential support of devotional service, without which a sadhaka,no matter how qualified, cannot attain his desired destination.

Narada Muni defines humility in the following way:

*yenasadharanasakta-*  
*dhama-buddhih sadatmani*  
*sarvotkarsanvite ’pi syad*  
*budhais tad dainyam isyate*

**“Wise men define humility, dainya,as the state in which one always thinks oneself exceptionally incapable and low, even when endowed with all excellences.”**

One should not mistakenly think that humility is a state of ignorance, poverty, or inability. To the contrary, a humble devotee is endowed with all good qualities, he follows all the regulations of bhakti,and he has a healthy fear of material life. Moreover, humility is not an artificial show of meekness by one motivated for ends other than pure devotion.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu has listed four primary symptoms of a sadhaka’shumility:

**To think oneself lower than the grass, to be more tolerant than a tree, not to expect personal honour, and to offer all respect to others.**

While humility has its external symptoms, most significant is a state of heart. That state of heart finds its perfection at the stage of prema,and is most fully felt by the gopiswho, by its influence, display an array of inconceivable transcendental symptoms of dainya.

A practising devotee creates a favourable environment for the internal appearance of dainyaby cultivating the limbs of bhakti. Such an environment manifests in regulated thoughts, words, and actions, which even in immature stages of devotion attract Krsna’s attention. By divine grace, a devotee’s determination bears fruit, and his success becomes the inspiration for facing further challenges in devotional service.

One of the greatest examples of Krsna’s mercy is the meeting with and guidance from the spiritual master. This is why Srila Prabhupada is addressed as His Divine Grace.

An example of Krsna’s direct grace to the world is His very special gift, Srila Prabhupada, by whose grace millions worldwide now (read the path of pure devotional service.

Krsna’s mercy is both direct and indirect: direct mercy comes from Him personally, indirect mercy through one of His innumerable agents.

Indirect mercy is beautifully described by the analogy of the spiritual-master-cloud, who draws mercy from the Krsna-ocean and then redistributes that mercy to those in need. Amazingly, there is no difference between grace that is direct or indirect. Indeed it is said that in some ways indirect mercy, the mercy of the spiritual master, is superior in attributes to direct mercy.

As with all limbs of bhakti,the intensity with which a sadhaka cultivates humility must correspond to the stage of devotion after which he aspires. The further one desires to advance, the greater must be his humility. If humility does not mature, a devotee’s inspiration to advance will be checked. The development of dainya finds its perfection in utter humility, an inseparable counterpart of prema.Thus, spontaneous absolute humility arises at transcendence, and it invokes premathrough the grace of Krsna and His associates.

In conclusion, we may examine an oft-raised argument that challenges the symptoms of humility. Some devotees are heard to say,

**“Since humility means that a devotee feels oneself to be worthless and unqualified, such negative sentiments make me disinclined to advance spiritually.”**

This objection is built on the false premise that a good practitioner can become tired of or discouraged in his devotions. Yet the very nature of bhaktiis that it is inexhaustible and that it thrives on itself. Krsna explained this to Narada long ago:

*svabhavo mat-krpa-bhakti-*  
*premnam vyakto ’yam eva yat*

**“My mercy, My devotional service, and ecstatic love for Me all have this nature \[that no one ever feels that they have had enough\]. That should be simply obvious.”**

Thus, as a devotee practises humility, his devotion naturally inspires him to serve Krsna in better and better ways. That is the way of real humility. Moreover, as Krsna is pleased with a devotee’s quest after Him, He further inspires His devotee as stated in the verse beginning with tesam evanukampartham:

**“To show them special mercy, I, dwelling in their hearts, destroy with the shining lamp of knowledge the darkness born of ignorance.”**

We thus conclude and reply to the objection:

**“For a devotee who is astute in devotional practices, intense humility will never cause him to be discouraged; to the contrary, humility will nurture his determination.**

\* \* \* \*

The Vedas declare that both the Supreme Lord and the living entities are in an eternal quest for the taste of transcendental pleasure. In this regard Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura cites the well-known verse, raso vai sah rasam by evayam labdhvanandi bhavati:

**“He Himself is rasa,the taste or mellow of a particular relationship. And one who achieves this rasacertainly becomes anandi,filled with bliss.”**

There cannot be any argument about the assertion that all living entities perform activities for the taste they derive from those acts— or more precisely, for the taste of the pleasure they derive from those acts. And the same can be said for any spiritual aspirant. Thus, the tastes a devotee derives from bhaktiinspires his advancement and nourishes his determination. Rasanurtures sankalpa.

It should be emphasised that the tastes and moods of devotion in practice must be in conformity with a devotee’s aspired goal. Just as sadhanamust correspond to sadhya, sothe tastes of practice should also conform to the tastes one aspires for at perfection.

One may ask:

**“What happens when, in the matter of taste, there is incongruity to the principle of ‘the practitioner and the means of practice should be in accord with their goal’?”**

It is true that even spiritual tastes can become a distraction from, or even unfavourable to, the goal. Although this topic has been discussed in an earlier chapter, we quote Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami in our defence:

*api tyaktva Laksmi-pati-ratim ito vyoma-nayanim*  
*vraje radha-krsnau sva-rati-mani-dau tvam bhaja manah*

**“Give up attraction for Lord Narayana, which leads to the world of Vaikuntha. О mind, in Vraja worship Radha-Krsna, two philanthropists who give away the jewel of pure love.”**

Our answer to the question then is:

**“A devotee must abandon tastes that are not in conformity with his goal.”**

Returning to the tastes that nourish love, we should remember that sadhana-bhaktiis about a systematic awakening of the most coveted taste, krsna-prema.As a devotee becomes purified, he increasingly tastes the development of that love by virtue of decreasingly conditioned states. This is the exacting transition from lust to love.

In the following verse, Lord Krsna explains that the impetus to move up the staircase of sadhanais the increasingly spiritual tastes that a devotee relishes as he progresses:

*visaya vinivartante*  
*niraharasya dehinah*  
*rasa-varjam raso ’py asya*  
*param drstva nivartate*

**“Though the embodied soul may be restricted from sense enjoyment, the taste for sense objects remains.**  
**But, ceasing such engagements by experiencing a higher taste, he is fixed in consciousness.”**

Again, it should be noted that just as sadhanahas different tastes and moods, so too does prema.For that reason, a devotee must carefully chart the course for which he aspires. He should know the details of the goal through the guidance of his spiritual master, and through the scriptures approved by his guru.

Now let us turn to the tastes in the stages of sadhana.

The first stage of pure devotion is pure faith, and its mood is of conviction in the divinity of Krsna, and of service to Him. That conviction is a taste that flavours bhakti.But when faith is not pure, the resultant taste of bhaktiis mixed with a taste for enjoyment, yogicpowers, or liberation. By contrast, pure faith fixes a devotee to a spirit of conviction which can easily be called the foundation of all sankalpas.

The next stage is sadhu-sanga,or devotee association. Devotional service in either the practising or perfected stage is inseparable from devotee association. In the quest for the form of the Lord that attracts his devotions most, a Vaisnava finds that Krsna is never alone but is always in the company of devotees whose mood complements that form. That is the way of bhakti.

And a devotee should be keen to associate with Vaisnavas who are more advanced than he, for such devotees can bestow, enrich, and direct his relish for sadhana.Thus, a regulative principle of devotional service is:

**“Associate with devotees who are considered more advanced.”**

The additional taste brought by sadhu-sangais the fraternity and security of serving in the company of Krsna’s servants and associates.

When a devotee is inspired to systematically practise the regulative principles of devotional service, he has reached the stage of bhajana-kriya.Here, devotional service reveals a variety of tastes, including fulfilment coming from transcendental knowledge, a sense of direction from systematic practice, and optimism from a perception of sadhya.

Such devotion is unsteady at first due to the presence of bad habits; this is anartha-nivrtti.However, to the degree that bhakti frees a devotee of past karma,the taste for service solidifies. Rupa Gosvami gives two symptoms of such devotion, klesaghni,and subhada:

**Freedom from the effects of past karma,and entrance into a life of auspiciousness, respectively.**

The steady stage of practice is known as nistha.Progressive regulated devotional service is very much dependent on nama-sankirtanaand hearing Srimad-Bhagavatamin the association of advanced devotees. Caitanya Mahaprabhu expects that a practising devotee has the discrimination to engage in sadhanawith sainis who have a similar, but more elevated, relish for bhakti:

*srimad-bhagavatarthanam*  
*asvado rasikaih saha*  
*sajatiyasaye snigdhe*  
*sadhau sangah svato vare*

**“One should taste the meaning of Srimad-Bhagavatam in the association of pure devotees, and one should associate with the devotees who are more advanced than oneself and who are endowed with a similar type of affection for the Lord.”**

The feeling of being “fixed up” in bhakti,wherein spiritual life is no longer mostly a battle with past bad habits, is a breath of fresh air that spurs a practitioner forward. This phrase “fixed up” was used by Srila Prabhupada to denote a devotee’s steadiness in bhakti,and specifically to denote the stage of nistha.

When a devotee matures to the stage of ruci,his devotional service is driven by taste itself, and thus bhaktibecomes spontaneous in its motivation, although still not enriched with pure greed. Narada Muni explains how the taste for nama-sankirtanaand hearing Srimad-Bhagavatammakes a devotee oblivious of the taste for material pleasures:

*yatra bhagavata rajan*  
*sadhavo visadasayah*  
*bhagavad-gunanukathana-*  
*sravana-vyagra-cetasah*

*tasmin mahan-mukharita madhubhic-caritra-*  
*piyusa-sesa-saritah paritah sravanti*  
*ta ye pibanty avitrso nrpa gadha-karnais*  
*tan na sprsanty asana-trd-bhaya-soka-mohah*

**“My dear King! In the place where pure devotees live, following the rules and regulations and thus purely conscious and engaged with great eagerness in hearing and chanting the glories of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, in that place if one gets a chance to hear their constant flow of nectar, which is exactly like the waves of a river, one will forget the necessities of life—namely hunger and thirst—and become immune to all kinds of fear, lamentation, and illusion.”**

One can just imagine the enthusiasm that such taste generates in a devotee. And as wonderful as it is, it is supplanted by the stage of asakti,where the taste of true affection for Krsna dawns within a devotee’s heart. The mellows of attachment inspire a devotee to abandon his home and family, and in a state of complete detachment he incessantly chants Krsna’s names while always hoping lor the Lord’s special mercy. In such a dedicated devotee, taste is fuelled by true eagerness to hear about, and to enter into, Krsna’s pastimes.

These, then, are some of the varying tastes of sadhana-bhakti, which become more and more wonderful as a devotee climbs the staircase of service to Krsna.

It should be noted that the above-mentioned tastes of devotion are generally experienced during nama-sankirtana.Non-different from the Lord, Krsna’s names manifest their grace upon the eligible practitioner, enabling him to nourish his taste for the manifold aspects of devotional service.

\* \* \* \*

Indeed, there are many other features of bhaktiwhich nurture a devotee’s determination by the relish they afford. While much could be written about them, we make only mention of a few:

A devotee receives incredible reciprocation by participating in public nama-sankirtana,book distribution, speaking to others about Krsna, and arranging festivals to glorify Him.

Lord Brahma emphasises that such efforts to elevate others inspires both the hearers and the speakers:

*yatha harau bhagavati*  
*nrnam bhaktir bhavisyati*  
*sarvatmany akhiladhare*  
*iti sankalpya varnaya*

**“Please describe the science of Godhead with determination and in a manner by which it will be quite possible for the human being to develop transcendental devotional service unto the Personality of Godhead Hari, the Supersoul of every living being and the summum bonum source of all energies.”**

In addition to outreach activities, tastes for bhakticome from the encouragement of advanced Vaisnavas and from service to spiritual masters. Devotion to guruis the foundation of spiritual life, and the satisfaction of the spiritual master is a source of unlimited encouragement for the sincere servant. Without a doubt, the relish a devotee enjoys from pleasing his guruis a motivation that is second to none. This truth is confirmed by verses like yasya deve para bhaktir, and *yasya prasadad bhagavat-prasadah*.

Throughout his devotional journey, a devotee is blessed with euphoric experiences, usually during nama-sankirtana.Although these encounters with divinity are only the shadow of ecstasy, bhava-abhasa,they are powerful motivators for a practitioner. And as a devotee becomes situated in goodness, he is relieved from sinful reaction and experiences continual happiness in practising bhakti-yoga.

Srila Prabhupada’s liberal presentation of bhaktialso encouraged devotees to complement their blossoming attachment to Krsna with reverence for other forms of the Lord, such as Ramacandra and Nrsimhadeva. As Lord Rama is the guardian of regulative devotion, so Lord Nrsimha is the guardian of devotees. Sheltered in this way, devotees become increasingly determined to hear about Krsna’s wonderful pastimes in Vrndavana, and their intelligence deeply ponders how they, too, may enter into such unparalleled exchanges of love.

## Chapter Twenty-Two

**Results of Sankalpa**

Earlier chapters presented an overview of sankalpa,the importance of abhidheya-jnana,and the sources of inspiration for determinations. In this chapter we will review some of the results of sankalpa,as well as the spiritual consequences of not making a sankalpa.As with other aspects of devotional service, determination has defined characteristics and results. A devotee will know if he is progressing towards bhavaif the outcome of his efforts meets authorised criteria.

Scriptures and saints affirm that sustained determination results in, among other things,

**Faith; transcendental knowledge; attentiveness in following the regulations of bhakti,especially in chanting mantras;inspiration for sadhana;eagerness for spiritual success; dissatisfaction with anything other than the goal; and, most important of all, the blessing to see the lotus feet of the Lord.**

We begin by exploring how determination—which itself is born of faith—also leads to faith.

Although the very act of making a sankalparequires faith in bhakti,the psychological effects of making a vow, and the conviction arising from its subsequent results, fortifies a practitioner’s faith. A faithful devotee whose determination is fixed on the path to Krsna is granted spiritual rewards, which result in increased faith. Krsna Himself emphasises:

*yatha sankalpayed buddbya*  
*yada va mat-parah puman*  
*mayi satye mano yunjams*  
*tatha tat samupasnute*

**“A yogiwho has faith in Me, absorbing bis mind in Me and knowing that My purpose is always fulfilled, will always achieve his purpose by the very means he has determined to follow.”**

After his spiritual master brought to Gopa-kumara’s attention that chanting his mantrawas also service to Jagannatha, the boy began to chant with a renewed determination. As a result, his faith in the transcendental goal of life intensified.

Faith, we must remember, is the qualification for devotion, which means that higher grades of bhaktirequire higher grades of faith. And the contribution made by a sankalpato the growth of faith is significant.

Faith is weak, strong, or deep, corresponding to a devotee’s level of attainment, namely kanistha, madhyama,and uttama.And these divisions can each be further subdivided, grouping devotees as kanistha-kanistha, madhyama-kanistha,and so on. The fact of the matter is that in return for a devotee’s increased efforts to hear about Him, the Lord within cleanses the sadhaka’sheart and thus increasingly refines his faith. The verse beginning with satatam kir-tayanto mamconfirms the dynamic connection between determination and faith-led sadhana.Therein Krsna says,

**“Always chanting My glories, endeavouring with great determination, bowing down before Me, these great souls perpetually worship Me with devotion.”**

Faith develops in the same way in which bhaktiprogresses: both quantitatively and qualitatively. In describing the three levels of faith, Lord Caitanya and Rupa Gosvami explain them in terms of the three levels of qualification:

**An uttama-adhikariis said to have faith that is firm, drdha,and deep, praudha;a madhyama-adhikarihas full faith, sraddhavan,though it lacks the strength and depth of the uttama,whilst a kanistha-adhikarihas faith that is soft and pliable, komala.**

These terms are not categorically identical since some are qualitative and others quantitative. Firm, soft, and pliable are qualitative terms, while deep and full are quantitative terms. Moreover, it is interesting to note that in describing firm faith, both Lord Caitanya and Rupa Gosvami use the word drdha,which is often associated with determination, as in drdha-vrata.Thus firm faith is determined faith.

To conclude, determined devotion leads to faith, which then becomes the fertile soil in which further determination grows.

Let us now examine another outcome of determination, and that is transcendental knowledge: a spiritual topic shared abundantly in this book.

In the Bhagavad-gita,Krsna says,

*tesam satata-yuktanam*  
*bhajatam priti-purvakam*  
*dadami buddhi-yogam tam*  
*yena mam upayanti te*

*tesam evanukampartham*  
*aham ajnana-jam tamah*  
*nasayamy atma-bhava-stho*  
*jnana-dipena bhasvata*

**“To those who are constantly devoted to serving Me with love, I give the understanding by which they can come to Me. To show them special mercy, I, dwelling in their hearts, destroy with the shining lamp of knowledge the darkness born of ignorance.”**

In the two verses cited above, constant devotion is shown to give rise to both knowledge and the intelligence by which to grasp knowledge. This path of devotion invokes a vision of constant determination to progress from one stage of bhaktito the next. Stage-to-stage advancement means that a devotee must have corresponding stage-to-stage knowledge, which is:

**Knowledge of whatever stage one is on; knowledge of the duties that correspond to that stage; knowledge of the succeeding stage; knowledge of qualification for that stage; knowledge of duties that correspond to the succeeding stage; knowledge of how to rise from the current stage to the next, and so on.**

Yet knowledge and understanding of any stage of devotion are only accessible to a practitioner when he is determined to progress to that stage. And that knowledge comes from Krsna, Who, as the indwelling guru,teaches a practitioner either directly from within his heart, or indirectly from the hearts of his gurus.However knowledge is received, it is administered according to the recipient’s eligibility, and one aspect of eligibility is the willingness to move forward on the path of devotion. To make a sankalpa!

The Lord describes this progressive reciprocation between determination and knowledge in this way:

*sanaih sanair uparamed*  
*buddhya dhrti-grhitaya*  
*atma-samstham manah krtva*  
*na kincid api cintayet*

**“Gradually, step by step, one should become situated in trance by means of intelligence sustained by full conviction, and thus the mind should be fixed on the self alone, and should think of nothing else.”**

\* \* \* \*

We have briefly shown the power of sankalpain occasioning transcendental knowledge. Our next topic is attentiveness.

As a sincere devotee climbs the ladder of pure devotional service, the determination fuelling his ascent from rung to rung brings ever-new rewards. Knowing this through personal experience, a devotee becomes inspired to ever-heightened levels of attentiveness. This is but one way in which sankalpagives rise to absorption in bhakti-bhajana.

Furthermore, as a sadhakaseeks such higher states of advancement, he does so with the knowledge that success in progressive bhaktidemands increased attentiveness in practice. This is another way in which sankalpagives rise to mindfulness.

When Advaita Acarya descended to the world and saw peoples’ miserable condition, He resolved that He would invoke the appearance of Sri Krsna. With this thought in mind, He began to carefully worship a saligramadeity with tulasileaves and Ganges water, all the while observing a strict fast.

In his commentary to Caitanya-bhagavata,Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura writes that Advaita’s vow resulted in service “with a determined and unwavering heart.” And when the Lord appeared before His devotee, Caitanya Mahaprabhu said to Advaita,

**“I have descended to fulfil Your vow, for You have profusely worshipped Me.”**

This is an example of how sankalpainspires one to be especially attentive in sadhana.

Additionally, Srimad-Bhagavatamdeclares that a devotee must embrace an ever-enhanced attentiveness with each successive vow he takes:

*bhaktyavesya mano yasmin*  
*vaca yan-nama kirtayan*  
*tyajan kalevaram yogi*  
*mucyate kama-karmabhih*

**“The Personality of Godhead, who appears in the mind of the devotee by attentive devotion and meditation and by chanting of the holy name, releases the devotee from the bondage of fruitive activities at the time of his quitting the material body.”**

We have shown how determination fuels attentiveness. By contrast, it is well known that in the absence of strong determination, a devotee will struggle with attention during nama-sankirtanaand gayatrimeditations, among other services. One result of inattention is that seeds of new anarthasare sown within the heart.

Thakura Bhaktivinoda describes three kinds of inattentiveness:

**Apathy, laziness, and distraction.**

Apathy means a lack of determination, which, like the other kinds of inattentiveness, can be eradicated by the association of advanced devotees—determined devotees. And inattentiveness is the breeding ground for all kinds of offences, which then sap a devotee’s bhakti.

Lord Kapila explains that the Lord gifts attentiveness to devotees when He sees their sincere effort for the same:

*na casya kascid dayito*  
*na dvesyo na ca bandhavah*  
*avisaty apramatto ’sau*  
*pramattam janam anta-krt*

**“No one is dear to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, nor is anyone His enemy or friend. But He gives inspiration to those who have not forgotten Him and destroys those who have.”**

In the above verse, the words “attention” and “care” are both synonyms for apramatta,which is a negation of pramatta.And pramatta means “deluded,” “bewildered,” and “maddened by desire.”

The implication is that those who are not attentive will slide down the bhaktiladder. For this reason, a practitioner must make sincere efforts to rise to perfection and invoke the blessings of the Lord in the form of renewed attentiveness, which then protect the sadhakafrom material desires and, worse yet, from offences to Krsna’s names.

In this section we have shown with both positive and negative reasoning that sankalpaand attentiveness are intrinsically linked. The former results in the latter.

As with attentiveness in nama-sankirtana,a devotee knows that spiritual advancement requires carefully following both guidelines and prohibitions of sadhana.He knows that neglecting the rules of devotion will undermine desired results.

The proclamation of sankalpa-mantras,for example, has this very purpose at heart, as illustrated by the following vow, a part of the Karttika-vrata:

**“О Lord Damodara! О Lord Who rescues the devotees from sufferings! О master of the demigods! To please You and Goddess Radha, I shall bathe every morning during the month of Karttika.”**

Similarly, at the time of initiation, a devotee vows to follow the four regulative principles and to chant sixteen rounds of the maha-mantra.Such a sankalpais not a one-off event, because attention to following the principles and nama-sankirtanarequires successively higher grades of determination.

For example, the vow to chant sixteen rounds is a vow to chant sixteen rounds minimum without offence. When a devotee decides to increase the number of rounds he chants, either provisionally or permanently, he makes a vow or vows to do so. Additionally, as a devotee attempts to raise the quality of his chanting, he precedes the same with a corresponding sankalpa.

In other words, the very act of a determination has as its purpose the means as much as the attainment. Thus, since every successive attainment is a heightened attainment, it always requires a heightened sadhana.This principle is in accord with the rule, sva-sadhananurupam hi phalam sarvatra sidhyati:

**“In all spheres of activity, the results one achieves match the discipline one has practised.”**

Thus, determination is also a pillar of ever-refined practice.

Upon making a sankalpa,a devotee is always eager for success. Determination is like the starting point of a race, which all participants are eager to win. That eagerness or enthusiasm is integral to progressing on the path of devotion, and to reaching its end. Rupa Gosvami ascertains this enthusiasm, utsaba,to be one of the six ingredients required to bring bhaktito completion, bhaktih prasidhyati.

The example of Gopa-kumara’s vows to go spiritually higher and higher is evidence that determination inspires one for progressively superior attainments.

By taking a vow to embrace the next stage of spiritual development, a sincere devotee achieves his goal, which only goes to increase further his eagerness for the next stage of Krsna conscious ness and the sankalpathat stage entails. This dynamic is expressed in the Naradiya Paranain this way:

*sad-dharmasyavabodhaya*  
*yesam nirbandhini matih*  
*acirad eva sarvarthah*  
*sidbyaty esam abhipsitah*

**“Those who are eager to awaken their spiritual consciousness and who thus have unflinching, undeviated intelligence certainly attain the desired goal of life very soon.”**

Thus we see that sankalpainspires devotees to spiritual advancement.

\* \* \* \*

A corollary of this eagerness for success is that determination also makes a devotee indifferent to or unfulfilled by anything but his goal.

Dhruva Maharaja is the sterling example of a devotee who cared for nothing other than his determined goal—a planet superior to Brahma’s. Even when Narada tried to discourage him, even when the demigods came to tempt him, Dhruva remained resolute. To Narada, Dhruva almost impudently replied,

*padam tri-bhuvanotkrstam*  
*jigisoh sadbu vartma me*  
*bruhy asmat-pitrbhir brahmann*  
*anyair apy anadhisthitam*

**“O learned brahmana!I want to occupy a position more exalted than any yet achieved within the three worlds by anyone, even by my fathers and grandfathers. If you will oblige, kindly advise me of an honest path to follow by which I can achieve the goal of my life.”**

This exclusive devotion is praised by Krsna throughout the Bhagavad-gitaas ananya,or undeviating, and its personification, Hanumanji, is praised by Narottama Dasa as an ekanta-bhakta,or a single-minded devotee.

Sri Kavi explains that such indifference to material and spiritual enticements develops in proportion to one’s degree of surrender to the Lord. As one becomes more and more committed, one is enriched with detachment:

*bhaktih paresanubhavo viraktir*  
*anyatra caisa trika eka-kalah*  
*prapadyamanasya yathasnatah syus*  
*tustih pustih ksud-apayo ’nu-ghasam*

**“Devotion, direct experience of the Supreme Lord, and detachment from other things—these three occur simultaneously for one who has taken shelter of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, in the same way that pleasure, nourishment, and relief from hunger come simultaneously and increasingly, with each bite, for a person engaged in eating.”**

So influential is the one-pointed vision arising from a devotee’s vow to reach his goal that in the absence of its attainment the entire world appears like a void. Devotees know well Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s feelings in this regard:

*yugayitam nimesena*  
*caksusa pravrsayitam*  
*sunyayitarm jagat sarvam*  
*govinda-virahena me*

**“O Govinda! Feeling Your separation, I consider a moment to be like twelve years or more. Tears are flowing from My eyes like torrents of rain, and I feel all vacant in the world in Your absence.”**

The final result of sankalpato be mentioned is its ability to give a devotee vision of the lotus feet of the Lord. Evidence of this is given in the previously-cited verse beginning with sad dbarmasyavabodhaya.And Vedic literature is replete with histories of great Vaisnavas who, as a result of their determination in bhakti, received darsanaof Lord Krsna.

Dhruva is an example of a devotee who saw the Lord as a result of his sankalpas.His mother told him that Krsna was to be found in the forest, and so the boy retired to Vrndavana and performed austerities until the Lord appeared to fulfil his desire.

His first vow was to eat fruit every third day, his second vow to eat leaves every sixth day, the third to drink water every ninth day, the fourth to inhale every twelfth day, the fifth to stand on one leg, and the sixth to fix his mind exclusively on the form of the Lord.

A result of these successive sankalpaswas that Dhruva took control of the airflow within the universe, causing all creatures to struggle with their breathing. When the confused demigods came to the Lord for shelter, Narayana explained that their suffering was due to Dhruva’s determination. The Lord said,

**“It is due to the severe austerity and full determination of the son of King Uttanapada, who is now fully absorbed in thought of Me.”**

The Lord reassured the demigods that He would resolve their crisis, and then He kindly appeared before the boy to appease him.

Srimad-Bhagavatamgives further examples of Narada Muni, Kardama Muni, Maharaja Prthu, Ajamila, King Citraketu, and Mother Diti as just some of the devotees who, with strong determination, were able to see Lord Krsna face to face.

Such perfection is equally accessible to anyone with strong determination and a commitment to progressive devotional service. Krsna encourages Arjuna to be equally determined, sa niscayena yoktavyo yogo ’nirvinna-cetasa:

**“One should engage oneself in the practice of yogawith determination and faith and not be deviated from the path.”**

When a devotee follows this advice of the Lord, he eventually attains the ultimate goal of going back home to Godhead.

In this regard, Srimati Radharani secured from Krsna a promise that a devotee’s determined sadhanawill eventually lead to Krsna’s personal audience and hence the perfection of life:t

*athapidam astu*  
*cirad asa-matram tvayi viracayantah sthira-dhiyo*  
*vidadhyur ye vasam madhṝrima-gabhire madhu-pure*  
*dadhanah kaisore vayasi sakhitam gokula-pate*  
*prapadyethas tesam paricayam avasyam nayanayoh*

**“Still, please grant this one benediction: To those devotees who reside in the profoundly sweet land of Vrndavana and who for a long time yearn with a steady heart to someday attain You, please Î master of Gokula, appear before their eyes as their youthful friend.”**

Krsna agreed to Her proposal, which means that every practitioner can be assured that his determined effort will result in a personal audience with the Lord.

\* \* \* \*

The rest of this chapter elaborates on the consequences of a devotee neglecting to advance in Krsna consciousness. Rather than progressing from one sankalpato the next, for reasons of his own a practitioner becomes involved in vikalpa,rejecting the path to bhava.

No doubt readers will wonder:

**“What can a devotee expect in such a calamity?”**

Such an unfortunate devotee will:

**“Be unable to control his mind and senses, be victimised by thoughts of sex, succumb to material allurements resulting from bhakti,lose his taste for nama-sankirtana,be unable to attain or remain in goodness, be distracted from Ins path, and lose Krsna’s favour and the chance to see Him.”**

The long list above is by no means exhaustive. From it, readers will conclude that in the absence of the determination to progress in bhaktiand the strength to sustain vows, a devotee will fall away and resume material pursuits, or in a best-case scenario remain a religious neophyte.

Scriptures repeatedly emphasise how determined devotion is essential to the challenge of mind and sense control. For example, Krsna gives Arjuna no alternative to determined practice in the matter of self-restraint:

*asamsayam maha-baho*  
*mano durnigraham calam*  
*abhyasena tu kaunteya*  
*vairagyena ca grhyate*

**“O mighty-armed son of Kunti! It is undoubtedly very difficult to curb the restless mind, but it is possible by suitable practice and by detachment.”**

In a later verse the Lord also uses the word dhrtyatmanato describe a devotee who controls his mind with determination, something that Krsna considers crucial for spiritual progress. This evidence confirms that without determination, the basic tools to bring the mind and senses under control are wanting.

When the mind and senses are uncontrolled, they are then drawn into sense objects, most prominent of which are the bodies of the opposite sex—or alternatively of the same sex. And when attachment to those bodies grows, sex desire becomes uncontainable.

Because his determination was weak, to the dismay of the demigods, Lord Brahma became sexually attracted to his own daughter. Similarly, at an inauspicious hour Kasyapa Muni succumbed to union with his wife, Aditi. These are but some examples of becoming victimised by lust, also known as visaya-sangara.

A more subtle result of sporadic devotion is succumbing to the opulences that accrue from devotional service.

For example, as one progresses in sadhana,the attractive nature of bhaktiradiates from the practitioner and attracts followers, the results of which are wealth, adoration, and distinction. If a sadhakais not steady in determination, then instead of offering these results to Krsna, he will be tempted to become their enjoyer. Succumbing to such temptation is called taranga-rangini.

Krsna and devotion to Him are like a desire tree, but in order to receive the ripe fruit of that tree a devotee must remain determined in his purity and not be distracted by the unripe fruit of mundane allurements. Sukadeva Gosvami says, muktim dadati karhicit sma na bhakti-yogam:

**“Those engaged in getting the Lord’s favour attain liberation from the Lord very easily, but He does not very easily give the opportunity to render direct service unto Him.”**

These words of wisdom warn a devotee to be focused on the very rarely attained goal of prema-bhakti.Krsna will readily give every other perfection—wealth, followers, even liberation—but He will be reluctant to give the kind of devotion that controls Him.

In the way that irresolute devotion leads to a loss of self-control, ṝ also leads to a loss of spiritual attraction.

Queen Kunti says that taste and attachment for nama-sankirtana is dependent on concentrated devotion, which is possible only when a devotee is resolute in his determination. Although she is Krsna’s success potency, the potency that brings determinations to fruition, still she prays,

*tvayi me ’nanya-visaya*  
*matir madhu-pate ’sakrt*  
*ratim udvahatad addha*  
*gangevaugham udanvati*

**“O Lord of Madhu, as the Ganges forever flows to the sea without hindrance, let my attraction be constantly drawn unto You without being diverted to anyone else.”**

In other words, should a devotee not repeatedly buttress his efforts for perfection, should he become negligent in his practices, he risks losing attraction for the very thing that is his means of success.

The mode of goodness is the foundation upon which the sadhana of a progressive Vaisnava stands. And goodness, in turn, is depend ent on the “great determination” of the practitioner. Conversely, in the absence of such determination, dhrti,the foundation of a devotee’s spiritual practices becomes compromised and contaminated by the lower modes. Needless to say, without being resolute in purpose, a less advanced devotee will not be able to rise to the higher stages of devotion characterised by goodness—to nisthaand beyond.

In one Bhagavad-gitapurport Srila Prabhupada says,

**“Without such determination, one cannot make tangible progress.”**

And it is interesting to note that in this purport Srila Prabhupada equates steadiness, which is a quality of goodness, with determination.

A forest wanderer who neglects to follow his map inevitably becomes lost. Similarly, a devotee who does not follow the direction shown by sadhuand sastrais inevitably distracted from his goal by the play of the illusory energy.

Thus, at the very beginning of the Bhagavad-gita,Krsna makes known that in the absence of resolute determination, practitioners of any spiritual path will be diverted from their purpose. He says, babh-sakha hy anantas ca buddhayo ’vyavasayina:

**“The intelligence of those who are irresolute is many-branched.”**

And later the Lord repeats Himself, saying, sa niscayena yoktavyo yogo ’nirvinna-cetasa:

**“One should engage oneself in the practice of yogawith determination and faith, and not be deviated from the path.”**

Finally, and perhaps most crucially, when one or many of the above defects come into play, when a devotee loses momentum in his practices, then Krsna’s mercy and the chance for His darsana become all the more elusive—indeed, unlikely.

King Prataparudra was a great devotee, and he made repeated attempts to see Caitanya Mahaprabhu. However, because the Lord was a sannyasiwhose dharmaforbade association with materialists, the Lord refused the invitations. The king, on the other hand, was so determined that in the absence of such an audience he considered his life futile, and was ready to abandon his kingdom.

Hearing of these developments, the prime minister, Sarvabhauma Bhattacarya, reassured the monarch, deva na kara visada tomare prabhura avasya ha-ibe prasada:

**“My dear King! Do not worry. Because of your firm determination, I am sure that Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s mercy will definitely be bestowed upon you.”**

In other words, there is a direct connection between determination and attaining the mercy of the Lord. The determined receive mercy, the faint of heart do not.

The ultimate mercy of Krsna towards the sadhakais to bestow His darsana.And Bilvamangala Thakura emphasises that such mercy is the result of avowed devotion:

*bhaktis tvayi sthiratara bhagavan yadi syad*  
*daivena nah phalati divya-kisora-murtih*  
*muktih svayam mukulitanjali sevate ’sman*  
*dharmartha-kama-gatayah samaya-pratiksah*

**“O my Lord! If one engages in Your pure devotional service with determination, You become visible in Your original transcendental youthful form as the Supreme Personality of Godhead. As far as liberation is concerned, she stands before the devotee with folded hands waiting to render service. Religion, economic development, and sense gratification are all automatically attained without separate endeavour.”**

The shortcoming of sadhanain which a devotee does not face the renewed challenges that come with the fight for liberation can be best summarised by Lord Krsna’s instructions to Uddhava:

*sve sve ’dhikare ya nistha*  
*sa gunah parikirtitah*  
*uiparyayas tu dosah syad*  
*ubhayor esa niscayah*

**“Steadiness in one’s own position is declared to be actual piety, whereas deviation from one’s position is considered impiety. In this way the two are definitely ascertained.”**

The progression from faith to attachment brings with it duties that correspond to each stage of bhakti.A devotee must be determined to move from one stage to the other when he has the qualification to do so, and equally determined not to progress when he lacks such qualification. Thus, the sadhakamust embrace duties for the stage for which he is qualified. Neglect of such determinations is called niyamagraha.

The word niyamdgrahahas two meanings:

**Adopting spiritual practices for which a sadhakahas no qualification is called niyama-agraha,and neglecting practices for which he is qualified is called niyama-agraha.**

For example, at the stage of faith, a devotee is encouraged to just chant Hare Krsna. To reach the stage of steadiness, he must then take initiation, avoid the offences to the holy name, follow regulative principles, and so on. If a Vaisnava refuses to take initiation from a living gurubut begins to worship the deity, he commits the offence of niyama-agraha.Why? Because he has embraced practices for which he has no entitlement. The result is that he is barred from the very devotion he covets.

Similarly, a devotee steady in nama-sankirtanabut negligent in the study of Srimad-Bhagavatamis equally remiss for not endeavouring to take steps in devotion for which he is eligible and hence obliged. Thus he commits the offence of niyama-agraha.

Thakura Bhaktivinoda sums up his commentary on the niya-magrahaoffence with the following words:

**“The conclusion is that the practitioner attains a higher level of devotion as a result of following the rules prescribed according to his qualification. He should not maintain attachment for the rules of his previous level of practice. Keeping this instruction always in mind, he should always engage in chanting and remembering Lord Krsna and thus continue advancing to higher levels.”**

This chapter has illustrated the spiritual benefits of taking vows lor determined devotion and the handicaps for not doing so. Obviously, determined effort cannot be over-emphasised. Perhaps one of the best examples of the sanctity of determination is given by the Lord when He says,

**“Even if one commits the most abominable action, if he is engaged in devotional service he is to be considered saintly because he is properly situated in his determination.”**

In the matter of pure devotion, determination in service is a superior criterion than purity of conduct. This truth is praised again by the Lord to Uddhava in the following verse:

*jata-sraddho mat-kathasu*  
*nirvinnah sarva-karmasu*  
*veda duhkhatmakan kaman*  
*parityage ’py anisvarah*

*tato bhajeta mam pritah*  
*sraddhalur drdha-niscayah*  
*jusamanas ca tan kaman*  
*dubkhodarkams ca garhayan*

**“Having awakened faith in the narrations of My glories, being disgusted with all material activities, knowing that all sense gratification leads to misery, but still being unable to renounce all sense enjoyment, My devotee should remain happy and worship Me with great faith and conviction. Even though he is sometimes engaged in sense enjoyment, My devotee knows that all sense gratification leads to a miserable result, and he sincerely repents such activities.”**

So glorious is a Vaisnava’s determination to attain perfection that Krsna is willing to overlook His devotee’s accidental entanglement in material affairs. This determination, of course, must be aimed at spiritual perfection and the pleasure of the Lord; then, like Maharaja Prataparudra, a practitioner is assured of eventually attaining Krsna’s mercy. It is but a matter of time!

## Chapter Twenty-Three

**Loss of Sankalpa**

The subject of sankalpawould not be complete if we did not elaborate somewhat further on the factors that cause a devotee loss of determination. While this has already been touched on in the previous chapter, the subject deserves further attention.

The importance of determined progress in devotional service cannot he underestimated. In elaborating on the principle of enthusiasm, utsahan,Thakura Bhaktivinoda calls it the “life of faith,” a spiritual ingredient without which faith becomes “meaningless”. While determination and enthusiasm are not synonymous, they are certainly closely related. To move from one level of devotion to another requires enthusiasm. Thus, determination is very much related to faith, which is the qualification and foundation of bhakti.When a devotee loses his determination, his faith cannot help but be affected and he falls into a perilous condition full of unexpected consequences.

Of the many factors responsible for a loss of determination, we have selected the following:

**Misconduct, bad association, lack of discrimination, doubtfulness, and faulty sadhana.**

First let us consider the kinds of actions unbefitting a Vaisnava, which we have grouped under the title of “misconduct.”

In the verse beginning with yesam tv anta-gatam papam,Krsna prescribes the ingredients essential for a solid footing in determined bhajana. These ingredients have already been elaborated on and they are:

**Devotional piety, proper conduct, and spiritual self-identity.**

When a devotee neglects to abide by some or any of these three items, when he is sinful, bad-mannered, or illusioned, then he undermines his own ability to remain resolute in the face of challenges to progressive spiritual life.

Moreover, a devotee’s reluctance to abandon material desires and sinful acts constitutes offence to the holy name. Whether done accidentally or deliberately, the result of offences is a loss of determination. The misconduct most condemned by acaryasand sastrais vaisnava-aparadha,offence to Vaisnavas.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu says,

*yadi vaisnava-aparadha uthe hati mata*  
*upade va chinde, tara sukhi’ yaya pata*

**“If the devotee commits an offence at the feet of a Vaisnava while cultivating the creeper of devotional service in the material world, his offence is compared to a mad elephant that uproots the creeper and breaks it. In this way the leaves of the creeper are dried up.”**

Offences to Vaisnavas, what to speak of to one’s spiritual master, uproot a practitioner’s creeper of devotion and cause the leaves of bhakti,like determination, to dry up.

Serious devotees therefore ask:

**“How to avoid offences?”**

We answer:

**“Be proactive! Behave respectfully with devotees, avoid thinking badly of them, and always be submissive to your guru.”**

If one suspects that he has committed an offence he will enquire:

**“How can one detect that an offence has been made?”**

The answer of acaryaswho have elaborated on this topic is:

**“With introspection an intelligent person can himself detect reactions to offences, and through the eyes of well-wishers such defects can be exposed fully.”**

The reaction to such distasteful conduct includes a loss of enthusiasm, a loss of determination, and a loss of taste for nama- sankirtana.And if that is not bad enough, in addition the offender is burdened with an increasingly agitated mind.

The inevitable question is:

**“How to rectify offences?”**

The simple and unavoidable answer is:

**“One must ask for forgiveness from the offended Vaisnava and sincerely chant Krsna’s holy names.”**

By adopting a humble and respectful demeanour, the creeper of devotion will again receive proper nourishment, its leaves will unfold to regain their original lustre, and eventually the buds of devotion will begin to blossom.

In addition to vaisnava-aparadhaand guru-aparadhaare a further eight offences to the holy name. They too need pre-emptive attention. Since a practising devotee often recites the ten offences in the morning, it goes without saying that he should be wise enough to avoid them. As already mentioned, the effects of offence carry over to transcendence and remain stumbling blocks for even the advanced sadhaka.

Thus, an astute and sincere devotee shuns the degrading conduct which undermines his progress to the goal of prema.Having come to the path of pure devotion, a sadhakashould, at all cost, avoid losing that good fortune. It is the greatest tragedy!

\* \* \* \*

The next obstacle to determined devotion is incompatible association. We use the word “incompatible” to include bad association, as well as association whose goal diverges from the goal of the vraja-sadhaka.

Much can be written on the topic of association, which, in this verse, Caitanya Mahaprabhu calls the root of devotion:

*krsna-bhakti-janma-mula haya ‘sadhu-sanga’*  
*krsna-prema janme, tenho punah mukhya anga*

**“The root cause of devotional service to Lord Krsna is association with advanced devotees. Even when one’s dormant love for Krsna awakens, association with devotees is still most essential.”**

Before describing two kinds of undesirable association, we shall clarify what association is.

One thing it is not, and that is mere physical proximity!

Association primarily means a connection with other people on whom we are mentally, emotionally, and spiritually dependent. The dictionary defines association as:

**“A co-operative link between people; a mental connection between things.”**

Interaction based on the conception that someone will enhance our spiritual life is the primary aspect, svarupa-laksana,of association, and physical proximity is the secondary characteristic, tatastha-laksana.

Thus, a devotee like Prahlada Maharaja may be in the physical proximity of non-devotees, of demons, but because he does not think that such company has anything to offer him, he is not associating with them.

A similar situation may be the reality for many working householders who either employ, or are employed by, materialistic people and who, as part of their profession, must socialise with the same. Such devotees can protect themselves from the effects of bad association by externally acting dutifully while internally remaining insulated.

To summarise, association is not about physical proximity, but about receptivity to others’ views, values, and spirituality. Good association is when others’ spiritual perspective is beneficial; bad association is when others’ spiritual perspective is detrimental.

Let us now look at the effects that bad association has on a devotee’s sankalpas.

When a devotee keeps company with Mayavadis and materialists, his determination to advance spiritually is foiled and the creeper of his devotion uprooted. Moreover, Bhakti-devi is offended and withdraws her mercy from even fortunate devotees.

Ramacandra Puri is an example of such a hapless soul. Although fortunate enough to be a disciple of Madhavendra Puri, by associating with Mayavadis, Ramacandra Puri himself became a Mayavadi who took pleasure in finding fault with Vaisnavas. When Madhavendra Puri was departing from this world, Ramacandra Puri criticised him; he later also criticised Caitanya Mahaprabhu when visiting Jagannatha Puri.

Unsavoury conduct was also found in Bhagavan Acarya, whom Svarupa Damodara repeatedly upbraided for favouring Mayavadis. Bhagavan Acarya’s brother was a Mayavadi poet, and when he came to Jagannatha Puri, Bhagavan Acarya wanted to hear from him about Mayavada philosophy, but Svarupa Damodara forbade him to do so.

So powerful and deceptive is the enticement of bad association that Bhagavan Acarya, an eternally liberated cowherd boy associate of the Lord, succumbed to its allurements a second time. This took place when a friend wanted to read a composition to Caitanya Mahaprabhu. What kind of play can a Mayavadi compose that would be pleasing to the Lord? Fortunately, Svarupa Damodara Gosvami saved the situation.

Sometimes a devotee is attracted to a circle of scholars or a group of accomplished musicians whose underlying conclusion is that Krsna’s form and pastimes are maya.A practitioner may think that he can remain free of contamination while learning from such people; however that may well be wishful thinking, as was the case with Mukunda Datta.

Mukunda Datta was a contemporary and associate of Lord Caitanya in Navadvipa, however he, too, liked to mix with Mayavadis, and for that offence he was severely punished by the Lord.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu warned His followers that even an advanced Vaisnava could become contaminated by agreeing to hear the teachings of Sankaracarya. The Lord said,

*jivera nistara lagi' sutra kaila vyasa*  
*mayavadi-bhasya sunile haya sarva-nasa*

**“Srila Vyasadeva presented the Vedanta philosophy for the deliverance of conditioned souls, but if one hears the commentary of Sankaracarya, everything is spoiled.”**

And even if, for the sake of argument, a devotee is not contaminated by Mayavadis, why would someone want to associate with those who believe Krsna to be a temporary mundane illusion? Why would someone want to hear derogatory statements about the Lord Whom he aspires to love?

If devotees reflect on how Lord Caitanya rejected Mukunda Datta for befriending impersonalists, they will conclude that Mayavadi association is like playing with fire. It should be clear, therefore, that impersonalist association will weaken or completely destroy one’s determination to attain Krsna.

Another kind of bad association is the association of materialists—those interested in wealth, women, and fame.

When Caitanya Mahaprabhu was asked to meet Maharaja Prataparudra, the Lord declined the request even though the king was a great devotee. In response to the king’s invitation, Lord Caitanya cited the following verse:

*niskincanasya bhagavad-bhajanonmukhasya*  
*param param jigamisor bhava-sagarasya*  
*sandarsanam visayinam atha yositam ca*  
*ha hanta hanta visa-bhaksanato ’py asadhu*

**“Alas, for a person who is seriously desiring to cross the material ocean and engage in the transcendental loving service of the Lord without material motives, seeing a materialist engaged in sense gratification or seeing a woman who is similarly interested is more abominable than drinking poison willingly.”**

This slokais self-explanatory. What devotee can expect to maintain spiritual vows after having poisoned the soil in which his devotional creeper grows?

\* \* \* \*

Let us now move from bad association to consider the demerits of divergent association.

Many kinds of association may cause a practitioner to digress from his goal and thus undermine his determination. Of these we will name a few. However, the litmus test is expressed by the principle of sajatiyasaye snigdhe sadhau sangah svato vare.This saying is derived from the following instruction of Caitanya Mahaprabhu:

*srimad-bhagavatarthanam*  
*asvado rasikaih saha*  
*sajatiyasaye snigdhe*  
*sadhau sangah svato vare*

**“One should taste the meaning of Srimad-Bhagavatam in the association of pure devotees, and one should associate with the devotees who are more advanced than oneself and who are endowed with a similar type of affection for the Lord.”**

The essence, svarupa-laksana,of this teaching is:

**“One should associate with the devotees who are more advanced than oneself and who are endowed with a similar type of affection for the Lord.”**

Hearing Srimad-Bhagavatamamong those devotees is secondary, the tatastha-laksana.Moreover, the word sajatiyasayeis most significant. It indicates that a devotee should keep company with those who have a similar kind of aspiration and affection for the Lord.

Thus, at a certain stage of advancement, devotees who are very fixed in regulated devotion will find that they are not suitable association for those following the path of spontaneous devotion—and vice versa. Because the devotion of these two kinds of devotees diverge, neither one can fully inspire the other in confidential talks about Krsna.

When Jagadananda Pandita, a regulated devotee, wanted to go to Vrndavana, Caitanya Mahaprabhu warned him not to mix with the locals, who were all spontaneous devotees. Srila Prabhupada comments on this instruction as follows:

**“Devotees on the platform of vidhi-marga\[regulative devotional principles\] may misunderstand the activities of those on the platform of raga-marga(devotional service in spontaneous love\]. Therefore, Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu instructed Jagadananda Pandita to remain apart from the residents of Vrndavana.”**
