Moreover, devotees who are keen to attain shelter of one of Krsna’s incarnations will not be suitable association for practitioners aspiring after Vraja-krsna. Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami says,

*api tyaktva Laksmi-pati-ratim ito vyoma-nayanim*  
*vraje radha-krsnau sva-rati-mani-dau tvam bhaja manah*

**“Give up attraction for Lord Narayana, which leads to the world of Vaikuntha. O mind! Worship Vraja’s Radha-Krsna, two soft-hearted philanthropists Who give away the jewel of pure love.”**

And in a similar vein Srila Prabhupada says,

**“There are hundreds and thousands of Visnus, but for a devotee no form of Krsna is important but the original form, two-handed Syamasundara.”**

Gopa-kumara, with his travels through different planets, exemplifies how one’s determination wanes in the company of any devotee other than one whose affection is the same as one’s own. Whether with the Kumaras on Tapaloka or the Yadus in celestial Dvaraka, after taking in the environment, its residents, and its Lord, Gopa-kumara’s spiritual inspiration eventually waned.

To summarise: we know that Vaisnavas of the Sri-sampradaya do not associate closely with devotees of the Kumara-sampradaya, because divergence between their respective teachings challenges the resolve each has for their own kind of practice and attainment. Similarly, Vaisnavas of the Gaudiya-sampradaya do not associate closely with worshippers of other forms of Krsna, like Lord Ramacandra, because by so doing their determination will slacken. That is the result of divergent association.

We conclude this topic by citing the example of Gopa-kumara, who throughout his travels associated with great devotees, the Lord’s companions, and the Lord Himself. And although the boy always tried to make himself at home with whomever he was with, still, because he was not in the company of the sajattyasaye,he could not find peace.

Sri Narada informed Gopa-kumara that he would never be satisfied with any company other than one that harmonised with his own type of love for Krsna. The sage voiced the boy’s inner dissatisfaction in the following way:

*sri-vaikunthe ’tula-sukha-bhara-pranta-simaspade 'sya-*  
*yodhya-puryam tad-adhika-tare dvarakakhye pure ’smin*  
*dyatasyapi tava balate durghatam citta-duhkham*  
*svargadau ca prabhu-vara-padabjeksanenapy abodhah*

**“Even when you came to Sri Vaikuntha, the Lord’s abode of limitless, incomparable joy, and to His transcendental city of Ayodhya, and to this city of Dvaraka, even greater than both, your heart’s distress only multiplied in a most unlikely way.”**

Now let us examine the effects of a dearth of spiritual discrimination.

A devotee’s lack of discrimination results from his spiritual immaturity and lack of learning. In the absence of careful guidance and strict adherence to the regulative principles, a sadhakawill inevitably stumble into wrong places, wrong association, wrong situations, and wrong practices.

The principle of siddhasya laksanam yat syat sadhanam sadha-kasya tatdenotes a straight line between sadhanaand sadhya. However, a lack of discrimination in what constitutes real sadhana and how to implement it will result in a devotee straying into territories divergent from his declared goal. Needless to say, being so sidetracked will compromise his determination.

Additionally, learning unnecessary rituals, adopting extraneous spiritual practices, or travelling to irrelevant holy places are some examples of poor spiritual judgement. As Narottama Dasa Thakura writes,

*tirtha-yatra parisrama kevala manera bhrama*  
*sarva-siddhi govinda-carana*

**“The struggle to travel to various holy pilgrimage places is simply a mistake of the mind, because to make spiritual advancement one only needs the lotus feet of Govinda.”**

One of the most common examples of misjudgement is a devotee’s excessive emphasis either on outreach preaching or on focused sadhana.Srila Prabhupada expected his followers to keep a balance between the two. And while both preaching and sadhanaare equally important, balance is sometimes absent in the conduct of devotees.

On the one hand, devotees can become so absorbed with preaching and its supporting duties that they neglect reading, the morning programs and attentive japa.On the other hand, devotees can sacrifice the blessings of outreach to retire to academic institutions or holy places to enrich themselves with knowledge similar to the way of jnani-bhaktas.Both groups have ideologies to support their lack of discrimination, but both fall short of the balance that Krsna recommends in the Bhagavad-gita.

The standard of discriminating devotion recommended by the Lord is to be seen in the conduct of Haridasa Thakura. In praise of the namacarya, Caitanya-caritamrtasays,

*apane acare keha, na kare pracara*  
*pracara karena keha, na karena acara*  
*‘acara’, ‘pracara',—namera karaha‘dui’ karya*  
*tumi—sarva-guru, tumi jagatera arya*

**“Some behave very well but do not preach the cult of Krsna consciousness, whereas others preach but do not behave properly. You simultaneously perform both duties in relation to the holy name by your personal behavior and by your preaching. Therefore, you are the spiritual master of the entire world, for you are the most advanced devotee in the world.”**

In summary, an over-zealous preacher risks the offence of inattentiveness, thereby dampening his determination for sadhana.

Likewise, blinkered scholars often neglect preaching at the cost of Gauranga’s blessings, which results in a sadhanathat is solely dependent on their own limited efforts. In either case, a lack of discrimination compromises sankalpa.

A final example of a lack of spiritual acumen was spoken of by Uddhava to Gopa-kumara, who, in his attempt to attain Krsna’s mercy, contemplated going to Jagannatha Puri.

Uddhava informed the boy that Puri, with its festivals, darsana of Jagannatha, and unlimited prasadamwas so enjoyable that the boy’s feelings of separation from Krsna would be checked, so much so that true humility would evade him. Uddhava advised Gopa-kumara to go to Vraja where festivals were absent, where Krsna was not readily visible, and where the necessities of life were sparse. Since Vraja and its pastime places would invoke great separation, humility would manifest and from that, prema.For Gopa- kumara, Vraja was a more advisable place to go to than Puri.

Although he had advanced to the doorstep of prema,Gopa-kumara still lacked the discrimination to know what was best for him. Uddhava awoke the boy to the truth that the wealth of one kind of bhaktiwould weaken his enthusiasm for the treasure of another, the kind of bhaktihe so dearly coveted.

\* \* \* \*

Next, let us examine doubtfulness as a mindset that gets in the way of making and keeping to one’s sankalpa.

In the Bhagavad-gitaKrsna reassures Arjuna that by following the path of bhaktihe will attain its perfection without a doubt, asamsayah. And yet, accomplishing the perfection of prema sometimes appears to be such a lofty goal that devotees doubt their ability to attain it. Rupa Gosvami expresses such doubtfulness on more than one occasion. For example, he writes,

*kva jano ‘yam ativa pamarah*  
*kva durapam rati-bhagbhir apy adah*

**“Where am I, an insignificant fool? And where is that divine love which even great devotees cannot attain?”**

Sadhana-bhaktiis usually a trying and lengthy process. Considering the time and effort it took a great devotee like Brahma to attain success, a standard devotee may become doubtful, and his doubtfulness may cause him to despair.

In another verse, Rupa Gosvami echoes a similar melancholy:

*pracinanam bhajanam atulam duskaram srnvato me*  
*nairyasena jvalati hrdayam bhakti-lesalasasya*

**“I am very weak and lazy to do even the smallest devotional service, and so when I hear of the peerless and difficult-to-accomplish services performed by the great devotees in ancient times, my heart burns with despair.**

But then in the second part of the same verse, the acaryaexpresses optimism and hope:

*visva-dricim aghahara tavakarnya karunya-vicim*  
*asa-binduksitam idam upety antare hanta saityam*

**“O Lord! Î killer of Aghasura! But when I hear that Your waves of mercy splash everyone from the demigod Brahma down to the most insignificant creature, then my heart becomes sprinkled with a cooling drop of hope.”**

The two parts of the verse and their translations are explained thus: From the first part of the verse, it appears that being doubtful of success is natural, at least for some sadhakas.If, however, those devotees succumb to an attitude of faithlessness, then their determination will be seriously impaired. The solution is to face an impending obstacle as a welcome challenge and a good opportunity to invoke Krsna’s mercy.

For intimacy with a woman, a sannyasidisciple of Srila Prabhupada committed suicide. He thought that the path to Krsna had become impassable for him. But upon hearing of such conduct, Srila Prabhupada disapproved. His Divine Grace emphasised the redeeming nature of devotional service, by which that sannyasi could have continued his sadhana,albeit in a different asrama.

And that mood leads us to the second part of the verse in which Rupa Gosvami reassures his readers that the nature of offenceless bhaktiis to inspire the practitioner with both renewed enthusiasm and hope in Krsna’s merciful nature.

And such hope does not go in vain! Sudama Vipra was penniless and a social outcast, yet Krsna, the Supreme Lord and master of six opulences, embraced him with both arms and showered him with untold wealth. The result of offenceless devotion is beyond a devoice’s imagination, beyond his wildest dreams. Gopa-kumara’s guru said, vanchatitam ca setsyati:

**“Indeed, you will attain more than you desire.”**

So, while a devotee may sometimes become doubtful and apparently weakened in his resolve, if he remains patient and confident in the words of scripture, his determination will be redoubled by the grace of Krsna and Bhakti-devi.

The final factor that undermines determination is faulty sadhana.

The overall effect of shoddy devotional practice is obvious: a sadhakadoes not advance in Krsna consciousness; he loses his enthusiasm. And while the varieties of defective sadhanaare legion and their descriptions voluminous, certain defects should be detailed here.

One defect is to deviate from the spiritual practices for which one is qualified.

Devotional service from sraddhato asaktiis systematic. When a devotee violates the methodical structure with which Krsna imbued the process of bhakti,when he adopts spiritual practices that are above his level of qualification, or when he neglects to take up spiritual practices for which he is qualified, his spiritual advance ment is hampered.

In the latter case, a devotee may wrongly think that meeting the next challenge to his sadhanais “just too much.” The underlying reasoning for failing to meet this challenge may be due to apathy or laziness, and is often expressed by the words, “I am not so advanced.” Obviously, such an attitude is counter-productive to generating enthusiasm.

In the following verse Krsna outlines the conduct of both the faithful and the unfaithful devotee. This quote is a compound of two similar verses that are combined by Bhaktivinoda Thakura in his teachings on niyamagraha:

*sve sve ’dhikare ya nistha*  
*sa gunah parikirtitah*  
*viparyayas tu dosah syad*  
*ubhayor esa niscayah*

*desa-kaladi-bhavanam*  
*vastunam mama sattama*  
*guna-dosau indhiyete*  
*niyamartham hi karmanam*

**“Steadiness in one’s own position is declared to be actual piety, whereas deviation from one’s position is considered impiety. In this way the two are definitely ascertained. Î saintly Uddhava! In order to restrict materialistic activities, I have established that which is proper and improper among all material things, including time, space, and all physical objects.”**

The stages of devotion each have their specific dos and don’ts. Whichever stage a devotee has reached, he is duty bound to honour its corresponding practices. To act beyond or below one’s eligibility is to seriously handicap one’s advancement. We have spoken about this topic extensively in the previous chapters and so shall not comment further here.

The verse above may also be viewed from another interesting and relevant perspective: that of the instructions given by the guru to the disciple.

Are the spiritual master’s instructions below or above the eligibility of the follower?

If the sadhana-siksagiven by the spiritual master is not appropriate, if it is too elementary or too advanced, one way or the other the disciple may feel handicapped in his progress. Thus it is the duty of the guruto provide instructions according to time, place, and eligibility so that the disciple can feel inspired to take successive steps to perfection.

\* \* \* \*

Another fault of sadhanaoccurs when a devotee, undoubtedly an immature one, becomes proud of his spiritual attainment.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu taught that the key to progressive devotion is humility. He writes,

*trnad api su-nicena*  
*taror iva sahisnuna*  
*amanina manadena*  
*kirtamyah sada harih*

**“One who thinks himself lower than the grass, who is more tolerant than a tree, and who does not expect personal honor but is always prepared to give all respect to others can very easily always chant the holy name of the Lord.”**

Since pride is the antithesis of humility, as one would expect it produces regressive devotion, which the examples below illustrate:

A neophyte sometimes foolishly thinks that because he has learned some mantrasand taken diksahe has mastered all that is to be known. And then, a somewhat more advanced sadhakamay become proud of his immature realisations, mistakenly thinking that he has reached the goal, while actually he is revelling in mental speculation.

While the illusions of both the neophyte and the slightly more advanced devotee are equally detrimental to sadhana,even more so is a pride that causes a devotee to offend Vaisnavas. The common characteristic of these three devotees, their pride in spiritual attainment, is known as utsaha-mayi.

Another defect is sometimes seen in a more advanced Vaisnava Although he is free of pride, his defect is that he has not yet developed utter humility, dainya.This indispensible ingredient of prema can only be attained by those who have developed feelings of separation from Krsna. And there are different reasons why a devotee has not learned to cultivate vipralambha-seva.

One reason for the absence of dainyacan be attributed to a devotee feeling contentment, meaning the freedom from suffering that accompanies the mode of goodness. Krsna describes this defect in the following words:

*tatra sattvam nirmalatvat*  
*prakasakam anamayam*  
*sukha-sangena badhnati*  
*jnana-sangena canagha*

**“O sinless one, the mode of goodness, being purer than the others, is illuminating, and it frees one from all sinful reactions. Those situated in that mode become conditioned by a sense of happiness and knowledge.”**

Another reason a devotee may not have developed dainyais insufficient spiritual guidance. This relates to the earlier defect wherein the spiritual master’s instructions are below or above the eligibility of the follower.

Like all stages of devotional service, transcendence requires direction from a qualified spiritual master. If a spiritual master is not sufficiently advanced, or not sufficiently realised, he may be unable to guide a qualified disciple in matters of separation. Srila Prabhupada describes the limitations of different grades of gurusin this way:

**“In this verse Srila Rupa Gosvami advises the devotee to be intelligent enough to distinguish between the kanistha-adhikari, madhyama-adhikari,and uttama- adhikari.The devotee should also know his own position and should not try to imitate a devotee situated on a higher platform.**

**“Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura has given some practical hints to the effect that an uttama-adhikariVaisnava can be recognised by his ability to convert many fallen souls to Vaisnavism.**

**“One should not become a spiritual master unless he has attained the platform of uttama-adhikari.A neophyte Vaisnava or a Vaisnava situated on the intermediate platform can also accept disciples, but such disciples must be on the same platform, and it should be understood that they cannot advance very well toward the ultimate goal of life under his insufficient guidance. Therefore a disciple should be careful to accept an uttama-adhikarias a spiritual master.”**

The final fault in sadhanato be mentioned here are the distractions that come from bhakti.

One such distraction is the material opulence that follows devotees, especially preachers, specifically leaders, sannyasisand gurus. Unless devotees are careful to engage wealth and followers in Krsna’s service, they may develop a sense of entitlement which redirects their aspiration from premato that of material enjoyment.

Another kind of distraction is when devotees develop excessive attachment to other forms of the Lord, like Nrsimha or Rama, forms that are meant to facilitate attraction to Krsna, but not to be the ultimate goal of attraction. This phenomenon has been described previously from a different perspective under the title of “divergent association.”

In short, these distractions weaken determination to attain loving devotion to Krsna.

In this chapter we have described five factors that result in a decrease in, or complete loss of, determination. They were:

**Misconduct, bad association, lack of discrimination, doubtfulness, and faulty sadhana.**

While there are other factors that have the same unfortunate result, we have selected those that are given the most emphasis by acaryas, primarily Sanatana Gosvami in Brhad-bhagavatamrta.

In summary, the lesson to be learned is that only appropriate devotional practice can protect a Vaisnava’s determination from being sapped away by the material energy. For this reason it is said, sadhu savadhana:

**“Sadhu! Be careful!”**

## Chapter Twenty-Four

**Summary: Sadhana And Sankalpa**

Part Five of Sankalpa-kaumudi,“Determinations in Sadhana,” concludes with this current summary-chapter, the main purpose of which is to emphasise that sadhana-bhaktiis best visualised as a stepwise process of spiritual development rather than a one-step process to perfection. Indeed, the stage of perfection itself, prema, also has a similar stepwise development that facilitates its unending growth.

The aspect of sadhanain which a devotee rises from one step to the next is known as sankalpa.Generally, books on sadhana-bhaktielaborate on the symptoms and practices of each step, but say little on how to transit between those steps. As a result devotees often enquire about the means to progressive advancement. To fulfil the need for such a book we have composed Sankalpa-kaumudi with emphasis on what it means to move from one step to another.

Upon deep contemplation, readers will conclude that the primaeval impelling force of determination is the calling of the soul for love. And one impetus for love is dissatisfaction with the status quo, hence the need for spiritual progress.

We shall now explain this quest for love, which is implicit in Rupa Gosvami's definition of sadhana-bhakti:

*krti-sadhya bhavet sadhya-*  
*bhava sa sadhanabhidha*  
*nitya-siddhasya bhavasya*  
*prakatyam hrdi sadhyata*

**“When transcendental devotional service, by which love for Krsna is attained, is executed by the senses, it is called sadhana-bhakti,or the regulative discharge of devotional service. Such devotion eternally exists within the heart of every living entity. The awakening of this eternal devotion is the potentiality of devotional service in practice.”**

The constitution of the living entity is existence, knowledge, and pleasure, sat, cit,and ananda.The essence of ananda,or the hladini-sakti,is love, and the essence of love is spiritual emotion, bhava.This bhavais not to be confused with the stage of love by the same name. The pleasure potency, hladini,has two aspects: pure love of Krsna, and impure love that excludes Krsna.

Although by nature the jivais a lover of the Lord, being distracted by the material energy he searches for happiness in the temporary creation. In excluding Krsna from his outlook, the bewildered jivaexchanges the bliss of real love for the unsatisfying happiness of impure love for family, home, country, and so on. And because that love is unconstitutional, the jivatastes its essence, which is the emotion of unhappiness.

Unhappiness is so much against the inherent make-up of the living entity that it ferments a constant sense of dissatisfaction within him. This dissatisfaction manifests within all the jiva’sattainments and compels him to continually search for real happiness, real love, and real emotion.

Kapiladeva explains that the materialist searches among the thorn bushes of economic development and sense gratification, and for a little enjoyment he undergoes untold suffering:

*grhesu kuta-dharmesu*  
*duhkha-tantresv atandritah*  
*kurvan duhkha-pratikaram*  
*sukhavan manyate grhi*

**“The attached householder remains in his family life, which is full of diplomacy and politics. Always spreading miseries and controlled by acts of sense gratification, he acts just to counteract the reactions of all his miseries, and if he can successfully counteract such miseries, he thinks that he is happy.”**

In time, even the most diehard materialist concludes that he has a duty to the world around him, and so he undertakes a variety of pious activities, learning to taste pleasure from giving along with taking.

More advanced than the gross materialist is the pious soul who realises his duty to the Creator is as imperative as his duty to the creation, and so he searches for happiness in religiosity.

More advanced still is the spiritualist who realises that happiness is not found in this world, and so he wisely aspires for liberation, which is still not real happiness, but rather a suspension of distress.

Out of many such brahmavadis,barely a few are actually liberated, and of those who are, almost all abandon their attainment in dissatisfaction because they have not found what they are looking for. Unless they are blessed with the association of Vaisnavas, even the liberated remain ignorant of real happiness, which is the satisfying shelter found under Krsna’s lotus feet.

Rupa Gosvami quotes an unknown Vaisnava poet who expresses amazement at the bewildering influence of the material energy over these jnanis.Even though they adopt burdensome spiritual disciplines, they remain as illusioned as their materialistic counterparts:

*hanta citnyate mitra*  
*smrtva tan mama mahasam*  
*vivekino ‘pi ye kuryus*  
*trsnam atyantike laye*

**“Many intelligent people thirst after impersonal liberation. O friend! When my heart considers their folly it becomes struck with wonder.”**

Yet a truly intelligent soul who continues to search after the real path to happiness comes to the conclusion, either through philosophical research or by meeting with Vaisnavas, that the abode and object of love is the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

But among the devoted, most are satisfied to he believers and to worship from a distance, with only a lew taking up the challenge of bhakti—“become a sadhaka!”

Those who actually practise regulated devotion are exception ally wise, for they have concluded that devotional service in practice, not lip service to Krsna, is the panacea for dissatisfaction with life and love. In that way, through sadhana-bhakti,they begin in re-awaken their dormant, pure love for Krsna.

As the cleansing process of sadhana,especially nama-sankirtana, gradually reveals love by stages, two things happen:

**A devotee becomes increasingly satisfied with the process of sadhana,and increasingly dissatisfied with his current attainment, the status quo.**

As a result, the sadhakawants to move on to the next stage of bhakti,and to the next stage, and the next—on to bhava.This eagerness for dynamic progress is the sign of a healthy practitioner

In the way that a person becomes eager as he nears the completion of a prolonged assignment, or in the way that one becomes anxious upon sighting the end of an arduous journey, in his enthusiasm for ecstatic devotion a sadhakabecomes increasingly eager to progress from one stage of devotion to the next. Thus we see that spiritual eagerness, anxiety, and enthusiasm are at the heart of sankalpa.

\* \* \* \*

While instructing Uddhava, Krsna explains how the combination of satisfaction and dissatisfaction nourishes a devotee’s Krsna consciousness:

*yatha yathatma parimrjyate ’sau*  
*mat-punya-gatha-sravanabhidhanaih*  
*tatha tatha pasyati vastu suksmam*  
*caksur yathaivanjana-samprayuktam*

**“When a diseased eye is treated with medicinal ointment it gradually recovers its power to see. Similarly, as a conscious living entity cleanses himself of material contamination by hearing and chanting the pious narrations of My glories, he regains his ability to see Me, the Absolute Truth, in My subtle spiritual form.”**

The inability of a person to see impels him to apply a medication that will restore his vision. Similarly, a devotee’s dissatisfaction with the suffering inflicted upon him by material nature inspires him to attain a state transcendental to the modes. In both cases an unsatisfactory condition is the impetus for attaining satisfaction, and to the degree that dissatisfaction wanes, to that extent satisfaction waxes.

At this point we request the reader to note the following clarification:

**Although dissatisfaction with his conditioned state is a pure devotee’s impetus for sankalpas,the reason for dissatisfaction is not because he wants to be liberated from misery. The reason is that services at a lower stage of bhaktiare less suited to being offered to Krsna than are those at a higher stage. Moreover, in the ultimate issue, loving devotion is the only bhaktithat is suited to Krsna’s pleasure. Thus a pure devotee does not undertake sankalpasto be relieved of suffering in the way of a jnani.He wants only what is best for the Lord.**

As already mentioned, one should not think that having attained prema,dissatisfaction with the existing condition or with the quest for love comes to an end. Indeed, the very nature of pure love is that it always strives to increase itself, by itself. This is made possible through the agency of Krsna’s pastimes, which are themselves manifestations of love between Krsna and His devotees. Thus, once again, we see in action the principle of bhaktya sanjataya bhaktya, “*bhakti* begets *bhakti*.” In this case, prema-bhaktibegets more prema-bhakti.

In his dissertation on divine love, called Prema-samputa, Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains how love nurtures itself, by itself. He writes,

*loka-dvayat svaj anatah paratah svato va*  
*prana priyad api sumeru-sama yadi syuh*  
*klesas tad apy ati-bali sahasa vijjitya*  
*premaiva tan harir ibhan iva pustim eti*

**“As a lion is nourished by defeating many elephants, similarly all-powerful love is nourished by defeating many troubles as great as Mount Sumeru, troubles that come from the two worlds, from one’s kinsmen, from outsiders, from oneself, and even from the beloved who is more dear than life itself.”**

This verse is spoken by Sri Radha wherein She reveals that the many obstacles scattered throughout Her pastimes with Krsna an actually food to nourish Their love.

**“What are these obstacles?”**

In the order corresponding to how they are listed, beginning with “The troubles that come from the two worlds,” these obstacles are:

**The forbidden nature of paramour love; the wickedness of Her in-laws; the gossip of the Vrajavasis; Radha’s own contrary nature; and finally, Krsna’s infidelity.**

The troubles to which Srimati Radharani refers are constituted of prema,they nurture prema,and the intent to overcome them is the expression of prema,the sankalpaof prema.

From the evidence given thus far it is clear that the quest for love is never-ending; even after one has attained it, one is always seeking to enhance love more and more. Since that is the case for Sri Radha and Krsna, then what can be said of devotees.

This divine quest, however, is not initiated by any form of unhappiness, but by a transcendental bliss that ever-expands itself. And the impetus for such increase is divine greed.

The following well-known verse, while commonly explained as the price of pure devotional service in practice, can also be understood as the price of loving devotional service. The price spoken of is greed, and since love breeds greed, greed for love, like love, is ever increasing. That is the case no matter how much of it Krsna, or a premi-bhakta,tastes. Rupa Gosvami has written:

*krsna-bhakti-rasa-bhavita matih*  
*kriyatam yadi kuto ’pi labhyate*  
*tatra laulyam api mulyam ekalam*  
*janma-koti-sukrtair na labhyate*

**“Pure devotional service in Krsna consciousness cannot be had even by pious activity in hundreds and thousands of lives. It can be attained only by paying one price—that is, intense greed to obtain it. If it is available somewhere, one must purchase it without delay.”**

We have spoken of the cause of love and of the impetus for love, which are love and greed respectively. But there is another important aspect to transcendental life, and that is the nourishment of love. The question then arises:

**“What nourishes love?”**

Scholars in devotion, Krsna and His associates, and Caitanya Mahaprabhu all know the secret that responds to this enquiry:

**“The eternal dynamic between the meeting and separation of the lover and the beloved nourishes love.”**

This well-known principle of sambhogaand vipralambhaeternally pervades Krsna’s pastimes, nourishes pure love, expands it, and keeps it fresh. These two poles of spiritual magnetism are described in the following two verses.

Rupa Gosvami defines separation, vipralambha,thus:

*yunor ayuktayor bhavo yuktayor vatha yo mithah*  
*abhistalinganadinam anavaptau prakrsyate*  
*sa vipralambho vijneyah sambhogonnati-karakah*  
*na vina vipralambhena sambhogah pustim asnute*

**“When the lover and the beloved meet, they are called yukta\[connected\]. Previous to their meeting, they are called ayukta\[not connected\]. Whether connected or not connected, the ecstatic emotion arising due to not being able to embrace and kiss each other as desired is called vipralambha,separation. This vipralambhahelps nourish emotions at the time of meeting.”**

And Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura cites the following definition of meeting, sambhoga:

*darsanalinganadinam anukulyan nisevaya*  
*yunor ullasam arohan bhavah sambhoga iryate*

**“Meeting each other and embracing each other are aimed at bringing about the happiness of the lover and the beloved. When this stage becomes increasingly jubilant, the resultant ecstatic emotion is called sambhoga.”**

Such is the dynamic of eternal sankalpa.As will be explained in a subsequent part of the book, the sankalpasat the time of separation from Krsna are the various means by which to meet with Him again, and the sankalpasat union are arrangements for pastimes of pleasure.

Readers will by now be familiar with the oft-cited principle of siddhasya laksanam yat syat sadhanam sadhakasya tat:

**“The practitioner and the means of practice should be in accord with their goal.”**

For those who have contemplated this maxim, it stands to reason that if prema,the goal of sadhana,is characterised by sankalpa, then sadhana,the means to prema,must also be characterised by sankalpa.This is confirmed by the reverse form of our maxim:

**“The characteristics of the goal indicate the nature of practice to be followed by the practitioner.”**

Thus sankalpasin perfection are an indication of sankalpasin practice.

\* \* \* \*

With that final declaration, let us leave the realm of love and return to the realm of practice.

While a sadhakaprogresses from stage to stage, relishing the success of his determinations, he occasionally succumbs to the effects of the material energy, and makes sankalpasin the wrong direction, into maya’sdomain.

These steps away from Krsna include forays into sense gratification and worse yet, acts offensive to Vaisnavas. Such faulty conduct is likened to trying to light a fire while simultaneously pouring water on it. While defective sadhanais characteristic of anartha-nivrtti,a devotee conditioned by the modes of nature remains susceptible to making offences at more advanced stages.

An internal tug of war with the mind and senses can certainly be a cause of discouragement, but for a devotee whose heart is dedicated to attaining bhava,his goal is assuredly within reach.

Krsna speaks of two kinds of sadhakaswho are torn between Him and His illusory potency:

**One is in the realm of sensual acts, and the other in the realm of mental contemplations.**

We begin with the former, less-advanced devotee, who executes plans both for bhaktiand for sense enjoyment. The Lord says,j

*ata-sraddho mat-kathasu*  
*nirvinnah sarva-karmasu*  
*veda duhkhatmakan kaman*  
*parityage ’py amsvarah*

*tato bhajeta mam pritah*  
*sraddhalur drdha-niscayah*  
*jusamanas ca tan kaman*  
*duhkhodarkams ca garhayan*

**“Having awakened faith in the narrations of My glories, being disgusted with all material activities, knowing that all sense gratification leads to misery, but still being unable to renounce all sense enjoyment, My devotee should remain happy and worship Me with great faith and conviction. Even though he is sometimes engaged in sense enjoyment, My devotee knows that all sense gratification leads to a miserable result, and he sincerely repents such activities.”**

The devotee in question has faith in nama-sankirtanaand knows the liabilities of material happiness. Still, he is weak! He is unable to abandon sense gratification.

An example is a devotee’s struggle with the “fourth principle,’ namely the vow of initiation that says “no illicit sex.” Grhasthas, brahmacaris, vanaprasthas,and sadly sometimes even sannyasis transgress this principle.

Magnanimous as He is, Krsna reassures the devotee that service to Him will bear fruit. The Lord is more interested in His devotee’s sincere motivation than in the sadhaka’sspiritual weakness Because He takes only the essence of a devotee’s service attitude, Krsna is known as bhava-grahi janardana.

Perhaps the most striking counsel Krsna offers above is that a devotee should remain happy despite his shortcomings. Happiness may not be a devotee’s immediate mindset following a falldown. Yet it is reassuring that despite such humiliation, the Lord encourages the practitioner to be positive in conduct, mind, and heart.

The second type of sadhakais more advanced. He does not indulge his senses in gratification but he still has the mental inclination to do so, and may also daydream in that way. To this devotee Krsna says,

*badhyamano ’pi mad-bhakto*  
*visayair ajitendriyah*  
*prayah pragalbhaya bhaktya*  
*visayair nabhibhuyate*

**“My dear Uddhava! If My devotee has not fully conquered his senses, he may he harassed by material desires, but because of his unflinching devotion for Me, he will not be defeated by sense gratification.”**

Controlling the mind is more difficult than controlling the gross senses. If a devotee entertains thoughts of enjoyment or remembers past indulgences, his mundane sankalpais a distraction from spiritual ones. As with the devotee who yields to sensual pursuits, if this devotee’s heart is given to the Lord and to the Lord’s service, the purifying effect of nama-sankirtanawill give him the strength to control his mind and to completely turn away from the inferior energy.

In the Bhagavad-gita,Krsna urges Arjuna to make it known that both these devotees are under His personal protection and so they are never vanquished by maya:

*ksipram bhavati dharmatma*  
*sasvac-chantim nigacchati*  
*kaunteya pratijanihi*  
*na me bhaktah pranasyati*

**“He quickly becomes righteous and attains lasting peace. Î son of Kunti! Declare it boldly that My devotee never perishes.”**

In both of the above cases, to succeed in bhakti-yogaa devotee’s practices must be pragalbhaya,strong, and drdha,resolute. In other words, his sadhanamust meet the standard set by the acaryas.If it does, a devotee can be assured that quality practice at any stage of bhaktiwill make for a successful sankalpaand victory over the mundane distractions plaguing his senses and mind. Thus he will resolutely move along to the next step of his journey.

Having given emphasis to the strength of a practitioner’s bhakti, let us now examine the quality of his service. By quality we mean the purity of the faith upon which devotional acts are based.

The above two verses spoken by the Lord refer to a pure devotee and to pure devotion, uttama-bhakti.It is a devotee’s purity of purpose that makes Krsna supportive of shortcomings. Pure devotion means that despite a rebellious mind, despite contrary senses, despite unintentional falldowns, a devotee abhors mayo'' siren song. In Krsna’s words, nirvinnah sarva-karmasu,the devotee is “disgusted with material life” and he also detests sense gratification. That type of purity of purpose is called sincerity.

Once a practitioner has attained steadiness of mind as well as steadiness in sense control, both sadhanaand sankalpabecome effortless, the impetus for both being inspired by duty, taste, and attachment. That said, the anchors of past offences slow forward progress and compromise the taste derived from bhakti Nonetheless, at these stages of devotion, reactions are a burden on bhaktirather than a distraction from it.

From the beginning of sadhu-sangato the last stage of asakti, devotional service in practice has these two aspects: sadhanaand sankalpa.This is expressed by Rupa Gosvami in the following way

*sadhakanam ayam premnah*  
*pradurbhave bhavet kramah*

**“Gradually emotions intensify, and finally there is an awakening of love. This is the gradual development of love of Godhead for the devotee interested in Krsna consciousness.”**

No doubt there are other features of devotional service. However, practice and motivation to reach the goal are the two that Rupa Gosvami highlights in his definition of sadhana.

The yearning for love drives devotees ever forward, and so devotional activities and progressive determinations are also the hall mark of bhavaand prema.

At stages of love, the yearning for loving exchange continues but the dynamics of sankalpatake new forms, because devotion is spontaneous and propelled by ecstasy and love. In Rupa Gosvami's presence at Prayaga, Caitanya Mahaprabhu named the different stages of love:

*prema vrddhi-krame nama—sneha, mana, pranaya*  
*raga, anuraga, bhava, mahabhava haya*

**“The basic aspects of prema,when gradually increasing to different states, are affection, abhorrence, love, attachment, further attachment, ecstasy and great ecstasy.”**

With premaas the first stage of love, there are seven further stages, making a total of eight. However, since bhava,which also goes by the name of rati,is the sprout of love, it too may be counted as a preliminary stage, thus making nine in all. Many are the wonders of transcendental emotion! Since this book confines its scope to sadhana-bhakti,we will not delve any further into the truths of sankalpain transcendence. Perhaps that can be the subject of a future book!

In summary, the process of sadhana-bhaktihas two main aspects: cultivation and determination. Because of a dearth of books on the latter, it is the theme and substance of this book.

The recognition of such constant endeavour and the importance of knowing it is emphasised by the Lord to the creator, Brahma:

*pramanais tat-sad-acarais*  
*tad-abhyasair nirantaram*  
*bodhayan atmanatmanam*  
*bhaktim apy uttamam labhet*

**“The highest devotion is attained by slow degrees by the method of constant endeavour for self-realisation with the help of scriptural evidence, theistic conduct and perseverance in practice.”**

Sankalpa-kaumudiinvestigates the various aspects of sankalpa based on the definition of bhakti,a definition that establishes bhava as the goal of sadhana,and thus a devotee’s motivation for practice.

However, this book has not yet reached its conclusion. In Parts Six, Seven, and Eight we present three important foundations of the sankalpaprocess: attentiveness in nama-bhajana,chanting with emotion, and divine grace, respectively. We are certain that readers will find these topics worthy of their attention and worthy of application in their own devotional life. Jaya Radha Syama!

## Part Six

**Sankalpa and Attentive Nama-Bhajana**

## Chapter Twenty-Five

**Attentive and Inattentive Sadhana**

Considering the intense absorption generated by the non-stop thoughts of an uncontrolled mind, it is astonishing—nay, almost perplexing—how difficult it is to maintain attentiveness in sadhana. In Part Three we have written extensively about the factors and agents contributing to such difficulty, a difficulty that poses a daunting challenge to sadhakasother than just the spiritual novice. And yet, as difficult as spiritual attentiveness may be, for practitioners to stay successfully on the path of bhaktiit is an indispensable must. Otherwise, as the Upanisadssay, sadhana-bhaktiis a razor’s edge and for the careless, mishaps are inevitable:

*uttisthata jagrata*  
*prapya varan nibodhata*  
*ksurasya dhara nisita duratyaya*  
*durgam pathas tat kavayo vadanti*

**“O jiva! Wake up! Wake up! Make the most of the unique boon that the human form of life offers you: the opportunity to break the cycle of repeated birth and death. But take heed! Learned transcendentalists warn that the path of spiritual realisation is difficult and as sharp as the edge of a razor.”**

The message of scripture is clear. Yet while attentiveness is a must for spiritual development, it is not unique to Krsna consciousness or even yogain general. It is an essential aspect of everyday life. Whether crossing a street, slicing bread, or playing sports, inattentiveness can cost us a life, a finger, or a game. Attentiveness is a trait that contributes to success in endeavours and good relation ships.

The same can be said for attentiveness in bhakti-yoga.It is instrumental in ensuring success in sadhanaand in establishing a good relationship with Krsna. Those who are not alert during nama-sankirtanaor Srimad-Bhagavatamclass, intentionally or otherwise, are signalling to Bhakti-devi and Sri Krsna that they are not interested in the yuga-dharmaor in glorification of the Lord. Hardly a formula for spiritual success!

Readers may ask:

**“What is the connection between attentiveness, systematic steps in bhakti,and bhakti-sankalpas?’’**

The short answer is:

**“Since sankalpasare the steps that break new ground in a devotee’s spiritual life, it is clear that the direction sankalpastake are, spiritually speaking, the direction in which a devotee is headed.”**

If a man navigating a ship carelessly steers off course even a little, he will end up many kilometers from his scheduled destination. However, in Krsna consciousness there are no “many kilometers” from Krsna. The sadhakaeither attains bhavaor he does not.

We can highlight three important ways in which attentiveness navigates and effects our ability to make successful determinations:

**It makes sankalpaseffective; steers the aspirant in the right direction; and avoids contrary results.**

We begin with effectiveness. Being attentive makes sankalpaseffective, meaning successful. Attentiveness means that determinations are knowledgably formulated to attain a corresponding goal, and such repeated conduct paves the shortest route to bhava.

The second value of attentiveness is that it steers the aspirant in the right direction; it keeps his eye on the goal and keeps the goal in focus. In ISKCON the word “deviate” is often used to indicate someone who has gone off track. It is an accurate explanation of what happens when a sadhakaeither purposely or carelessly drifts from the path of the mahajanas.We may add that even purposeful deviation usually starts with innocent negligence, which then results in loss of taste, faith, and strength. An enfeebled condition contorts the consciousness, and a practitioner begins to think of other goals in life outside of his original aspiration for perfection. That is how a devotee deviates.

The third contribution of attentiveness is its effect in avoiding contrary results. Inattention in Krsna consciousness may give a result in a determination that is opposite to what a practitioner desires.

For example, if a person is not concentrating while walking upstairs, he may slip and fall. In other words, a misplaced effort will culminate in a result different to that which is expected and desired. Attentiveness avoids mishaps in devotion.

A contrary result is exemplified by the story of how Vrtrasura was conceived from fire with the goal of killing Indra. The mispronunciation of a mantra by an inattentive priest resulted instead in a devotee who would be killed by Indra. Sukadeva Gosvami describes this event in the following way:

*hata-putras tatas tvasta*  
*juhavendraya satrave*  
*indra-satro vivardhasva*  
*ma ciram jahi vidvisam*

**“After Visvarupa was killed, his father, Tvasta, performed ritualistic ceremonies to kill Indra. He offered oblations in the sacrificial fire, saying, ‘O enemy of Indra, flourish to kill your enemy without delay.’”**

In his commentary to this verse Srila Prabhupada writes:

**“There was some defect in Tvasta’s chanting of the mantrabecause he chanted it long instead of short, and therefore the meaning changed. Tvasta intended to chant the word indra-satro,meaning, ‘O enemy of Indra.’ In this mantra,the word indrais in the possessive case, sasthi,and the word indra-satrois called a tat-purusacompound, tatpurusa-samasa.Unfortunately, instead of chanting the mantrashort, Tvasta chanted it long, and its meaning changed from ‘the enemy of Indra’ to ‘Indra, who is an enemy.’ Consequently, instead of an enemy of Indra’s, there emerged the body of Vrtrasura, of whom Indra was the enemy.”**

From the three examples above, it would be shortsighted to argue that a sankalpais gainful regardless of whether a devotee is alert to its necessities or not. The reality is that attentiveness is the key to a fruitful sankalpa.

In the world today, attentiveness has become fashionable under the name of “mindfulness.” Of course, that mindfulness is not a limb of yogabut a narcissistic social fad by which practitioners increase their awareness of the present and embrace as reality the products of their conditioning—their thoughts, feelings, and sensations. There is no spiritual value to this kind of mindfulness. Its worth, if any, lies solely in the cultivation of a kind of absorption, which, were it focused on sadhana-bhakti,would acquire some tangible value.

\* \* \* \*

We begin this section by examining Sanskrit synonyms for attentiveness. We do so in order to acquire a better grasp of the different meanings of the word in a bhakticontext.

We begin with the word savadbana.Pariksit Maharaja utters this word to solicit his mother’s special attention for the very confidential topic he is about to divulge—how in Dvaraka, Lord Krsna suffers due to His ecstatic feelings of separation from Vraja. The king says, be man-matar idanim tvam savadbana-tara bhava:

**“My dear mother! Please now be fully attentive.”**

Another example is the following stanza which all devotees are familiar with:

*sri-guru-carana padma kevala-bhakati-sadma*  
*bando mui savadbana mate*

**We sing these lines daily during guru-pujaas part of Narottama’s song, Sri-Guru-vandana. Srila Prabhupada translates the word savadhanaas, “Worship him with great care, great awe.”**

The verbal root of savadhanais dha,which means “to put,” and the prefix avameans “down,” so avadhanameans “putting down.” To put unnecessary things away, or by contrast, to place an essential thing in its place, is called avadhana.Add the prefix saand we have the adverb savadhana,meaning “with attention.”

With these two examples we have the following meaning for being attentive:

**To place our wandering minds and devotions where they belong, in guruand Krsna.**

The next synonym for attentiveness is avahita.It is similar to savadhanain that the root dbaand its prefix avahave basically the same meaning. We may note that this verbal root dhahas many meanings, depending on the context in which it is used. An example of this use is when Brahma offers prayers to the Lord. Sukadeva describes the attitude of the creator saying, girbhis tv avahitendriyah:

**“With a fixed mind he \[Brahma\] offered the Lord prayers as written or approved by Vedic literature.”**

In other words, the creator was “fixed in mind, without deviation;” avahitendriya,is a compound of avahitaand indriya.

From avahitawe acquire further insight into the meaning of attentive, which is,

**To be fixed in mind and not deviate from an intended purpose.**

How else could sadhakasattain bhava!

The next synonym is wonderfully graphic. In his plays Lalita-madhavaand Vidagdha-madbava,Rupa Gosvami employs the word utkarna,a word that conjures a true picture of what attentiveness is meant to be. The prefix udmeans “up” and karna means “ear.” Utkarnatherefore means,

**“Perking up your ears.”**

When Krsna hears the sound of Radha’s ankle bells, or when Madhumangala hears the flute song, they “listen with rapt attention,” or they “raise their ears.” Here is one example in which the narrator introduces Krsna using utkarna:

\[punar utkarno bhavan sapulakam\]

*madhurima-laharibhih stambhayaty ambare ya*  
*smara-mada-sarasanam sarasanam rutani*  
*iyam udayati radha-kinkini-jhankrtir me*  
*hrdi parinamayanti vikriya-dambarani*

**\[“Again He listens with rapt attention, perking His ears. Then, His bodily hairs standing in ecstasy He says:\] ‘Moving through the air in waves of sweetness, the tinkling sound of Radha’s ankle bells silences the cooing of the sarasabirds maddened with amorous passion, and fills My heart with a host of ecstasies.’”**

Here, attentiveness is nicely described as lending an ear to something that is taking place or is being spoken.

Without reviewing the grammar in much detail, let us look at a few more informative synonyms for the word attentive: apramatta, samahita, susamahita,and atandrita.

Apramattaliterally means “not intoxicated” or “not mad.” It is the opposite of the extreme mode of ignorance. This means that attentiveness is a state of spiritual sobriety. In other words, if one is not fixed in devotional service, be one a yogior a jnani,he is distracted and captured by the Lord’s illusory potency.

The word samahitaimplies a bringing together and assembling of things. When samahitarefers to the mind or consciousness it means,

**“To collect thoughts; to concentrate the mind in meditation.”**

Thus, attentiveness also means bringing together one’s faculties in one place. For devotees that one place is sadhana.

When the prefix suis added to samahita,then we have susama- hita,which further amplifies attentiveness in both its intensity and attainment. This makes clear that attentiveness means concentrating the mind and senses, a concentration that has both qualitative and quantitative gradations.

And finally, we have atandrita,which is the opposite to being lazy or wearied. This word indicates a foundation of attentiveness, which is to be well rested and free of lassitude. An alternative meaning of atandritacan refer to a marginal attainment of developed attentiveness, which is that sadhakasbecome free of all bodily demands. One verse that exemplifies this attainment was spoken by King Pariksit to Sukadeva Gosvami:

*naisatiduhsaha ksun mam*  
*tyaktodam api badhate*  
*pibantam tvan-mukhambhoja-*  
*cyutam hari-kathamrtam*

**“Because of my vow on the verge of death, I have given up even drinking water, yet because I am drinking the nectar of topics about Krsna, which is flowing from the lotus mouth of Your Lordship, my hunger and thirst, which are extremely difficult to bear, cannot hinder me.”**

The above Sanskrit synonyms for “attentive” are meant to give us a deeper understanding of what being attentive is and why it is important for the sadhaka.Let us now assemble the essence of those Sanskrit words to give a comprehensive meaning to attentiveness as viewed from the context of sadhana-bhakti:

**“Attentiveness in devotion means to fix the mind without deviation on the goal of attaining bhava.This attentiveness entails carefully hearing from saints and making the instructions of guruand Krsna one’s life. By investing all his faculties in the process of sadhanawithout lassitude, a practitioner regains his spiritual sanity. Then, by the strength garnered from nama-sankirtanaand Srimad-Bhagavatam,he systematically plumbs the depths of smaranato reach the state of Krsna consciousness where, among other things, he is free from all bodily demands, such as weariness. That is the way of attentive sadhana.”**

**In studying these and other synonyms for attentiveness, the one which most represents the paragraph above is the word ekagra, which literally means “one-pointedness” or “with one-pointed attention.”**

Brahma-sutrasays yatraikagrata tatravisenat. This aphorism implies that the only requirement for sadhanais one-pointed attention, ekagrata,a topic that is discussed in detail in the following section. Our point here is that for this unique quality, Vyasa chose the word ekagrata.Thus we take it to be unique.

In the Bhagavad-gita,Lord Krsna repeatedly uses the same word and stipulates that the qualification of a yogiis an attentive mind, ekagram manah krtva yata-cittendriya-kriyah:

**“The yogishould then sit very firmly and practice yoga to purify the heart by controlling his mind, senses, and activities and fixing the mind on one point (eka- agram).”**

And at the conclusion of His teachings, Krsna asks Arjuna, kaccid etac chrutam partha tvayaikagrena cetasa:

**“Have you heard this with an attentive mind \[eka-agrena\]?”**

In both references Krsna uses the word ekagra.

As already mentioned in the Introduction, Srimad-Bhagavatam repeats the use of ekagrain exacting contexts, thus emphasising the need of a devotee’s one-pointedness in sadhana.

Following these examples, we too have chosen to use the word ekagrain this chapter. Therefore, based on the definition of attentiveness above, readers will know clearly what we mean when writing “one-pointedness,” “one-pointed attention,” ekagra,or its derivatives.

\* \* \* \*

Let us now take a brief look at the teachings and examples of the Lord and His devotees on the importance of single-pointed concentration in affecting successful sankalpas.

The Brahma-sutraverse yatraikagrata tatravisenatemphasises the stature of ekagrata,attentiveness, as the unique, overriding requirement for effective meditation.

The verse literally translates as,

**“Where is single-pointed concentration, there, because nothing is specific.”**

If we unpack the translation, then its full meaning is:

**“Wherever the yogican find single-pointed concentration, at that place he may practise meditation. This is because scriptures make no other requirement on which location a yogimust practise in.”**

A reader may raise the following objection to this translation:

**“Surely being in a holy place like Vrndavana in more important for practising Krsna consciousness than attentiveness!”**

The short answer of Brahma-sutrais:

**“No! The overriding factor for sadhanais the ability to be attentive.”**

This objection is not new, but was current during the time of Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s followers. To allay that argument. Baladeva Vidyabhusana wrote an extensive commentary which confirms our summary-answer above. Because it is so relevant and instructive we reproduce the acarya’scommentary in full:

**“This sutrameans, ‘In whatever direction, place, or time \[yatra\],that the mind finds single-pointed concentration \[ekagrata\],in that direction, place, or time \[tatra\],one should worship Lord Hari’.**

“The meaning is that in the worship of the Lord there is no restriction of direction, place, or time. Why is that?

The sutraanswers, avisenat,‘because there is nothing specific,’ which means, ‘because in this matter, scriptures give neither specific prohibitions nor make specific prescriptions.’

“The Varaha Puranaoffers full confirmation of this conclusion. It says,

*tam eva desa seveta*  
*ta kala tam avasthitim*  
*tan eva bhogan seveta*  
*mano yatra prasidati*

*na hi desadibhih kascid*  
*visenau samudiritau*  
*manau-prasadanartha hi*  
*desa-kaladi-cintanam*

**“‘One should seek a place, time, situation, and sensory environment where the mind becomes peaceful and cheerful. Other than that, there is no specific instruction regulating these factors. Place, time, situation, and sensory environment may be chosen to facilitate a peaceful and cheerful mind.’**

**“Someone may still object, saying,**

**“It is not so! Scriptures do establish rules regarding the suitable place for worship. For example, in the Svetasvatara Upanisadit is said,**

*same sucau sarkara-vahni-valuka-*  
*vivarjite sabda-jalasrayadibhih*  
*mano ’nukule na tu caksu-pidane*  
*guha-nivatasrayane prayojayet*

**‘“One should practise yogain a solitary place free from stones and wind; it should be clean, pure, flat, pleasing to the mind, not unpleasing to the eyes, secluded, and far from noisy bathing places.**

**“‘Additionally, it is commonly thought that one must meditate in a holy place, for holy places bring liberation.’**

**“To this I reply,**

**“‘Yes! It is true! Still, there may be an unfortunate situation where one is unable to take shelter of a holy place. If there is no such misfortune, then one should stay in a holy place and worship the Lord there. Nevertheless, the verse above offers the final conclusion in the words mano ‘nukule,meaning ‘One should find a place that is pleasing to the mind.’ And that is the overriding consideration of all other requirements.”**

The gist of the great acarya’sargument is that holy places, the brahma-muhurta,the bank of a body of water, and where people do not congregate are all helpful in the practice of Krsna consciousness. But more important than these considerations is the place where one can be attentive. If attentiveness is more easily attained in the absence of these criteria, or if a sadhakahas no access to them, then the most important thing is one pointed attention of the mind.

This reasoning is supported by other acaryas.For example, in translating and commenting on the verse beginning with krsnam smaran janam casya,Srila Prabhupada translates the phrase kuryad vasam vraje sadaas:

**“And one should live in Vrndavana. If one is physically unable to go to Vrndavana, he should mentally live there.”**

Elsewhere Srila Prabhupada comments on the same verse:

**“The purport is that if it is possible one should go and physically be present at Vrajabhumi, Vrndavana, and be engaged always in the service of the Lord, following the devotees in Vraja-dhama, the spiritual realm of Vraja. If it is not possible, however, to be physically present at Vrndavana, one can meditate anywhere upon living in that situation. Wherever he may be, one must always think about life in Vraja-dhama and about following in the footsteps of a particular devotee in the service of the Lord.”**

In these quotations we see that to practise spontaneous devotion, the dominant constant is attentive meditation on service to Krsna and the supporting variant is living in Vraja, either directly or indirectly. This conclusion is strongly emphasised by Rupa Gosvami, Jiva Gosvami, and Visvanatha Cakravarti. In summary, attentive ness is key to sankalpa.

Moving from Brahma-sutrato its commentary, Srimad-Bhagavatam,we see the same principle explicitly conveyed. After Nrsimhadeva killed Hiranyakasipu, Prahlada Maharaja approached the angry Lord to pacify Him. By Nrsimhadeva’s kindly touch the boy attained a transcendental nature, and in that perfected state he prepared himself to offer prayers. In other words, Prahlada made the sankalpato pray.

**“What preparation was relevant to such a determination?”**

Narada says,

*astausid dharim ekdgra-*  
*manasa susamahitah*  
*prema-gadgadaya vaca*  
*tan-nyasta-hrdayeksanab*

**“Prahlada Maharaja fixed his mind and sight upon Lord Nrsirnhadeva with full attention in complete trance. With a fixed mind, he began to offer prayers in love with a faltering voice.”**

The answer to our question is quite clear:

**“Prahlada did only one thing, and that was to steady his mind and senses by fixing them on the Lord.”**

With such single-pointed attentiveness, he then began to offer prayers, prayers that are revered by all Vaisnavas today. Again, through the conduct of Prahlada Maharaja, we see how attentiveness is a primary constituent of a successful sankalpa.

Finally let us see Krsna’s instruction on the subject.

While teaching Uddhava the science of bhakti yoga,the Lord prefaces description of His appearance as the Hamsa-avatara thus:

*apramatto ’nuyunjita*  
*mano mayy arpayan chanaih*  
*anirvinno yatha-kalam*  
*jita-svaso jitasanah*

*etavan yoga adisto*  
*mac-chisyaih sanakadibhih*  
*sarvato mana akrsya*  
*mayy addhavesyate yatha*

**“A person should be attentive and grave and never lazy or morose. Mastering the yogaprocedures of breathing and sitting properly, one should practise fixing the mind on Me at dawn, noon, and sunset, and thus gradually the mind should be completely absorbed in Me. The actual yogasystem as taught by My devotees, headed by Sanaka-kumara, is simply this: having withdrawn the mind from all other objects, one should directly and appropriately absorb it in Me.”**

Krsna’s definition and summary of yogais simple:

**“Absorb the mind in Me.”**

From the highest authority we again hear that the step-by-step process to transcendence has attentiveness as its essence. The Lord, acaryas,and scripture make this abundantly clear.

\* \* \* \*

Let us now look at attentiveness in sadhana-bhaktifrom a different perspective, one that we find acaryaslike Thakura Bhaktivinoda employ to emphasise the importance of the subject. This approach is to study the opposite of attentiveness, which is inattentiveness.

When sincere devotees see the spiritual devastation that inattention causes, they take seriously the importance of attention in their services, especially in the japaof the holy names.

The question devotees ask is:

**“What is inattentiveness in sadhana-bhaktiand what are its consequences?”**

In summary:

**“Inattentiveness means to be distracted from the practice and purpose of one’s bhajana;its ramifications are a variety of offences to the holy name.”**

As short as is the answer above, that lengthy an explanation we offer below. And we begin our commentary on inattentiveness by studying the Sanskrit synonyms for the word.

Bhaktivinoda Thakura uses the word pramadafor inattention, which is commonly used in Sanskrit to denote:

Intoxication, madness, insanity, negligence, and carelessness.

For example, there is the well-known verse spoken by Maharaja Rsabha to his hundred sons:

*nunam pramattah kurute vikarma*  
*yad indriya-pritaya aprnoti*  
*na sadbu manye yata atmano ’yam*  
*asann api klesada asa dehah*

**“When a person considers sense gratification the aim of life, he certainly becomes mad after materialistic living and engages in all kinds of sinful activity. He does not know that due to his past misdeeds he has already received a body which, although temporary, is the cause of his misery. Actually the living entity should not have taken on a material body, but he has been awarded the material body for sense gratification. Therefore I think it not befitting an intelligent man to involve himself again in the activities of sense gratification by which he perpetually gets material bodies one after another.”**

In this case pramattahmeans “mad.”

And in another example Kaviraja Gosvami writes,

*bhrama, pramada, vipralipsa, karanapatava*  
*arsa-vijna-vakye nahi dosa ei saba*

**“Mistakes, illusions, cheating, and defective perception do not occur in the sayings of the authoritative sages.”**

In this verse pramadameans illusion, and in his purport Srila Prabhupada writes,

**“Pramadarefers to inattention or misunderstanding of reality.”**

Herein Srila Prabhupada shares the same usage as Bhaktivinoda Thakura. Thus, for the purposes of this book, just as ekagratais our word for attentiveness, pramattatais our word for inattentiveness.

The verbal root here is mad,which means “mad,” and the prefix praamplifies the meaning so that pramadacan be understood as “utter madness.”

When a person is mad, he certainly has no control over his mind or senses, and so he cannot be attentive. Hence madness and inattention are closely related and so share the same Sanskrit word usage. Conversely, when one is not mad, not deluded by sense gratification, then one is sober and attentive, not negligent in one's duty.

With reference to the verse immediately above, we must admit that as conditioned souls we, unlike authoritative sages, are subject to the four defects. Thus, inattentiveness is inherent in us all. And that is a problem. With the rare exception, attentiveness in bhakti does not come naturally to a sadhaka.For that reason he must make serious efforts to attain it.

The main obstruction caused by inattentiveness, particularly inattentive chanting of the maha-mantra,is offence to Krsna’s holy names. Pramadaresults in nama-aparadha.

It is well known that Krsna and His name are one. There is no difference between the two. That is the nature of the supreme absolute reality. Like all persons, Krsna likes to be addressed attentively. He does not like to be called on with a dismissive or inattentive attitude. But when we chant with that careless attitude, He is offended.

We should add that offences to Krsna’s name are incurred nor just from negligent chanting but from a list of other transgressions. Padma Purananames ten. Inattentiveness is sometimes connected to the ninth and sometimes added as the eleventh, all-encompassing offence. It also includes not listening carefully to an exalted speaker. For example, prefacing a mantrawith which he would initiate the Pracetas, Lord Siva said,

*idam viviktam japtavyam*  
*pavitram mangalam param*  
*nihsreyasa-karam capi*  
*sruyatam tad vadami vah*

**“Now I shall chant one mantrawhich is not only transcendental, pure, and auspicious, but is the best prayer for anyone who is aspiring to attain the ultimate goal of life. When I chant this mantra,please hear it carefully and attentively.”**

We may note how the word sruyatamis translated as,

**“Hear it carefully and attentively.”**

Implicit in that instruction is the consequence of not following it, which Srila Prabhupada expounds in his purport:

**“Lord Siva advised the sons of the King to hear him attentively, for inattentive hearing is offensive.”**

The conclusion is that just as it is an offence to the holy name to be inattentive while chanting Hare Krsna, it is equally offensive to be inattentive while hearing Srimad-Bhagavatamor the person bhagavata.After all, those two are both expansions of the holy name.

Some devotees have said that chanting Krsna’s name offensively is like beating Krsna with a stick. What a frightening picture that conjures! And yet the incident of Jagai and Madhai beating Lord Nityananda is evidence of the assertion. The two cousins were offence personified, and Lord Nityananda is the presiding deity of the holy name, glorified with the following words:

*nityanandam aham naumi*  
*sarvanatida-karam param*  
*hari-nama-pradam devam*  
*avadhuta-siromanim*

**“I bow down to the Supreme Lord, Nityananda Prabhu! He is the awarder of the highest joy to all, the bestower of the holy name, and the crest jewel of all paramahamsamendicants.”**

A lesson to be learned from this incident is that offences to the holy name do personal harm to the Lord.

And that is not all! If not checked, inattentiveness becomes the root of other offences, as well as the cause of persistent bad habits Jagai and Madhai’s offensive conduct resulted in Vaisnava aparadha,the results of which extend even into the realm of bhava.

Thus, even though a devotee may make sankalpaswith the aim of advancing in bhajana,if in so doing he commits offences, the results he attains pale in comparison to his efforts. Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami writes,

*bahu janma kare yadi sravana, kirtana*  
*tabu ta’ na paya krsna-pade prema-dhana*

**“If one is infested with the ten offences in the chanting of the Hare Krsna maha-mantra,despite his endeavour to chant the holy name for many births, he will not get the love of Godhead that is the ultimate goal of this chanting.”**

Srila Prabhupada’s translation of this slokais very significant. The word “endeavour” indicates determinations, sankalpas.A devotee may make repeated efforts to progress in Krsna consciousness, but the sprout of love of God will continue to evade him until, like Jagai and Madhai, he stops his offensive ways and follows the path of pure devotees, the path of the mahajanas.

Another aspect of the above is that a lack of progress over many years may well cause a devotee to become discouraged and so even more negligent.

And finally, the burden of offences and the distraction caused by the bad habits that offences bring make sadhanaall the more difficult. It is like running waist deep in water.

In short, inattentive chanting of Krsna’s holy names drains a sadhaka’sinspiration, encumbers his efforts, and compromises his success in sankalpas.Not a good formula for spiritual advancement!

Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura records a conversation between Haridasa Thakura and Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu on the glories of Krsna’s name. The namacaryadescribes how Lord Caitanya always emphasised the importance of offenceless chanting. Haridasa said,

**“O Lord! To Sanatana Gosvami here in Jagannatha Puri and to Gopala Bhatta in South India, You taught that the holy name must be chanted attentively, that inattention in chanting is an offence, and that a devotee may carefully avoid all other offences yet still not experience the ecstasy of the pure name. Due to the offence of inattentiveness, pramada,the chanter is obstructed in efforts to reach the stage of nistha,firm faith, and so growth of the devotional creeper is stunted, divesting it of the potential to flower into krsna-prema.”**

With that final judgment from He Who brought the holy names of Krsna to the world, let us recap what we have heard of the effects of inattentiveness:

Because inattentive chanting is an offence to the holy name, it is the source of especially resilient bad habits.

The anarthasresulting from past pious or sinful activity are relatively easy to eradicate. But the anarthasresulting from offences to Krsna’s names are more difficult to purify—much more.

In addition to breeding new anarthas,inattention also breeds further offences. Inattention is a habit that pervades a devotee’s attitude, causing him, for example, to wrongly respect demigods or be disrespectful of other scriptures. Hence, by a negligent psychology, a sadhaka is prone to commit other offences.

The cumulative effect of these new anarthasand aparadhasis to constrain the devotee to the stages of anisthita bhajana-kriyaand to ban him from the stages of nisthaand beyond. In other words, a devotee’s sankalpasbecome ineffective. It is like walking up a down-moving escalator.

The effects of inattentiveness are frightening! Under the influence of such an adverse habit there is every chance that some devotees will fall away from the path of pure devotion, while those who do not are on a slow-boat to bhava.

\* \* \* \*

In the following section we shall look at three kinds of inattentive ness and some recommended means to overcome them. Haridasa Thakura names the varieties of inattentiveness as:

Apathy, laziness, and distraction.

Unfortunately, a devotee’s long-standing connection with sense gratification conditions him in ways that are generally unfavourable for attentive sadhana.Sensual acts, among other things, have left their impressions within the subtle body, which means that a sadhaka’smemories are full of thoughts of the past. Ideally, harinamashould be accompanied by remembrance of Krsna. But deep conditioning suppresses spiritual thoughts with mundane ones. Hence a devotee’s inability to focus on Krsna’s names and pastimes results in inattentiveness.

Thakura Bhaktivinoda warns that unless a devotee resolutely steers away from this ingrained habit, even chanting sixty-four inattentive rounds a day will not produce a “drop of taste” for the Lord’s name. How frightening!

Apathy means a lack of feeling, emotion, interest, or concern. It is the same indifference that the jivaexhibited to Krsna before entering the material world, and the same indifference that led to its attraction for sense gratification. The cause for attraction to mayais that apathy is not a natural attribute of the soul. The jiva must exhibit emotion for and interest in something, and if that something is not spiritual, it will be material. Thus, while apathy can be a state of mind, it is a temporary one, and if the practitioner does not conquer it, he is conquered by it.

The Sanskrit word for apathy is audasinya.The root asmeans “to sit,” and with the prefix adthe meaning becomes “to sit apart” or “to take no interest in.” Udasinameans “sitting apart” or “indifferent,” and audasinyais what is related to udasinawhich is:

Indifference, apathy, disregard.

Indifference to a person is certainly offensive. And indifference to an activity renders it ineffective and sometimes dangerous, as in the case of cutting bread with a knife. What, then, of inattentiveness in sadhana-bhakti,which scriptures say is already like walking a razor’s edge.

We see that the word udasinais repeatedly used in the Bhagavad-gitato express a sense of neutrality, such as when Krsna says,

*udasina-vad asinam*  
*asaktam tesu karmasu*

**“I am ever detached from all these material activities, seated as though neutral.”**

Srimati Radharani also uses udasinain the context of transcendental indifference, during a pastime wherein She thinks that Krsna had abandoned Her:

*grhantah khelantyo nija-sahaja-balyasya balanad*  
*abhadram bhadram va kim api hi na janimahi manak*  
*vayam netum yuktah katham asaranam kam api dasam*  
*katham va nyayya te prathayitum udasina-padavi*

**“I was engaged in My own playful activities at home, and because of My childish innocence I did not know right from wrong. Therefore, is it good for You to have forced us into being so much attracted to You and then to have neglected us? Now You arc indifferent to us. Do You think this is right?”**

There are different ways for a devotee to rid himself of apathetic inattention, udasina-pramada.The most preferred solution is to chant by the side of an advanced Vaisnava, taking note of his mood in japaand any visible signs of the pleasure he tastes from the holy names. In a humble state of mind, the neophyte may emulate these attributes with the aspiration that in due course, he too will become fixed in chanting and privileged to taste its nectar.

In the absence of a great Vaisnava, a devotee can also chant in a temple or holy place in the company of peers and in the presence of Tulasi-devi. Needless to say, the number of rounds chanted must be fixed at a minimum of sixteen. However, if it is possible, then the more rounds the better.

For devotees so inclined and somewhat self-controlled, for devotees who will not fall asleep, Bhaktivinoda Thakura suggests that they retire to a solitary place and chant japawith their heads covered with a cloth. The reasoning is that the sound of the holy name will awaken attraction and melt the heart, dispersing the attitude of apathy and indifference.

To know which of these solutions is most suited for him, a devotee can ask his spiritual master, other senior Vaisnavas, or his counsellor.

The second type of inattentiveness is laziness, jadya-pramada. Jadameans:

**Cold, rigid, dull, dumb, apathetic.**

Readers may enquire:

**“What is the difference between apathy and laziness?”**

The two are certainly similar, although they have distinguishing characteristics. In the context of nama-sankirtanawe answer:

**“Apathy indicates a lack of attraction and motivation to chant; laziness is the unwillingness to make the physical effort to chant.”**

One is about the lack of feeling and the other a lack of activity.

The lazy devotee may have some attraction to chanting, hut due to the mode of ignorance he is too slothful to chant. The apathetic sadhakalacks attraction, but at the same time is not averse to sadbana.When he chants it is mechanical!

A lazy devotee finds chanting burdensome and will quickly fall asleep or become distracted by some non-devotional activity. Such a devotee is someone who is expert at wasting time, and can never finish his rounds.

As with apathy, the best panacea for this disease is to chant with an advanced devotee. The sound vibration he emits will give a lazy neophyte the inspiration and strength to sever the bonds of ignorance. Moreover, the conduct of the advanced devotee is such that he never wastes a moment of his time but is always engaged in service or in chanting Krsna’s names. When a lazy practitioner sees such intense dedication, his heart is stirred and his attitude to nama-sankirtanachanges.

Thus enthused to overcome the lower modes, a neophyte gradually takes shelter of the holy names and dedicates himself to increasing the quality and quantity of his chanting. If Krsna, who is within His devotee’s heart, senses that such determination is sincere, He removes the inertia anchoring His devotee to ignorance. And if a devotee remains resolute, the Lord blesses him with ever-increasing taste for chanting. How this wonderful reciprocation unfolds is described in this beautiful verse:

*srnvatam sva-kathah krsnah*  
*punya-sravana-kirtanah*  
*hrdy antah stho hy abhadrani*  
*vidhunoti suhrt satam*

**“Sri Krsna, the Personality of Godhead, who is the Paramatma \[Supersoul\] in everyone’s heart and the benefactor of the truthful devotee, cleanses desire for material enjoyment from the heart of the devotee who has developed the urge to hear His messages, which are in themselves virtuous when properly heard and chanted.”**

The third form of inattentiveness is distraction, viksepa.The root ksipmeans “to throw,” and when prefixed with a vithe meaning is “to throw, scatter, disperse.” Thus, viksepameans:

**Throwing, scattering, distraction.**

Distraction, viksepa-pramada,takes place when a devotee’s attention is habitually taken from meditation on nama-sankirtanato petty, non-devotional acts or thoughts. Most often a devotee’s mind is distracted by thoughts of sense gratification. The word viksepais evocative. When a devotee scatters his mind to everywhere other than where it should be, namely Krsna’s names, then he is said to be distracted.

This kind of inattention is particularly pernicious. The offences caused by distracted sadhanasow seeds of deeply-rooted material attachments that sadhakasfind difficult to overcome.
