The effect of hearing about Krsna’s pristine qualities is like that of hearing about His divine form, in that Krsna’s qualities further blossom in the heart when they are heard of. The unfolding of Krsna’s qualities follows in sequence the increased appearance of His name and form, and the same may be said of the unfolding of His pastimes.

Since the name of Krsna appears first, it is more prominently manifest than His form, which in turn is more prominently manifest than the qualities, and those more than the pastimes. As meditation matures, these attributes gain strength and influence in the graded way already explained. And they will become equally prominent when love appears. The influence of premais such that Krsna is no longer able to hide His opulences or sweetness from His devotee.

The reader will do well to note that this development of Krsna’s form, qualities, and pastimes is wholly and solely dependent on chanting His holy names. Nama-sankirtanais like the motor which reveals Krsna’s other attributes. When nama-sankirtanastops, these attributes again recede into their source, the holy names. As in all stages of smarana,meditation depends upon consistent progress in chanting. There is no other way.

In this way, while describing dhyana-smaranawe have shown how proficiency in nama-bhajanareveals Krsna’s attributes both sequentially and increasingly.

\* \* \* \*

We had paused our deliberation on dbyanato elaborate on how nama-sankirtanadevelops during meditation and also cultivates the appearance and presence of Krsna’s other attributes, such as His form. Admission into progressive stages of smarana-dasaare made possible solely by the grace of the holy name. Having covered that topic, we now continue our deliberation on meditation.

As dhyanamatures, Krsna’s presence becomes increasingly apparent in the sadhaka’sexternal conduct. One way is that a pure devotee sees His worshipable deity in everyone and in everything. Krsna says, yo mam pasyati sarvatra sarvam ca mayi pasyati:

**“A devotee sees Me everywhere and sees everything in Me.”**

Caitanya Mahaprabhu further elaborates on this way of behaviour to Ramananda Raya:

*sthavara-jangama dekhe, na dekhe tara murti*  
*sarvatra haya nija ista-deva-sphurti*

**“The maha-bhagavata,the advanced devotee, certainly sees everything mobile and immobile, but he does not exactly see their forms. Rather, everywhere he immediately sees manifest the form of the Supreme Lord.”**

Seeing Krsna’s form everywhere means that a devotee is reminded of Krsna wherever he looks. Objects and people become a stimulus lor a further awakening of thoughts of the Lord, and this enables meditation to continue even at times other than secluded bhajana.

A devotee may see a cloud whose colour reminds him of Krsna’s bodily complexion, a river that reminds him of the Yamuna, or a bill of Govardhana,

Another way in which the appearance of Krsna within the heart is perceived externally is in a devotee’s features. Although Kardama Muni had performed severe austerities, because of his Krsna consciousness he appeared healthy and effulgent. In the same way, Krsna’s presence radiates through a devotee’s appearance and demeanour.

**The third way is how a devotee adopts the very qualities upon which he meditates. For example, as a devotee appreciates Krsna’s habit of pleasing speech, he increasingly reflects that conduct by becoming more politely spoken. Even though his father persecuted him in so many ways, when addressing Hiranyakasipu, Prahlada Maharaja remained gracious, addressing him as asura-varya,“the very best of the dynasty of demons.”**

And still another way in which a devotee displays the Lord’s qualities is by perceiving them in the things around him. This is similar to seeing something that reminds the devotee of Krsna’s form, but the devotee now sees His qualities. In the following verse Krsna explains how this takes place:

*raso’ham apsu kaunteya*  
*prabhasmi sasi-smyayoh*  
*pranavah sarva-vedesu*  
*sabdah khe paurusam nrsu*

**“O son of Kunti! I am the taste of water, the light of the sun and the moon, the syllable omin the Vedic mantras; I am the sound in ether and ability in man.”**

In ways like these, spiritualisation of a Vaisnava becomes increasingly apparent, indicating the maturing of nama-bhajanaand the depth of meditations. For an advancing Vaisnava, meditation is not a part of his life, it is his life. And so the discerning observer will be able to appreciate a sadhaka’sspiritual journey by noting how he walks, talks, and conducts himself. Krsna has explained these things to Arjuna in the Bhagavad-gita.

Just as bell metal produces gold when treated with mercury in a fiery crucible, the combination of Krsna’s name, form, and qualities brings into view the pastimes of the Lord. And the appearance of pastimes includes the presence of Krsna’s abode and transcendental associates. This is the mature way in which Krsna’s pastimes make their appearance during nama-sankirtana.

The touchstone of Krsna’s holy name can manifest any and every pastime of the Lord, independent of any effort. Yet the science of bhakti-yogafollows the imperishable laws that were laid down by Krsna Himself. Those laws dictate that just as a devotee must have heard of Krsna’s name, form, and qualities before accessing them through bhajana,in that very same way a devotee must hear of Krsna’s pastimes in order to meditate on them.

Without belabouring a point emphasised several times in this book, the reader cannot underestimate the importance of hearing and reading Srila Prabhupada’s books. How will a devotee remember pastimes if he has not heard them!

The stage of meditation will generally feature remembrance of an individual pastime, which may be about how Krsna runs from His mother in protest to the threat of being tied down, or even a single frame of that pastime, such as His crying elephant tears. Or, a devotee may remember a certain mantra,meditating on the scene it depicts one aspect at a time. This is mantra-dhyana-upasana,or mantramayi-upasana,a topic that has been discussed earlier.

If a devotee does not have an affinity for Krsna’s pastimes, nama-bhajanawill continue to have its purifying effect, and as taste becomes richer, so too will the desire to hear of Krsna’s sports. If, on the other hand, a devotee is mature in spontaneous devotion, he will meditate on pastimes that correspond to the Vraja resident whom he seeks to serve.

Devotees often ask:

**“Is it acceptable to make efforts at meditating on individual or even sequential pastimes?”**

This is similar to questions regarding meditating on krsna’s form or qualities. We answer:

**“Such efforts are acceptable provided that they do not interfere with hearing the holy name.”**

Attentive nama-sankirtanais not only the priority, but it is nourishment for the appearance and development of Krsna’s form, qualities, and pastimes. There is little meaning to nama-bhajanaif the sadhaka’sfull attention is not on the maha-mantra.

Meditation on Krsna’s pastimes should nurture hearing Krsna’s names. Hearing the maha-mantrais so important that it supersedes even meditating on it. Jiva Gosvami says that nama-sankirtana is more effective than nama-smarana. Meditation on pastimes should result in bonding with earlier attainments of name, form, and qualities into a unified whole. If, however, any question remains in the mind of the devotee, then full dependence on the holy names to manifest pastimes is the unerring path to lila-smarana.

While we have already made the upcoming point, because of its importance we shall repeat it again, as it is never redundant:

The offenceless chanting of Krsna’s names spontaneously manifests Krsna’s forms, qualities, and pastimes within the sincere sadhaka’sheart. This takes place without any effort on part of the practitioner to meditate on those attributes. By hearing and reading about Krsna’s qualities, forms, and pastimes, a devotee will gain the favour of those attributes, which will inspire him to elicit their sequential appearance in his nama-bhajana.However, if for example a devotee can meditate on Krsna’s pastimes while remaining fully attentive to the sound vibration of the maha-mantra,then there is no harm in the additional effort. If, however, by such effort hearing the holy names is compromised, then the practitioner should abandon his extra meditation and be confident that chanting will reveal everything in due course.

As meditation on pastimes matures, a taint glimmer of true devotional mellow appears in the heart. Because all the aspects of the holy name are present, albeit in stages of development, the mellow of devotion makes itself known ever so slightly. This attraction towards a mood of bhaktiis characteristic of the stage of asakti, and becomes more persuasive at the next two levels of remembrance, anusmrtiand samadhi.

We close this discussion of dhyanaby citing a verse that shows the power of even this stage of smarana-dasa.A person who meditates on the Lord thus attains a rare devotional liberation:

*yasmin janab prana-viyoga-kale*  
*ksanam samavesya mano ’visuddham*  
*nirhrtya karmasayam asu yati*  
*param gatim brahma-mayo ’rka-varnah*

**“Anyone, even a person in an impure state, who absorbs his mind in Him for just a moment at the time of death burns up all traces of sinful reactions and immediately attains the supreme transcendental destination in a pure, spiritual form as effulgent as the sun.”**

\* \* \* \*

The fourth level of remembrance is constant remembrance, anu- smrtior dhruvanusmrti.

As a sadhakaenters into deep meditation, the ecstasy and success he experiences are addictive, and thus dhyanabecomes continual and known as anusmrti.

Acaryashave likened anusmrtito a stream of oil, or more aptly to a river in spate—an unending, uncontrollable torrent that empties into the ocean of Krsna’s pastimes. In either case constant remembrance is a flood of nectar, and its practitioner the foremost of Vaisnavas, vaisnava-agryah. Since the remembrance of Krsna’s pastimes is continual, anusmrtidisplays the natural characteristic of being sequential. Such a sequence may or may not follow Krsna’s daily eightfold pastimes, depending on the expertise and spontaneity of the sadhaka.

Jiva Gosvami quotes the following definition of constant remembrance by Lord Kapila:

*mad-guna-sruti-matrena*  
*mayi sarva-guhasaye*  
*mano-gatir avicchinna*  
*yatha gangambhaso ’mbudhau*

*laksanam bhakti-yogasya*  
*nirgunasya hy udahrtam*  
*ahaituky avyavahita*  
*ya bhaktih purusottame*

**“The manifestation of unadulterated devotional service is exhibited when one’s mind is at once attracted to hearing the transcendental name and qualities of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Who is residing in everyone’s heart. Just as the water of the Ganges flows naturally down towards the ocean, such devotional ecstasy, uninterrupted by any material condition, flows towards the Supreme Lord.”**

Just as constant remembrance facilitates meditation on Krsna’s pastimes, remembrance of Krsna’s pastimes facilitates constant remembrance. This is the dynamic of raganuga-bhakti,a dynamic that will initiate some level of spontaneity even in the vaidhi-bhakta. This is confirmed by the phrase mano-gatir avicchinna,meaning that the mind is at once attracted.

Scriptures including Srimad-Bhagavatampraise continual remembrance for exhibiting the symptoms of pure devotion, including being free of personal motivation.

A sadhakais never hampered in or deviated from thoughts of Krsna, and would not exchange his devotional wealth for all the treasures of the three worlds. Because of his deep connection to Krsna’s internal potency, and because of his blossoming attachment to remembrance, the practitioner is indifferent to material acquisitions and the miseries of the world. And yet Krsna is mindful not to bestow material opulence on His devotee, as was the case with Bali Maharaja. Where there is wealth and distinction, there is always a risk that a practitioner becomes distracted from his bhajana.Sukadeva Gosvami says,

*na vai bhagavan ñuñaṁ amusyanujagraha yad uta punar*  
*atmanusmrti-mosanam mayamaya-bhogaisvaryam evatanuteti.*

**“The Supreme Personality of Godhead did not award His mercy to Bali Maharaja by giving him material happiness and opulence, for these make one forget loving service to the Lord. The result of material opulence is that one can no longer absorb his mind in the Supreme Personality of Godhead.”**

In the verse that begins with yasyaham anugrhnami,and those following it, Krsna admits that His strategy to ensure that a sadhaka is not distracted again by mayais to divest him of all his personal opulences. Krsna may allow a devotee to accumulate opulence for the purpose of service, notably preaching, but not for sense gratification.

As already mentioned, constant remembrance facilitates a smooth meditation on Krsna’s pastimes that is rich with the ornaments of the Lord’s name, form, associates, and qualities. In tandem with such absorption, a devotee is always eager to hear from other devotees about Krsna’s pastimes and to glorify those pastimes himself, in the way Krsna explains in the Bbagavad-gita.

**“What kind of pastimes is a devotee attracted to?”**

**“Those to which he is attached!”**

**“What if a vaidbi-sadhakadoes not have such attachment?”**

**“Then he should study the truths of pastimes as described in Srimad-Bhagavatam.”**

By doing so he will connect with those pastimes he most resonates with intellectually, and acting on that he will activate his spontaneous life. If he studies which pastimes are the most varied, which influence remembrance the most, and which saints have recommended above others, he will come to a rational conclusion. When he applies that conclusion to his bhajana,his attachment will take root.

These three truths of pastimes are signposts that can direct the path of a regulated devotee’s meditation. Again, they are:

Which pastimes are the most varied; which pastimes influence remembrance the most; and which of the Lord’s sports the saints have recommended above all others.

These are briefly explained below, beginning with:

Which pastimes are the most varied.

Krsna has two kinds of pastimes: those of creation and those of pleasure-sports. Hearing and chanting of the former results in piety and liberation, while that of the latter in love. And the same can be said of remembering His pastimes. The reason for the transcendental superiority of the pleasure pastimes is their captivating nature. They attract the heart, which in a captive state comes under their transcendental influence and becomes the beneficiary of the supreme opulence of prema.

How this happens is connected to the second truth:

Which pastimes influence remembrance the most.

By hearing Krsna’s pleasure-sports, the sadhakais first blessed with transcendental knowledge, which gradually dissolves the knots with which the modes of nature bind the heart. Thereafter the senses loosen their grip on sense objects, and the mind finds increasingly greater delight in remembering that which it has heard. In this way a practitioner becomes attached to thinking of Krsna’s diversion of killing demons and playing with His friends. By this attachment to pastimes he becomes attached to Krsna.

Success in hearing of the Lord is possible in the association of other like-minded saintly souls. By hearing from them, chanting with them, and exchanging realisations, a devotee can become proficient in constant remembrance and thus taste a transcendental pleasure accessible only in advanced association. Narada Muni glorifies the benefits of such sadhu-sanga:

*yatra bhagavata rajan*  
*sadhavo visadasayah*  
*bhagavad-gunanukathana-*  
*sravana-vyagra-cetasah*

*tasmin mahan-mukharita madhubhic-caritra-*  
*piyusa-sesa-saritah paritah sravanti*  
*ta ye pibanty avitrso nrpa gadha-karnais*  
*tan na sprsanty asana-trd-bhaya-soka-mohah*

**“My dear King! In the place where pure devotees live, following the rules and regulations and thus purely conscious and engaged with great eagerness in hearing and chanting the glories of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, in that place if one gets a chance to hear their constant flow of nectar, which is exactly like the waves of a river, one will forget the necessities of life—namely hunger and thirst—and become immune to all kinds of fear, lamentation and illusion.”**

The third truth of hearing pastimes is:

Which of the Lord’s sports the saints have recommended above all others.

Great devotees say that the pastimes of Krsna and His incarnations as described in Vedic literatures are the best. Of those sacred texts, the pastimes in Srimad-Bhagavatamare considered superior, because it is both the essence of the Vedas and the spotless Purana. Among the pastimes glorified in Srimad-Bhagavatam,Krsna’s pastimes are superlative, because as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, His pastimes alone can award the supreme benediction. And because both Krsna and Caitanya Mahaprabhu descended to make known and available the sweetness of vraja-lila,those are the most worthy pastimes of Krsna to hear, chant, and remember.

Vaisnavas opine that the chapters spoken by and about the gopisare better still. And while a transcendental comparison of all Vrndavana pastimes confirms that gopi-lilamanifests the fullness of truths and the pinnacle of sweetness, topics for remembrance cannot be mandated, just as spiritual attraction cannot be legislated. Avirhotra Navayogendra argues that a devotee’s preference is his prerogative, one that is to be confirmed with his spiritual master:

*labdhvanugraha acaryat*  
*tena sandarsitagamah*  
*maha-purusam abhyarcen*  
*murtyabhimatayatmanah*

**“Having obtained the mercy of his spiritual master, who reveals to the disciple the injunctions of Vedic scriptures, the devotee should worship the Supreme Personality of Godhead in the particular personal form of the Lord the devotee finds most attractive.”**

Thus, some devotees will prefer to remember Krsna as the son of Yasoda, others as the friend of Subala, and still others as the beloved of Radha. And a few, like Anupama and Murari Gupta, will be attracted to a Vaikuntha deity like Rama or Narayana, for They, too, are exquisite and attractive in Their own way.

This is the way in which a vaidhi-sadhakaconcludes on what pastimes to hear. By doing so, the effect of those pastimes will be to gradually infiltrate his nama-sankirtanaand—preceded by the appropriate form and qualities of the Lord—they will make their own gradual appearance.

And whatever form of the Lord a devotee concludes is best for him, is best. At least until he concludes otherwise.

\* \* \* \*

Absorbed in nama-bhajana,a devotee’s identification as a specific kind of servant of Krsna becomes increasingly attractive and increasingly dominant. For the sadhakafollowing the vraja vasis,his inclination to a gopior gopa—young or old—indicates readiness for a certain form and service, which naturally become an aspect of his remembrance. These—form and service—are two of the eleven bhavasthat define a resident of Vraja, gopaor gopi When he attains ecstatic devotion, a devotee will confirm or modify those bhavasand also realise the other nine in consultation with a suitably qualified spiritual master.

Cakravarti Thakura says that the very power of remembrance, including a devotee’s awareness of his spiritual identity, is made possible by the Lord’s anusandbana-sakti. This is the potency by which living entities closely inspect or investigate. When applied to bhaktiand specifically to smarana,it is the natural enquiry into one’s original identity and the contemplation thereof.

Krsna also says,

*sarvasya caham hrdi sannivisto*  
*mattah smrtir jnanam apohanam ca,*

**“I am seated in everyone’s heart, and from Me come remembrance, knowledge, and forgetfulness.”**

Thus a devotee’s ability to know his constitutional position is completely dependent on the Lord’s mercy. Even the actual power of remembrance is possible by grace alone. A sadhakamay show eagerness for such attainment, however if he is not qualified for Krsna’s mercy, artificial attempts to impose such realisation will be futile. Not only will they not bear fruit, they will be counterproductive and jeopardise the health of the devotional creeper. For this reason, advanced spiritual guidance is more than helpful.

If for some reason a devotee is qualified for mercy yet does not have access to such a qualified spiritual master, then Krsna will direct the devotee from within his heart.

In this regard we may refer to Krsna’s own statements in the Bhagavad-gitaand their clear commentary by Cakravarti Thakura. To avoid extensive repetition we summarise here the essence of these verses and the acarya'steachings, as reproduced in their entirety in Appendix Six.

The Lord’s instruction addresses the unmotivated devotee absorbed in nama-bhajanaand fully immersed in remembrance of His attributes. How will this devotee proceed without external guidance? How will he realise his svarupa? How will he attain Krsna’s lull mercy? Krsna answers by saying that even without being asked, He will give devotees instruction from within, He will reveal the devotee’s svarupa,and He will bestow His mercy by His personal appearance. Such dedicated devotees need not worry. Ma sucah!

When Krsna’s name is chanted with love, and His form, qualities, and pastimes remembered with affection, a sadhakaattracts the attention of the Lord. And because these attributes of name, form, qualities, and pastimes are part of His constitutional nature, their bhajanaimpels Krsna to become absorbed in affection for His devotee. When a devotee thinks of Krsna’s love for him, he becomes even more absorbed in nama-bhajana,so much so that even hearing a part of the Lord’s name swells the tide of his love for Krsna. Lord Siva tells His wife,

*ra-karadini namani*  
*srnvato devi jayate*  
*pritir me manaso nityam*  
*rama-nama visankaya*

**“O Goddess! Whenever I hear any word beginning with the letter ‘r’ love is awakened in my heart because I think that it may be the name of Rama.”**

In this way, true to His promise, Krsna plays the role of the guru and bestows the fruit of loving devotion to Him.

This chapter has described the first four stages of smarana-dasa, the development of the holy name through those stages, and how the attributes such as form appear by the grace of the name and become more pronounced with deepening remembrance. Furthermore, we have described how the regulative devotee can gradually acquire spontaneity, and the spontaneous sadhakawill develop attraction to a specific name and form of Krsna and His corresponding qualities, pastimes, and associates. We conclude om study of dhruvanusmrtiby emphasising that the attainments of each division of smarana-dasaare cumulative, which means that the attainment of each division, such as the attainment at smarana, is contained within every successive stage, such as in dharana.Thus dhruvanusmrtipossesses the attainments of the first four levels of smarana-dasa.

## Chapter Thirty

**Attaining Trance**

Earlier chapters have outlined the progressive stages of the devotional cultivation known as remembrance in nama-sankirtana, which has as its culmination trance, or samadhi.The current chapter is dedicated to describing the trance of great devotees. This account will enable the reader to envision the perfection of sadhana, bhava,as it unfolds through the samadhiof transcendentalists. Then in the following chapter we will describe the characteristics of, and the means for attaining, smarana-samadbi.In this way readers may become eager for the sadhyathis book has so often spoken of, and knowledgeable of that very last stage of sadhanawhich precedes and strives for that sadhya. We begin by reviewing a practitioner’s progress in smarana-dasa,which was elaborately described in the preceding chapter.

At the first stage, called smarana,the sadhakatries to underhand the Lord, a process that gradually awakens tangible attraction to Krsna in his heart. That attainment is known as dharana, the second step of nama-bhajana.With firm attraction the devotee now meditates not just on Krsna’s name, form, and qualities, but also on His pastimes. This practice is known as dhyana,and its accomplishment gradually submerges the sadhakain the nectar of krsna’s sweetness. Swimming in the ocean of nectar is known as dhruvanusmrti,and diving to the depths of that ocean to collect the pearls of Krsna’s personal appearance is what we know as samadbi—the subject at hand.

\* \* \* \*

After many years of sincere effort, a fortunate devotee arrives at this very last stage of sadbana,the supreme attainment of deep attachment to the Lord. His body, mind, and senses motionless, the trance of the perfected sadhakaresembles the calm waters of the ocean when the wind has ceased.

In the stage of trance, a pure devotee is no longer aware of distinctions like meditator and meditation. What to speak of external things, the only reality for him is the object of meditation, and nothing else.

While absorbed in samadhiin his Himalayan hermitage, Markandeya Rsi’s material mind stopped functioning and he could not notice that Lord Siva and his consort had come to visit him. He was so rapt in thoughts of Krsna that he lost all awareness of himself and the external world. Lord Siva had to invoke his mystic powers to enter the sage’s heart and so rouse him to awareness of his presence.

Such is true samadhi!No longer does the concept of “I am meditating” exist, a consciousness still slightly present at the stage of anusmrti.In samadhithe advanced devotee is submerged in the Lord’s pastimes and attributes. He is like a great shark fearlessly plying the deep waters of the ocean, oblivious to the movements of lesser fish, even more so of those insignificant men on land.

And such was Markandeya trance, which Jiva Gosvami gives as the example of a sadhaka’s samadhi:

*tayor agamanam. saksad*  
*isayor jagad-atmanoh*  
*na veda ruddha-dhi-vrttir*  
*atmanam visvam eva ca*

**“Because Markandeya’s material mind had stopped functioning, the sage failed to notice that Lord Siva and his wife, the controllers of the universe, had personally come to see him. Markandeya was so absorbed in meditation that he was unaware of either himself or the external world.”**

Devotional samadhiparallels the eighth stage of astanga-yoga attained by yogiswith great difficulty, but realised by a pure devotee with relative ease. By the grace of nama-sankirtana,and by serving Krsna and things related to Him, a devotee’s remembrance matures to its perfection. At this stage of devotion, even the vaidhi-sadhakahas an exclusive preference lor the form of Krsna, while the raganuga-bhaktahas a well-defined vision of who he desires to emulate, and in what service to the Divine Couple. Short of transcendental revelation, samadhigives the fullest mental conception of a devotee’s spiritual identity.

In his extensive commentary to the Srimad-Bhagavatamverse beginning with sravanam kirtanam visnoh,Srila Prabhupada summarises this fifth stage of smarana-dasa,saying,

**“\[Samadhior trance is\] awakening a likening for concentration upon a particular form \[of Krsna\]... Therefore samadhi,trance, can be possible in five different ways in terms of one’s relationship.”**

In short, this state of illumination, in which a devotee sometimes relishes a direct vision of the Lord, learned scholars call samadhi and generally is referred to as self-realisation.

Although the practitioner may worship Krsna’s name, form, qualities, and pastimes through the stages of smarana-dasa,with each successive step of his meditation to samadhithese attributes become clearer, sweeter, and fuller, manifesting fullness at the final phases of trance. As stated in the previous chapter, every successive step includes within it the attainments of the previous step, with trance possessing the attainments of all five steps of smarana-dasa.

Moreover, the first four levels of smarana-dasaare sometimes exhibited to their perfection by sadhakaswho have advanced beyond them. Similarly, devotees who have attained transcendence in bhavaand premasometimes exhibit transcendental versions of these five states, especially that of samadhi.While both practitioner and transcendentalist exhibit similarities in the external manifestation of these forms of remembrance, their internal experiences differ significantly. And again, this is very much the case with their absorption in samadhi.

Therefore one must be careful to distinguish the samadhidescriptions of practising devotees from that of their liberated counterparts. As mentioned earlier, we will now give examples of the trance of great devotees and transcendentalists, and in this way illustrate the goal of sadhana-samadhi.

At the beginning of Satya-yuga, Kardama Muni underwent devotional meditation—yoga-misra-bbakti,also known as kriya-yoga with the aim of satisfying the Supreme Lord. Maitreya narrates how Kardama sat in samadhi:

*tatah samadhi-yuktena*  
*kriya-yogena kardamah*  
*samprapede harim bhaktya*  
*prapanna-varadasusam*

**“During that period of penance, the sage Kardama, by worship through devotional service in trance, propitiated the Personality of Godhead, who is the quick bestower of all blessings upon those who flee to Him for protection.”**

The sage was successful in his sadhana,and the Lord appeared to fulfil his desires. However, from the ensuing description it is clear that Lord Visnu appeared not in Kardama’s heart, but externally before his eyes. This exceptional darsanawas possible because of the extreme compassion the Lord felt for Kardama’s austerities. Readers may note just how appreciative Krsna is of the devotee who has attained the very difficult stage of samadhi. After the Lord’s departure, Kardama made his hermitage and underwent penance on the shores of a lake whose name Srimad-Bhagavatam explains:

**“It was called Bindu-sarovara because drops of tears, asru-bindavah,had fallen there from the eyes of the Lord, who was overwhelmed by extreme compassion for the sage who had sought His protection.”**

Kardama Muni was clearly a practitioner, for he harboured a material desire—a good wife who would satisfy his “lustful desire.” It is unusual that at this stage of devotion such desires persist. In pure devotional service, samadhiis characterised by freedom from material desires. The heart is pure. Nonetheless, the Lord considered the sage so dear that He not only fulfilled Kardama’s desires, but became his son.

One may question how it was possible for a yogilike Kardama to become an object of Krsna’s affection, even as his heart was still tainted by lust.

The answer is that while Kardama’s yogic powers elevated him to samadhi,the mercy was made possible by the power of his attachment in devotion. Such is the power of even mixed devotional service. In other words, while a batha-yogimay not see the Lord even after lifetimes of effort, Kardama was able to do so in a relatively short time by being steeped in bhaktias much as he was in yoga.The Lord confirms the power that devotional yoga-samadhihas in attracting Him:

**“O Devarsi! The yogisengaged in meditation are not able to satisfy Me as fully as those engaged in kriya-yoga \[yoga-misra-bhakti\].The kriya-yogiswho have attained dhyana,can, by My grace, rise to the stage of samadbi.”**

It is a rare samadhirevelation that enables a devotee like Kardama Muni to see the Lord with his eyes. If Krsna appears to the sadhaka,He usually does so within their minds.

Pippalayana gives the example of Lord Brahma as a devotee who saw the Lord within himself while in trance. Not only did Brahma see Krsna, but he saw Vaikuntha, was greeted by the Lord with a handshake, and heard Srimad-Bhagavatamin four essential verses. And although all this took place in his heart, Brahma’s experience was one that gave the impression of seeing the Lord with his eyes and experiencing Vaikuntha through his senses. Such is the power of devotional samadhi.The Navayogendras said,

**“When the Lord expands His special mercy, one sees the Lord within by meditation as if directly with the eyes. This we can understand from what happened to lotus-born Brahma.”**

Trance at the stage of ecstatic devotion is the goal of earnest sadhakas.Bilvamangala Thakura is an example of a sadhakaat the advanced stage of bhava.In his Krsna-karnamrtahe reveals the trance of devotees in this formative stage of love for Krsna. The Thakura writes,

*punah prasannendu-mukhena tejasa*  
*puro’ vatirnasya krpa-mahambudheh*  
*tad eva lila-murali-ravamrtam*  
*samadhi-vighnaya kada ñu me bhavet*

**“When will the sweet flute-sound of that youth Who earlier appeared before me and Who is said to be a great ocean of mercy, appear again, displaying the full beauty of His joyful moon-like face and thus destroy the agony of my mind, and the misery of my lonely trance.”**

This verse expresses the author’s yearning for the enchanting modulations of Krsna’s flute-song to interrupt his samadhi-meditation Yet in his commentary, Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami offers a more confidential purport, one that reflects Srimati Radharani’s thoughts in Her samadhi:

**“When will the flute-song of that youth, Who had appeared earlier and directed Me to this grove for pastimes, finally appear carrying the wealth of His joyful, moon-like face, and with that enchanting beauty, destroy the intense pain of My mind.”**

Pausing for a moment, Radha questions whether such good fortune is possible. She then answers Her own doubt.

**“After all! He is an ocean of mercy and as such He can certainly relieve My suffering.”**

With the exception of Radha’s samadhi,these are examples of the trance of great devotees at varying degrees of bhava.And since bhaktimanifests in five different mellows—neutrality, servitorship, friendship, parenthood, and conjugality—the samadbiof devotees differs according to the mood that they adopt.

A practitioner initiates the flow of his meditations, but when his trance gains spontaneous momentum, it is self-propelling. By contrast, the samadhiof a bhava-bhaktarequires no effort; indeed, sometimes it is only with great effort that such trance can be broken. Prahlada Maharaja explained to his teachers that he had no control over his devotion to Krsna. It was controlling him:

*yatha bhramyaty ayo brahman*  
*svayam akarsa-sannidhau*  
*tatha me bhidyate cetas*  
*cakra-paner yadrcchaya*

**“O brahmanas\[teachers\]! As iron attracted by a magnetic stone moves automatically toward the magnet, my consciousness, having been changed by His will, is attracted by Lord Visnu, Who carries a disc in His hand. Thus I have no independence.”**

\* \* \* \*

When ecstatic devotion fully blossoms into prema,the fully spiritual energy of the internal potency fuels the motor of a devotee’s meditations, a samadhiwhich has no comparison to anything within this miserly creation.

A well-known example of prema-samadhiis that of Narada, when he was the son of a maidservant in a previous birth.

Narada relates the events of his spiritual development as they look place in the service of some great devotees who passed the months of caturmasyanear his home. After the death of his mother, even though just a boy, he took to the life of a mendicant and travelled the earth. Finally, in the depths of a jungle beneath the shade of a great banyan tree, he took rest, and after purifying himself, entered a trance of meditation in which he came face to face with the Lord. The sage narrates,

*tasmin nirmanuje ’ranye*  
*pippalopastha asritah*  
*atmanatmanam atmastham*  
*yatha-srutam acintayam*

**“After that, under the shadow of a banyan tree, in an uninhabited forest, I began to meditate upon the Supersoul situated within, using my intelligence, as I had learned from liberated souls.”**

By following the regulative principles of devotion, Narada first attained bhavaand thereafter prema.He was a vaidhi-siddha. Sitting beneath the tree, he followed the process taught to him by the bhaktivedantas,chanting the mantrawith which he was initiated and meditating on the Paramatma in love:

*dhyayatas caranambhojam*  
*bhava-nirjita-cetasa*  
*autkanthyasru-kalaksasya*  
*hrdy asin me sanair harih*

**“As soon as I began to meditate upon the lotus feet of the Personality of Godhead with my mind transformed in transcendental love, tears poured from my eyes, and without delay the Personality of Godhead Sri Krsna appeared on the lotus of my heart.”**

As Narada’s mind was flooded with love, the Lord progressively appeared within his senses: his nose, ears, and eyes. First Narada experienced the fragrance of the Lord’s body, next his ears heard the Lord’s approaching ankle-bells, and finally he beheld the Lord’s beautiful features, beginning with his face:

*prematibhara-nirbhinna-*  
*pulakango ’tinirvrtah*  
*ananda-samplave lino*  
*napasyam ubhayam mune*

**“O Vyasadeva! At that time, being exceedingly overpowered by feelings of happiness, every part of my body became separately enlivened. Being absorbed in an ocean of ecstasy, I could see neither myself nor the Lord.”**

Overwhelmed by symptoms of ecstasy, Narada fainted and so he lost awareness of the Lord and, of course, of himself. When the hoy returned to consciousness, he immediately wanted to invoke his previous vision, and thus undertook the same meditation and chanted the same mantra.Nothing! Try as he might, Narada could not again invoke darsanaof Krsna. After long hours of effort, he heard the Lord’s voice once more:

*hantasmin janmani bhavan*  
*ma mam drastum iharhati*  
*avipakva-kasayanam*  
*dnrdarso ’ham kuyoginam*

**“O Narada! I regret that during this lifetime you will not be able to see Me anymore. Those who are incomplete in service and who are not completely free from all material taints can hardly see Me.”**

It is fascinating that the Lord calls Narada a kuyogi,an incomplete, faulty yogi.After all, he has reached perfection, prema,so how is he incomplete? But the words avipakvaand kasayanammean “immature” and “possessing material dirt respectively.” And the voice continues to tell Narada that in this life he will not be able to see the Lord again. Why? Because the boy’s ensuing fever of separation, his intense desire to see the Lord again, will cleanse his heart of all material desires, hrc-chayan.

Cakravarti Thakura explains that Krsna’s “standard” is to only show Himself once to a devotee who has attained premain a sadhakabody. The reason is that the initial stage of love is still immature, and maturing takes place in the siddha-dehaunder the benevolent effect of intense separation. That separation is made intense by a devotee longing after the vision he once had as a sadhaka.And if there are any defects in the devotee’s heart, they too are burned up in the fire of longing.

What was the contamination in Narada?

Jiva Gosvami explains that Narada had already declared that by realising premahe was free from passion and ignorance. The contamination that he had was of a sattvikanature, which the acarya says was attachment to residence in the forest. What other impurities Narada may have had were not specified, but they too would have been in the same mode of goodness.

Our reader should note that the impurity or impurities of a premi-bhaktalike Narada are not active, but dormant. In other words, the devotee is not actively combating the effect of such an attachment, indeed he is not even aware of it, and yet it remains lodged in the corner of the heart.

To better understand Narada’s attachment we may refer to Jiva Gosvami’s description of three kinds of realised devotees. They anknown as prapta-bhagavat-parsada-deha, nirdhuta-kasaya,and murcchita-kasaya:

**These are devotees who have eternal forms as Krsna’s associates, devotees whose desires are completely washed away, and devotees whose material desires are inactive, respectively.**

Examples of these are Narada when he attained his eternal form, Sukadeva Gosvami, and Narada as a sadhakain his previous life when harbouring the dormant desire to reside in solitude. Bharata Maharaja is also an example of a murcchita-kasaya.His kingly propensity to give shelter to others remained in him, and surfaced as the protector of a deer fawn.

In the paragraphs above, we have shown the samadhiof devotees on the threshold of prema.Vyasadeva is the example of a devotee whose premais mature. Sri Jiva Gosvami cites the follow ing verse as indicative of Vyasa’s trance of love:

*atho maha-bhaga bhavan amogha-drk*  
*suci-sravah satya-rato dhrta-vratah*  
*urukramasyakhila-bandha-muktaye*  
*samadbinanusmara tad-vicestitam*

**“O Vyasadeva! Your vision is completely perfect. Your good fame is spotless. You are firm in vow and situated in truthfulness. And thus you can think of the pastimes of the Lord in trance for the liberation of the people in general from all material bondage.”**

In this verse Narada is requesting his disciple to enter samadhiin which he can see the pastimes of Krsna so that he can later describe them. After Narada’s departure, Vyasa made the most of this blessing and entered into a trance of love which is described in Srimad-Bhagavatam. One may ask:

**“What did he see in trance?”**

The obvious answer is:

**“Vyasa transcribed the contents of his samadhiin Srimad-Bhagavatam.Thus the contents of Srimad-Bhagavatam are the vision of Vyasa.”**

In Tattva-sandarbha,Sri Jiva analyses Vyasadeva’s trance in detail. He does so to show that Vyasa’s samadhiis a product of mature prema,a premathat revealed the original Personality of Godhead, Krsna, in the company of His full potencies.

It is important to show that Vyasa was mature in realisation for two reasons.

First, the ultimate teaching of Srimad-Bhagavatamis how to attain premathrough the practice of sadhana-bhakti.This is conveyed in verses like,

*rajan patir gurur alam bhavatam yadunam*  
*daivam priyah kula-patih kva ca kinkaro vah*  
*astv evam anga bhagavan bhajatam mukundo*  
*muktim dadati karhicit sma na bhakti-yogam*

**“My dear Maharaja Yudhisthira! The Supreme Personality of Godhead Krsna is always ready to help you. He is your master, guru,God, very dear friend, and head of your family. Yet sometimes He agrees to act as your servant or order carrier. You are greatly fortunate because this relationship is possible only by bhakti-yoga.The Lord can give liberation \[mukti\]very easily, but He does not very easily give one bhakti-yoga ,because by that process He is bound to the devotee.”**

Acaryasall agree that the words bhakti-yogain the verse refer to prema.Srila Prabhupada writes in this regard,

**“Krsna readily grants liberation but does not very readily grant perfection in devotional service.”**

Perfection in devotional service means love of God. To properly transmit the truths of prema-bhakti,the author himself must be fully experienced in the same.

The second reason Vyasa’s attainment is important is because he is the teacher of Srimad-Bhagavatam’steacher. To explain the truths of bhaktito their perfection, Sri Suka must also be experienced in prema.And that is only possible if his teacher is similarly spiritually perfected. One can only give what one has.

In conclusion, we must admit that Vyasa’s trance transpired through his mature expression of love for Krsna. After all, scriptures note that the sage Apantaratama became Dvaipayana Vyasa. Some say he is an empowered jiva,an avesa-avatara,while others that he is visnu-tattva,an amsa-avatara.Srila Prabhupada opines for the former. In either case, it is clear that his spiritual identity eminently qualifies him for a samadhiof love.

We have gone to some length to explain Vyasa’s trance of prema, to show the importance that that kind of samadhiplays in the composition of our most authoritative scripture and hence in the subject matter that it presents. By experiencing premaone can teach it and transmit it—bhaktya sanjataya bhaktya, bhaktibegets bhakti.

\* \* \* \*

Finally, we show an example of samadhias experienced by Krsna’s personal associates, the gopis.In His instructions to Uddhava, the Lord remembers the young damsels of Vraja and describes their samadhiof absorption in Him. With great feeling Krsna said,

*ta navidan mayy anusanga-baddha-*  
*dhiyah svam atmanam adas tathedam*  
*yatha samadhau munayo 'bdhi-toye*  
*nadyah pravista iva nama-rupe*

**“My dear Uddhava! Just as great sages in yogatrance merge into self-realisation, like rivers merging into the ocean, and are thus not aware of material names and forms, similarly, the gopisof Vrndavana were so completely attached to Me within their minds that they could not think of their own bodies, or of this world, or of their future lives. Their entire consciousness was simply bound up in Me.”**

The gopisexperienced this state of trance both in Krsna’s presence and in His absence. Whether they were separated from their beloved and meditated on their pastimes with Him, or whether they were actually dancing with Him beneath a moon-lit sky, their absorption surpassed the samadhiof the greatest yogi.

The reader may immediately appreciate how intensely the gopiswere absorbed in Krsna. Even when Krsna was in faraway Dvaraka, they were just as engrossed in meditating on the rasa dance as when they were actually with Him in Vraja, singing, dancing, and embracing. For the gopisthere was no difference between sitting still or dancing, keeping silent or singing, alone or among millions of others; these were all parts of the same trance. And that trance was powered by an extraordinary kind of love known only to them, called adhirudha-mahabhava.

When separated from Krsna, continuous thought of Him so absorbed the gopis’attention that they forgot who they were or where they were. They remembered only pastimes with Him, and that remembrance was so intense that they thought they were actually with Him, relishing His association and the bliss of the rasadance.

Similarly, when the gopiswere actually with Krsna, they forgot where they were or where they had come from. Their minds were so captivated by Krsna that they were not even sure that they were actually with Him. They thought,

**“Surely this is too good to be true. I must be dreaming it all.”**

In other words, the gopis’existence, their constant consciousness, was so much bound up in Krsna that they could not tell whether they were in His manifest or unmanifest pastimes, whether they were dreaming or awake, whether their experience was real or just meditation.

In the pastime of dancing in Lord Jagannatha’s Ratha-yatra, Caitanya Mahaprabhu exhibited the same samadhi.Taking the role of Srimati Radharani, He conversed with Lord Jagannatha in an attempt to bring the Lord back to Vrndavana. During that exchange Jagannatha spoke of the gopis’ecstasy of separation and disclosed its special power:

*mora bhagya mo-visaye, tomara ye prema haye,*  
*sei prema—parama prabala*  
*lukana ama ane, sanga karaya toma-sane,*  
*prakateha anibe satvara*

**“Our loving affairs are more powerful because of My good fortune in receiving Narayana’s grace. This allows Me to come there unseen by others. I hope that very soon I will be visible to everyone.”**

Here and elsewhere, Krsna admits that the samadhiof Radha and Her gopisis so powerful that it forcibly brings Krsna from Dvaraka to Vrndavana, makes Him a living part of their meditations, and facilitates real-life exchanges. Despite that, the gopis continue to think that their pastime with Krsna is a dream. This is the super-excellence of their samadhi.It is second to none.

Although the gopis’ samadhiis compared to that of great sages, the analogy is merely a limited indication, in the way of sakha-candra-nyaya,showing the moon by pointing out the branches of a tree. Great sages have no attraction to Krsna, and neither has He any for them. On the other hand, the gopishave so fully given themselves to Krsna that He feels that even giving Himself to them, still He remains in their debt.

The analogy is valid in the sense that, just as the minds of yogis attain oneness with the object of their meditation, the gopis’minds attained a superlative oneness with their meditation on Krsna.

We may add that the gopisspoken of above were of two kinds. Some, like Radha and Lalita, were Krsna’s eternal associates, while many, many others were pure devotees who became qualified for the Lord’s company as sadhana-siddhasthrough association with the nitya-siddha-gopis.

There are many examples of the trance experienced by Krsna’s eternal associates. Are they relevant to our study of sadhana-sankalpa ?Very much so! Determinations have goals as their aspiration, and the devotion of the gopisdescribed by Krsna is the Vraja-aspiration of Gaudiya Vaisnavas.

In his purport to the verse above, Srila Prabhupada explains that a sadhaka’ssincere aspiration ends in such a wonderful attainment, Because of its relevance we quote the purport in its entirety:

“Krsna has two kinds of presence—prakataand aprakata, manifest and unmanifest. These are identical for the sincere devotee. Even if Krsna is not physically present, the devotee’s constant absorption in the affairs of Krsna makes Him always present. This is confirmed in the Brahma-samhita (5.38):

*premanjana-ccburita-bhakti-vilocanena*  
*santah sadaiva hrdayesu vilokayanti*  
*yam syamasundaram acintya-guna-svarupam*  
*govindam adi-purusam tam aham bhajami*

**“Due to his intense love, the pure devotee always sees Lord Krsna present within his heart. All glories to Govinda, the primeval Personality of Godhead! When Krsna is not manifest before the inhabitants of Vrndavana, they are always absorbed in thoughts of Him. Therefore, even though at that time Krsna was living in Dvaraka, He was simultaneously present before all the inhabitants of Vrndavana. This was His aprakatapresence. Devotees who are always absorbed in thoughts of Krsna will soon see Krsna face to face without a doubt. In other words, devotees who are always engaged in Krsna consciousness and are fully absorbed in thoughts of Krsna certainly return home, back to Godhead. They then see Krsna directly, face to face, talk with Him, and enjoy His company. This is confirmed in the Bhagavad-gita(4.9):** ***tyaktva deham punar janma naiti mam eti so ’rjuna.***

**“Because during his lifetime a pure devotee is always speaking of Krsna and engaging in His service, as soon as he gives up his body he immediately returns to Goloka Vrndavana, where Krsna is personally present.**

He then meets Krsna directly. This is successful human life. This is the meaning of prakateha anibe satvara:

**The pure devotee will soon see the personal manifestation of Lord Sri Krsna.”**

Of course, there are varieties of trance that are unique to Lord Caitanya, Krsna, and Radha, samadhisno other living entity can exhibit. Many of these, along with their symptoms of ecstasy, arc described in Caitanya-caritamrta.They are recorded for us, to encourage us to strive for the kind of samadhifor which we as sadhakasand later as siddhasare eligible for. To progress in the realm of sankalpas,the goal must always be in sight.

Having extensively discussed different kinds of samadhi,we will now return to the trance of the sadhakaand describe their characteristics in the following chapter.

## Chapter Thirty-One

**Perfecting Trance**

Readers will have noted that the sadhanasfor the preceding four stages of smarana-dasaare very similar, in that the activities are primarily chanting, hearing, and remembering under the guidance of qualified spiritual masters. What varies from stage to stage is the subject matter for hearing and remembering, as well as an increased attraction for spontaneous practice by both the regulated and the spontaneous sadhaka.In the same way, the last stage of sadhana,trance, generally shares the practice common to the preceding stages.

The regulated and mostly-regulated devotee will transit along the stairway of samadhimainly by hearing and remembering the names of Krsna. His sadhanawill not include a deeply-felt identity as a vraja-vasi,nor will it intently follow any of Krsna’s associates.

His general devotion finds its strength in its knowledge, faith, and attraction to Krsna.

The spontaneous devotee, on the other hand, will increase hearing and learning about the vraja-vasiswhom he aspires to follow. As he does, his sense of identity as a gopior gopaboth deepens and widens. “Deepens” means that he increasingly identifies with the Vraja service and form that he covets, and “widens” means that his inclination to a Vraja-identity expands to aspire for some or all of the remaining nine aspects of ekadasa-bhavas.

These are the two general paths taken by the regulated and the spontaneous devotee through the stages of samadhi,from where Krsna’s grace will finally elevate them to bhava.While there is more to the sadhanajourney of these devotees, scripture and acaryasdo not give much detail. Bhaktivinoda Thakura elaborates somewhat further on the perfection of the raganuga-bhakta,however we have already mentioned that the path of siddha-pranaliis not one taught by his successors and thus we do not write further on it. Readers wishing to know what Bhaktivinoda Thakura wrote may research Jaiva-dharmaand Harinama-cintamani.

In preceding chapters we have explained how a sincere devotee is never bereft of suitable spiritual guidance. Either his spiritual masters or the Lord within will ensure that the advanced sadhaka has the proper instruction to follow the devotion of his choosing, be that regulated or spontaneous. The Lord gives this assurance as a personal guarantee:

*ananyas cintayanto mam*  
*ye janah paryupasate*  
*tesam nityabhiyuktanam*  
*yoga-ksemam vahamy aham*

**“But those who always worship Me with exclusive devotion, meditating on My transcendental form—to them I carry what they lack, and I preserve what they have.”**

Seasoned wood and air from bellows employed in greater quantity can transform a small fire for boiling water into an inferno for melting gold. Similarly, attentive nama-sankirtanaand regular hearing of Krsna’s pastimes can elevate smaranathrough the stages of remembrance to samadhi.What is possible for the experienced blacksmith is also possible for the spiritually enlightened sadhaka. The same spiritual intelligence with which a practitioner attained lower stages of devotion will enable him to attain the exalted stage of trance. Of this process no more need be said.

We shall dedicate the rest of this chapter to describing the attributes of the sadhakaascending the stage of samadhi.The attributes of the fortunate Vaisnava who has reached the doorstep of samadhi are of vital relevance to this book, because trance is the stage of devotion from which one is elevated to bhava.These attributes are an indication of what attracts Krsna’s attention and of the eligibility to attain His grace. A devotee who is in knowledge of these qualities knows the markers that signal the approach to love.

In this age of Kali it is rare to find people who are interested in, what to speak of who will attain, samadhi.By contrast, in Satya-yuga everyone lives in a state of divine trance. Thus they have no interest in economic development or sense gratification. Rather, they are self-satisfied, merciful, friendly, peaceful, sober, and tolerant. They take pleasure from within, see all things equally, and, endeavouring for spiritual perfection, they worship the Supreme Personality by austere meditation and internal and external sense control.

These characteristics of trance are also introduced at the beginning of the Bhagavad-gita.In the second chapter Krsna calls upon Arjuna to transcend the modes of nature. In response Arjuna asks,

**“What are the symptoms of such a perfected soul?”**

Krsna’s answer is summarised as follows:

**One who has attained samadhihas given up all desire for sense gratification. His purified mind finds satisfaction in the self and is neither disturbed when subjected to the threefold miseries, nor elated when showered with happiness. Unaffected by whatever evil or good may come his way, he neither despises nor praises it, but remains steady—free from attachment, fear, and anger. When in trance the devotee withdraws all his senses from sense objects in the way that a tortoise draws its limbs within the shell. And although he has abandoned sense enjoyment, even if a slight taste for sense objects remains in him, he remains fixed in consciousness by experiencing a higher taste from within.**

Some of the characteristics mentioned above, as well as some not mentioned, are worthy of elaboration. The features of samadhiwe have chosen to emphasise are:

**Its liberated status, the realisations it affords, freedom from bodily identification and other illusions, freedom from karma, fearlessness, exclusive interest in Krsna’s pastimes, the qualification to see Krsna, and spiritual perfection from which fall down is rare.**

We begin by showing bow a devotee in trance, while not yet fully liberated, has the symptoms of a liberated soul, or one absorbed in brahmananda.

When Prajapati Daksa was beheaded at the demigods’ sacrifice, they were advised by Lord Brahma to ask Lord Siva’s forgiveness for their offences. When a delegation of demigods arrived at Kailasa, they found Lord Siva in a trance of meditation. Maitreya described that greatest of Vaisnavas in this way:

*tam brahma-nirvana-samadhim asritam*  
*vyupasritam girisam yoga-kaksam*  
*sa-loka-pala munayo mañuñam*  
*adyam manum pranjalayah pranemuh*

**“All the sages and demigods, headed by Indra, offered their respectful obeisances unto Lord Siva with folded hands. Lord Siva was dressed in saffron garments and absorbed in trance, thus appearing to be the foremost of all sages.”**

The verse equates Lord Siva’s trance with brahma-nirvana,or the bliss of liberation brahmananda.Clearly a great devotee is not absorbed in impersonal meditation. Thus we may understand that Siva’s complete absorption in his worshipable Lord Sankarsana equals the stage of liberation. In his purport Srila Prabhupada confirms this conclusion:

**“Samadhimeans particularly concentrated attention, so one who has achieved the qualification of always meditating on the Personality of Godhead is to be understood to be always in trance and enjoying brahma- nirvana,or brahmananda.”**

How does the samadhiof the sadhakaequate to the bliss of a liberated jnanior yogi? Prahlada Maharaja answers:

*tad brahma-nirvana-sukham vidur budhas*  
*tato bhajadhvam hrdaye hrd-isvaram*

**The boy tells his schoolmates that all learned men know well that complete meditation on Krsna gives a pleasure that equals or surpasses the pleasure of liberation. In short, the bliss of samadhi equals the bliss of liberation.**

This is further confirmed by Krsna when He declares that pure devotion is superior to liberation in this well-known verse:

*brahma-bhutah prasannatma*  
*na socati na kanksati*  
*samah sarvesu bhutesu*  
*mad-bhaktim labhate param*

**“One who is thus transcendentally situated at once realises the Supreme Brahman and becomes fully joyful. He never laments or desires to have anything. He is equally disposed toward every living entity. In that state he attains pure devotional service unto Me.”**

\* \* \* \*

The next feature of samadhiis that the advanced sadhakais endowed with realisation of devotional truths.

A consequence of intense nama-bhajanaand absorption in Krsna’s form and pastimes is that a devotee naturally becomes realised in the confidential truths regarding Krsna. Such realisation comes from hearing, but it also awakens spontaneously as he progresses through the stages of smarana-dasa.This devotional wonder is confirmed by Suta Gosvami at the beginning of Srimad-Bhagavatam:

*vasudeve bhagavati*  
*bhakti-yogah prayojitah*  
*janayaty asu vairagyam*  
*jnanam ca yad ahaitukam*

**“By rendering devotional service unto the Personality of Godhead, Sri Krsna, one immediately acquires causeless knowledge and detachment from the world.”**

In commenting on Krsna’s assertion that is in samadhia devotee experiences a divine state that is free of all miseries, Srila Prabhupada says,

**“One in full samadhihas realised Brahman, Paramatma, and Bhagavan.”**

His Divine Grace emphasises that the stage of trance gives a devotee full realisation of the three features of the Absolute Truth. This is because he is increasingly in contact with Krsna’s samvit-sakti. cognitive potency. As such the sadhakais empowered with both knowledge, jiiana,and realised knowledge, vijnana.

In his Krsna-samhita,Thakura Bhaktivinoda highlights fifteen truths that are realised by a devotee who has attained samadhi.The Thakura says that these truths are both very subtle and otherwise inconceivable to the unqualified speculator.

While words represent objects, they cannot fully convey the experience an object transmits. The word “apple” offers the con cept of a fruit, but cannot convey the taste of an apple. Similarly, the following words represent certain truths which can only be experienced by the realised soul. They are but some of the spiritual treasures awaiting serious practitioners. These realisations are the truth of:

**The self; the insignificance of the self; the supreme shelter, Krsna; the relationship between the shelter and the sheltered, the devotee; the beauty of the qualities, activities, and form of the shelter; the relationships amongst the sheltered; the abode of the shelter and the sheltered; the absolute time factor; the various moods of the sheltered; the eternal pastimes between the shelter and the sheltered; the energies of the shelter; both the advancement and degradation of the sheltered by the energies of the shelter; the misidentification of the degraded sheltered; the cultivation of devotional service for restoration of the degraded sheltered; and the degraded sheltered regaining their constitutional position through devotional service.**

These are some of the realisations that result from samadhi.

The next characteristic to be studied is how trance frees one from every aspect of bodily identification.

Freedom from all bodily-related illusions is also a separate characteristic of the brahma-bhutastage and so we give it special emphasis. The reason is because of the significant role that attachment to and detachment from the body plays in the relative bondage and liberation of a practitioner.

Freedom from the demands of the body does not mean that the body ceases to exist. Although Krsna takes charge of His devotee, He does not free a surrendered soul from all traces of karma. Were He to do so, the sadhakawould be unable to complete his devotional service without a body. Therefore both the gross and subtle body, along with the vital air and senses, must continue under the control of divine destiny. However, the self-realised practitioner is a master of his body and no longer a surrendered slave of its demands or its various manifestations. Neither will he ever he! Indeed, the advanced sadhakalooks upon his body as no more than something that is experienced in a dream.

Although Gaudiya Vaisnavas intensely engage their bodies and the world in spreading Lord Caitanya’s sankirtanamovement, they always remain aloof from illusion by remembering that those things are not the ultimate reality but a temporary one. Despite hands-on contact with the material world, realised detachment creates a chasm between the sadhakaand sense objects. He may appear attached, but he is not.

The Hamsa-avatara reveals how far removed from the body a devotee really is. While an avadhutamay externally exhibit the detachment in this example, most Gaudiyas internalise it. The Lord says,

*deham ca nasvaram avasthitam utthitam va*  
*siddho na pasyati yato ’dhyagamat svarupam*  
*daivad apetam atha daiva-vasad upetam*  
*vaso yatha parikrtam madira-madandhah*

**“Just as a drunken man does not notice if he is wearing his coat or shirt, similarly one who is perfect in self-realisation and who has thus achieved his eternal identity does not notice whether the temporary body is sitting or standing. Indeed, if by God’s will the body is finished or if by God’s will he obtains a new body, a self-realised soul does not notice, just as a drunken man does not notice the situation of his outward dress.”**

Prahlada Maharaja is an example of a devotee in samadhiwho, as mentioned previously, was completely oblivious of the needs or workings of his body. Narada Muni explains that the boy was so engrossed in thoughts of Krsna that he went about his daily activities out of habit. Prahlada was unaware of his own actions, which were directly carried out on his behalf by the Supreme Lord.

After Hiranyakasipu was killed and the boy was enthroned as the emperor of the three worlds, Prahlada Maharaja went about the duties of a king with attention to the welfare of all his subjects. In both boyhood and monarchy, Prahlada Maharaja was situated in the same spiritual trance. However, once kingly duties demanded his attention to the kingdom, he internalised the same detachment from his body that he had once manifest externally. This illustrates how extreme indifference to the demands of the body are manifest and unmanifest by self-realised souls.

A devotee in trance exhibits and experiences no connection to his own body. He sees his body as the property of the Lord, an instrument to be engaged exclusively in Krsna’s service. Scriptures are replete with descriptions of this attainment, for it is the goal of all practising Vaisnavas.

In Srimad-Bhagavatamthere are two almost identical verses that praise the detachment at smarana-samadhi.One is spoken by Kapiladeva and the other by the Hamsa-avatara. This is the one spoken by the son of Devahuti:

*deho ’pi daiva-vasagah khalu karma yavat*  
*svarambhakam pratisamiksata eva sasuh*  
*tam sa-prapancam adhirudha-samadhi-yogah*  
*svapnam punar na bhajate pratibuddha-vastuh*

**“The body of such a liberated yogi,along with the senses, is taken charge of by the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and it functions until its destined activities are finished. The liberated devotee, being awake to his constitutional position and thus situated in samadhi, the highest perfectional stage of yoga,does not accept the by-products of the material body as his own. Thus he considers his bodily activities to be like the activities of a body in a dream.”**

\* \* \* \*

The material energy is an unlimited storehouse of illusions. And these are largely connected to the material body, as it is a most suitable vehicle for the illusory energy to fulfil its purposes. A further bodily illusion is the urge to sleep.

Srila Prabhupada would say, “Sleep is death.” However, intense attachment to Krsna overcomes this bodily function, which generally drags a person into ignorance. Arjuna is an example of a devotee who had overcome the urge to eat and sleep by unceasing remembrance of Krsna. For that reason, Krsna calls him Gudakesa, “one who has conquered sleep.”

Even when asleep an advanced devotee is never derelict in thinking of Krsna’s name, form, qualities, and pastimes. By such constant absorption in Krsna, a devotee connects with the internal potency, by grace of which he conquers both sleep and ignorance. Srila Prabhupada says,

**“This is called Krsna consciousness, or samadhi,”**

In addition to false bodily identification and ignorance, three other kinds of illusion are primary causes of material bondage—attachment, hatred, and pride. Krsna says that these and all other kinds of illusion are no longer known to the devotee in trance. To Uddhava the Lord explains, yoganam atma-samrodhah:

**“Among the eight progressive states of yogaI am the final stage, samadhi,in which the soul is completely separated from illusion.”**

The final characteristic of illusion and bodily identity is the influence of the modes of nature.

Devotees are often curious:

**“Is an advanced sadhaka,such as a devotee at the stage of samadhi,a transcendentalist?”**

The short answer is:

**“No! But neither is he a victim of the modes of nature.”**

An advanced devotee is completely free of ignorance and passion that has already been explained. And yet the mode of goodness endures until a devotee attains bhava,of which the sadhakasitu ated in samadhifalls short. And yet we have clear scriptural statements that a devotee surrendered to Krsna, one fully engaged in undeviating devotion, is above the modes of nature.

For example, Krsna tells Uddhava, nirguno mad-apasrayah:

**“A worker who has taken shelter of Me is understood to be transcendental to the modes of nature.”**

And to Arjuna the Lord speaks this well-known verse:

*mam ca yo ’vyabhicarena*  
*bhakti-yogena sevate*  
*sa gunan samatityaitan*  
*brahma-bhuyaya kalpate*

**“One who engages in full devotional service, unfailing in all circumstances, at once transcends the modes of material nature and thus comes to the level of Brahman.”**

These references clearly indicate that the devotee fully immersed in trance is transcendental to the modes of nature even if he has not attained full liberation at bhava.

This interesting dichotomy can be explained in the following way:

An accomplished practitioner fully absorbs his senses in Krsna’s name, form, pastimes, and so on. By so doing, the Lord’s transcendental qualities are the objects of his gross and subtle senses, and so his body and mind transcend the influence of the modes, even of goodness. In that sense he is transcendental, or as we have explained earlier, he is spiritualised.

However, when the sadhakacomes out of his trance of devotion and goes about activities like eating and bodily maintenance, his senses contact mundane sense objects and take on their qualities. Since an advanced devotee will associate with things in the mode of goodness, he adopts that mode. So in this sense the practitioner is conditioned.

In other words, while the sadhakais engaged in trance he is transcendental, but when he is not in trance he is in the mode of goodness. From this we conclude that a practitioner who attains samadhihas both a transcendental and a mundane disposition. Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains this phenomenon in his commentary to a verse of Srimad-Bhagavatam.

That said, accomplished devotees who have strong attachment to the Lord remain absorbed in trance even when not engaged in nama-sankirtana.These devotees are of two types:

Those who continue to actively remember Krsna and so do not relate well to practical duties, and those whose bhajanais so powerful that the momentum of their trance carries them through practical, day-to-day dealings.

CakravartI Thakura points out that the extent to which a devotee is absorbed in trance, to that degree his body and mind are transcendental, the balance remaining material. But when that devotee attains prema,the material aspect of his body disappears and he becomes fully transcendental: not spiritualised, but spiritual. This proportional relationship between absorption in nama-bhajanaand transcendence is revealed in the following words of Sri Kavi:

*bhaktih paresanubhavo viraktir*  
*anyatra caisa trika eka-kalah*  
*prapadyamanasya yathasnatah syus*  
*tustih pustih ksud-apayo 'nu-ghasam*

**“Devotion, direct experience of the Supreme Lord, and detachment from other things—these three occur simultaneously for one who has taken shelter of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, in the same way that pleasure, nourishment, and relief from hunger come simultaneously and increasingly with each bite for a person engaged in eating.”**

To further respond to the earlier question:

**“In the time that a devotee is in trance he is transcendentally situated, and in the time that he is otherwise engaged he remains above the modes to the degree that he retains his absorption of trance.”**

A sadhaka’stranscendence is based on his connection with the transcendental, not with his own liberated condition. This is the way references to the practitioner being above the modes should be understood. This understanding applies to other stages of smarana-dasa,indeed to any stage of pure devotion. By deep absorption, a devotee even at the beginning stage of sadhanacan experience occasional freedom from the modes.

How the sadhakaenjoys the state of liberation at the stage of trance is praised in this way:

*cetah khalv asya bandhaya*  
*muktaye catmano matam*  
*gunesu saktam bandhaya*  
*ratam va pumsi muktaye*

**“The stage in which the consciousness of the living entity is attracted by the three modes of material nature is called conditional life. But when that same consciousness is attached to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, one is situated in the consciousness of liberation.”**

This concludes, albeir at length, the quality of a devotee’s freedom from the influence of the material body. The next attribute of a devotee in trance is how he is free from bad habits, karma.

Bad habits, anarthasthat result from past karma,are completely washed away for a devotee who is constantly engrossed in thoughts of Krsna. He is not only free of karma—an attainment reached with steady recollection—but of all impressions and effects of karma.He does not even remember them.

Yet there are other anarthasthat are more pervasive than those resulting from past pious or sinful acts.

These are obstructive habits that result from offences to the holy name.

Since the means of success for a devotee is the quality of his nama-bhajana,those activities which offend the holy name are clearly counterproductive. Indeed, when the holy name is offended, the devotee is faced with resilient reactions. Remembrance effectively purifies these offences, and the stages of smarana-dasasystematically clear them from the heart. By the time a devotee reaches samadhi,the effect of such offences in bhajanais minimal. Yet they can be discerned by how quickly the Lord’s grace is achieved.

Another symptom of samadhiis fearlessness.

The yogiswho are in trance in remote places, like the heart of the jungle or the cave of a mountain, are easy prey for wild animals or snakes. Yet they are so absorbed in meditation that they are unaware of external circumstances. Their faith is in Krsna, Who controls the activities of all living things, wild or good-natured. And because of their strong faith they have nothing to fear.

The same may be said of devotees relishing the trance of nama-bhajana.Like Haridasa Thakura, who shared a cave with a poisonous snake, they have given themselves to Krsna. It is now up to Him whether they live or die. They are fearless.

*The Srimad-Bhagavatamsays,*  
*bhayam dvitiyabhinivesatah syad*  
*isad apetasya viparyayo ’smrtih*

**“Fear arises when a living entity misidentifies himself as the material body because of absorption in the external, illusory energy of the Lord.”**

A devotee in samadhihas no attachment to or identification with either his body or mind, and he is free from the influence of the modes; how then can fear enter his heart? And because he is always absorbed in Krsna, he partakes of Krsna’s quality of fearlessness He is abhaya-carana.

Prabodhananda Sarasvati describes the fearless sadhakain this way:

*na tapah sadhunam akrtisu tatha sadhu-krtisu*  
*prakampah kalaher api na hi na va deha-dalane*  
*praharso na brahmady-adhikavi-bhave napi parama-*  
*mrta-brahmanande samadhigata-vrndavana-bhuvah*

**“A devotee relishing the mellows of samadhiin the land of Vraja neither suffers from impious or pious deeds, nor does he tremble in fear of his body’s demise due to the snake of time. He is not interested in the opulences of Brahma or other demigods, and he has no inclination to taste the eternal bliss of impersonal Brahman.”**

\* \* \* \*

The aforementioned characteristics of trance may be said to be its marginal features, tatastha-laksana.Its principal attribute, svarupa-laksana,is disinterest in anything other than thoughts of Krsna, the pastimes of Krsna, and chanting the names of Krsna.

Jiva Gosvami gives the sage Markandeya as the example of a devotee who is so absorbed in trance that he has no awareness of what is happening around him, even when Lord Siva and his wife appear in person:

*tayor agamanam saksad*  
*isayor jagad-atmanoh*  
*na veda ruddha-dbi-vrttir*  
*atmanam visvam eva ca*

**“Because Markandeya’s material mind had stopped functioning, the sage failed to notice that Lord Siva and his wife, the controllers of the universe, had personally come to see him. Markandeya was so absorbed in meditation that he was unaware of either himself or the external world.”**

An advanced devotee’s obsession with Krsna is obvious in his dealings. He is always talking about Krsna, whether asked to or not. As a preacher, such a devotee is willing to take any risk to give others the holy name, because to him that is the only thing of value or importance in the universe. Absorption in Krsna is spontaneous and effortless, therefore sometimes such a devotee becomes distracted from his preaching, his household affairs, or work, and returns to thoughts of the Lord’s pastimes, which is his default mode.

A devotee whose attachment to Krsna has just matured will be new to the current of devotion sweeping his heart downstream towards the cascading waterfall of ecstasy. As a novice in managing external symptoms of devotion, he may sometimes startle observers with his behaviour, giving them the impression of being a daydreamer, or even mentally disturbed. Ignorant people will be apologetic, offenders will call him a sahajiya,but learned Vaisnavas will know that he has fallen into the celestial river of trance, relishing the sweet nectar of attachment to Krsna’s pastimes.

This wonderful state of devotion brings along with it one extraordinary quality: it qualifies the devotee to see Krsna.

That qualification is not like the access to pastimes of the premi-bhakta,or the occasional vision of the bhava-bhakta.But it is an eligibility brought about by intense attachment nonetheless.

Readers may question:

**“How does a practitioner have the qualification to see Krsna?”**

The answer is:

**“Sadhana-bhakticaptivates Krsna and also controls Him. Therefore, if the sadhaka’sdesire is strong enough, it is not impossible for him to see Krsna.”**

Of course, this control is not the control that loving devotion exerts over the Lord, but it is control nonetheless. Were that not the case, Krsna would not make attachment a condition for awarding love, a topic we have already discussed. How Krsna is con trolled by sadhanais explained in the following verse:

*na sadhayati mam yogo*  
*na sankhyam dharma uddhava*  
*na svadhyayas tapas tyago*  
*yatha bhaktir mamorjita*

**“My dear Uddhava, the unalloyed devotional service rendered to Me by My devotees brings Me under their control. I cannot be thus controlled by those engaged in mystic yoga, sahkhyaphilosophy, pious work, Vedic study, austerity, or renunciation.”**

With the use of the word sadhayati,Krsna clearly says that bhakti brings Him under its control.

**“Does bhaktihere refer to practice or perfection?”**

**“Jiva Gosvami argues that because bhaktiis contrasted with other sadhanaslike yogaand sankhya,Krsna must be speaking of sadhana-bhakti.”**

The rule is that like must be contrasted with like. So when this verse speaks of bhaktiit speaks of sadhana-bhakti,the means to control Krsna at any stage of its practice, what to speak of at its culmination, trance.
