Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s sole written instruction to the world is contained in His Sri Siksastaka.These eight verses are named “teachings” but they are actually “teachings on nama-bhajana.” The introductory verse describes the seven perfections of nama-sankirtana,and the next verse the unfortunate condition of the people of this age who have no taste for chanting. The third verse sets out the primary qualification for steady sadbana,which is humility. The fourth verse expresses the natural detachment of one who has taste for chanting, ruci;the fifth of a devotee attached to Krsna, praying for admittance into ecstatic devotion. The sixth verse describes the external symptoms of the fortunate Vaisnava who has attained bhavaand is hankering after prema,while the seventh and eight verses praise the perfected soul who tastes premain separation and meeting, respectively. The reader will find Appendix Seven, the eight verses of Sri Siksastaka,useful to refer to while reading this chapter.

Bhaktivinoda Thakura instructs us that a devotee’s nama-bhajanashould follow the guidance of the verses of Siksastaka.By such smaranaa devotee will eventually awaken all transcendental truths, free himself of all impiety, and perceive the eightfold pastimes enacted within his purified heart.

Srila Prabhupada would regularly cite the seventh verse of Siksastakaas the example of what chanting in separation was all about. Another verse that Srila Prabhupada was fond of quoting as an example of vipralambha-bhajanawas the eighth verse of Srinivasa Acarya’s Sad-gosvamyastaka.

We shall briefly review both verses, beginning with the one spoken by Caitanya Mahaprabhu:

*yugayitam nimesena*  
*caksusa pravrsayitam*  
*sunyayitam jagat sarvam*  
*govinda-virahena me*

**“My Lord Govinda! Because of separation from You, I consider even a moment a great millennium. Tears flow from My eyes like torrents of rain, and I see the entire world as void.”**

On a morning walk in Bombay, Srila Prabhupada called this verse, and the mood of chanting it inspires, the summit of Krsna bhajana:

**“This is the summit of bhajana,when one will be crying and there will be torrents of tears, and one will see everything as vacant for being separated from Govinda. That is the topmost summit of Krsna bhajana.”**

Srila Prabhupada, like his spiritual master, was emphatic that Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s path to perfection “for the common person” was learning to feel separation from Krsna. That was what the Lord had descended to teach, and that lesson is clearly expressed in the words yugayitam nimesenaand sunyayitam jagat sarvam.This is the standard of feeling separation, Every second, every blink of the eye that separates one from Krsna appears like an age, and a universe teeming with life, crowded with stars and planets, yet without Him, is like a Buddhist void. The gopisactually felt like that, and so they criticised Brahma for creating eyelids that blinked and obstructed them from seeing Krsna. The gopissaid,

*atati yad bhavan ahni kananam*  
*trutir yugayate tvam apasyatam*  
*kutila-kuntalam sri-mukham ca te*  
*jada udiksatam paksma-krd drsam*

**“O Krsna, when You go to the forest during the day and we do not see Your sweet face, which is surrounded by beautiful curling hair, half a second becomes as long as an entire age for us. And we consider the creator, who has put eyelids on the eyes we use for seeing You, to be simply a fool.”**

The sadhanain which a devotee attempts to see Krsna and the one in which he cries after Krsna are both valid. However, the path of sambhogais for a very rare and qualified sadhaka,whereas the path of vipralambhais for the common person, and thus it is both faster and more assured.

One may compare the two to the process of self-realisation through either meditation or through sankirtana.Both are possible, but who has the purity of mind or the lifespan to meditate for thousands of years? Better we adhere to the path of nama-sankirtanaas recommended by scripture and by Gauranga. Similarly, better to follow the process of vipralambha-sevaas endorsed by Caitanya Mahaprabhu and His acaryas.

And yet we see even today that immature and unqualified pseudo-devotees futilely follow the sadhanaof sambhoga.Because they are like a baby monkey hanging onto its mother’s back, such foolish devotees fall from the path due to its difficulty. They do not advance in bhakti,nor do they enjoy Gaura’s shelter, and so they become victimised by sex life, intoxication, and other wanton ways. And yet some foolish neophytes still continue to follow this dead-end road to spiritual destruction.

In general these practitioners are grouped into the category of sahajiyas,or those who have rejected the authorised siddha-pranali m exchange for a cheap sadhanaconcocted by tiny minds. Indeed, our acaryasconsidered all sadhanasthat do not follow the process of vipralambha-sevato be averse to the process of pure devotional service. Those who take up such paths are not followers of Caitanya Mahaprabhu.

In the course of Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s pastimes, His associates never assisted Him in conjugal affairs.

**“What did they do?”**

**“They saw themselves as helpers in nourishing the Lord’s feelings of separation.”**

In searching after Krsna, Caitanya Mahaprabhu would fall into the ocean, or wander around Puri in the dead of night. And when the Lord momentarily saw or felt Krsna, He very quickly lost that darsana,only to be plunged into even deeper feelings of separation in which He relished even wilder ecstasies than before. In a bewildered state He would hold Svarupa Damodara by the neck and cry,

“Where is Krsna? Please show Him to Me.”

That is the perfection sadhakasare meant to emulate, but not imitate.

Lord Caitanya taught us to feel separation. From whatever stage of sadhanawe can experience a distance between us and Krsna, from that stage we should try to feel separation from Him. And from whatever stage of sadhanawe can experience a distance between us and bhava-bhakti,from that stage we should try to feel separation from perfection. Then we should incorporate those feelings, that bhava-seva,into our sadhanaand our life. A sadhaka must make the sankalpato adopt such a mood of service, and as he progresses through the stages of bhakti,the mood of vipralambha should be the ever-brighter beacon that illumines his determinations.

Indeed, a measure of spiritual advancement is how much we can feel separation. The more we feel separation, the more we are advancing.

An intelligent sadhakawill conclude that the process of seeing Krsna is actually through learning to cry after Him in the way that Caitanya Mahaprabhu cried. Such a wise devotee will learn to feel how time without Krsna is the creator’s form of punishment, and he will learn to be satisfied with nothing and no one, save Krsna. That is the path of perfection, the siddha-pranali.

We conclude this review of the Siksastakaverse with a beautiful quote from Srila Prabhupada, spoken on the appearance day of Srimati Radharani:

**“This process of devotional service is taught by Caitanya Mahaprabhu. Not that very easily, ‘We have seen Krsna or seen Radharani in rasa-lila.’ No! Not like that. Feel the separation. The more you feel separation from Krsna, you should understand that you are advancing. Don’t try to see Krsna artificially. Be advanced in separation feeling, and then it will be perfect. That is the teachings of Lord Caitanya... Don’t try to see Krsna. You cannot see Krsna with your material eyes. Neither you can hear about Him with your material ears. Neither you can touch. But if you engage your tongue in the service of the Lord \[by chanting Hare Krsna and taking prasadam\],then He’ll reveal Himself to you, ‘Here I am.’ That is wanted. So feel separation of Krsna just like Radharani, as Lord Caitanya teaches us, and engage your tongue in the service of the Lord; then, one day, when you are mature, you’ll see Krsna eye to eye.”**

Let us now scrutinise the verse in Sad-gosvamyastakathat Srila Prabhupada was so fond of quoting.

\* \* \* \*

The teachings of Caitanya Mahaprabhu have been preserved in all their perfection by His devoted followers. From the Six Gosvamis to Srila Prabhupada, the sadhanaand sadhyathat Lord Caitanya brought from Goloka has been passed down through the parampara.Unfortunately, deviations from Gauranga's siddha-pranali abound even today. Such is the expected influence of Kali.

Integral to both practice and perfection is their corresponding mood, the mood of separation. Srinivasa Acarya narrated how he witnessed the Gosvamis of Vrndavana—eternally liberated souls— express and taste their perfection in devotion:

*he radhe vraja-devike ca lalite he nanda-suno kutah*  
*sri-gouardhana-kalpa-padapa-tale kalindi-vane kutah*  
*ghosantav iti sarvato vraja-pure khedair maha-vihvalau*  
*vande rupa-sanatanau raghu-yugau sri-jiva-gopalakau*

**“I offer my respectful obeisances unto the Six Gosvamis, namely Rupa Gosvami, Sanatana Gosvami, Raghunatha Bhatta Gosvami, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami, Jiva Gosvami, and Gopala Bhatta Gosvami, who were chanting very loudly everywhere in Vrndavana, shouting, ‘Queen of Vrndavana! Radharani! Î Lalita! Î son of Nanda Maharaja! Where are you all now? Are you just on the hill of Govardhana, or are you under the trees on the bank of the Yamuna? Where are you?’ These were their moods in executing Krsna consciousness.”**

Like the Siksastakaverse, the first-hand testimony of Srinivasa Acarya paints a lucid picture of the bhajanapractised by the founders of the Krsna consciousness movement. Their example for succeeding generations was to cultivate feelings of separation that made one literally “mad after Krsna.”

Obviously, the extreme display of separation shown by the Gosvamis is the perfectional stage. Yet bhajanameans to gradually learn this process, which may begin by appreciating Krsna’s all-pervasiveness with one’s intelligence. That kind of meditation establishes a dynamic wherein a devotee recognises that Krsna is present everywhere, while at the same time hidden from view. It is an intellectual tension that awakens an eagerness to see Krsna, and cultivating that eagerness nurtures nascent feelings of separation.

The books composed by the Gosvamis and their followers are the inspiration for a sadhaka.By reading them, the tad-bhavaeffect further awakens the desire for vipralambhaand gradually nurtures it. This is the understanding of Narottama Dasa Thakura’s plea, rupa-raghunatha-pade haibe akuti:

**“When shall I become very eager to study the books left by the Six Gosvamis?”**

Once feelings of separation become an integral aspect of a devotee’s sadhana,then bhava-sevaand nama-sankirtananourish each other. As Srila Prabhupada says,

**“Bhajanameans how to become mad after Krsna.”**

Success in bhajanafrees a devotee of material inebrieties and inspires him to follow the simple life of dedication set by the Gosvamis. Rising through the stages of nama-smarana,the practitioner can search after Radha and Krsna—meaning, search after Them within his heart. When that sadhanais mature, and when Caitanya Mahaprabhu is pleased by the effort, He will reveal Himself. It cannot happen otherwise.

Readers may wonder how feelings of separation actually develop the quality of a practitioner’s bhajana,what to speak of enriching the love of a siddha.The answer is twofold.

One part of the answer, its marginal characteristic, lies in the basic psychology of separation, which is that when a person hankers after something of value he becomes all the more eager for it. The converse of this is that when a person finally acquires that valued object, he becomes accustomed to it. Applied to Krsna consciousness, this means that when a devotee values Krsna and is unable to see Him, the devotee becomes all the more eager. In other words, vipralambhaincreases the desire to meet Krsna.

The obvious stipulation is that a sadhakavalues Krsna. Such appreciation comes from a thorough knowledge of relationships, sambandha-jnana.A devotee must have firm faith that Krsna is the Supreme Lord, while he is but an insignificant servant whose life is meaningless without attaining eternal service to Krsna. One who has such firm faith will value Krsna; others will not. In the absence of such conviction, sadhanaremains mechanical and a devotee’s attachment remains rooted in family, home, and mundane pursuits.

The other part of the answer, the primary characteristic, is that vipralambhais an inherent quality of prema.

Love for Krsna remains fresh and is enhanced by eternal pas- times of meeting and separation. So, wherever vipralambhais cultivated, there premagrows. Krsna gives a poignant explanation of this dynamic to the gopisafter they accused Him of ingratitude for disappearing in the middle of loving exchanges with them. He said,

*nabam tu sakhyo bhajato 'pi jantun*  
*bhajamy amisam anuvrtti-vrttaye*  
*yathadhano labdha-dhane vinaste*  
*tac-cintayanyan nibhrto na veda*

**“But the reason I do not immediately reciprocate the affection of living beings even when they worship Me, O gopis, is that I want to intensify their loving devotion. They then become like a poor man who has gained some wealth and then lost it, and who thus becomes so anxious about it that he can think of nothing else.”**

Krsna keeps devotees in anxiety in order to increase their desire and affection for Him. This means that vipralambhacultivates prema.

A reader’s immediate response may be:

**“That is understandable in Krsna’s relationship with the gopisor with other siddhas,but what about the regular sadhaka?”**

We reply:

**“Krsna’s words are quite specific. He was not addressing the gopisdirectly, but anyone who worships Him. Therefore, He uses the word jantun,‘with living beings’—regular sadhakasincluded.”**

Still the reader may not be satisfied:

**“But what about Krsna’s use of the word anuvrtti, meaning the propensity for pure love. Where is the propensity for such pure love in a sadhaka?”**

We answer:

**“That propensity is there in every living thing.”**

The propensity to love is there in every living entity because it is part of his constitutional makeup—sat, cit, ananda.The combination of the citand anandapotencies result in prema.Service in separation is the mixing agent of these two energies.

**“But if separation results in prema,then that prema should be visible in a devotee’s sadhana.Is it?”**

We answer this question by first paraphrasing the teachings of Bhaktivinoda Thakura.

The acaryaoffers a practical example which follows Visvanatha Cakravarti’s quantitative evaluation of the degrees of premapresent in the stages of devotion from faith to love:

Ecstatic devotion, bhava,is also referred to by acaryasand sastra as rati.The two terms are each a synonym of the other. Ratiis the smallest divisible portion of prema,beyond which further integral division is not possible. In the way that the number one hundred is made up of many indivisible units, so premais made up of indivisible parts called rati.And ratiis the love present in bhava.

The primary stage of premasystematically thickens step by step to mahabhava,which can be compared to a number like one billion or one trillion. Caitanya Mahaprabhu instructs Rupa Gosvami about the development of prema:

*prema vrddhi-krame nama—sneha, mana, pranaya*  
*raga, anuraga, bhava, mahabhava haya*

**“The basic aspects of prema,when gradually increasing to different states, are affection, abhorrence, love, attachment, further attachment, ecstasy, and great ecstasy.”**

Similarly, ratiis manifest—not divided—to different degrees in the stages of sadhanaranging from sraddhato asakti.And although love at these stages manifests only a fragment of the power of rati, it is spiritual love nevertheless. This is how premais present in sadhana.

And because love is present in sadhana,it responds to the emotion invoked by the awareness of being separated from Krsna. The more a devotee feels separation from Krsna, the more love in sadhanagrows, and the more the sadhakais freed of inauspicious things. This applies to both regulated and spontaneous devotees. Narada is an example of a regulated devotee for whom separation from Krsna removed impurities and matured love.

As a final point on how vipralambhacan act on a sadhaka,readers may remember that separation and meeting are eternal conditions in which pastimes of love are manifest. This means that premaand vipralambhaare eternally connected. Service in separation is like the incline of the river of love, drawing all its water downstream to the ocean of Krsna. Where vipralambhais cultivated, there premaflows.

An inevitable question that relates to Krsna’s reply to the gopis is:

**“If Krsna does not reciprocate with His devotee’s service and sadhana,will practitioners not become discouraged?”**

In his commentary to the verse beginning naham tu sakhyo, Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura gives this enchantingly conclusive answer. He quotes Krsna’s explanation to the gopis:

**“For those surrendered souls who worship Me through nama-sankirtanaand other means, I do not respond in order to make their worship more perfect. Not seeing Me, those surrendered souls develop deep humility thinking,**

**“‘Alas! Everything I have done has been useless. Because I am an offender Krsna has not shown me the slightest favour.’**

**“By constantly meditating in this way, devotees who have not yet developed love for Me become free of lust and anger, and in time, their hearts awaken to pure devotion full of power and brilliance.”**

That is the perfect answer, from the all-knowing physician with a remedy for every ailment.

\* \* \* \*

We now return to explaining the additional benefits of vipralambha on a devotee’s sadhana.

As separation-induced attachment to Krsna increases, so too does a devotee’s desire to hear and chant about Him. And while vipralambha-bhavamay not reveal much of its riches, chanting and hearing do. Thus at sadhanathe pain of separation already invokes a simultaneously occurring emotion of joy.

A greatly anticipated gift is more valued than one immediately delivered. Similarly, many years of service in separation increases the sadhaka’spleasure when he finally meets Krsna face to face.

And so it continues for eternity in pastimes of love—vipra-lambbaforever increases the pleasure of sambhoga.Indeed, the happiness of meeting is not fully appreciated without a corresponding experience of separation. Just as salt keeps water fresh, vipralambhakeeps the joy of meeting ever relishable, ever enhanced.

**“The ornaments of love in separation decorate the mood of love in union.”**

As inseparable as vipralambhais from prema,so too is dainya, humility. In chapter twenty-one we have explained the relationship between utter humility and love for Krsna, as well as the important role that humility plays in sadhana.Since both humility and separation are limbs of love, they are thereby interrelated.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu stresses the importance of humility as a prerequisite for a sadhakato gain firm faith and to become steady in nama-bhajana.Moreover, in the absence of efforts to cultivate humility, a devotee will commit offences and so curtail every chance at winning Krsna’s favour. The Lord does not like proud devotees. Kaviraja Gosvami therefore suggests that a sadhaka keep the culture of humility in the forefront of his meditations. Commenting on the verse beginning with trnad api sunicena,the acaryawrites,

*urdhva-bahu kari' kahon, suna, sarva-loka*  
*nama-sutre ganthi’ para kanthe ei sloka*

**“Raising my hands, I declare, ‘Everyone please hear me! String this verse on the thread of the holy name and wear it on your neck for continuous remembrance.’”**

In short, humility is essential for a sadhaka.In a siddhait is raised to the superlative stage of utter humility, dainya.As premaappears in degrees of excellence through practice to perfection, so too does dainya.Yet whether in sadhanaor in sadhya,humility needs to constantly be honed, and the ability to humble a Vaisnava is one of the wonderful effects of vipralambha.

**“How does this honing take place?”**

**“Humility and separation nurture each other.”**

If we follow how Caitanya Mahaprabhu would recite His own Siksastakaprayers, we see a relationship of mutual and escalating cause and effect between separation, humility, and love. They each nurture and intensify the other. This has also been explained by Krsna in the earlier commentary by Cakravarti Thakura.

After glorifying the holy name in the first verse, the humility of a beginner who feels unqualified for nama-sankirtanaarose in the Lord, and so He spoke the second verse beginning with namnam akari bahudha.

Thereafter, Caitanya Mahaprabhu took heart and spoke the key to awakening love of God in the third verse, which describes the humility of a true sadhaka.Tasting the meaning of this verse with His associates, Lord Caitanya thought that although feeling distant from it, perhaps He too could one day practise pure devotion. A symptom of pure devotion is that a devotee always feels himself unworthy, and with increased humility Caitanya Mahaprabhu then spoke the fourth verse.

Considering Himself a conditioned soul, yet having great faith in the power of pure devotion, Lord Caitanya expressed His desire for eternal service, and with even greater humility He spoke the fifth verse, which addresses the Lord as the son of Nanda Maharaja.

Would Krsna again accept Gauranga as His servant? Great hope arose in Caitanya Mahaprabhu that Krsna would. After all, Krsna is an ocean of mercy! Feeling great eagerness for bhavabut considering Himself unqualified for it, the first stirrings of real dainya appeared in the Lord as He spoke the sixth verse as a prayer for ecstatic devotion.

Although separation was always the undercurrent of the Lord’s prayers, it now became a roaring wave of loving devotion that awoke feelings of distress, lamentation, and humility. Overwhelmed, Caitanya Mahaprabhu spoke like one deranged, pouring the sorrow of His heart into a verse symbolising the vipralambhaof a true lover, yugayitam nimesena.

At this point Caitanya Mahaprabhu assumed the role of Srimati Radharani, whose inconceivable love flooded His heart and awakened a host of ecstatic symptoms in which humility was manifest along with envy, eagerness, and pleading.

Seeing His associates as gopis,Lord Caitanya looked around to see whether anyone else was within earshot. Reassured that they were alone, He spoke the eighth and final verse, in which He totally enveloped Himself in the mood of Radha:

*aslisya va pada-ratam pinastu mam*  
*adarsanan marma-batam karotu va*  
*yatha tatba va vidadhatu lampato*  
*mat-prana-nathas tu sa eva naparah*

**“Let Krsna tightly embrace this maidservant who has fallen at His lotus feet, or let Him trample Me or break My heart by never being visible to Me. He is a debauchee, after all, and can do whatever He likes, but still He alone, and no one else, is the worshipable Lord of My heart.”**

In the sequence of verses above, the reader may observe the development of humility through the stages of sadhana, bhava, prema,and finally mahabhava.Such advancement is also possible in the devotee who embraces Lord Caitanya’s mood of separation. And that is because separation contributes to the development of the extraordinary quality of dainya,the harbinger of prema.In the chapter that follows, we shall present certain principles that Vaisnavas can apply in cultivating vipralambha-bhava.

## Chapter Thirty-Five

**Cultivating Vlpralambha**

A confidential aspect of separation is the bliss it generates in both lover and beloved. This is not an easy topic to comprehend, for it has both contradictory and inconceivable aspects and thus requires faith and spiritual maturity.

To an uninformed observer, the result of separating a lover from a beloved is that both will suffer anguish in proportion to their love. In one sense this is true even in the sphere of bhakti,and the external symptoms of vipralambhaseem to confirm it. Taken to its rare extreme, separation can even result in death. For example, Maharaja Dasaratha died in the anguish of separation from his exiled son Rama.

When witness to such manifestations of distress, some devotees, like the residents of Tapaloka, may opt for devotional meditation in favour of devotional service. In that way, they reason, they can always see Krsna within themselves and never be separated from Him. On the other hand, the spiritually impoverished may completely abandon bhaktiand take up jnanaor yogato attain freedom from all misery through liberation, while those seeking a reason for sense enjoyment may forswear spiritual life altogether and follow the way of karmaor hedonism.

But devotees who are fixed in devotional service will place themselves in the hands of Bhakti-devi, firm in the faith that she will always do for them what is spiritually best.

If we reflect for a moment on the nature of pure devotion, we can better understand the nuances posed by the concept that, concurrent with the pain of separation, it is a most wonderful joy. We have already given the example that the pangs of hunger are integral to the enjoyment of eating. Similarly, the pain of separation is integral to the enjoyment of meeting.

But the question still remains:

**“How can that separation be happiness?”**

We introduce the entirety of our answer by fist replying:

**“The logic of neti-netinecessitates that the agony of separation cannot really be distress.”**

The reason is that even the most rudimentary sadhanagives relief from distress and awards auspiciousness. Therefore we are led to conclude that what appears to be suffering must be something else.

**“What is that something else?”**

Sanatana Gosvami offers an example to answer our question. The acaryapoints out that even in everyday life, something can manifest symptoms opposite to its inherent nature. For example, if one is exposed to ice for an extended period of time, what at first feels cold later gives the sensation of burning. The ice appears to be hot, and the result of such prolonged exposure is a medical condition called ice-burn. And so it is with bhakti-yoga.

Thus we answer:

**“Separation is sometimes experienced as happiness, sometimes as sorrow, and at other times a combination of both. But at all times vipralambhais a form of ecstasy. Ectsasy is the ‘something else!’”**

By the agency of the Lord’s internal potency, the ecstasy of separation manifests the contradictory characteristics of pain and bliss, which may appear individually or concurrently.

When sunlight passes through a crystal, its component colours are broken up and they appear individually on a reflected surface as red, green, blue, and their rainbow combinations. Similarly, the one ectsasy of vipralambhamanifests through the prism of the svarupa-saktiupon the heart of a devotee. As a result, the devotee experiences different sensations such as the burning of red, the cooling of blue, the pleasing of green, and the endless rainbow combinations of these three.

This is how the one bliss of separation can be seen either as happiness or as pain, or as a combination of the two.

We can further understand the blissful nature of separation by observing the confusion it causes in advanced devotees. Intense separation can give the joyful perception that the devotee is with Krsna, and direct union with Him can bring about the painful condition of pending separation. Once again, the deceptive effect of separation acts in different ways, sometimes appearing as happiness, sometimes as sorrow. Furthermore, when union is confused as separation, it causes a pain that is a contrast to the naturally joyful state it inspires. This spiritual science is blissfully confusing and contradictory!

\* \* \* \*

The wise have determined that vipralambhagenerates happiness in three ways:

**By inducing meditation on Krsna; through the anticipation of meeting; and—the most intense of the three—by the taste of separation itself.**

When Krsna called the gopiswith the song of His flute, some ladies were restrained by their husbands and unable to leave their homes. These women meditated on Krsna, and in that way they experienced the bliss of His embrace. Sukadeva Gosvami says,

**“By meditating upon Him they realised His embrace, and the ecstasy they then felt exhausted their material piety.”**

Then there is the happiness of an anticipated meeting. In Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet,the young girl says to her lover,

**“Parting is such sweet sorrow that I shall say goodnight ’til it be morrow.”**

Here the oxymoron “sweet sorrow” means that their parting is sweet because it forces them into thoughts of their next meeting and the happiness it will bring.

True, the happiness from thoughts of a future meeting is a way in which vipralambhagenerates happiness. But it is not the main way. The mellow of separation itself, like union, is the direct cause of the most wonderful transcendental bliss. How that is so defies material logic, but faithful Vaisnavas accept it as truth and realist it through experience.

One may ask:

**“But is the pain of separation, sometimes referred to as poison, really that, or something more nuanced?”**

We may reflect:

**“Looking more deeply into the verses cited above gives a hint of the answer.”**

Sukadeva Gosvami describes the situation of the gopiswho could not go to the rasadance in this way:

*duhsaha-prestha-viraha-*  
*tivra-tapa-dhutasubhah*  
*dbyana-praptacyutaslesa-*  
*nirvrtya ksina-mangalah*

*tam eva paramatmanam*  
*jara-buddhyapi sangatah*  
*jahur guna-mayam deham*  
*sadyah praksina-bandhanah*

**“For those gopiswho could not go to see Krsna, intolerable separation from their beloved caused an intense agony that burned away all impious karma.By meditating upon Him they realised His embrace, and the ecstasy they then felt exhausted their material piety. Although Lord Krsna is the Supreme Soul, these girls simply thought of Him as their male lover and associated with Him in that intimate mood. Thus their karmic bondage was nullified and they abandoned their gross material bodies.”**

The first of the two verses is most relevant, particularly the words tivra-tapa,which translate as “intense burning pain.” The common understanding shared in the commentaries of acaryasSridhara, Sanatana, and Jiva is that tivra-tapais an intense affliction, while Visvanatha says it is an immeasurable sorrow.

**“So the pain of separation is actually suffering?”**

Ḍṁðṁis a noun from the root tap.Kaviraja Gosvami has this to say about a derivative of the same root, tapta:

*ei prema-asvadana, tapta-iksu-carvana,*  
*mukha jvale, na yaya tyajana*  
*sei prema yanra mane, tara vikrama sei jane,*  
*visamrte ekatra milana*

**“If one tastes such love of Godhead, he can compare it to hot sugar cane. When one chews hot sugar cane, his mouth burns, yet he cannot give it up. Similarly, if one has but a little love of Godhead, he can perceive its powerful effects. It can only be compared to poison and nectar mixed together.”**

In this verse Kaviraja Gosvami elaborates on how the heat of intense burning acts. He gives the brilliant example of hot sugar cane, which is simultaneously intolerably hot and irresistibly sweet. It is both painful and pleasurable. The acaryasupports his statement by quoting Rupa Gosvami, who says,

**“The poisonous effects of love of Godhead defeat the severe and fresh poison of the serpent. Yet there is simultaneously transcendental bliss, which pours down and defeats the pride of nectar and diminishes its value.”**

In other words, pain and pleasure are simultaneous effects of love for Krsna in separation.

Many other authorities confirm this, like Narada when he tells Gopa-kumara,

**“Premain separation is full of both the greatest ecstasy and the worst anguish.”**

When the verse of Srimad-Bhagavatamemphasises separation as an intense agony, it should be understood that there is an unstated simultaneous bliss. And, as we have mentioned, bhaktirelieves one of all distress. Thus if the pain and pleasure of separation are weighed against each other, the balance tips strongly on the side of pleasure.

So our answer to the question is:

**“The pain of separation is both distressful and blissful.”**

But there is more!

Other authorities—sometimes the same authorities—also say that there is no pain. They argue that the inner feeling is bliss, but its external expressions, caused by Krsna’s absence, are symptoms of great misery. Krsna, being away from the devotee, invokes reactions of separation like crying, incoherent talks, and facial transformations. But they reason that these are very special symptoms of ecstasy that manifest when Krsna is absent.

For example, Gopa-kumara in his spiritual identity as Sri Sarupa says,

*tatratyam yac ca tad duhkham*  
*tat sarva-sukha-murdhasu*  
*sa narinarti sokas ca*  
*krtsnananda-bbaropari*

**“There, in Goloka, sorrow dances vigorously on the head of every kind of happiness, and anguish gives a joy more intense than any bliss.”**

In his commentary Sanatana Gosvami says,

**“In Goloka the apparent misery of separation from Krsna is in fact the greatest happiness, and the anxiety felt by the Goloka-vasis is more ecstatic than any other pleasure.”**

Elsewhere in the same book Narada Muni says,

**“From the purely spiritual point of view, this so-called suffering is actually the most sublime ecstasy.”**

Thus there are two possible answers to the question, “So the pain of separation is actually suffering?”:

**“Concurrent with the sorrow of separation is a corresponding happiness, and the sorrow of separation is merely an external expression of an internal emotion of bliss.”**

We choose not to resolve these two answers in this book. The topic of premacannot be fully explained; it can be understood only by being realised. However, readers can be assured that there is bliss in the sorrow of separation.

Moreover, and most importantly, Krsna cannot tolerate seeing His devotees suffer. He cannot bear to see them calling after Him or sobbing uncontrollably, even if He knows that these are not symptoms of pain but of ecstasy. This is because He is Bhagavan, which also means “the most loving.”

And finally, there is an unspoken truth among Krsna and His devotees. The ecstasy that comes with separation—whether alone or accompanied by distress—is so extraordinary, so tasty, so superlative, that both Krsna and His devotees hanker to taste it. In other words, although they always strive to meet, in a secret recess of their hearts the Lord and His devotees think,

**“When we are separated, we will taste that special bliss.”**

\* \* \* \*

Practitioners can be assured that Krsna is sympathetic to the ago nies they face in their attempt to reach Him. He will certainly come to quell the sadhaka’sdistress of separation. But in His time!

Krsna has reasons for tempering His devotee’s eagerness to see Him, just as a smith tempers a sword by repeatedly heating, beating, and cooling it.

After giving His darsana,the Lord told Narada that the boy would not see Him for the rest of his life. Similarly, when Krsna abandoned the gopisprior to the rasa-dance, He watched their exhibitions of separation and then quickly returned. In both cases He wanted to hone His devotees’ love on the whetstone of separation from Him. For Narada that would take considerably longer than it would for the gopis.In either case the result would be the same.

And a similar result is shared by the sadhaka.Krsna oversees His devotee’s advancement and reciprocates according to what He considers is best for awakening love.

Feelings of separation are obviously invoked by not seeing Krsna, but more so by not obtaining the immediate result of the effort a practitioner puts into his sadhana.When a serious devotee does not feel he is advancing at pace, or when he is hankering after the symptoms described in Siksastaka,it should be known that Krsna is withholding Himself and withholding that special devotion to Him. He wants to see how the devotee will respond. Krsna makes a sadhakafeel this kind of separation as a test.

The overarching reason for Krsna playing hard to get is that He wants to see how much His devotee values Him.

After all, loving devotion will purchase Him Who is the personification of all that exists. Krsna is not a dollar-store trinket. And when He gives Himself, He does so unconditionally and totally. A practitioner should be willing to respond in kind: he should be willing to pay the price of such attainment, whatever the cost. And to see that he does, the following are some of the points on which Krsna assesses His devotee:

How steady is a devotee in service even without the reward of advancement? Does the devotee opt for liberation as an alternative to hard-to-attain bhava? Does he actually feel separation, or at least try to feel it? Is the devotee content to remain instead in goodness as a pious brahmana? Is the devotee distracted by material allurements like wealth or sense gratification, which are by-products of bhakti?

If Krsna sees that the sadhakais neither distracted nor discouraged from his goal, He will gain faith that His devotee values Him. Then gradually, in different ways, kind-hearted Krsna, Who is purchased by honest, steadfast devotion, will reveal Himself. In the interim, as the determined devotee gains increasing attachment to the Lord, he also gains a corresponding insight to the mercy that separation bestows upon him, and is grateful.

Some people may complain that in consideration of the difficulties posed by this age of Kali, Krsna is too demanding. Indeed, they may even say that taking pleasure in His devotee’s pain of separation is cruel.

Not so! Krsna does not take pleasure in the suffering of devotees, but He does take pleasure in the underlying devotion that generates their struggles.

By speaking to the gopis,Krsna addresses the world of Vaisnavas. He assures devotees — from beginner sadhakato advanced siddha—that He knows their sacrifice and surrender. Moreover, He reminds us that His responding to our devotion in His time, not ours, is for our spiritual benefit, not for His entertainment. Knowing these things, we should not fault Him. These are the Lord’s words to the vraja-devis:

*evam mad-arthojjhita-loka-veda*  
*svanam hi vo mayy anuvrttaye ’balah*  
*mayaparoksam bhajata tirohitam*  
*masuyitum marhatha tat priyam priyah*

**“My dear girls! Understanding that simply for My sake you had rejected the authority of worldly opinion, of the Vedas, and of your relatives, I acted as I did only to increase your attachment to Me. Even when I removed Myself from your sight by suddenly disappearing, I never stopped loving you. Therefore, My beloved gopis,please do not harbour any bad feelings toward Me, your beloved.”**

In the way that Krsna appeared to the gopis.He will also appeal before every sincere devotee. Even though He knows that His devotee’s feelings of separation are actually feelings of bliss, He can not long stand to see the symptoms of his suffering. Therefore, the sooner that a sadhakacan spontaneously shed tears, roll on the ground, and call out in anguish—all to see the Lord—the sooner Krsna will appear.

And when Krsna does appear, then the sadhakaand siddhaforget all their suffering and simply bask in the most sublime happiness. To behold Krsna with the eyes is the ultimate purpose of bhaktiand its fullest reward, a reward that uproots every illusion and impurity within the heart. With all obstacles removed, the devotee’s love can grow from strength to strength, blossoming in the special ecstasies that only Krsna’s company can bring.

\* \* \* \*

We should briefly emphasise the connection between cultivating emotion and hearing.

The correlation between the two is straightforward. The subjects a devotee hears make an impression upon his consciousness, thus the emotional experience and emotional influence of the subjects are impressed into the consciousness of the hearer, and the two become one.

Everyone has experience of even mundane things like movies, books, and songs being the source of emotional and psychological involvement. We identify with what we hear. A love narrative induces a feeling of romance, a horror story of fear, an action drama pumps adrenaline. This is akin to mantrasor incantations that are able to invoke weapons, subtle beings, or events. The reason is that words or combinations of words are endowed with certain powers. This holds true for both the mundane and the spiritual sound vibration, the two clearly differing in their potency and the results that they invoke.

The process by which any kind of sound vibration induces a corresponding feeling, and which is called tad-bhava,is explained in the following words of Sri Prahlada, a verse we have amply quoted in this book:

*tada puman mukta-samasta-bandhanas*  
*tad-bhava-bhavanukrtasayakrtih*  
*nirdagdha-bijanusayo mahiyasa*  
*bhakti-prayogena samety adhoksajam*

**“The devotee is then freed from all material contamination because he constantly thinks of the Lord’s pastimes and because his mind and body have been converted to spiritual qualities. Because of his intense devotional service, his ignorance, material consciousness, and all kinds of material desires are completely burnt to ashes. This is the stage at which one can achieve the shelter of the Lord’s lotus feet.”**

The significant words in this verse are tad-bhava-bhavanu-krtasayakrtih,which can be translated to mean,

**“By hearing or thinking, bhava,one’s mind and body, asaya-akrtih,assume the same qualities of what has been heard or thought of, anukrta.This is called tad- bhava."**

Caitanya Mahaprabhu gave an example of how this visual and auditory contact with an object creates an impression within the mind and body. He says that when a man sees a woman, or even hears her name, the image of a woman brings about certain transformations within that man’s mind and body.

Most men have experience of the metamorphosis that simply a name can conjure within one’s being. When a lusty man hears the name of a beautiful woman and dwells on her, he envisages the lady in his mind, begins to think of a romantic encounter, and when fully absorbed in lusty thoughts his body quickly becomes sensually agitated. He may be so absorbed in thought of this woman that the resulting impressions will colour his consciousness during waking hours and cause a sensual dream in his sleep. And that is all from a mundane name!

This is tad-bhava;the transformative potency of conveying images and impressions through the agency of sound, thereby inducing both psychological and physiological changes in the hearer.

Now, if mundane sounds and ideas have such power, what then of the spiritual sound vibration, or sabda.

By the same principle of tad-bhava,transcendental sound invokes spiritual transformations in the hearer. The more empowered the sound, the greater the spiritual effect. Similarly, a specific spiritual sound has a corresponding effect. The general principle is laid out by Vedanta, anavrttih sabdat:

**“One is liberated by spiritual sound.”**

Spiritual sound makes a liberating impression on the hearer.

Of course, liberation may mean many different things depending on the subject and purpose of spiritual sound. It may mean either attaining detachment from all that is material, acquiring the seed of devotion, attraction to the Supreme Lord, love for Krsna, or it may mean being submerged in great feelings of separation from Radha’s lover.

For a gaudiya-sadhaka,especially for one who is at the stage of smarana,the subject matter for hearing is Krsna’s pastimes in Vraja.

In the Lord’s original abode, His mercy, beauty, qualities, and pastimes are manifest to ultimate perfection. By hearing of them, a devotee tastes the limit of attraction to Him. Sanatana Gosvami calls the splendour of Krsna’s pastimes vilasa-Laksmi, and points out that they have a magical power to awaken prema within the heart. That awakening process takes place as soon as a devotee begins to hear vraja-lila.And when a thoughtful devotee carefully contemplates those pastimes with attention during nama-sankirtana,then love for Krsna imbued with feelings of separation begins to mature in bis consciousness.

Such perfection is made possible by the innate potency invested in the words describing the Lord’s pastimes. Materialists may not understand, but it is a transcendental reality. Caitanya Mahaprabhu addresses Krsna, saying, *namnam akari bahudha nija-sarva-saktis tatrarpita*:

**“You have invested all Your potencies in Your names.”**

And so it is with the Lord’s pastimes. They are pervaded by a power to vanquish all material contamination and invoke spiritual emotions tî the summit of vipralambha-bhava.Sukadeva Gosvami explained this power of Krsna’s pastimes when he revealed the eternal identity of Nanda and Yasoda. The sage quoted Drona and Dhara as saying,

*jatayor ñau mahadeve*  
*bhuvi visvesvare harau*  
*bhaktih syat parama loke*  
*yayanjo durgatim taret*

**“Please permit us to be born on the planet earth so that after our appearance, the Supreme Lord, the Personality of Godhead, the supreme controller and master of all planets, will also appear and spread devotional service, the ultimate goal of life, so that those born in this material world may very easily be delivered from the miserable condition of materialistic life by accepting this devotional service.”**

In his commentary Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura confirms that with the words parama bhakti,the two sadhakasDrona and Dhara prayed for the loving devotion suited to parents of the Supreme Lord. The acaryafurther paraphrases their request in this way:

**“In the future, others who hear about and glorify the services we rendered to the cowherd boy Krsna will easily attain that same liberation most rare.”**

The concluding verse of the same chapter of Srimad-Bhagavatam confirms that Drona and Dhara’s desires were fulfilled. They entered into the forms of the eternal Nanda and Yasoda, and by witnessing Krsna’s pastimes, they experienced the love of parenthood through the agency of Krsna’s internal potency:

*krsno brahmana adesam*  
*satyam kartum vraje vibhuh*  
*saha-ramo vasams cakre*  
*tesam pritim sva-lilaya*

**“Thus, the Supreme Personality, Krsna, along with Balarama, lived in Vrajabhumi, Vrndavana, just to substantiate the benediction of Brahma. By exhibiting different pastimes in His childhood, He increased the transcendental pleasure of Nanda and the other inhabitants of Vrndavana.”**

In his commentary Cakravarti Thakura confirms that Drona and Dhara attained the parama bhaktifor which they prayed, and by observing the wonderful childhood pastimes of Krsna and Balarama they, like the other inhabitants of Gokula, relished ever-increasing love, priti.

The conclusion to be drawn from the evidences of Srimad-Bhagavatam and its commentator is that the love that devotees attained by directly seeing Krsna’s pastimes is available at any time to Vaisnavas by attentively hearing them.

This wonder is due to the power invested in the words that glorify Krsna’s pastimes. Because Gopa-kumara had not systematically heard these pastimes from pure devotees, the Visnudutas told him that he had to hear Srimad-Bhagavatamand thus be empowered with the kind of love that would qualify him for the Lord’s association.

But it should be emphasised that the appearance of premais a gradual process.

As soon as one steadily hears Krsna’s pastimes, premamakes its appearance in incremental degrees, manifesting different aspects at taste and attachment. Although sraddha, ruci,and asaktiare not mature expressions of love, they are nonetheless its spiritual portions. When bhavais attained, then the sadhakawill be able to appreciate the beginning stage of real, transcendental love. More will be said of the development of premathrough hearing krsna-lila.However, we must concur that emotion is awakened and cultivated by hearing of Krsna.

Indeed, as elsewhere in this book, we now emphasise the importance of hearing from sadhuand sastrato understand the science of bhava-seva,of vipralambha,and consequently the science of service to Krsna. Even without systematically hearing, a devotee can still progress spiritually; however, that progress will be very much dependent on the quality of his chanting, which for the average sadhakameans that their advancement will be protracted.

The clear example is Gopa-kumara, a highly-qualified sadhaka who was favoured in many ways by the Lord. But without systematic education in nama-sankirtana,he was clueless about the process of bhava-seva.

His chanting was formulaic and its ultimate result was liberation. But when he studied Srimad-Bhagavatamunder the guidance of pure devotees, the boy’s spiritual life transformed. He was immediately qualified to hear further details of the esoteric practices of mantrameditation, in response to which his spiritual master again appeared and instructed him accordingly. Then, by the combined grace of sadhu, guru,and sastra,Gopa-kumara could chant with feeling and thus gain access to Vaikuntha.

A serious sadhakamust similarly practise devotional service under the guidance of bhagavatas.In that way he can access the standard process of devotional meditation—nama-bhajanain the mood of separation. As already mentioned, at some stage in his journey a practitioner must awaken an attraction to the Vraja-vasis, and that attraction must become his guiding star.

According to Rupa Gosvami, a devotee who understands the essence of teachings becomes a vraja-jananuga:

*tan-nama-rupa-caritadi-sukirtananu-*  
*smrtyoh kramena rasana-manasi niyojya*  
*tisthan vraje tad-anuragi jananugami*  
*kalam nayed akhilam ity upadesa-saram*

**“The essence of all advice is that one should utilise one’s full time—twenty-four hours a day — in nicely chanting and remembering the Lord’s divine name, transcendental form, qualities, and eternal pastimes, thereby gradually engaging one’s tongue and mind. In this way one should reside in Vraja \[Goloka Vrndavana-dhama\] and serve Krsna under the guidance of devotees. One should follow in the footsteps of the Lord’s beloved devotees, who are deeply attached to His devotional service.”**

The desire to follow the Vraja-vasis is a general attraction. Time specifies which of the Vraja-vasis a devotee has the most attraction for, perhaps for the young gopifriends of Srimati Radharani, the manjaris.And that same sadhana-laden time clarifies which of the manjarisattracts him the most.

Attraction for those divine beings who are out of reach is the genesis of natural feelings of separation.

As a devotee’s attraction grows, so do his feelings of separation from his Vraja role models. Those feelings of separation will inspire him to hear about Krsna’s corresponding pastimes with the gopis, and those topics will imbed themselves in his heart and become the source of meditations during nama-smarana.This is expressed above by the words anu-smrtyoh kramena rasana-manasi niyojya. Thus vipralambha-seva.becomes a function of hearing, a progressive dynamic by which a devotee acquires partial realisation of service in separation. Such progressive understanding of vipralambha gradually matures into an understanding of its transcendental details.

Following this all-perfect process of nama-bhajana,a devotee eventually receives the blessings of his worshipable deities, the Vraja-vasis for whose service he exists. In that way he attains the perfection of bhava.Ecstatic devotion soon matures, and bhajana becomes heavily laden with premaand its magical blessings. This is the process of vipralambha-sevaspoken of in Vaisnava literature, a path of perfection that Caitanya Mahaprabhu personified, a path of perfection His followers taught.

And while devotional literatures emphasise that pure devotion in the mood of separation can only be known and practised by those who have acquired knowledge of it, once that process has been perfected, service to the associates of Radha-Krsna progresses without dependence on other sources. It is self-manifest and fully spontaneous. This is the process of awakening, cultivating, and perfecting feelings of separation.

\* \* \* \*

We may reflect further on the process of cultivating vipralambhain the way that Srila Prabhupada repeatedly encouraged his followers with words like,

**“So we have to develop such Krsna consciousness. Our Gaudiya-sampradaya, our line of God realisation is that separation, feeling of separation. Not that we have got Krsna within our hand. No! The feeling of separation, worship of Krsna by feeling of separation, is better than the worship by directly meeting. Vipralambha-seva.”**

In the quote above, Srila Prabhupada calls upon his followers to “develop” feelings of separation for Krsna.

**“How are they to do that?”**

**“Just as they develop the physical aspects of sadhana- bhakti,the aspects known as cesta-rupa!”**

Therein a devotee first embraces the regulative principles. Those practices result in purification, and purification then leads in succession to taste, attachment, spontaneity, and ultimately ecstasy.

Feelings of separation are in the category of bhava-ruðṁ,and they are cultivated in the same way as cesta-rupa.

First a devotee understands the truths of service in separation and why it is Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s path to perfection. Then he offers prayers, submits before the deity, meditates on diksa-mantras,and chants Hare Krsna—all the while attempting to feel the separation that he intellectually comprehends. By empathising with the separation of great devotees as recorded in scripture, the effort of feeling gains substance through the principle of tad-bhava.

Thereafter, taste for the sweetness of vipralambhaawakens natural attraction, which with its moods increasingly suffuses a devotee’s nama-bhajanathrough the stages of smarana, dharana, dhyana, anusmrti,and samadhi.With the awakening of attach ment, a sadhakaexperiences the real pains of separation, and those enable him to actually cry after Krsna. When Krsna is addressed with such heartfelt pleas, He eventually bestows bhavaand thus the power to fully appreciate His presence.

In the sequence outlined above, two spiritual principles play a dominant role: invoking the sentiment of separation, and imbibing the mood of the great devotees of which one hears, tad-bhava.

We have repeatedly cited the maxim,

**“The practitioner and the means of practice should be in accord with their goal.”**

To experience separation in loving devotion, a devotee must cultivate separation in sadhana-bhakti.Similarly, to cultivate separation in sadhana,a devotee must desire to do so—bbaktya sanjataya bhaktya.By a desire for vipralambhathe bud of separation will manifest, and from that bud the blossom of loving devotion, rich with the fragrance of parting.

That perfection for which a practitioner aspires is described by the servants of Lord Narayana thus:

*namam tu sankirtanam arti-bharan*  
*megham vina pravrsi catakanam*  
*ratrau viyogat sva-pate rathangi*  
*vargasya cakrosana-vat pratihi*

**“Like the distressed crying of the catakabirds on a cloudless day of the rainy season, or the lamenting of a flock of cakravakibirds when parted from their husbands at night, the sankirtanaof the Lord’s names arises when one is burdened by too much pain.”**

Although the nama-sankirtanadescribed above is the mature manifestation of the holy names upon the tongue of a loving devotee sorely afflicted by the pangs of separation, the picture that it paints is one hankered after by the true sadhaka.

To feel separation from vipralambhais the beginning. The dynamic of tad-bhavacreates an impression within the heart, and that impression gradually ignites feelings within the practitioner.

A roaring fire within a hearth can be transported by a sliver of wood to another cold hearth where, with proper care, one can start a similar blaze. In like manner, hearing about the vipralambhain the associates of the Lord eventually brings about corresponding feelings in a sadhaka.Like the catakaand cakravakibirds in the last verse, a devotee must learn to call out for feelings of devotion, call out for Krsna’s mercy, call out for eternal service. Srila Prabhupada says that a devotee must learn how to cry for Krsna. This need is beautifully detailed by His Divine Grace in the The Nectar of Devotion:

**“In the same Narada-pancaratra,there is another expression of submission, wherein the devotee says,**

**‘My dear Lord, O lotus-eyed one, when will that day come when on the bank of the Yamuna I shall become just like a madman and continue to chant Your holy name while incessant tears flow from my eyes?’... One should feelingly pray and become eager to render his particular type of service to the Lord. This is the teaching of all great devotees, especially Lord Caitanya.**

**“In other words, one should learn how to cry for the Lord. One should learn this small technique, and he should be very eager and actually cry to become engaged in some particular type of service. This is called laulyam,and such tears are the price for the highest perfection. If one develops this laulyam,or excessive eagerness for meeting and serving the Lord in a particular way, that is the price to enter into the kingdom of God.”**

And so one asks:

**“Since conditioning by the modes of nature subdues pure emotions, what does it take to cry for Krsna?”**

**“The key to jump-start the process is to hear pastimes in which emotion is prominent, in which vipralambha is prominent.”**

When nama-bhajanais done with remembrance of those pastimes, the holy name cultivates those feelings and enables the sadhakato gradually appropriate them as his own.

This process of sharing the emotion of others is made possible in two ways:

**By hearing of Krsna’s potencies, or by hearing of His pastimes.**

If a devotee is not yet attracted to hearing Krsna’s pastimes, then studying how the Lord manifests His potencies in the world is a way to develop attachment to and separation from Him. A sadhakacan very easily lament that while Krsna is everywhere, He remains hidden by the covering of maya.

There are many passages in Srimad-Bhagavatamand Bhagavad- gitathat describe manifestations of the Lord’s potencies in this world. Being conscious of them naturally awakens devotional separation in a regulated devotee. Krsna emphatically declares,

*etam vibhutim yogam ca*  
*mama yo vetti tattvatah*  
*so ’vikalpena yogena*  
*yujyate natra samsayah*

**“One who is factually convinced of this opulence and mystic power of Mine engages in unalloyed devotional service; of this there is no doubt.”**

However, hearing of the feelings of separation expressed in Siksastaka,the songs of the acaryas,the pastimes of Caitanya Mahaprabhu, or the pastimes of Sri Krsna is a more direct and effective way to acquire the “small technique” of learning to cry after the Lord.

On sharing Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s feelings of separation, Srila Prabhupada emphasised embracing feelings of both worthlessness and disqualification as a foundation for service with emotion. In the same breath he would encourage devotees to trust in Krsna’s kindness and remain determined in their devotion:

**“What qualification do I have!... Still, I cannot give up Krsna consciousness!...That is wanted.”**

The songs of Narottama Dasa Thakura and Bhaktivinoda Thakura are especially rich in expressions of separation. Singing and meditating on these songs are wonderful ways to voice and feel the vipralambhaof liberated souls. Such practice quickly scatters seeds of spiritual emotion within the heart of a sadhaka,and with further watering and careful tending, manifests that yearning after Krsna.

Those prayers of great devotees that are filled with longing for eternal service are also effective means to awaken feelings of separation. A sadhakawill repeat and even memorise certain prayers with which he identifies, and thus be blessed by the moods of his predecessors.

The following is an example of a prayer that spontaneous devotees will covet:

*devi duhkha-kula-sagarodare*  
*duyamanam ati-durgatam janam*  
*tvam krpa-prabala-naukayadbhutam*  
*prapaya sva-pada-pankajalayam*

**“O goddess! Kindly hear this unfortunate person now drowning in an ocean of pain. Place him on the sturdy boat of Your mercy, and ferry him to the wonderful realm of Your lotus feet.”**

Sharing emotion-rich songs and prayers are part of the aforementioned direct way of awakening feelings of separation by hearing of Krsna’s pastimes.

Hearing these pastimes and reciting their verses not only endows a devotee with feelings of separation, but also gives him relief from Krsna’s absence, and so are sources of much needed enthusiasm for sadhana.A wonderful example of such verses is the concluding portion of Brhad-bhagavatamrta,which are excerpts from Brahma-samhitaand Srimad-Bhagavatam.Because these verses assuage the pain of separation from Krsna and His devotees, the) are known as a rasayana,or medicinal tonic for the ears and heart of a sadhaka.Some Vaisnavas recite them daily and in that way they memorise them. Then by repeating those verses they are able to taste the nectar of devotion.

## Chapter Thirty-Six

**The Perfection of Separation**

Thakura Bhaktivinoda suggests that devotees hear two kinds of pastimes to awaken and nurture feelings of separation: pastimes of separation prior to meeting Krsna, and pastimes in which Krsna has left His devotees. They are called purva-ragaand pravasa, respectively. Verses describing these pastimes and how Vraja-vasis feel in these situations are especially favourable for a devotee’s bhajana.When a sadhakastudies and learns these verses, they become a stimulus for deep meditation in nama-bhajana,enabling a practitioner to experience the moods of perfected devotees.

The pastimes of purva-raga,or attachment before meeting, are especially relevant to a sadhaka.The reason for this is that the practitioner shares the circumstance of Krsna’s associates—he, too, has not met Krsna.

Rupa Gosvami defines this condition of separation in this way:

*ratir ya sangamat purvam*  
*darsana-sravanadi-ja*  
*tayor unmilati prajnaih*  
*purva-ragah sa ucyate*

**“When attachment produced in the lover and beloved before their meeting by seeing, hearing, and so on becomes very palatable by the mixture of four ingredients, such as vibhavaand anubhava,this is called purva-raga.”**

A sadhakadoes not have the ingredients of love mentioned above. But, like the lover, he has not had the good fortune of meeting

Krsna, and like the lover he has developed a degree of attachment for the Lord. These comparable characteristics enable a sadhaka to closely identify with expressions of separation from Krsna and make them his own. In a way, a practitioner’s adopted feelings may be called the shadow, dbhasa,of purva-raga.

For example, before Srimati Radharani met Krsna in person, She had heard that there was a gopain Vraja by the name of Krsna. The two syllables of that name acted on Her just like a mantra by which vasita-yogisbring others under their control. Her mind hopelessly captivated, Her tongue constantly echoed the name “Krsna! Krsna! Krsna!”

Then one day while fetching water from the Yamuna, Radha heard some flute music. It was not ordinary flute music, but the kind by which snake charmers bring serpents under their control. Radha felt Her mind slacken and Her senses charmed by the melodies coming from an unidentified person in an unidentified place.

On another day, Radha saw the picture of a very beautiful youth with a dusky complexion, captivating smile, and roaming eyes. While looking at that picture, Radha felt Cupid’s influence enter Her heart and gradually spread a nectarean poison throughout Her being. In this way the picture awakened passionate thoughts that She had never before known.

As a newly-wedded bride, Srimati Radharani was perplexed. Unaware that Krsna the flute player and the person in the picture were one and the same, She thought that not only had She become unfaithful, but that She had become attracted to three paramours at once. “How immoral!”, She thought.

Taking Lalita into confidence, Radha revealed Her dilemma:

*ekasya srutam eva lumpati matim krsneti namaksaram*  
*sandronmada-paramparam upanayaty anyasya vamsi-kalah*  
*esa snigdha-ghana-dyutir manasi me lagnah pate viksanat*  
*kastam dhik purusa-traye ratir abhun manye mrtih sreyasi*

**“Since I have heard the name of a person called Krsna, I have practically lost My good sense. Then, there is another person who plays His flute in such a way that after I hear the vibration, intense madness arises in My heart. And again there is still another person to whom My mind becomes attached when I see His beautiful lightning-like effulgence in His picture. Therefore I think that I am greatly condemned, for I have become simultaneously attached to three persons. It would be better for Me to die because of this.”**

While a sadhakawill not exhibit the loving bewilderments of Srimati Radharani, he will share attraction to Krsna’s name, flute playing, and form. And he too is yet to meet Krsna. Therefore he can identify with Radha’s separation. Mounting the chariot of Her words, he can travel to the domain of Her vipralambhaand there collect keepsakes of separation to recall in smarana.

In their books glorifying Krsna and His pastimes, Vaisnavas have often included episodes of purva-raga,and in that way given an opportunity for their readers to advance in feelings of separation.

One extensive narration of purva-ragain Srimad-Bhagavatamis the Venu-gita.In this chapter the gopis,who have as yet not met Krsna, indirectly glorify Him by speaking about His flute and the effect that its music has on Vrndavana. Another famous passage is Rukmini-devi’s letter to Krsna in which She pleads with Him to kidnap and marry Her. Vaisnavas read, memorise, and sing verses from these episodes and in that way nourish their spiritual emotions.

Readers may think that because purva-ragais based on Krsna’s amorous dealings it is relevant only for devotees attracted to madhurya-bhava.While the separation of purva-ragais fully relevant to devotees who follow the gopisor queens, it is still relevant to devotees of all spiritual disposition.

The reason is that conjugal love contains the sentiments of all other mellows, and thus devotees who appreciate its feelings of vipralambhawill find nourishment for their own kind of eternal service. After all, Vaisnavas of all dispositions meditate on the Siksastakaprayers, which are spoken by Caitanya Mahaprabhu in the mood of Sri Radha.

Moreover, becoming attracted to Krsna before meeting Him is possible in every mellow. In Krsna’s earthly pastimes, His association with His servants, friends, seniors, and lovers unfolds over time and generally begins with separation, develops into meeting, and concludes in separation. In any case, devotees who hear sys fanatically, following the path of krama-suddha-sravana-dasa,will not neglect important passages describing purva-raga.

The second kind of pastimes recommended by Thakura Bhakti vinoda are those in the category of pravasa,wherein Krsna leaves His associates. Rupa Gosvami defines this separation as follows:

*purva-sangatayor óuñîr bhaved desantaradibhih*  
*vyavadhanam tu yat prajnaih sa pravasa itiryate*

**“Pravasais a word used to indicate the separation of lovers who were previously intimately associated. This separation is due to their being in different places.”**

The difference between purva-ragaand pravasais that in the latter, devotees have already met Krsna. Clearly, this kind of separation is generic over all mellows.

Kaviraja Gosvami cites a very important verse for devotees who are serious about cultivating love in separation. It was spoken by the acaryaMadhavendra Puri on his deathbed:

*ayi dina-dayardra natha he*  
*mathura-natha kadavalokyase*  
*hrdayam tvad-aloka-kataram*  
*dayita bhramyati kim karomy aham*

**“O My Lord! O most merciful master! O master of Mathura! When shall I see You again? Because of My not seeing You, My agitated heart has become unsteady. O most beloved one, what shall I do now?”**

These words were originally spoken by Srimati Radharani upon Krsna’s departure for Mathura, and it was Madhavendra Puri who made Her feelings known to the world.

Srila Prabhupada says that this verse is,

**“The seed of Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s cultivation of love of Godhead.”**

We have discussed at length how Caitanya Mahaprabhu has taught His followers how to cultivate chanting in separation. It seems that the teachings of Madhavendra Puri summarised in this verse are the seed of Gauranga’s line of devotional service. Caitanya Mahaprabhu received these teachings from His guru,Isvara Puri, and so we have continued to receive it through the Gaudiya parampara.

Kaviraja Gosvami makes a similar comment on the poetry of Madhavendra Puri. He writes,

*ei sloke krsna-prema kare upadesa*  
*krsnera virahe bhaktera bhava-visesa*

**“In this verse Madhavendra Puri teaches how to achieve ecstatic love for Krsna. By feeling separation from Krsna, one becomes spiritually situated.”**

Krsna’s departure for Mathura is described in Srimad-Bhagavatam, as is the pathos of the residents of Vraja. When the gopisheard the proclamation from Nanda Maharaja that Krsna and Balarama would be leaving with Akrura, they were heartbroken. In a state of confusion they abandoned all feminine reserve and publicly disclosed their feelings in verses like this:

*sri-gopya ucuh*  
*ahî vidhatas tava na kvacid daya*  
*sathyojya maitrya pranayena dehinah*  
*tams cakrtarthan viyunanksy aparthakam*  
*vikriditam te ’rbhaka-cestitam yatha*

**\[The gopissaid\] “O Providence! You have no mercy! You bring embodied creatures together in friendship and love and then senselessly separate them before they fulfil their desires. This whimsical play of yours is like a child’s game.”**

As always, Sukadeva Gosvami did not directly describe Srimati Radharani’s plight. However, others—like Rupa Gosvami in books like Lalita-madhavaand Hamsaduta—thoroughly describe the sorrow and madness that Radha experienced upon Krsna’s departure from Vrndavana.

The verse of Madhavendra Puri encapsulates the intensity of Radha’s separation and therefore Gaudiya Vaisnavas constantly keep it on their tongues, knowing well its spiritual significance. By remembering this verse, devotees can connect with the vipralambha of Sri Radha according to their spiritual qualification.

Through Madhavendra Puri, Srimati Radharani teaches the world how Krsna is loved in separation. Even the uninformed reader can recognise that service in separation is the central theme of Radha’s appeal.

Calling Krsna Dina-dayardra and Natha, or the compassionate master of the poor and neglected, reflects the foundational feelings of worthlessness, disqualification, and determination explained in the previous section. Srila Prabhupada repeatedly emphasises that although a devotee feels himself helpless and neglected by Krsna, still He remains the only hope and shelter. This kind of thinking, followed by a corresponding feeling, leads to the highest emotional ecstasy. Caitanya Mahaprabhu always revelled in these expressions of exalted love in separation.

\* \* \* \*

The feelings in the verse beginning with ayi dina-dayardra natha heare similar to those expressed by Radha when She met Uddhava and heard the message he had brought from Krsna.

Srimad-Bhagavatamrecords the essence of that exchange in the Song of the Bee,which is ten verses laden with feelings of separation, hearing which greatly benefits a practitioner’s bhajana. Those verses recount extreme pronouncements of separation in which Radha rambles on to a bumblebee, whom She presumes to be a messenger from Mathura-Krsna. The verses correspond to ten kinds of impulsive speech, which range from the derogatory to the respectful. While they are symptomatic of Radha’s unique maha- bhava,their underlying feelings of separation are nourishment for the receptive devotee.

An extensive narration of even more extreme symptoms of Radha’s vipralambhais found in Rupa Gosvami’s Hamsaduta.

The book is Lalita-devi’s message to Krsna depicting the pathetic condition of Srimati Radharani in His absence. The author describes extraordinary declarations of vipralambhawhich will leave the reader in awe of the apparently destructive power of divine love. Sometimes Radha thinks She is Krsna, sometimes She embraces His picture, sometimes She repeatedly collapses, somenines Her life airs seem to have departed.

The narrative recounts dozens of devastating events of Radha’s forlorn condition and how Lalita plays on Krsna’s intolerance of His devotee’s suffering. And yet the book does not conclude with Krsna’s return. Its purpose is to further inflame Krsna’s feelings of estrangement from His true love, and in the process to share with the reader His untold reaction to Radha’s laid-bare suffering. The relentless instances of Her ecstatic symptoms wear away any mundane conceptions a reader may have of Vipralambha-seva,and jars him into appreciating the confidential truths of love of God.

One of the introductory verses describe Radha’s extreme anxiety in which Her thoughts alternate between dying and living:

**First She thinks, “I can no longer tolerate the suffering that Krsna’s departure causes Me and so I shall give up My body. That will surely oblige Krsna to return to see Me.”**

**Then She has second thoughts, “But hearing of My death will be a shock to Him and cause Krsna unhappiness.”**

**And finally She concludes, “I cannot cause distress to My beloved. Therefore, I shall not die.”**

Radha’s suffering in Krsna’s absence is then expressed by Rupa Gosvami in this way:

*yada yato gopi-hrdaya-madano nanda-sadanan*  
*mukundo gandinyas tanayam anurundhan madhu-purim*  
*tadamanksic cinta-sariti ghana-ghurnaparicayair*  
*agadhayam badhamaya-payasi radha virabini*

**“At the request of Akrura, Krsna and Balarama left the house of Nanda Maharaja for Mathura. At that time Srimati Radharani’s mind was disrupted, and She became almost mad because of extreme separation from Krsna. She experienced great mental pain and agitation, which caused Her to drown in mental speculation in the river of anxiety.”**

The literary works of great authors like Vyasa and Rupa almost always describe the visible external symptoms of love in separation Only occasionally do they refer to the internal experience of vipralambha,which Vaisnavas revere as a most extraordinary bliss that cloaks itself in symptoms of suffering.

At times when He collapses unconscious, we read of Caitanya Mahaprabhu becoming an assistant to the gopiswho picks flowers for the Divine Couple, or watches Krsna and the gopisin water fights. At other times while desperately searching for Krsna, Caitanya Mahaprabhu encounters Him, only to again lose sight of Him.

While narrations of internal transformations are infrequent, devotees are constantly reminded that the experience they do afford is a bliss to which even the happiness of meeting with Krsna can not compare. That bliss is so extraordinary that the conventional and relatively passive symptoms of happiness, like smiling, are not representative. And so vipralambha-sevafinds its expression in the contrary and extreme symptoms usually associated with suffering. But it is all bliss!

In the preceding pages we have shown how to cultivate feelings of separation and thereby gain entrance into the mood of sadhana which concludes with bhava.Practising devotees must be knowledgeable in the concepts of bhava-sevaand in how to wed bhavato cestain the determinations they make in sadhana.

While feelings of separation are generally spoken of as feelings of separation from Krsna, they are not exclusively so.

Rupa Gosvami encourages the sadhakato become a vraja-jananuga,or a follower of a role-model Vraja-vasi. As a devotee becomes attached to an associate of Krsna, he naturally feels distant from them. Moreover, any devotee who hears regularly will become attached to the Vraja-vasis like Mother Yasoda, Subala, and Vrnda-devi, and of course to Vrndavana itself. And until he is re-established in his constitutional position, a devotee will taste increasingly intense sentiments of vipralambha,which will significantiló contribute to his purification and qualification.

In his Utkalika-vallari,Rupa Gosvami calls out to Subala, Lalita, Visakha, Vrnda-devi, and the residents of Vraja in general. That same mood is reflected in Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami’s Vraja-vilasa-stava,where the author entreats the birds, cows, and Govardhana Hill, along with both well-known and less-known Vrajavasis.

In his book of songs, Gita-mala,Bhaktivinoda Thakura instructs us to entreat all the residents of Vrndavana in this way:

*e heno radhara carana-jugale*  
*paricarya pa’bo kabe*  
*haha braja-jana more doya kori'*  
*kabe vraja-vane lo’be*

**“When will I be so fortunate as to serve Radha’s two lotus feet? O people of Vraja, when will you shower me with your mercy and take me with you to the forests of Vraja?”**

While Srimad-Bhagavatamexemplifies separation from Krsna, and while Caitanya Mahaprabhu personified it, there is another related separation which has been the personal trait of our acaryas—feelings of separation from Radha.

It is significant that in light of the voice of both Srimad-Bhagavatam and Caitanya Mahaprabhu, our acaryas’emphasis on Vipralambha-sevatakes an apparently different perspective. And the perspective of separation from service to Radha is pervasive, dominant, and prolific through the centuries, from Rupa Gosvami to Bhaktivinoda Thakura. And while Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura and Srila Prabhupada did not write explicit prayers or books in pursuance of service to Radha, they certainly elaborated on the principle.

Srila Prabhupada writes,

**“In Vrndavana all the pure devotees pray for the mercy of Srimati Radharani, the pleasure potency of Lord Krsna. Srimati Radharani is a tender-hearted feminine counterpart of the supreme whole, resembling the perfectional stage of the worldly feminine nature. Therefore, the mercy of Radharani is available very readily to the sincere devotees, and once She recommends such a devotee to Lord Krsna, the Lord at once accepts the devotee’s admittance into His association. The conclusion is, therefore, that one should be more serious about seeking the mercy of the devotee than that of the Lord directly, and by one’s doing so (by the good will of the devotee) the natural attraction for the service of the Lord will be revived.”**

Someone may ask:

**“Is separation from Sri Radha a digression from the standard teachings of feeling separation from Krsna?”**

The answer is:

**“No, it is not!”**

And in the above quote Srila Prabhupada addresses the underlying reasoning why it is not.

Without doubt the general principle taught by scripture and Lord Caitanya is separation from Krsna. But those same authorities also taught the process of approaching Krsna was through His devotees. There is no precedent for a direct approach to the Lord. To get the mercy of Krsna, one must get the mercy of His devotee, yasya prasadad bhagavat-prasadoand tasmat parataram devi tadiyanam samarcanam.

In our Gaudiya lineage the spiritual master is almost always an associate of one of two servitors of Krsna—Srimati Radharani or Lord Balarama-Nityananda.
