Having heard of the fidelity of Srimati Radharani’s maidservants, a practitioner hopes to one day enter into their midst and assist them in their service to Radha’s meetings with Krsna.

Although disappointment leads a mortal to abandon a material undertaking, the power of the internal potency makes a devotee experienced in separation even more determined to attain his goal. His hope is like an ocean without shores, in which undercurrents are expressions of humility such as, “What is the use of living without Radha;” the incoming tide is the force of affection that makes him whisper, “What would I do with Krsna, without Her;” the rising and falling of endless waves are the relentless emotions that wash his heart of every last trace of selfishness, “I am so wretched.”

The Supreme Lord and His consort are persons. While a mother will hold a toy out of reach of her child to make him more appreciative of it, her heart can only bear so many tears. Similarly, Radha and Krsna may withhold love from a devotee to make him all the more eager for it, but the devotee’s sincere solicitations soften the Divine Couple’s hearts.

While winter nights may appear endless, they do come to an end. By the grace of the sun, the darkness and cold are dispelled. Similarly, just when a sadhakathinks,

**“It is easier to make the sun rise than to get Radha’s mercy,”**

She relents.

Finally, the mercy comes!

It may come through one of many channels—the spiritual master, the holy name, the deity, or from within the heart. The Supreme is unlimited; so too are the ways it can manifest mercy. Notwithstanding, the recognised path is that mercy, in the form of a ray of pure goodness, comes from the heart of the advanced devotee. That is the law of bhaktimost preferred by Krsna.

**“How will the mercy appear?”**

It may come in any one of these four ways:

**“Through instructions, blessings, a darsana,or from the heart.”**

This mercy can come in the waking state, in a trance of bhajana, or in dream. However it comes, this mercy is the natural culmination of a life dedicated to quality sadhana.

When Narada was serving the great devotees, they instructed him to sit down and hear their talks of Krsna. In that way the boy was blessed with ecstatic devotion through hearing krsna-katha.Some devotees take Srila Prabhupada’s instruction to chant sixteen rounds and follow the regulative principles as a similar instruction, following which the serious practitioner will awaken ecstatic devotion.

Similarly, a devotee may receive the blessing of bhavaof his spiritual master with words like,

**“May you have undeviating devotion to the Divine Couple.”**

Although the Mathura brahmanaheard the narration of Gopakumara’s quest from its beginning to its completion, he was unstirred. With the order of Radha in his heart, Gopa-kumara blessed the brahmanawith love by embracing him.

The mere presence of a great devotee, of one’s Vraja role model, or of Krsna Himself, may give rise to bhavain the heart. Just as the full moon causes high tide in the ocean, one who is heavy with love can cause a surge of bhavawithin another. A devotee may also attain bhavaby seeing the deity of Krsna. Jiva Gosvami refers to the following verse, a favourite of Srila Prabhupada, as an illustration of mercy by seeing the deity of the Lord:

*smeram bhangi-traya-paricitam saci-vistirna-drstim*  
*vamsi-nyastadhara-kisalayam ujjvalam candrakena\|*  
*govindakhyam hari-tanum itah kesi-tirthopakanthe*  
*ma preksisthas tava yadi sakhe bandhu-sange ’sti rangah*

**“My dear friend! If you are indeed attached to your worldly friends, do not look at the smiling face of Lord Govinda as He stands on the bank of the Yamuna at Kesighata. Casting sidelong glances, He places His flute to His lips, which seem like newly-blossomed twigs. His transcendental body, bending in three places, appears very bright in the moonlight.”**

If real devotion manifests in a sadhakain the absence of the above causes, then it is to be understood that it has awakened from within. Krsna and His associates are within the heart of a devotee, and they can accomplish the same thing from within that they could accomplish from outside.

Because of the importance of a devotee’s grace, the following are two examples—both involving Narada Muni—of how a devotee bestows bhava.

Describing his disciple Prahlada Maharaja, the great sage says,

*gunair alam asankhyeyair*  
*mahatmyam tasya sucyate*  
*vasudeve bhagavati*  
*yasya naisargiki ratih*

**“Who could list the innumerable transcendental qualities of Prahlada Maharaja? He had unflinching faith in Vasudeva, Lord Krsna \[the son of Vasudeva\], and unalloyed devotion to Him. His attachment to Lord Krsna was natural because of his previous devotional service. Although his good qualities cannot be enumerated, they prove that he was a great soul \[mahatma\].”**

Prahlada was in the womb of his mother while she lived in Narada’s asrama.While the sage explained the science of devotion to the good lady, the boy heard everything, and this created a devotional impression that appeared as bhavaat the time of his birth. The words naisargiki ratihmean that he attained bhavaby the favour, nisarga,of Narada.

The other example is the equally well-known story of Narada and the hunter Mrgari that Caitanya Mahaprabhu narrated to Sanatana Gosvami. By Narada’s instructions and well-wishes, a sinful man became a pure devotee imbued with love of God.

Such is the power of the mercy of a great devotee. Fortunate is the sadhakawho attains his shelter.

## Chapter Forty

**Attaining Krsna’s Grace**

Our praise of divine grace would be incomplete if we did not say something about the power of the holy name to manifest bhava. Since Krsna and His name are one and the same, it stands to reason that the holy name can enact the same spiritual transformation within a sadhakathat Krsna can. Caitanya Mahaprabhu has said, namnam akari bahudha nija-sarva-saktis:

**“O Krsna! You have invested all Your potencies in Your names.”**

Since Rupa Gosvami has not separately listed the holy name as a means for attaining bhava,we shall not do so. We shall assume that it is part of giving mercy by instructions, as it is the order of the Lord and His devotees that a sadhakaexclusively dedicates himself to nama-sankirtana.We may also consider it to be included in the mercy given by a devotee, since the holy name is received from the Vaisnavas.

To indicate the power of the holy name we include a beautiful song by Thakura Bhaktivinoda which is laden with the truths and mercy of the holy name. Devotees who have been blessed by the grace of the name will identify with these verses:

*krsna-nama dhare koto bal*  
*visaya-vasananale, mora citta sada jvale,*  
*ravi-tapta maru-bhumi-sam*  
*karna-randhra-patha diya, hrdi majhe pravesiya,*  
*varisoya sudha anupam*

**“How much power does the name of Krsna possess? Like a desert scorched by the sun, my heart constantly burns in the fire of worldly desires. The holy name then enters my heart through my earholes to shower my soul with unparalleled nectar.**

*hrdoya hoite bole, jihvara agrete cale,*  
*sabda-ruðṛ nace anuksan*  
*kanthe mora bhange svara, anga kanpe thara thara,*  
*sthira hoite na pare caran*

**“It speaks from within my heart, moves on the tip of my tongue, and constantly dances on it in the form of transcendental sound. My throat becomes choked up, my body violently trembles, and my feet move uncontrollably.**

*cakse dhara, dehe gharma, pulakita saba carma,*  
*vivarna hoilo kalevara*  
*murchita hoilo man, pralayera agaman,*  
*bhave sarva-deha jara jara*

**“Rivers of tears flow from my eyes. Perspiration pours from my body. My body thrills with rapture, causing my hair to stand on end and my skin to pale and discolour. My mind grows faint, and I begin to experience devastation. In this way my entire body is shattered by a host of ecstasies.**

*kori’ eto upadrava, citte varse sudha-drava,*  
*more dare premera sagare*  
*kichu na bujhite dilo, more to’ batula koilo,*  
*mora citta-vitta saba bare*

**“While causing such an ecstatic disturbance, the holy name showers liquid nectar on my heart and drowns me in the ocean of divine love of God. He does not allow me to understand anything, for He has made me truly mad and has stolen away my heart and my wealth.**

l

*oinu asroya ja’r, heno vyavahara ta'r,*  
*varnite na pari e sakal*  
*krsna-nama iccha-moy, jahe jahe sukhi hoy,*  
*sei mora sukhera sambal*

**“Such is the behaviour of Him Who is now my only shelter. I am not capable of describing all this. The holy name of Krsna is independent and thus acts according to His own sweet will. In whatever way He becomes happy, that is also my way of happiness.**

*premera kalika nam, adbhuta rasera dham,*  
*heno bala karaye prakas*  
*isat vikasi’ punah, dekhay nija-rupa-guna,*  
*citta hari’ loya krsna-pas*

**“Krsna’s name is the bud of the flower of divine love, the abode of devotion’s wonderful mellows. Such is the power that He manifests that although He displays His power only slightly, He reveals His own divine form and qualities, steals my heart, and takes it to Krsna.**

*purna vikasita hoiya, braje more jaya loiya,*  
*dekhay more svarupa-vilas*  
*more siddha-deha diya, krsna-pase rakhe giya,*  
*e dehera kore sarva-nas*

**“Being fully manifest, the holy name of the Lord takes me to Vraja and reveals to me His own love dalliance. He gives me my eternal body, keeps me near Krsna, and completely destroys this mortal frame of mine.**

*krsna-nama-cintamani, akhila rasera khani,*  
*nitya-mukta suddba-rasa-moy*  
*namera balai jata, saba lo'ye hoi hata,*  
*tabe mora sukhera udoy*

**“The name of Krsna is touchstone, a mine of all devotional mellows, eternally liberated, and the embodiment of pure rasa. When all impediments to the pure chanting of the holy name are taken away and destroyed, then my happiness will know its true awakening.”**

\* \* \* \*

The grace of Krsna first manifests in the life of a devotee when, through some divine arrangement, he meets a Vaisnava and accomplishes some semblance of devotional service. From that time on, a gradual rise through the stages of devotion are constantly nurtured by divine grace, which grows ever more assertive with the attainment of every new frontier of self-realisation.

The mercy that manifests at the mature stage of attachment introduces the practitioner to ecstatic devotion in the way that a friend extends his hand to one needing assistance stepping over an obstacle. Although that obstacle is the unsurpassable ocean of material existence, by the grace of the Lord it has now become small enough to hop over with a little help.

Lord Brahma voices this truth with the unparalleled beauty of Srimad-Bhagavatam’spoetry. Even one unversed in Sanskrit tastes pleasure in reading such a composition:

*samasrita ye pada-pallava-plavam*  
*makat-padam punya-yaso murareh*  
*bhavambudhir vatsa-padam param padam*  
*padam padam yad vipadam na tesam*

**“For those who have accepted the boat of the lotus feet of the Lord, Who is the shelter of the cosmic manifestation and is famous as Murari, the enemy of the Mura demon, the ocean of the material world is like the water contained in a calf’s hoof-print. Their goal is param padam,Vaikuntha, the place where there are no material miseries, not the place where there is danger at every step.”**

As a Vaisnava revels in the wonders of transcendence and in the novelty of a blossoming svarupa,divine grace nudges him forward through the heavenly stages of ecstatic devotion to mature love. The realised soul has many steps to take before being fully qualified to enter Radha-Krsna’s entourage. And while he continues to hear and chant of the Divine Couple, his devotions are continually honed by moods of ecstasy that become ever more forceful and blissful with every step he takes towards Vraja.

As already described, the constitutional characteristic of bhava-bhakti,its svarupa-laksana,is ecstasy which appears both as cause and effect.

This means that by the influence of the pleasure potency, the sadhakaexperiences bhavaas ecstasy, and by the influence of the knowledge potency, he simultaneously perceives bhavaas the cause of ecstasy. This is the wonderful way in which suddha-sattva blesses the devotee. By contrast with the emotions a practitioner encounters during sadhana,the emotions at bhavaare fully transcendental and cleanse away all material contamination.

The influence of ecstasy is to soften the heart, and this marginal characteristic, tatastha-laksana,is responsible for external symptoms such as shedding tears, shivering of the body, and faltering of the voice. In the mood of a sadhaka,Caitanya Mahaprabhu prayed for these symptoms. And while the expressions of spiritual emotion are beyond the range of material contamination, from the spiritual point of view they are relatively mild and undeveloped. As prema matures, the emotions it generates proliferate and their external manifestations become all the more intense.

Softening of the heart results in a spontaneous desire to serve Krsna.

If a sadhakadid not develop spontaneity at practice, he does now. Raganaturally arises as a consequence of bhavaand makes itself known by three desires or tastes. These are the desires to meet Krsna, to please Him with services, and to gain His confidence in the way of a close friend. These desires individually and combinedly propel a devotee forward to ever-new spiritual frontiers until they realise their fulfilment in prema.

In addition, a bhava-bhaktadisplays nine behavioural characteristics, anubhavas,that are reliable indicators of true attainment. There are people who pose as advanced devotees by imitating some of these external symptoms, like crying. Srila Prabhupada speaks extensively about such imitators and so we shall not talk of them other than to remind the reader that since a real bhava-bhakta hides his tears, expressions of ecstasy are not a fair indicator of spiritual attainment. However, the following nine anubhavasdefine the external characteristics of a bhava-bhaktain both reliable and perceivable ways.

Rupa Gosvami lists these subordinate signs of ecstatic emotion as follows:

*ksantir avyartha-kalatvam*  
*viraktir mana-sunyata*  
*asa-bandhah samutkantha*  
*nama-gane sada rucih*

*asaktis tad-gunakhyane*  
*pritis tad-vasati-sthale*  
*ity-adayo ’nubhavah syur*  
*jata-bhavankure jane*

**“When the seed of ecstatic emotion for Krsna fructifies, the following nine symptoms manifest in one’s behaviour: tolerance, not wasting time, detachment, pridelessness, confidence in the Lord’s mercy, longing for the Lord, a taste for chanting the holy name of the Lord, attachment to descriptions of the transcendental qualities of the Lord, and affection for those places where the Lord resides—that is, a temple or a holy place like Vrndavana. These are all called anubhava,subordinate signs of ecstatic emotion. They are visible in a person in whose heart the seed of love of God has begun to fructify.”**

Tolerance means to remain undisturbed even when there is reason lor being perturbed, just as Pariksit Maharaja remained composed even in the face of death.

A devotee does not waste a moment of his time; he wants always to serve and glorify Krsna. Srila Prabhupada would exemplify this when be would regret having to sleep because it was “a waste of time.”

Natural attachment to Krsna means that a sadhakais truly detached and has no taste for sense objects. In his prayers to the Lord, Yamunacarya disclosed that he spat at the thought of past sense gratification.

Pridelessness is seen when a person in an important position still remains humble. A devotee is the most exalted of humans, and yet be always thinks of himself as worthless. An example is Maharaja Bharata, who is said to have begged door to door even from his enemies.

Confidence means that an advanced devotee has firm faith that he will meet with Krsna face to face. Why not! He has already come this far. By the same holy name and by the same mercy, he will certainly attain his objective. Sanatana Gosvami expresses this beautifully in the following verse, which practising devotees may embrace as an inspiration for never giving up:

*na prema sravanadi-bhaktir api va yogo 'tha va vaisnavo*  
*jnanam va subha-karma va kiyad aho saj-jatir apy asti va*  
*hinarthadhika-sadhake tvayi tathapy acchedya-mula sati*  
*be gopi-jana-vallabha vyathayate ha ha mad-asaiva mam*

**“O my Lord, I do not have any love for You, nor am I qualified to discharge devotional service by chanting and hearing. Nor do I possess the mystic power of a Vaisnava, knowledge, or pious activities. Nor do I belong to a high-caste family. On the whole, I do not possess anything. Still, Î beloved of the gopis,because You bestow Your mercy on the most fallen, I have an unbreakable hope that constantly in stirs my heart and pains me endlessly by its overwhelming presence.”**

A devotee has an insatiable longing or eagerness to be with the object of His desire, Krsna, an emotion that Bilvamangala Thakura vividly expresses in the poetry of his Krsna-karnamrta.

It goes without saying that an accomplished bhava-bhaktahas a taste for nama-sankirtana.Even while engaged in household duties, Srimati Radharani would give away Her thoughts by inadvertently singing about Krsna. And Arjuna would chant Hare Krsna even in his sleep. At the stage of bhava,chanting is a devotee’s constant companion.

And just as a devotee can never give up Krsna’s names, he cannot give up talking of Krsna’s qualities and pastimes. In his interaction with his disciples or with non-devotees, Srila Prabhupada always glorified Krsna by speaking the teachings of the Bhagavad-gita.His constant preaching was a sign of his attachment to glorifying the Lord.

And finally, a devotee is always attached to living in a place where Krsna enacted His pastimes. This may be in holy places like Vraja, Mayapur, or any temple of iskcon around the world, places that are all home to Lord Caitanya’s preaching pastimes.

A familiar verse that we chant while residing in New Vraja-dhama is found in Sri Padyavaliand spoken by Kavisekhara:a

*trasit kila nanda-sadma sakatasyatrabhavad bhanjanam*  
*bandha-ccheda-karo ‘pi damabhir abhud baddho ‘tra damodarah*  
*ittham mathura-vrddha-vigalat-piyusa-dharam pibann*  
*anandasru-dharah kada madhu-purim dhanyas carisyamy aham*

**“When will I become fortunate to visit Mathura Puri and shed tears of bliss as I drink from the stream of nectar words flowing from the mouths of the old guides there who say, ‘Here was Nanda Maharaja’s home. Here the cart was broken. Here Lord Damodara, who breaks the bonds of birth and death for His devotees, was Himself tied up with ropes by Mother Yasoda’?”**

As a devotee passes through the stage of sadhana-bhakti,he will gradually acquire a semblance of these qualities. Sometimes a few of those traits are visible, at other times they are not. At all times manifest characteristics are the shadow of the real thing. The genuine anubhavasof a bhava-bhaktaare always present, and they differ from those of the sadhana-bhaktain that the former are expressions of transcendence, the latter—while admirable—are, at best, expressions of goodness.

The characteristics of a devotee who has attained bhava-bhakti cannot be fully enumerated even by an august poet. Great demigods are in awe of a devotee who has reached this success in bhakti,knowing that his path to the pinnacle of spiritual achievement is almost a given. It is just a matter of a little mercy from the Lord.

\* \* \* \*

Introducing bhava-bhakti,Rupa Gosvami raises a few topics that are helpful in understanding the destination for which a sadhaka aspires.

There is such a thing as the semblance, abhasa,of bhava,also known as rati,which is called ratyabhasa,and which may be seen in two kind of devotees:

**One is aspiring for liberation and sense gratification, the other is ignorant of bhakti,curious, and socially conscious.**

Given the right circumstances and association, they both can experience a semblance or reflection of bhavaknown as prati-bimba-ratyabhasaand chaya-ratyabhasa,respectively.

Since Krsna reluctantly gives bhavato even pure devotees, it will be clear to the reader that He will definitely not give it to the impure practitioner, to those who are self-interested. Nonetheless, under certain circumstances, even those impure devotees may experience spiritual emotions, seeing which some neophytes become impressed.

**“How do impure people experience even a reflection of bhava?”**

Rupa Gosvami answers:

The beams of pure devotion from real devotees shine upon them either in kirtana,a festival, or parikramaof holy places, and make an impression that produces the semblance of the real thing.

Of the two kinds of ratyabhasa, prati-bimbais more intense and may be likened to a reflection. However, because its motivation is very bad, it cannot lead to pure devotion, although it can result in elevated stages of sense gratification and even liberation.

The other, chaya,is weaker, resembling a shadow. But its advantage is that the motivation is innocent. Of the two it is the better, because by further association with an advanced devotee, the practitioner with chaya-ratyabhasacan be elevated to pure devotion, and in time to pure ratior bhava.

The topic of prati-bimbais of no further interest. However, we should consider certain features of chaya-ratyabhasathat are relevant to the true sadhaka.

It happens that on occasion, a practising devotee has an overwhelming spiritual experience. He feels an upsurge in emotions like humility and happiness, accompanied by externally uncontrollable symptoms like crying and trembling. After the symptoms subside, the sadhakais generally confused and worries that he has become a sahajiya,an imposter.

The concept of chaya-ratyabhasahelps explain this phenomenon and lay a devotee’s mind to rest—he is not an imposter.

As already explained, the moonrays of bhavafrom a great devotee, from the holy name, or from Krsna Himself, may touch the heart of an inexperienced and immature devotee. Because he is not qualified for it, the devotee cannot be elevated to the stage of bhava.And yet the mercy is not ineffective. It will touch the devotee and induce a semblance of bhavain him that lasts for a while before it wanes.

And although the influence of ratyabhasawanes, the memory of it does not; neither does the purification it affects. A sincere devotee remembers such experiences and so becomes determined for advanced devotion. Additionally, the intense experience burns up material attachments and makes advancement that much easier and that much more rewarding. But it should he emphasised that only quality association will further the cause of pure devotion and bring about the blessings of transcendence. It is not possible without serving, hearing from, and being blessed by an advanced devotee.

In summary, a devotee should not misunderstand when forceful feelings of ecstasy overtake him while still in an immature stage of devotion. He should recognise such events to be made possible by the mercy of his guruor other advanced devotees. Such epiphanies or spiritual incidents should be cherished and used by the devotee as inspiration for quality sadhanaand recommitment to attaining bhava.Many disciples of Srila Prabhupada had similar experiences in his presence, and those experiences remain with them as one of the landmarks of their spiritual journey. Other devotees have similar spiritual encounters that are occasioned in different ways.

But just as a devotee’s sadhanaor ratyabhasacan be elevated to their culmination by sadhu-sanga,similarly sadhana, ratyabhasa, and even bhavacan be hampered and even destroyed by offences to a sadhu.This unfortunate topic requires careful attention. Rupa Gosvami explains why:

*hari-priya-janasyaiva prasada-bhara-labhatah*  
*bhavabhaso ’pi sahasa bhavatvam upagacchati*  
*tasminn evaparadhena bhavabhaso ’py anuttamah*  
*kramena ksayam apnoti kha-sthah purna-sasi yatha*

**“By the boundless mercy of a dear devotee of the Lord, the semblance of bhavasuddenly transforms into real bhava.But by offending that devotee, even the best bhavabhasagradually wanes as does the full moon in the sky.**

*kim ca—*  
*bhavo ’py abhavam ayati krsna-presthaparadhatah*  
*abhasatam ca sanakair nyuna-jatiyatam api*

**“Moreover, it should be added that by a grave offence to a dear devotee of the Lord, even real bhavawill be destroyed; by an intermediate offence, bhavawill degrade to bhavabhasa;and by a slight offence, bhava will deteriorate to an inferior quality.”**

In his teachings to Rupa Gosvami, Caitanya Mahaprabhu warned of the dangers of offences to Vaisnavas, likening them to a mad elephant that tramples underfoot the flowering garden of the creepers of devotion. In the above verses, Rupa Gosvami highlights offences to a great devotee and is very specific about what it means to trample the creeper of devotion.

Whether a devotee has attained bhavaor merely its semblance, the taste of devotion is the inspiration for its execution, in the way that the taste of food is the reason for eating. If that taste is lost, the inspiration for bhakti,as it does for eating, wanes and dies.

Commentators Jiva and Visvanatha detail the intent of the author of Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu,which we shall summarise.

Offences are of two kinds: those to Krsna, and those to His dear devotee.

Although Jiva Gosvami seems to weigh them equally, it is commonly accepted that the latter is more grievous than the former. That said, it seems that both still have the same effect on the bhakti of the offender.

If the sinner is a bhava-bhakta,then his punishment varies with the severity of his offence, which is graded as extreme, intermediate, and slight. No mention is made of how that assessment is made, however we have the example of Brghu Muni, whose offences corresponded to the above grading when they were physical, verbal, and mental. Even today the Lord has the footmark of Brghu on His chest, a reminder of where the brahmanakicked Him—a very severe offence.

The reaction to an extreme offence committed by the bhava-bhaktais that he is deprived of his bhava;he becomes abhava. That means he again becomes a sadhana-bhakta,and one without even a semblance of bhava.

The reaction for an intermediate offence is that the offender is again deprived of his transcendental attainment; he becomes a sadhana-bhakta,but he retains a semblance of bhava, bhavabhasa.

Finally, the reaction for a slight offence is that the permanent mood, sthayi-bhava,of the offender is lowered. Acarya Visvanatha says that if the devotee is in the conjugal mellow, his mood is changed to servitude, and if it is servitude, that is changed to neutrality. We know that the conjugal mood is the richest in mellows and has the tastes of all other rasas.In this case the slight offender is deprived of his natural inclination and receives an identity that has less qualities.

An example of an offender is the Dvivida gorilla, who was part of Lord Kama’s entourage and rendered extraordinary service in the war against Ravana. Some say that he is even an eternal associate of the Lord. Yet Dvivida had some disagreement with Laksmana; he could not surrender to the Lord’s brother and became offensive to Him. As a result he lost his bhava,and by association with the demon Naraka, he too became a full-fledged demon who was later killed by Lord Balarama. In this instance an associate of the Lord is converted to a demon by vaisnava-aparadha.

The reactions for offences committed by a sadhana-bhaktawith bhavabhasaare not detailed in the same way. Yet Rupa Gosvami says,

**“The best bhavabhasagradually wanes.”**

This indicates that there are grades of bhavabhasa,and according m the weight of offence, as in the case of the bhava-bhakta,the offender either loses his bhavabhasaaltogether or is demoted to semblances of bhavaof decreasing intensity.

A similar loss of bhava,or a loss of the semblance of bhava, takes place when a sadhakakeeps intimate association with a Mayavadi or someone strongly drawn to impersonal liberation. As Caitanya Mahaprabhu said, mayavadi krsne aparadhi:

**“Mayavadas are offensive to Krsna.”**

By keeping company with Mayavadis, a devotee also becomes offensive and is thereby deprived of his bhava.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu warns His followers to be alert and avoid all offences and bad association. He says to Sri Rupa,

*tate mali yatna kari' kare avarana*  
*aparadha-hastira yaiche na haya udgama*

**“The gardener must defend the creeper by fencing it all around so that the powerful elephant of offences may not enter.”**

The practical means by which a sadhakacan protect his devotion is by avoiding bad association and staying always in the company of pure devotees, especially advanced devotees. That way a practitioner can freely taste the nectar of bhavabhasaor of bhava,as the case may be.

Aside from that, a Vaisnava must remain alert against weeds that take root within the best fenced-off garden, weeds that can choke off the actual creeper of devotion and cause offensive conduct. The most obvious weeds are those that promote:

**“Material enjoyment, liberation, unacceptable behaviour, diplomatic behaviour, desires for worship, and recognition as a great devotee.”**

As water nourishes weeds and healthy creepers alike, nama-sankirtananourishes the weeds of bad habits growing alongside the creeper of devotion. If, with the help of advanced association, the weeds are not pulled out at the root, they can cause havoc in a sadhaka’sattempts at perfection. But when such weeds are uprooted, then the devotional creeper quickly bears the fruit of premain the shade of Krsna’s lotus feet. At that stage of devotion, the bhaktais no longer susceptible to offences or deviant behaviour. That is the perfection of life.

\* \* \* \*

Some devotees argue that because Krsna’s mercy is very difficult to attain, it is more desirable to strive for Lord Caitanya’s mercy. After all, Srila Prabhupada often said that Gaura was more merciful than Krsna. To court Gauranga’s favour, they say, one need not be learned in scripture, or versed in the ways of bhakti.One has only to chant Hare Krsna and Caitanya Mahaprabhu will do the rest. After all, they reason, the Lord came to give krsna-prema to the most fallen; they are fallen and so premawill come in this last-track way.

This reasoning, however, is flawed, because it does not reconcile the speciality of the Lord’s limited pastimes on Earth with the greater purpose of His teachings for the future generations of followers. A proper understanding of the Lord’s appearances cannot ignore what both Krsna and Gaura said while present.

Although Lord Caitanya transformed sinners like Jagai and Madhai into lovers of Krsna, these miraculous conversion of krpa-siddhi,like the Lord’s physical presence, are a special feature of the

Lord’s pastimes. They are not the standard path to perfection.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu displayed bhavaimmediately after initiation to show the power of diksaand the diksa-mantra.However, we do not see devotees today making such extraordinary transformations after their initiation. In short, the miraculous deliverance of devotees we read about in biographies like Caitanya-caritamrta are exceptional occurrences, limited to the Lord’s pastimes.

Vaisnavas must view Lord Caitanya’s pastimes of mercy in tandem with His teachings. The former take place exclusively during the time of His appearance, the latter are for everyone, for all time.

It is like the difference between vapu-sevaand vani-seva.The physical presence of a great person facilitates some unique exchanges for a limited audience and for a certain era. However, it is the teachings of a great person, which are not dependent on geography or time and so are universal in application, that are his greatest gifts to mankind.

A reader may then ask:

“Then what is that special feature of Caitanya Maha- prabhu’s mercy that Vaisnava texts extol?”

To this question acaryas,including Srila Prabhupada, reply:

**“It is the unqualified, publicly proclaimed, and freely distributed means to attain perfection. We repeat, ‘the means to attain perfection,’ not ‘perfection itself.’”**

The special mercy of Caitanya Mahaprabhu was to disclose to the world the most confidential perfection of spontaneous loving devotion and the path to its attainment:

*anarpita-carim cirat karunayavatirnah kalau*  
*samarpayitum unnatojjvala-rasam sva-bhakti-sriyam*  
*harih purata-sundara-dyuti-kadamba-sandipitah*  
*sada hrdaya-kandare sphuratu vah saci-nandanah*

**“May the Supreme Lord, Who is known as the son of Srimati Saci-devi, be transcendentally situated in the innermost chambers of your heart. Resplendent with the radiance of molten gold, He has appeared in the Age of Kali by His causeless mercy to bestow what no incarnation has ever offered before: the most sublime and radiant mellow of devotional service, the mellow of conjugal love.”**

Moreover, the Lord gave access to both this sadhyaand sadhana through the simple process of nama-sankirtana.And because He is the same Supreme Being who establishes the laws of bhakti-yoga, He could dispense with all the qualifications of purity, learning, and high birth that would be obstacles for the average person of this age. And so through His teachings and example, Caitanya Mahaprabhu opened the door to the very secret storehouse of love of God, thereby making its contents available to anyone and everyone who was willing to accept it—with the minimal condition that they abandon sinful life.

Kaviraja Gosvami writes,

**“He wove a wreath of the holy name and prema,with which He garlanded the entire material world.”**

From this verse we should understand the wreath of the holy name and premato be the sadhanaof chanting Hare Krsna in the mood of separation from a Vraja associate. The Lord did not garland the world with premain a form that descends on people whether they want it or not, or make effort lor it or not. Rather, Caitanya Mahaprabhu freely garlanded the world with premain the form of the means by which people can attain prema.

The two ways in which premadescends is described by Narada to Gopa-kumara:

**One form is that love which comes fully manifest without any effort. The other is the love that scriptures describe, love which comes in an unmanifest form as sadhana-bhakti,and which manifests as a consequence of perfected practice.**

Narada explains these two processes in this way:

*yathodaran milaty annam*  
*pakvam va paka-sadhanam*  
*sadhakasyocyate sastra*  
*gatyayam sadhana-kramah*

**“Just as from a generous donor one might receive food already cooked or the means and ingredients for cooking food oneself, so according to the opinions of scripture one receives Krsna’s mercy through a method of devotional practice leither regulative or spontaneous\].”**

This example has been explained earlier. A well-wisher may show his mercy to a pauper in two ways:

**He may invite the beggar to a cooked meal, or he may give the poor man all the ingredients with which to cook his own meal.**

In both cases the pauper enjoys a meal as a result of his well- wisher’s kindness.

Another example is when one requests a flame with which to initiate a sacrifice. That flame may be given as a burning ghee wick ready to be placed in firewood, or one may receive the ingredients for the flame, namely, a piece of cotton, a container with ghee, a little camphor, and a few matches. In either case, the purpose of lighting the fire is achieved, albeit in different ways.

In summary, when Caitanya Mahaprabhu is said to freely distribute love of God, we should understand that during His appearance He gives both krpa-siddhiand sadhana-siddhi,and after His disap pearance that same premais available through sadhana-siddhi.

These are the features of Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s special mercy. These are the wonderful truths of devotion that Krsna did not explicitly reveal. This is the leniency that Krsna did not display. Of those rare souls who did understand His intent, Krsna was demanding. The Lord expected aspirants to surrender to Him and renounce the world as conditions for adopting the sadhanaof vraja- bhakti.Caitanya Mahaprabhu did not.

If we enquire what the teachings are for the present time, then the answer will be that it is the wisdom that Caitanya Mahaprabhu and His representatives taught! And that is the rigorous practice of sadhana-bhaktibased on knowledge and renunciation.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu described the path of perfection to Sanatana Gosvami, and these teachings were expanded on in books by His followers, which include Rupa Gosvami, Jiva Gosvami, Visvanatha Cakravarti, Bhaktivinoda Thakura, Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura, and Srila Prabhupada. The books of the acaryas lay the foundations of sadhana-bhakti,describing how devotees can rise from faith to attachment, and how by the additional grace of the Lord they can reach bhava,the juicy fruit of their practice. This book is an attempt to summarise those teachings and to emphasise the determination a sadhakaneeds, and the repeated sankalpashe must make to progress up the staircase of sadhana.

In conclusion, to avail themselves of Lord Caitanya’s special mercy, devotees must read the teachings of the Lord as they are found in the books of His followers, and systematically implement into their sadhanathe teachings they have learned from their gurus.

Yes, Lord Caitanya’s mercy is special! Kaviraja Gosvami says that a study of Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s life and teachings will reveal that,

*sri-krsna-caitanya-daya karaha vicara*  
*vicara karite citte pabe camatkara*

**“If you are indeed interested in logic and argument, kindly apply it to the mercy of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu. If you do so, you will find it to be strikingly wonderful.”**

Hut Krsna’s direct mercy is also special! After Rupa Gosvami describes how mercy makes bhavaavailable through sadhanaand through devotees, the author writes this verse to indicate that the most wonderful mercy of all is that very rare mercy which is given directly by Krsna. Putana is an example of such good fortune:

*lokottara-camatkara-karakah sarva-saktidah*  
*yah prathiyan bhaved bhavah sa tu krsna-prasadajah*

**“That bhavawhich is more amazing than anything in this world, which gives all powers, and which is very deep, is the bhavacaused by the mercy of Krsna.”**

May the grace of Gaura and Krsna bless us all with our most coveted goal, and may we attain the service to the Divine Couple that we most hunger for. Jaya Srila Prabhupada! Jaya Gaura-Nitai! Jaya Radha-Syama!

## Summary and Conclusion

In this final chapter we summarise the contents of each chapter, or select philosophical conclusions from those chapters in a way t hat the aggregate paints a comprehensive picture of the message of Sankalpa-kaumudi.The basic theme of this book is pure devotional service in practice; more specifically, how a devotee navigates the steps within sadhana-bhaktiwith the cherished aspiration of attaining bhava.

After reviewing the basics of bhakti-yogawe introduce the principles, psychology, and general examples of sankalpasin devotional service in practice. This preliminary knowledge facilitates the understanding of the subsequent theme, the stage-by-stage progression in attentive nama-bhajanaenriched with the mood of separation taught by Caitanya Mahaprabhu. When a devotee expertly applies himself to this process he can expect two things: systematically advancing to the stage of deep attachment to Krsna, and becoming the object of the Lord’s mercy. The attainment of those two will ensure entrance into the kingdom of ecstatic loving devotion.

We now begin our chapter-by-chapter summary.

\* \* \* \*

Part One, “Aspects of Sadhana,” lays a foundation of devotional truths on which the book rests. It gives a brief look at the basic elements of sadhana-bhakti,such as its place among other types of devotion, its purity, stages, underlying basic truths, how a devotee is recognised by qualification and attainment, and the spiritual transformation it brings about in a sadhaka’sbody—gross and subtle.

In Chapter One we introduce bhaktias the subject of the book, offering an unadorned description of pure devotional service. Although bhaktiis about practice and perfection, there is an intermediate stage which is the preliminary phase of perfection, and is called bhava.This exalted accomplishment is the goal of sadhana-bhaktiand the heartbeat of the serious practitioner Ecstatic devotion should be the urgent and immediate goal of even sadhakaand also the final attainment he can expect in this life. The reason is that bhava-bhaktiis the preliminary stage of love of God, one for which a practitioner’s body is suited, and one which then awards them the spiritual body in which they can further cultivate love under the direct tutelage of Krsna’s eternal associates in a setting where Krsna’s pastimes are concurrently manifest. Moreover, the body that corresponds to the stage of bhavais eminently suitable for cultivating loving devotion to its perfection.

Chapter Two is a summary of the stages of devotion from faith to love, and an explanation of the two approaches to sadhana— regulated practice and spontaneous practice. Throughout the book determinations are described in relation to both vaidhiand raga-bhakti,with the understanding that in the ideal, the former is meant to gradually transform into the latter. If that transforma tion does not take place in practice, it can alternatively take place with the attainment of bhava.In order to highlight the prominence of pure devotion, also known as svarupa-siddha-bhakti, this chapter also describes some impure forms of devotion, like aropa-siddha-bhakti.Impure devotion has its limited benefits, most significant of which is that it may give the practitioner access to pure devotees and their mode of pure worship. However, knowledge of impure devotion primarily serves the purpose of steering the sadhakaclear of this potentially spiritual hazard. The straight and effective path to Krsna is along the path of pure devotion.

Chapter Three studies how devotees are appreciated, namely according to their qualification for and attainment in devotion. In both cases there are three divisions, the beginner, intermediate, and advanced, and of these the intermediate is most suited to be a preacher. Yet there are two kinds of madhyama-adhikais:the practitioner who has risen to this stage of attainment, and the perfected devotee who has sublimated his ecstasy to embrace the qualities of

a preacher. He is the true acarya.As for the beginner, if he neglects both the study of Srila Prabhupada’s books and strict sadhana,he becomes entrenched in the introductory stage of devotion where minimal nama-sankirtanaand faith in Krsna’s deity are identified with Krsna consciousness. However, this religious life, while a preliminary stage of bhakti,should not be the proverbial spiritual rut in which a devotee becomes stuck, inasmuch as elementary school is fine for a child but not an adult.

The different stages of sadhanaand of sadhakasare the subject of the fourth chapter. Rupa Gosvami discloses that a bhava-bhakta is both a sadhakaand the upper limit of the intermediate devotee. Since sadhanais about purification, Chapter Four also describes bow the stages of bhaktifrom faith to love effect the spiritualisation of the two aspects of self-identification, “I” and “mine.” The degree of spiritualisation of these factors determines how well a devotee can be attentive in sadhana,specifically in nama-bhajana. Since attentive nama-sankirtanais the means by which a serious devotee can effectively pass through the stages of nistha, ruci,and asakti,it is imperative that the practitioner properly align his heart tî the needs that such purification effects. Surrender means to be willing to make those lifestyle adjustments that facilitate freedom from the contamination brought about by identifying with the gross material body. Krsna challenges the sadhanato be constantly endeavouring for perfection. And while such long-term effort may sound exhausting, the transcendentally uplifting nature of pure devotional service is invigorating and energising. Bhaktiproperly performed is never tiring.

In this book we repeatedly emphasise the indispensable need to study Vaisnava scripture, beginning with but not limited to Srila Prabhupada’s books. Chapter Five is the first essay on this subject, wherein we concentrate on why scripture emphasises the need to know tattva,and also give many examples of living entities—even animals—who achieved perfection without even a modicum of spiritual understanding. That said, the spiritual perfection of an ignorant animal, for example, should not be an excuse for a human to neglect his God-given intelligence and ignore the real challenge before him, which is studying the basic truths of sadhana-bhakti that he can apply for the attainment of bhava.Srila Prabhupada

has already summarised the Vedas in easily understandable language, and a devotee cannot seriously be called his follower with out respecting what His Divine Grace dedicated most of his time to, and which he referred to as his mission: presenting transcendental literature for the Vaisnava community.

\* \* \* \*

Part Two, “The Definition and Purpose of Sadhana,” is an essential read, a dedicated exposition of the definition of sadhana-bhakti with specific emphasis on its goal, bhava-bhakti.That definition makes clear the overarching purpose of a sadhaka’sdevotions, and it also serves as the inspiration for this book’s composition.

Chapter Six introduces two important subjects: the first is the correlation between a devotee’s practice and perfection, and the second, the definition of practice. Rupa Gosvami's definition of sadhana-bhaktireflects this correlation and makes clear to every sadhakawhat the real purpose of his devotion is, a purpose that should never be forgotten, but rather yearned after. Throughout Sankalpa-kaumudiwe cite a basic aphorism: practice must be in accord with its goal. Knowledge of practice is abhidheya-jnana, and knowledge of perfection, prayojana-jnana.In every endeavour one’s goal must be crystal clear, and the effort by which that goal is attained, equally so. Thus the sadhaka'sendeavours meet with success in the way that a traveller who is clear on his directions successfully reaches his desired destination. And of course, the foundation of such practice and perfection is based on sambandha-jnana, knowledge of relationships.

Devotional service is not manifest by physical acts, but it is self-manifesting, meaning it is Krsna’s mercy. The topic of Chapter Seven is circular causality, which indicates a mutual and perpetual interaction of cause and effect. As the wheel of bhakticontinues to rotate, a devotee advances through the stages of devotion, beginning with sraddhaand ending with asakti.With this spiritual development his false ego is systematically spiritualised, and although hidden behind the curtain of his conditioning, bhava becomes increasingly prominent. The neophyte devotee misunderstands the cause of bhaktito be his own activities, such as chanting

Hare Krsna. He does not recognise that the seed of devotion was received from his spiritual master and it is the sprouting of this seed that enables his practices to bear fruit. In time, as the neophyte matures, he understands the truths of devotion and realises that bhaktiis actually the manifestation of Krsna’s mercy upon his senses. And that mercy almost always appears through advanced Vaisnavas, most notably the diksa-and siksa-gurus.

Chapter Eight poses and answers a series of questions that devoices and non-devotees alike raise about the definition of sadhana- bhakti.Since non-devotees and impersonalists often challenge the definition of sadhana,answering their objections is as much a defence of our spiritual heritage as a means of education for studious Vaisnavas. The last question—how and why bhavafinally makes its appearance—is answered more elaborately in the following chapter. Of cardinal importance is a devotee’s own understanding of the purpose for which they are practising sadhana.While the definition repeatedly appears in Srila Prabhupada’s books, and while it is as perfect as all Rupa Gosvami's illuminations on bhakti- yoga,devotees often fail to grasp the importance of the stated goal of practice. The result of a lack of clear purpose in sadhanais that the practitioner remains either a perpetual sadhakaor abandons serious sadhanaaltogether. Both these undesirable results can be avoided when a devotee is directed to the objective of practice both by his own studies and the guidance of others.

Bhava-bhaktiappears by the grace of the Lord, when He or His representatives are satisfied by a sadhaka’sstrong attachment to Krsna. To properly understand how the bhavaconcealed in the heart of the devotee is revealed by the premaof the Lord, Chapter Nine further studies the definition of bhavaand the corresponding commentaries of our acaryas.This topic is important, because the awakening of ecstatic devotion through progressive stages of sadhanais the underlying theme of Sankalpa-kaumudi. And while bhavais the ultimate goal of sadhana,it is achieved by a sequence of intermediate goals, such as rising from steadiness to taste. However, these intermediate sankalpasmust clearly he in a straight line with the destination of bhava,which means that a sadhakamust be attentive and not distracted by unrelated devotional efforts. In the way that one who wants to quickly and securely arrive at his destination avoids detours, similarly a devotee who is eager for bhavaavoids dabbling in the spiritual practices like, for example, the practices or forms of worship of other Vaisnava sampradayas.

\* \* \* \*

Part Three, “The Sankhya of Sankalpa,” is an analytical study of exactly what sankalpais in relation to its prime movers: the mind, intelligence, and false ego. These three constitute the sub stratum of determination, and of taking the initiative to progress through the stages of sadhana.Since both determination and making determinations are functions of a subtle body purified by the power of bhakti,it is helpful for a student to have a basic grasp of Srimad-Bhagavatam’sapproach to this psychology.

Chapter Ten is an introduction to Part Three. The primary parts of the subtle mechanism that constitutes a sankalpaare the senses, mind, intelligence, and false ego. The purpose of this sankhya- analysis is to help prevent the practitioner from falling victim to the obstacles posed by his conditioned nature. Moreover, by the strength of his sadhana,he should engage his subtle faculties to progress along his spiritual journey. Throughout the Bhagavad-gita Krsna emphasises the importance of controlling the senses and mind by a spiritually empowered intelligence. Since sankalpasare based on a spiritual decision-making process, a sadhakawill find clarity in his determinations when he comprehends the mechanism underlying the interaction between the subtle and gross bodies. The intelligence becomes enlightened by transcendental knowledge, and in such an empowered state it can direct the soul to its destination without impediment.

Chapter Eleven describes the origin of the mind, its conduct under the modes of nature, and how devotional service purifies it. Where the mind was once the cause of the tribulations of material life, it can become the source of happiness in devotional service. After all, it is the controlled mind that enables the contemplation and realisation of a sankalpa.Because of its inherently sattvika nature, the mind is inclined to spiritual life; however, past karmic entanglement has habituated it to sense gratification. Controlled by the intelligence and purified by nama-sankirtana,the mind is the asset that a devotee needs not only for determinations, but also for meditation on the holy name, the means by which he can progress through the advanced stages of nistha, ruci,and asakti.That said, no matter how instrumental the mind may be in nama-bhajana, spiritual authorities advise practitioners never to put full faith in the mind. We have the example of many accomplished yogiswho fall down from their perfection by being victimised by the mind.

Chapter Twelve describes the all-important topic of empowering the intelligence to retake control over the mind. By gradually relinquishing its authority to the inferior mind, which then entangles the jivain unconstitutional acts, the bewildered intelligence assumed an inferior role to its subordinate. However, by the association of saints and by hearing devotional scriptures, the intelligence gradually reasserts its authority over the mind, recalibrates the ego as a servant of Krsna, and redirects the jivato devotional service. The intelligence is the immediate neighbour of the soul and also the medium through which Krsna communicates. When Krsna says that He gives a devotee intelligence, it means that He communicates transcendental knowledge through the medium of the intelligence. And because knowledge is the sustenance of the intelligence, in one sense there is no difference between knowledge and intelligence. For this reason scripture is replete with knowledge that nurtures the intelligence so that it can reassume its role in being the driver of the chariot of the body, and master of the mind.

The thirteenth chapter of Sankalpa-kaumudihighlights the role played by the false ego in the entanglement of the superior living entity in the inferior material energy. The first step in this process of degradation takes place when the pure living entity exhibits indifference to his eternal identity as the servant of Krsna. This unstable condition quickly leads to fascination with the temptations of maya,which then result in the acquisition of countless material bodies and the false identity of being an enjoyer. The false identity that the living entity embraces is central to its entanglement in fruitive activities. However, if the jivaembraces a real identity as servant of Krsna, that identity becomes instrumental to his emancipation. Reforming the false ego entails a gradual process of purifying the mind of its spiritual indifference and its material indulgences. This reformation is made possible by the power of sadhana-bhakti,a power with which the sadhakacan make successive sankalpastowards his quest. The sensual, mental, and intellectual engagements of sadhana-bhaktiare meant to effect the reformation of the ego, and when that reformation is complete, one is said to be self-realised and eligible for ecstatic devotion.

Chapter Fourteen employs the example of the ladder as a means to explain how the descent of the soul from a condition of liberation to bondage is akin to the ascent from bondage to liberation. The sankalpasin both directions are similar: it is a matter of whether the mind acts to degrade the conditioned soul or liberate him. The conduct of the mind, and thus the intelligence and ego, largely depends upon the type of association with which they connect. The association of a pure devotee is key in generating a spiritual inclination in the subtle body, which can then begin its journey of sankalpasto re-establish the soul in its constitutional position. The association of pure devotees and advanced devotees is not just an inaugural event, it is at the root and the crown of devotional service, and at all times in between. The implication of keeping good company is avoiding bad association, which is not about physical proximity to a non-devotee, but being dependent on them in a way that compromises one’s own spiritual values and practices.

\* \* \* \*

Part Four, “Types and Examples of Sankalpa,” gives practical examples of different sankalpasthat are characteristic of progress on the path of devotion. It begins with a description of the five basic kinds of determinations and their relative importance to the goal of sadhana.Knowledge of these types of sankalpasgives a thoughtful sadhakaa tool with which to measure the value of his devotional acts as they relate to the attainment of bhava.The chapters that follow set out examples of determinations made in Krsna consciousness, and offer practical advice on how a devotee can go about making a sankalpa.

Devotees can evaluate the relevance of a determination in elevating them to bhavabased on which of the following five categories their sankalpafalls into, which Chapter Fifteen describes as: determinations that are full of the desire for ecstatic devotion; those that are the ingredients to attaining bhava;those favourable for realising it; those that are unopposed to it; and those that are detrimental for its attainment. Scriptures are replete with recommendations that promote devotional progress. However, not all of these guidelines can be followed at once, and according to varying circumstances some may not be applicable and others may be impractical. For this reason a devotee must know which choices and practises in Krsna consciousness are principles and which are details, which are indispensable and which are dispensable. Once again, making these choices and decisions is the function of the intelligence, which must be crystal clear about the five kinds of determinations and how and when they are applicable in bringing the practitioner closer to his goal.

Chapter Sixteen cites sankalpasfrom scripture and the lives of our acaryas.These examples are educational for a practitioner because they reveal how the Lord and His devotees go about their determinations, and thus they teach what should—and in some cases what should not—be undertaken to formulate, execute, and perfect a sankalpa.In all cases we see that these sankalpasare characterised by three features: a clear goal, the means to attain it, and where that goal leads. A practitioner may question the sheer volume of things to be known in practising sadhana,but the truth of the matter is that material entanglement is convoluted enough to require at least a corresponding effort in becoming disentangled. Of these three characteristics of a sankalpa,the means of attainment is what requires a coherent approach that bears the knowledge of how tî evade the trappings of the material energy and maximise the benefits to be derived by spiritual practice. Additionally, the other two features of a sankalpa—a clear goal and where the goal leads—must also be in harmony with the dynamics of pure devotional service.

There are many examples of sankalpasupon which a devotee embarks upon in his personal sadhana.Chapter Seventeen describes some of these, such as the most obvious determination of chanting a minimum of sixteen offenceless rounds a day. And when a devotee becomes more advanced he may read books that nurture his specific aspiration in perfection, such as the parts of Srimad-Bhagavatamthat describe Krsna’s pastimes with the gopis.

A devotee who is serious about spiritual advancement should be clear about the determinations he needs to make in all areas of his life, such as sadhana, asrama,and lifestyle, just to name a few. Moreover, he should know which vows are voluntary, public, private, essential, optional, general, or personalised. An important takeaway from this chapter, as from the book, is that a serious sadhakais not someone who considers devotional service to be a process that functions on autopilot, where the practitioner mechanically plods along. To the contrary, a devotee is constantly assessing himself, makes adjustments in sadhanaas needed, and moves from stage to stage armed with the appropriate sankalpa.In Krsna’s words, those who are “constantly endeavouring for perfection are assured of liberation in the Supreme in the very near future.” In Chapter Eighteen we offer the ingredients for making a sankalpawhich are generic to the many determinations a devotee will make on his spiritual journey to ecstatic devotion. Some of these are: knowing at what stage one is in spiritual life; where one is going; having the qualification to get there; and how to actually best formulate a sankalpa.These ingredients of sankalpashould be put into practice under the governance of the earlier described five categories, such as determinations that are full of the desire for ecstatic devotion, or those that are the ingredients to attaining ecstatic devotion. The combination of these governing and subsequent aspects of sankalpamay be compared to how a cooked offering for the deity is prepared: the primary ingredients are the cooking utensils, fire, ghee, and vegetables. The spicing is secondary, its purpose to enhance the offering in different ways according to availability or taste. In either case, just as a cook carefully considers how to best prepare his offering to the deity, a sadhakaconsiders well the steps he makes towards ecstatic devotion.

\* \* \* \*

Part Five, “Determinations in Sadhana,” concludes the description of the concepts underlying determinations with an emphasis on factors that effect and possibly neutralise a devotee’s efforts in progressing through the stages of sadhana.It explores the role of sankalpain sadhana-bhaktiin terms of its causes, nourishment, and loss. The first five parts of Sankalpa-kaumudilay the groundwork for the last three—Six, Seven, and Eight—which investigate three essential pillars of sankalpa:attentiveness in nama-bhajana, chanting with emotion, and divine grace, respectively.

Chapter Nineteen begins with a summary of the preceding chapters and continues with both scriptural and historical examples of how, for different reasons, devotees express their determinations: to advance in Krsna consciousness, to attain a certain service, or to see the Lord. And while these are all perfect reasons for sankalpas, in the eyes of great devotees the best reasons are those which aim at pleasing one’s spiritual master, at pleasing Krsna, and at spreading the Krsna consciousness movement among conditioned souls. Devotees sometimes misunderstand the desire of sadhanato attain bhavaas a kind of spiritual selfishness, an attraction for liberation. However, the reality is that transcendental service is the goal of practice because it facilitates the best way to serve and please Krsna. Moreover, the attainment of bhavais most pleasing to Srila Prabhupada, because that was the gift that he came to give. After all, the success of the Krsna consciousness movement is not measured in mortar and bricks, but in the pure devotees that it creates as a consequence of chanting Hare Krsna.

Sankalpa-kaumudiplaces great emphasis on a devotee being properly versed in transcendental knowledge. In the preceding chapter we have brought to the foreground knowledge of relationships, or sambandha-jnana.Chapter Twenty then probes into knowledge of practice, or abhidheya-jnana.And while a devotee needs to be conversant with all nine limbs of devotion, his main attention must be on knowing how to put into practice the principles underlying offenceless nama-sankirtana.Since chanting of the holy names is the religious principle for this age, knowledge of the functional duties regarding nama-sankirtanais a sadhaka’sprimary area of study. Srila Prabhupada displayed the effortlessness of a pure devotee’s nama-sankirtana.And yet what is very natural for him and great devotees is often a struggle for their followers. For the sadhaka,chanting the sixteen-word maha-mantraturns out to be quite a spiritual science, but one that he cannot turn his back on. For this reason all devotees need to apply themselves to learning the science of attentive nama-bhajana.

Chapter Twenty-one is dedicated to studying the factors responsible for the cause and nourishment of sankalpas.What makes and what keeps a devotee determined in his ascent up the stages of pure devotional service? Among the many causes of sankalpas,the foremost is the quality devotee association with which a sadhaka is blessed. And a factor most responsible for the nourishment of sankalpasis the devotional taste, rasa,that a successful sankalpa brings forth. In the way that an ordinary person is impelled by the pleasure he derives from a successful endeavour, a devotee is inspired by the pleasure that he derives from devotional service, specifically nama-sankirtana.It is instructive to note the connection between association and the kind of taste of bhava-bhaktia devotee acquires. Because Narada associated with regulated devotees, he developed a taste for vaidhi-bhakti.Similarly, a devotee who associates with spontaneous devotees in the mood of madhurya-rasa will himself be attracted to the same savour of perfection. This is in conformity with the principle that bhaktibegets bhakti.This also implies that the taste of bhaktibegets the same taste of bhakti.

Chapter Twenty-two lists the various results of sankalpa,among which further eagerness for perfection and the greed for Krsna’s lotus feet stand out as foremost. The nature of bhaktiis to increase the desire for itself, and so it is natural that determination leads to further determination. The completion of successful sankalpas results in more than renewed confidence and faith: the primary result of successfully climbing the next step on the ladder of devotion, the treasure of a Vaisnava’s life, is heightened devotion for Krsna. Srila Prabhupada had said that we should become mad for Krsna. In the way that a mother is obsessed with care and concern for her children, a devotee should be similarly possessed by affection for Krsna. And while all perfected devotees love the form of the Lord Whom they serve, the love of the Vraja-vasis—and among the Vraja-vasis, the love of the gopis—is the most transcendentally intense. Therefore, Gaudiya Vaisnavas aspire to serve Krsna like the gopis,and so their eagerness in sadhanaand sadhyafollows in the gopis’footsteps.

In the next chapter, Twenty-three, we have described five factors that result in a decrease in, or complete loss of, determination. They are misconduct, bad association, lack of discrimination, doubtfulness, and faulty sadhana.Our experience of fifty years as a leader in the Society is that substandard spiritual practice and criticism of fellow Vaisnavas and Vaisnavis are the most widespread and debilitating factors in a devotee’s spiritual life. These unfortunate habits are like vampires that sap a devotee’s determination and ability to enthusiastically engage in sankalpas.It is more than lamentable that having become the beneficiary of pure devotion, a devotee can then jeopardise his very rare good fortune and the two things most instrumental to spiritual well-being—good sadhanaand respectful service to Vaisnavas. One of the factors responsible for such misconduct is iskcon’s lack of familiarity and connection with Vaisnava culture, something that we hope the future will bring.

Chapter Twenty-four is the summary and final chapter of Part Five. In essence it explains that the motivation driving a sadhaka from a lower stage of devotion to a higher is his dissatisfaction with his service to Krsna on the lower stage, and the promise of rendering a better quality service on the higher. Because real bhakti, loving devotion, only begins at bhava,a practitioner is relentless in his pursuit of that goal. And since his Krsna consciousness increases with every sankalpa,his eagerness for taking every successive sankalpaalso increases. Although there are many factors involved in a sankalpa,for a sadhakathey all translate into the quest to love Krsna. Everyone is looking for love and everyone wants to give love. A question that often arises is whether the desire for spiritual advancement is a selfish motive. If such a desire is driven by an eagerness to be free of material suffering, then the answer would be “Yes!” However, if the motive for advancement is to increase Krsna’s pleasure, then the answer is “No!” Of course, becoming a lover of Krsna means a Vaikuntha life. But that is simply a by-product of the endless drive of a devotee for increased service to his Beloved.

\* \* \* \*

Part Six is entitled “Sahkalpa and Attentive Nama-bhajana.” Devotional service really means chanting Hare Krsna, with all other limbs of bhaktienabling the development and perfection of nama-sankirtana,the religious practice for this age. Nama-bhajana is the systematic progress through stages of chanting that an accomplished by escalating determinations based on correspond ingly evolved faith, knowledge, and attachment. As chanting is enriched, it brings the sadhakain closer and closer proximity to Krsna in many varied and wonderful ways. These chapters are designed to assist the thoughtful sadhakain cultivating attentive ness, especially in the more advanced stages of nama-smarana. which scriptures consider to be the very essence of bhakti-yoga Such cultivation by stages is what lies at the very heart of sadhana sankalpa,especially in the transition from dhyanato samadhi.

Chapter Twenty-five prefaces the study of nama-bhajanaby exposing the primary obstacle to it, inattentiveness. The neophyte devotee does not have sufficient attachment to Krsna to keep hr. mind attached to the holy names or to keep it free of distraction. Therefore he must make extra effort to control his mind, avoid things that further agitate it, and ensure that his sadhanais exact ing and free of offence. While the list of dos and don’ts in the practice of attentiveness is not insignificant, they all serve the purpose of ekdgrata,or one pointed attention, colloquially known as having a “one-track mind.” A sincere practitioner must learn and cultivate those things that facilitate attentiveness until that time that his heart has become purified and naturally craves the sound of Krsna's names more than it craves anything else. While different dos and don’ts contribute to attentiveness, there is no replacement for repeated effort, which is something that Krsna is emphatic about in the Bhagavad-gita.

Having defined attentiveness and inattentiveness in the previous chapter, Chapter Twenty-six shows how attentiveness develops through the stages of regulated and spontaneous devotion. Attentiveness is integral to learning smarana.In the absence of natural attraction for Krsna, a regulated devotee must learn to control his mind and then fix his controlled mind on the sound of the holy names during nama-sankirtana.As purification of the heart takes place, either such attentiveness becomes increasingly effortless, or a devotee’s taste for Krsna’s names awakens and natural attraction replaces efforts at attentiveness. In either case, for both vaidhi-and raga-bhaktas,attentiveness becomes one of the mind’s proactive characteristics. Whether attentiveness is accomplished by practice

or taste, it is fully secured when the heart is purified of both the objects of distraction and the habits causing distraction. However, it is both practice and taste that enable nama-sankirtanato exercise ns purifying effect upon the heart. Therefore, seen from the perspective of cause and effect, regulative discipline or natural attraction of the mind are the cause of purification which effects further attentiveness.

Chapter Twenty-seven is entitled “Acceptance and Remembrance.” Its pages describe the all-important stage of varana- dasa,whereat a sadhakahas matured to the stage where he has a general conception of how he would like to serve as a siddha.This conception is based on both purity of heart and attachment to a resident of Vraja. The cultivation of this purity and attachment is enacted by nama-sankirtanaand is known as smarana-dasa,the subsequent stage of devotion. Srila Prabhupada and his spiritual master have strongly emphasised nama-sankirtanaas the means lor attaining all perfections in this stage of remembrance. And for their followers, nama-sankirtanameans personal sadhanaenhanced with outreach preaching that makes the most of the resources current technology facilitates. In this way, by both sadhanaand preaching, a practitioner is sure to invoke the grace of Caitanya Mahaprabhu. And for the sadhaka,the Lord’s grace is manifest as increased expertise in the kind of nama-bhajanathat facilitates spiritual advancement.

Chapter Twenty-eight is replete with the many principles that underlie nama-bhajanaand which form the basis by which a devotee can seriously progress through advanced stages of Krsna consciousness. A devotee arrives at the stage of smarana-dasa by perfecting the two preceding stages. He must have acquired a clear concept of his spiritual destination, which acquisition is sravana-dasa,and then made a firm commitment to that destination, which is varana-dasa.Then meditation can go forward apace. The five stages of smaranaare smarana, dharana, dhyana, anu- smrti,and samadhi,which are recollection, absorption, meditation, constant remembrance, and trance, respectively. And as always, the means for advancing through these stages is nama-sankirtana,in which the nature of the holy name unfolds along with the form, qualities, and pastimes of Krsna. Thakura Bhaktivinoda calls

the names corresponding to this development rupa-yukta-nama, guna-yukta-nama,and lila-yukta-nama,respectively. When the holy name is pleased with its worship, then it reveals its most desirable feature as rasita-nama,the rasa-enhanced name.

Chapter Twenty-nine describes the first four stages of smarana dasa,the development of the holy name through those stages, and how the attribute such as form appears by the grace of the name and becomes more pronounced with deepening remembrance. Furthermore, it describes how the regulative devotee can gradually acquire spontaneity, and how he and the spontaneous sadhakawill develop attraction to a specific name and form of Krsna and His corresponding qualities, pastimes, and associates. The chapter concludes its study of dbruvanusmrtiby emphasising that the attainments of each division of smarana-dasaare cumulative, which means that the attainment of each division, such as smarana,is contained within every successive stage, such as in dharana.Thus dbruvanusmrtipossesses the attainments of the first four levels of smarana-dasa.In this way a devotee becomes increasingly proficient in nama-sankirtana,and although his external appearance and conduct may remain unchanged, internally he experiences dramatic changes as a result of spiritual advancement.

In Chapter Thirty we begin our study of the fifth stage of remembrance, trance, by presenting the ideal of that attainment which is shown by great devotees like Kardama Muni, Markandeya Rsi, Brahma, Narada, and Bilvamangala Thakura. This account enables the reader to envision the perfection of sadhana, bhava,as it unfolds through the samadhiof transcendentalists. And while samadhi at sadhanais not the same as that at bhavaand prema,as with all practices devotional, a sadhakashould know the goal in order to have a correspondingly relevant practice. Because trance is the stage at which the transition to bhavatakes place and plays a critical role in the sadhaka’sjourney, Sankalpa-kaumudiglorifies it in three chapters. Moreover, trance is the most elusive aspect of sadhana to perfect. Although proficiency in nama-sankirtanaempowers the sadhaka,the attainment that he aspires for is more challenging than any other. As a devotee approaches bhava,Krsna becomes ever more attentive to him. The Lord is well aware that very soon there will be one more devotee who will be able to control Him.

The characteristics of perfection must be emulated in practice. Chapter Thirty-one emphasises that as the stage of samadhi approaches its goal, it must be perfectly aligned with bhava,in the way that a ship must dock exactly in its port at arrival. Since trance indicates the devotional stage of asakti,its primary characteristic of attachment to Krsna is the sattvikaversion of the love it aspires to awaken at bhava.Attachment is brought to maturity through nama-sankirtana,which also brings to light extraordinary attributes of trance, including: its liberated status; the realisations it affords; freedom from bodily identification; freedom from karma; learlessness; exclusive interest in Krsna’s pastimes; the qualification to see Krsna; and spiritual perfection from which fall-down is rare. A further attribute is the spiritualisation of a devotee’s body. To the extent a devotee is absorbed in trance, to that degree his body and mind are transcendental, with the balance remaining material. This proportional relationship between absorption in nama-bhajanaand transcendence is further dependent on the intensity of a devotee’s trance, his lifestyle, and possibly his environment. If these factors are extremely favourable, a devotee’s connection with transcendence may encompass all hours of the day. If, however, these factors are not so favourable, a practitioner’s spiritualisation may be limited to the time in which he does nama-sankirtana.

Chapter Thirty-two addresses the doubt that arises in devotees at every stage of devotional service. Looking at bhavain the far-off spiritual distance they wonder, “Can I do it?” The same doubt may arise at samadhi.Having come to the stage of trance was already an extraordinary spiritual achievement, enabled only by the grace of a qualified guru.In the process, the accomplished devotee will have seen many other practitioners languish or fall by the wayside. If attaining bhavais an even rarer attainment than samadhi, and if Krsna is generally reluctant to give it, the sadhakamay have good cause to doubt. But Krsna says, “No! Do not doubt Me.” The Lord assures a sincere sadhakathat just as Garuda helped the little sparrow retrieve its eggs from the ocean, He helps His devotee make that final crossing over the ocean of repeated birth and death. He says, “I and the acaryasare not small men, and we are here to help you.” After all, Krsna is interested in devotion, not mastery over yogic asanas.And the devotion that attracts Him most is vraja-bhaktihoned to a particular mellow following one of His eternal Vraja associates.

\* \* \* \*

Part Seven, “Sankalpa for Chanting with Emotion,” examines chanting with emotion and specifically vipralambha.In the many chapters preceding this we have described the sadhanaof true Gaudiyas. Systematic meditation in nama-sankirtanabraided with feelings of separation is the means by which devotees pass through the increasingly elusive stages of devotion from nisthato advanced asakti.

Chapter Thirty-three introduces the concept of bhava-seva,or service with emotion. If we apply to the perfection of premathe maxim that a practice and its goal must correspond, then it stands to reason that sadhanamust be enhanced by feelings of affection, and increasingly so as one advances in smarana-dasa.Indeed we see that faith, attraction to devotees, patience, enthusiasm, anti humility are just some of the emotions inherent in sadhana.And the more a devotee attentively cultivates these emotions favourable to practice, the more they manifest, in the way that love inherent within the heart also manifests with practice. The primary emotion that draws all other qualities after it in the way the current of a river carries leaves downstream, is vipralambha-seva,feelings of separation.
